I am writing this review based off a 'imagine if' kind of thing. So imagine this you're alone in the nazi zombie apocalypse no one to watch your back you're down to your last magazine 5 bullets 15 nazi zeds shambling towards your position it's hopeless you're not going to have a good time. No one to say goodbye to no one to latch on to before the horde overruns your position. You're not having fun.
Now imagine you were with 3 other people your friends your comrades people who have your back. Opening fire on the zombie hordes one bullet two bullets three bullets four. Ammunition running low. Joe has one sniper rifle cartridge, Anthony has 4 shotgun shells and Griffin has 7 shots in his pistol. You? You just have two sticks of dynamite. The situation is assessed, about 25 of those nazi zeds heading your way and they're blocking your path to the supply room. You make a rough plan of how to take them out.
I'll plant the dynamite on the pathway the zeds have to take to reach us. Can't plant it too far either because Griffin will use his pistol to detonate them. Shoot the dynamite before the zeds pass them or you won't be able to hit them. Anthony will take any that come too close. Joe will take out the more tougher armoured ones. Me? I will run out there and scavenge the dead undead.

If you enjoyed Hotline Miami DO NOT play this (I know that is a clickbatey intro line but it will make more sense upon further reading)
Hotline Miami didn't need backstory. It was surreal and symbolic and pretty much perfect in pacing and design; there is seriously nothing I would add or remove from it, I love it so much I'm building an arcade machine of it!
But Holine Miami 2 is here to fill in the void that was never there; gone is the mystery and symbolism and here is lore explaining away every single action. Thought that the constant russian killing was poking fun at the constant russian killing in many modern games? Nope! Turns out its because russia went to war and took over and blah blah who cares.
What is so perplexing about all this is that the first game actively went against the concept of plots; it was post modernist and abstract. It took things that in general works of fiction would be key plot points (for example the photograph that is ripped) and turns them into mere abstractions, general feelings rather than plot points. The game purposefully took out whatever narrative it had by swapping protagonists two thirds of the way through. A logical plot was only given as an alternate ending to OCD players that the game actively made fun of.
Despite all this intelligent and artistic game design in the first game Hotline Miami 2 decides that every single detail and metaphor from the original needed to be completely explained into a big cohesive plot that sucks out any life or symbolism that it all had. It's truly dissapointing and honestly feels detrimental to the orignal work.
So if you played and loved the first game I truly suggest you just skip over this! Do not play it at all, you'll enjoy the first more than if you had played this. And if you think you just want more of the gameplay you'd also be dissapointed; maps are too large to see most long distance enemies so almost every map becomes frustraiting, it is a lot less fun then the first.

I love this game. I really do. The game has amazing music, is graphically gorgeous for an imitation SNES-era topdown beat-em-up/shooter, and it controls very tightly and very, very precisely. So why don't a I reccomend this?
This screenshot is the level Takeover, in the 5th act/chapter of the game. In other words, its quite late in the game. I have tried to complete this mission many, many times to beat it, and this bug happens every time. I cannot kill them, as I used the knuckleduster enhancement (Deadly punches, no weapons). Sure, this could be totally avoided by choosing another enhancement and trying a different approach, and a different play style.This is why I don't reccomend this game. I will more than happily change it to a reccomend if this is fixed at all, but it will stay as it is until then. This may seem minor, but let me use the Soulsborne series as an example. In Demon's Souls, Dark Souls 1-3 & Bloodborne, every boss could be taken on and defeated regardless of your play style. Want to be lightly armoured and deal little damage, but be agile and get lots of hits in quickly? Do it. Want to be an absolute powerhousing tank that is slow as♥♥♥♥♥♥ but deals massive damage and takes all the hits, but you stay on your feet? Sure. Do you want to run around naked and punch everything in every game in the entire Soulsborne series to death at level 1 without ever resting at a bonfire? Do it. They were hard games, unfairly hard at times, but they always let you play the game how you liked, with any setup. I chose to use guns as little as possible, to stay quiet. But I would have to change that play style to one I am unfamiliar with and have to get used to frustratingly quickly. I don't like that at all. If it lets you choose a play style, I cannot recommend it if it then forces you into using another play style. Even in the missions where you start with guns, I usedd melee weapons once the ran out. I love this game, I really really do and I want to recommend it so much, but I cannot recommend that forces you into a certain play style, after having let you choose how to approach the levels and floors.

Want to play a game like Left 4 Dead but without zombies? Try Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide. Please note through out this whole review I will be comparing Vermintide to Valve's Left 4 Dead a lot
Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is a game developed by Fatshark and takes place in the Warhammer universe where the vermins of the sewers, rats, infest and infect the living world
The game offers nothing special in terms of gameplay as it is mostly the same as Left 4 Dead and I would call it as a Left 4 Dead clone. There are 4 players, this game is multiplayer only by the way, and they have to walk through a map whilst slaughtering a bunch of rats and trying not to die and survive
The enemies vary from regular rats to gas rats, exactly the same as Left 4 Dead which offers spitters and boomers and such. The enemy AI is dumb surprisingly, although Left 4 Dead offers very clever and scary AI, especially when the infected start running towards you, that doesn't happen in Vermintide, they pile up and just stay there. They don't run towards you no matter where you are and only attack you when they are near you, nothing else. The AI could vary depending on harder difficulties, however, on normal the AI is pretty dumb
The game does offer up a challenge and usually in Easy and Normal difficulty you will survive when playing online however when playing with companion AI, you will die for sure, as mentioned previously with the enemy AI, the companion AI is dumb as well, so much so that sometimes the companion AI would get stuck in the environment or get killed instantly by the vermin rats
It's very hard to get a game going in multiplayer as hardly anyone plays this game anymore, at least at the time I play. Most games (found in the lobby browser) are either locked or not enough players and don't expect your game request (for example, a game in Easy mode) to be requested as it took me ages to play the prologue on medium difficulty without entering the lobby browser
Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is a mixed bag. It offers nothing unique as it's mostly a clone of Left 4 Dead just with rats instead of zombies and the story offered to the players is nothing special and although Left 4 Dead to this very day is still being played from it's date of release which was 2008, Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide which was released in 2015, only a select few still play
I would only recommend Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide to either fans of the Warhammer franchise or if you have a couple of friends (which sadly I don't have any friends), then purchase the 4 pack, but if you are looking for another Left 4 Dead game, don't purchase this, stick with Left 4 Dead or Left 4 Dead 2 until Valve decides a third game is in order

If you are a D&D 3.5 fan, imagine every criticism you ever lobbed at 4E about it being "too much like a video game".
Now imagine a video game based on 4E that removed all the redeeming factors. You have no party. Your at-wills are on the hotbar, as are your encounter powers and daily powers, which are now keyed exclusively to real-time cooldowns themselves.
And it's all buggy as hell.
They could have made a wonderful, even FUNCTIONAL version of the D&D Tactics PSP game using the 4E ruleset. They decided to do precisely the opposite, creating a buggy hack-and-slash PC game based loosely on the 4E ruleset.
WOTC was on to something when they made the GBA Eye of the Beholder and the PSP D&D Tactics. They missed the target, but they got somewhere close. A proper D&D TRPG is just waiting to be made, but now it's looking it will never come to pass. A pity.

How does one approach this legendary game? One of the single silliest games ever produced. Super 3D Noah's Ark has you play as Noah, as you run around feeding all the animals in the Ark, as they've grown restless; and for some reason this makes them want to spit at Noah until he dies. Yeeeeeeeeah...
Super 3D Noah's Ark is, as I'm sure many of you know, a First Person Shooter, in fact; it is a direct; pound for pound, reskin of Wolfenstein 3D. Rumor surrounds it, that this is because Id Software was frustrated by the SNES port of Wolfenstein; in which the game was butchered; with things like the Nazis being turned into the "Master State" and blood being censored; so Id approached Wisdom Tree and gave them the Source code of Wolfenstein, telling them to make a game more suitable.
Since its the same as Wolfenstein with just new maps; one can jump into it all the same. All enemies and weapons function the same; this game also has the Flamethrower and Rocket Launcher that were present in the DOS and SNES ports. And the only newly added function are Bible Quizs which reward you health and ammo for guessing correctly. However, unless you are the type of person to memorize this stuff; you're probably just gonna end up looking up the answers anyway so you can always get the health. Or saving and reloading right before. Music gets insanely repetitive.
Pros
----
+ Addicting and fun gameplay.
+ Difficulty spike is fair and eases you in slowly (only bosses are a step up).
+ Lots of secrets to find encouraging exploration; and 2 hidden stages.
+ New maps for fans of Wolfenstein.
Cons
----
- Dying respawns you without your weapons, this can be avoided by saving at the start of each map.
- Bible Quizs punish players for not knowing the answer; in a game where Health and Ammo is vital.
- Repetitive music; mute the music and put on Wolfenstein 3D music via Steams music player.
- Stupid concept

There was a sequel, unfortunately... Something named Deus Ex 2. Something that should never have come between any gamer's hands. But hey, nobody is perfect.

Plus the graphics were good, the storytelling was great... A great game, what else can I say ?
Then there is Deus Ex : The Fall, coming after Human Revolution.
At first I was like "Hey, the last one was awesome, and this is supposed to be linked with it... Can't be anything but good".

I have decided to re-do my old review of Super Monday Night Combat.  The first one was not long after the game released and was only a sentence of praise, which at the time I felt was sufficient for the zero people that would read it.  I suppose at this point, years on, that I can talk about what SMNC once was and what happened to it.  This will be more informative rather than any sort of recommendation (or non-recommendation), but I will say up front that no matter how good this game was, it isn’t really populated enough today for much fun.
Super Monday Night Combat is a sequel to one of the first attempts to shake up the standard MOBA scene.  Monday Night Combat released in 2010 on Xbox 360 and some months later on PC in early 2011.  I ended up receiving it as a prize from a website and quickly fell in love with the entire concept.  The flow of pushing lanes in third person with these larger-than-life characters using their crazy abilities with the premise of a futuristic amped up sporting event made for a unique starting point.  Quality gameplay that relied a good bit on skill and a handful of strategy backed that up well.  The dialogue both from the characters and the announcer and the bright colors and elaborate design of every arena made each match feel like you were watching a crazy combination of the NFL and professional wrestling (XFL comparisons excused).   The exceptional game had a moderate following, but never really became the hit I think a lot of the playerbase believed it should be.
Some time went by and I moved on to new games with bigger and more populated games, all the while wanting more MNC.  Then late in 2011, I caught wind of a closed beta for SUPER Monday Night Combat.  I signed up as fast as I could and no long after I was locked in to more of that MNC goodness, but with some interesting twists.  I spent hundreds of hours in the beta, giving feedback and reporting bugs while simultaneously having a wonderful time.  They added new heroes to the game and old ones were improved.  The gameplay shifted more to the MOBA side of things, making players last longer in combat while also bringing more of an importance to pushing lanes and bots rather than just taking out players.  Maps became larger and more complex and effective strategies and tactics became more important if you wanted to win.  You couldn’t just get by being a good shot or having solid reaction time, you also had to worry about placement, momentum, and effectively spending your money on bots and upgrades rather than just dumping it in whatever seemed decent.
However, as the game progressed into 2012, issues started to come up.  The first one that caught many people by surprise is that the developers started selling cosmetics in the beta.  Looking back on it, it’s not so egregious considering today’s nearly ubiquitous “pay now, play later” environment, but at the time it seemed like desperation and a negative way to fund development.  This was before crowdfunding had really started up.  On top of that, new players saw veterans with cosmetics (both before and after launch) and assumed that their skill was associated with these purchased items.  Even though skill and game knowledge made it very easy for veterans to dominate new players.  This created a very limited playerbase even in the closed beta.  Keys started going out more and more, but players wouldn’t stick around.  Snowballing was just as much a real thing in SMNC as it was in any other MOBA.  The game desperately needed matchmaking.  However as this was being developed, a closed beta key somehow came in to existence that could be reused infinitely.  With little warning, an announcement was made in April that the game is going to be released because the news of the free key had people joining by the thousands with little information on how to play or what the game was about.  With no real launch buildup or advertising, no functional matchmaking, and next to no real training mode for new players, the game went live.
Development continued, but as new players poured in, they would be thrust in to matches with veterans decked out with both the cosmetics they paid for from beta and all of the endorsements and products (minor stat tweaks and buffs) that were earned over time.  Given that veteran players would already beat new players without any endorsements of products, having them from the start meant it was even more of a slaughter.  The consensus was that resetting these would have been the correct choice even if it upset veteran players.  Eventually, some rough matchmaking was implemented, a new tutorial area with more beginner information and unlimited practice also came along, and a couple of new heroes shook things up.  About a month after release, Uber introduced the Turbocross game mode.  It was a welcome addition for some, mainly those nostalgic for the original MNC’s gameplay, but for others it seemed regressive and lacked balance.  What did ultimately come from it though was splitting an already small playerbase.  Matchmaking had finally come making the original game mode, Supercross, more appealing to play from both ends of the skill spectrum, but for the top end players queue times became intolerable.  Now the split playerbase had both new and old players leaving.
The final nail in the coffin for Super Monday Night Combat came mid-August of 2012.  The start of the Kickstarter for Planetary Annihilation was the end of any significant support for SMNC.  Uber Entertainment stated that the game would still be supported, but few updates came after the success of PA’s Kickstarter.  The game slowly withered away, with the last update releasing March 13, 2013.  Not even a full year after the initial release date.  Uber Entertainment went on to release PA, first into Early Access, and then fully on September 5, 2014.  It received some mediocre to poor reviews, but development continued.  Despite this, Uber started another Kickstarter on October 2 for a new RTS called Human Resources.  While the concept appealed to many, the poor realization of previous titles prevented it from hitting its funding goals and it was cancelled within weeks.  Uber entertainment suffered some layoffs, but moved forward releasing a well-received standalone expansion to Planetary Annihilation called “Planetary Annihilation: Titans,” perhaps borrowing some elements from Human Resources.  Uber has also completed some games featured on Playstation VR including Wayward Sky and the soon-to-be-released Dino Frontier.
Super Monday Night Combat was a great game that had lofty aspirations but never got off the ground.  A spectacular blend of action and strategy that could have been as big as or bigger than Smite, a more traditional third person MOBA, had it been launched and completed properly.  One has to wonder if it was put together a year later when crowdfunding was taking off, could it have been completed properly and been the hit it deserved to be?  I suppose we’ll never know that particular case, but one thing I know for sure, I’ll be ready if the day ever comes that Ultra Monday Night Combat is ready to go.

Although Iam not a fan of resident evil games, I only played the first one and never really liked it but I was quite excited when the evil within game was announced, mainly because it ran on the wonderful id tech 5 engine and had this wonderful and detailed gore technics and gibbing which Iam a massive fan of ever since the first soldier of fortune. So after a few months of waiting for the game, some delays which had to happen, eventually the game came out late 2014 but I was unable to play the game due to poor optimization and mainly due to the pc port being a piece of turd...But after a few months in march 2015 I decided to finally play the game without those atrocious black bars and with the fov I wanted via the extremely handy flawless widecsreen tool. The game still has a few issues, like CTD or freezes but the game with highest possible AA and graphical settings on 1080p it never dipped below 60 fps, it fluctuated between 60 and 144 fps which is a perfect for a 3rd person action survival game.
Now that we have the technicalities out of the way I can finally talk about this game that will probably stay very dear to my heart, not because it sometimes was quite scary and unpredictable but because the attention to detail and the whole art side of the game and everything is just done with such care and passion.  a detail like Sebastian hair flowing in the air when you turn around or the simples of details like his extremely high quality texture of his coat or jacket...The game is just full of these wonderful suprises and attention to detail. The music is excellent, the visuals are breathtaking, the gameplay is engaging and satisfying and the story is well done too. If I can be honest I wasn't expecting an almost 19 hour story but when I finished the game after those 19 hours I was extremely satisfied with it as a whole. The Evil Within is a piece of art, the breathtaking, almost realisic visuals, the excellent atmosphere of a horror game, It's just that this game can be considered as the best in it's genre and probably among the very best inbetween the great games that came out over the years.

Star Trek Online is a very decent MMO that does a fair job at capturing the expansive Star Trek Universe. You will encounter a plethora of memorable personalities on your journeys throughout the game while exploring both the famous and uncharted systems across the galaxy.
At the time of this review you can currently play as a Star Fleet Officer, a Citizen of the new Romulan Republic, or a Warrior of the Klingon Empire. There are three career paths that you can chose - Tactical, Science, or Engineering - which determine what skills you have access to as well as what kind of ship you will command.
STO is one of my top 3 best MMOs and is the second best MMO for Free to Play Players as there are literally no content restrictions unlike games such as Star Wars: The Old Republic (End Game content + Expansion Pack) or The Lord of the Rings Online (all content beyond The Lone Lands (level 30ish) requires individual purchase or subscription). You can easily reach max level (50) and beyond without subscribing. That being said there are the common account restrictions for F2P players, such as a currency cap, limited character slots (3), no account bank, and limited character bank storage space.
If you do decide to play STO here are a few tips:
* Levels 1-49 are essentially a giant tutorial that helps familiarize you with the mechanics of the game.
* At level 50 the game content changes from Single Player to Group as you take part in STFs (Special Task Force) missions and their Elite counterparts where you fight extremely tough enemies such as the Borg and Tholians for reputation items.
* At End Game, Lock Box and Cryptic Store Ships are vastly superior to anything else. If you are serious about playing the game throughout the End Content you should consider purchasing one as well as a subscription.

A game I affectionally refer to as "Left 4 Ratmen", Vermintide is a stylish, four-player coop hack-and-slash set in the original Warhammer Fantasy setting. It is mechanically similar to Left 4 Dead in a number of ways, primarily in how it handles weapons and equipment in-game, as well as mission structure, and the use of an AI "Director" that influences when and where hordes or special enemies appear. However, combat is primarily melee-based and the melee system itself is much more complex then in L4D, but not to the extent of say, Chivalry. You can tap the left mouse button for a light swing or hold for a charged one, or hold right mouse to block, and press left while blocking to shove enemies back. Ranged weapons are available but ammunition for them is limited. You can also carry one healing item, either a self-healing potion or a medkit you can use either on yourself or others, as well as a single buff potion, either strength or speed.
Here's the plot: It is the End Times in the Old World, and war besets the human Empire from all sides. The Skaven, vicious, treacherous rat-men, considered a myth by some and a mere annoyance by others, are pouring forth from underground to assault the Imperial city of Ubersreik. Its town guard slaughtered, the city's salvation now falls to a small band of Imperial warriors: witch hunter Victor Saltzpyre, sergeant Markus Kruber, and bright wizard Sienna Fuegonasus, as well as their nonhuman allies: wood elf waywatcher Kerillian and dwarf ranger Bardin Goreksson. Under the guidance of savvy innkeeper, they journey on a series of standalone misisons in an attempt to thwart the Skavens' efforts and support the surviving townsfolk.
Aside from the melee system, Verminide defers from L4D primarily in its out-of-game mechanics: The missions are played individually instead of as a linked campaign, you earn experience from missions and level up, and you can configure your character's loadout of a melee weapon, ranged weapon and up to three trinkets that provide passive buffs. You recieve one new piece of equipment per level up or mission completed. At the end of a level, the game rolls a set of dice, with each face roll improving your odds of recieving better gear. You can find additional "loot dice" in missions, as well as special tomes or grimoires, which add dice at the end of a level. However, carrying a tome prevents you from carrying a health item and carrying a grimoire not only prevents you from carrying a buff poton but reduces the entire party's maximum health, but rewards a "cursed die" at level's end that guarentees a face-up roll. Loot is color-coded by rarity and rarer gear can come with passive buffs. Unfortunately, the table of gear you can recieve depends on the difficulty level you seleceted, and getting better gear all but requires you to play on a  higher difficulty then you are either equipped or practiced for: Vermintide's RNG god is a particular brand of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I personally haven't had much success on anything above hard, and there are another three difficulties past that.
The Skaven come in a variety of forms, mostly the swarming clan and slave rats, but there are specialist rats that somewhat parallel the special infected of L4D in functionality: The Packmasters grab players and drag them away, Gutter-Runners pin players to the ground, Globadiers hurl damaging gas bombs, Ratling Gunners deal heavy ranged damage, Stormvermin are armored and can come in packs, and the rare but dangerous Rat-Ogre smashes and smacks players about. There is also the extremely rare Sack-Rat, which will actually run away from players but if killed drops useful equipment.
Vermintide suffers somewhat in the longevity department: There are only so many levels, though the addition of a "last stand" mode and a story DLC containing three new levels somewhat alliviates this. Still, at the time of this writing there are few multiplayer lobbies that aren't farming for tomes on the first level, the Horn of Magnus, so if you'd like to play any other level you should probably bring friends.

The difficulty levels seperate the men from the boys. Experience matters and learning the maps truly makes a difference in your team's success. If you've got a few friends who love gaming, definetley give this game a try.

[Edit]While I still recommend this game to anyone who likes this type of cooperative gameplay, it occurs to me a few months after my review that there are some people who absolutely hate this type of game, who rebuke the gear system, and who hate the steep skill curve.  Please watch gameplay footage, abundant on youtube, before making a purchase decision!
Vermintide is set during the Warhammer universe' apocalypse, when all the chaos creepers attack at once. Vermintide focuses mainly on the Skaven, a race of intelligent humanoid rats, who are boiling out of the underground by the thousands to attack the city of Ubersreik.
You can be one of five classes-- The dwarf ranger, the waywatcher, the witch hunter, the imperial soldier and the bright wizard. Of those first four, the only major class distinction is the waywatcher's ability to move at full speed while blocking. And the dwarf can see under tall things. Other than that, the differences come with the nuances of their weapons. At first, the classes will feel samey, but after awhile, the differences in weapons will seem massive, and you'll think yourself a stupid fool for thinking that they were similar.
The bright wizard, though, stands well apart from the other four. The bright wizard casts fire magic which can vary in form and utility based on which staff she wields. Whenever she uses her flames, she builds up heat, which you can vent by holding reload. BUT, if you build up heat past a certain threshold, venting it will cause a small amount of damage to you. Which is a small sacrifice when compared to the alternative of building heat to maximum, because when that happens, your body explodes (which, though fatal, is an epic way to kill a few more rats).
You start in your inn, which is your base of operations. It has crafty things you can use to upgrade, salvage or reroll equipment, and choose which mission to do. It starts out a bit dark, but as you complete more missions at higher difficulties, the inn gets brighter, with more lit candles and the addition of trophies and banners to the walls of the inn. All four companions share the "host's" inn, so anyone who joins your game can admire your gains.
From the map, you can start missions.
You begin on The Horn of Magnus, and after completing this mission on easy (which you might not find all that "easy" your first time through), additional missions become playable. You can unlock a total of 13 missions in the base game, each of which is playable at 5 difficulties.
If you succeed at a mission, you roll some dice at the end to determine your reward. The dice have six sides, but only two sides are "hits". But you can get better dice (with more "hit" sides) by collecting special items within the missions like Tomes and Grimoires, which are dangerous to carry because they take up a spot normally used for a potion, or in the case of grimoires, actually lower the entire team's HP by 33% per grimoire. The more hits you get on your dice, and the higher the difficulty, the better quality equipment you receive.
There are only five equipment slots, and only three types of equipment-- You can carry one melee weapon, one ranged weapon and three trinkets on your person. Trinkets have a very wide variety of passive effects from decreasing the damage of specific enemies' attacks to giving a chance to duplicate healing items you pick up. Equipment has four quality levels-- white, green, blue and orange, because ♥♥♥♥ purple, apparently. Having good equipment is definitely an asset, but you will feel yourself getting better at the game faster than your equipment improves, so the game is not heavily gear-centric. However, I'd definitely feel more pressure in Hard difficulty if you replaced my blue gear with whites.
Great, great, so what do you DO? Every mission has you going somewhere to do something. This is usually something simple like go to A, pick up X and bring it to B. But it isn't so simple, because angry rat people run at you with spears because die-die man-thing. There are different varieties of rat men.
Slave rats are stupid and hairless and weak and slow and hairless and you'll laugh at them when you start out, and later on you'll get so good at blocking them and pushing them to interrupt them that they will almost never hit you. Poison Globadiers don't even look like rats because they're in frickin hazmat suits and carrying tanks full of poison and they throw balls of stink at you and the stink balls hit a surface and pop into green stink clouds which damage you for as long as you tarry in the stink. Don't tarry in stink. There are also rats with miniguns. What, there are! They're called ratling guns. WHAT.
I saved your least favorite types of rat for last, starting with the assassin rat. He jumps at you, gets on your back, and just starts a'stabbin'. And there's nothing you can do about this. At all. If he gets on you, and there isn't a teammate around to push him off or put a musket ball in his stupid, snorting, stab-stab face, he will stab you until you die, while being very obnoxiously super stoked about it. Apex predator♥♥♥♥♥♥ Last, the packmaster, or hook rat. The hook rat is slow and weak and it makes stupid wheezy noises whever it goes. The problem is that, like the assassin, if he gets you, you can't do anything about it. Unlike the assassin, which just stabs you in the spot he manages to jump on you, the packmaster does his tricksy horse♥♥♥♥♥♥with a long pole with a chokey bit on the end that he puts around your neck. He then proceeds to drag you away from your party, usually through untold stinking waves of bald, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ slave rats. He watches you shoot arrows at him. He watches you fly off the cliff he just slapped you off of.
As far as how you'll go about exterminating these little diseased baldies, it is important to note that, although everyone gets a lovely selection of ranged weapons, ammunition is very limited and you will be doing most of your rat slaying with melee weapons unless you play the bright wizard. But even the bright wizard will melee SOME of the time in order not to overheat. So how is the melee combat? It sounds simple but it FEELS great. Every melee weapon has a normal (l click) and charge (hold l click) and block (r click) and push (hold r click + l click). Each type of melee weapon has its own stamina bar as well, which is a fast-regenerating resource which is depleted when blocking or pushing. The damage inflicted by your weapons follows the weapon in exactly the way you would expect. If your weapon swings first from left to right, it will strike the enemies in that arc as the blade passes through them. If your weapon's combo does two slashes and then a stab, you can expect to hit several enemies with the first two hits and then a single enemy for high damage. If you're using a two handed hammer, you have to time your attacks to account for the time it takes to swing the thing. Every weapon has its own feel, and you will develop strong preferences for the way certain weapon types perform.

As mentioned in most reviews, this game is a lot like Left 4 dead which was a favorite game of mine. I love this style of cooperative game play where you are forced to rely on your teammates...or else you die. I was mostly pulled in by my love for Warhammer fantasy though and they definitely got that part right. Graphically the game is great, especially Drachenfels dlc, and there are some awesome looking weapons. So all that said:
The Good:
-Coop that demands teamwork or you fail.
-Nice weapon variety with lots to choose from, even though some are a bit underpowered.
-Lots of variety of levels to play and some are quite large and fun to explore and look amazing.
-This game can be very challenging and outright punishing if you choose it to be. That's a definite pro in my book.
-To expand on previous point, you can collect tomes which take up health slots, and grimoires which reduce whole
party's health. This is added optional challenge which rewards you with better chances at loot rolls.
-A loot system which gives you added incentive to keep playing.
-The combat is fun as hell! I never knew it could be so deeply satisfying to kill Rat men.
-The Rat AI is pretty good and does a great job at keeping the pressure on you at all times. I very much enjoy the rushes that come at random. I also love the randomness of mob spawns. It makes levels have a lot of replayability.
- Very dark and gritty feel to the game which is right up my alley.
-The Soundtrack is bad♥♥♥♥♥and totally fits Warhammer Fantasy.
The Not so good -
-Loot system has flaws - Namely It's completely RNG and you don't get much for failing a mission. It can be quite demoralizing when you fight tooth and nail for upwards of a half an hour and are rewarded with a few measly green coins ( at level 30, or nothing at all at the lower levels).
- No real reason to run some of the levels. A lot of people just farm the easiest ones over and over and avoid the more difficult maps. Should be an incentive to do all maps.
-Friendly BOT AI is horrendous. They are of little to no help to you.
- Need more variety of mobs. All of the special mobs in the game are great and each do a good job of causing you and your team problems, but I wish there was a few bosses to tackle at the end of some missions or some other races to kill besides rats.
- Some weapons are borderline useless. (Shortbows i'm looking at you). There's a few weapons where there just isnt' any scenario that it would be better to take them over others.
- Game isn't fully optimized yet, graphically. I'm running it on a 1080 and I get some frame dips in parts that really shouldn't be happening. (Overall though it works fine for me)
Overall, I feel like this game is worth playing especially if you can get it on sale. There's a lot to love here despite some things needing work. Yes the loot RNG is frustrating, Yes there's some problems with some of the weapons, and yes there's some glitches that still exist. But if you look past all that, there is a diamond in the rough here. It's a great game to play with friends and to try to beat some of the harder levels and difficulties. I can't count how many celebrations erupted (and frustrations too!) from the intense missions that we were put through in the last week or so that I've been playing. It can be quite exhilarating watching your last teammate come into the wagon at the end of a mission with a massive zerg of angry rats nipping at his heels. It can also be equally thrilling or frustrating when those dice come up big and you get that orange trinket or rare helmet. Bottom line, I personally recommend this game since I'm 70 hours into it and still having as much fun with it as i had on day 1.

I love this game. I really do. The game has amazing music, is graphically gorgeous for an imitation SNES-era topdown beat-em-up/shooter, and it controls very tightly and very, very precisely. So why don't a I reccomend this?
This screenshot is the level Takeover, in the 5th act/chapter of the game. In other words, its quite late in the game. I have tried to complete this mission many, many times to beat it, and this bug happens every time. I cannot kill them, as I used the knuckleduster enhancement (Deadly punches, no weapons). Sure, this could be totally avoided by choosing another enhancement and trying a different approach, and a different play style.This is why I don't reccomend this game. I will more than happily change it to a reccomend if this is fixed at all, but it will stay as it is until then. This may seem minor, but let me use the Soulsborne series as an example. In Demon's Souls, Dark Souls 1-3 & Bloodborne, every boss could be taken on and defeated regardless of your play style. Want to be lightly armoured and deal little damage, but be agile and get lots of hits in quickly? Do it. Want to be an absolute powerhousing tank that is slow as♥♥♥♥♥♥ but deals massive damage and takes all the hits, but you stay on your feet? Sure. Do you want to run around naked and punch everything in every game in the entire Soulsborne series to death at level 1 without ever resting at a bonfire? Do it. They were hard games, unfairly hard at times, but they always let you play the game how you liked, with any setup. I chose to use guns as little as possible, to stay quiet. But I would have to change that play style to one I am unfamiliar with and have to get used to frustratingly quickly. I don't like that at all. If it lets you choose a play style, I cannot recommend it if it then forces you into using another play style. Even in the missions where you start with guns, I usedd melee weapons once the ran out. I love this game, I really really do and I want to recommend it so much, but I cannot recommend that forces you into a certain play style, after having let you choose how to approach the levels and floors.

A good, solid survival/horror game at least as good as the predecessors it emulates. It's only fault was being a game in a very hard to please market for the genre where similar games (see resident evil) and some better games (see the last of us) have set the bar so high that new games in the genre have to be significantly better to gain the favor of their fans.
It's the same stigma that has killed the otherwise passable Resident Evil titles after RE4. The fanbase judges based on their childhood memories of how good the older games were, regardless of the fact that played side by side, you'd likely enjoy the newer ones more.
If you were not an uber-fan of the classic silent hill and/or resident evil games, or able to be completely objective about the subject (as is the case with my view) this is a very well made game that should make it's home among the greats.
Horror is a hard fanbase to please across all platforms, and in a society that has given us enough of it that we're completely desensitized us to it, even more so. This game deserves to be liked, but falls just short when played on nostalgia goggles.

I had a lot of hesitation upon purchasing this game and resolved to play Alien: Isolation instead. However after playing A:I I came back to this when it was on sale and for some unkown reason forked out the cash. Turns out The Evil Within in its current state is a good game and I will tell you why. Firstly immersion...this game has it, granted not always especially when the clunky♥♥♥♥♥Resident Evil-style movement and character world interactions wrench you out of it. But for the most part you will be surrounded by an all encompassing horrorifying assortment of creaking wood, flaking walls and rusted metal, the sound design and enemy design are spot on and feel completely right for the world. Next the pacing of the game is well done enough to feel cohesive. Furthermore while some textures are not up to scratch most are well done, voice acting is not always on par...the protagonist responds to reality bending horror with "Huh, that was weird"... I am not even exaggerating this, that is a direct quote. Meanwhile the story is well done except the inevitable ♥♥♥♥ing cliffhanger sequel bait ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t ending that should be written in barbed wire and shoved up the story writers♥♥♥♥♥(or at least the♥♥♥♥♥of who ever demanded that he put in this endiing). The game switches up its setting and atmosphere everytime you just start to feel like you can relax and things are under your control, resulting in a perfect sense of fear and caution at all times. The 'bosses' are beautiful in a horrorifying gore-splattered way and rival any beastie I enjoying cutting down to size in Dead Space in the intricacy of their design and the feeling of equal terror upon being ambushed by them and sense of achievement and respect when I put them down...or had I???
This game is well put together and a blast to play in chunks every evening once it is dark, hell if you can play it all through in one long blast with the curtains drawn and headset on! All in all: characters are a bit flat and pulled out of a stereotyped stage drama from the West End, level-design and atmosphere are brilliant, story is too subjective to person taste for me to really dictate to you on, enemy design is spot, great music and the gameplay is appropriate for the nature of the game. It feels cohesive and a product of love and care not a souless game, worth your time if you can get it just a bit reduced from its full price.

Okay, initially, I really enjoyed this game, but...As time went on, now the novelty has worn off, I will say that I'm cooling on this game pretty rapidly. The game is still pretty good - A very fast-paced bullethell dungeoncrawler sort of deal, but...There's flaws. Pretty big ones.
First off, the visuals. Again, Initially, I quite liked them...But soon after, I discovered that the vast majority of the visuals in this were taken from an asset pack with little to no alterations. Now, I'm all for using asset packs as a base, to get your project off the ground, but...At least tweak them a bit, ya know? It makes the game look a lot more cheaply constructed, and it DOES hurt the game.
Second...The difficulty curve is unfair, to say the least. I understand a game of this nature is meant to be difficult, yes, but as it stands now it's less of a difficulty curve and more of a difficulty wall when you reach a boss, a wall you need to smash through with your face. Now, yes, a game like this that you could get through on your first try without upgrading yourself would be lunacy, but at the same time, it can be critically disheartening if you can barely progress past the first boss. Maybe I just suck, but it's pretty harsh. There's also some issues that result in some very cheap deaths, such as some of the monsters doing far too much collision damage too quickly, and very limited feedback for when you're getting hit, meaning you can die very quickly without realising you're in danger.
However...I will still give this game a borderline positive review. It's still very playable, but these two things are pretty irksome. I understand there's probably more fixes to come, so...If they changed up the graphics and made the difficulty a bit less insane, I would find this game more approachable and easier to reccomend.
So, if anyone reads my review and wonders if they should try it or not - Put basically, It's alright, and honestly, I've paid far more for far worse games. Give the Demo a try if you're unsure.

Lot of bad press for this one. I had fun with it though.
The good:
- Look, feel, atmosphere of Deus Ex: Human Revolution. The yellowish tints, the music, and ambient sounds are all really good.
- Stealth gameplay is competent
- Hacking is lifted straight from Deus Ex: Human Revolution. It worked well there and it works well here.
- The game didn't crash on me, not once.
- Lighting effects are very good.
- Though the levels are small, there are still multiple ways to complete the objective
- Augmentations are back, and greatly varied
- Once you arrive in Panama City (where most of the game occurs), the story really improves and develops a great sense of urgency. After you get to know him a little bit, Ben Saxon is less stoic and more relatable than Adam Jensen.
The bad:
- Unfortunately, the game is too short to really explore Ben Saxon's character. If you skip side missions and non-essential hacking, you can complete the game in 4 hours or less.
- Stealth works well, but if you like to shoot your way out of trouble, good luck. The shooting mechanics work for occasional use, but if you like extended gunplay, you'll be frustrated quickly.
- Levels are small. Panama City has a number of places to explore, but be prepared for lots of loading screens.
- Lighting effects may be good, but facial animations are just awful, some of the worst I've seen. We're talking levels of animation from 10 years ago (except for Saxon). Anna Kelso in-game does not even appear close to the way she is depicted on the game banner.
- Textures are hit and miss. Overall, the game looks good, but if you get too close to anything, well, you won't be fooled.
- My Biggest Gripe: THIS IS ONE-THIRD OF A GAME!!! The plan was to release the story in three parts. The Fall is Part One. This is not advertised on the store page, but should be. When you reach the end (cliffhanger), you'll expect the next level to start, but instead you'll get a "To Be Continued" message. At time of writing, there is no indication that a follow-up is forth-coming.
For what we have, is The Fall a bad game though? No, not at all. It definitely felt like it belongs in the Human Revolution universe. If you want more of the Human Revolution story (this is a prequel), Deus Ex: The Fall suffices. But it's only one-third of a game. Skip it for the list price of $10; skip it at 50% off; get it when it goes to 75% off ($2.50).

As a species we've landed on the moon and split the atom, but we still struggle with making good edutainment games. Even our classics in the genre like Oregon Trail and Encarta MindMaze had their flaws, leaving us with no truly great educational games. Now, I'm not going to sit here and tell you that Super 3-D Noah's Ark is that game, or that it's even a great game. But it's plenty fun, and the way it manages to be fun deserves some recognition in how endearingly off-kilter it is.
So the Lord did his flood thing and Noah is cruising around on his spacious ark when all of a sudden the critters start getting rowdy. You're six days out from the waters receding so you've got to calm the animals before they get biblical on your♥♥♥♥♥ and that means force-feeding them until they pass out. Luckily Noah has all sorts of tools to help him do that, from souped-up slingshots to watermelon launchers. There's a whole mess of secrets to find in each level of the sprawling ark as well if you want to score some extra fruit.
The way this actually plays out is what's so great about S3DNA. This is a first-person shooter, practically a re-skin of the original Wolfenstein 3D. That means perfectly flat, gridded maps, 2D enemies and items, and mostly hitscan combat. You run around shooting enemies to put them down and reach the exit, except as it's posed here you're slingshotting animal feed into faces until they happily fall asleep. There's a fair bit of exploring too, to turn up new wep-er, feeding tools, health and ammo, and other secrets. And for the edutainment angle, there are items that quiz you on bible facts like the length of the ark in cubits and how many sons Noah had and reward you with health and ammo for getting them right.
I know this sounds like a cute family title but the action is 100% classic FPS. It's got a super weird feel to it (especially if you've ever played Wolf3D) because the combat is actually intense, requiring you to snipe from corners and strafe through danger. Your feeding tools behave exactly like guns, with varying attack speeds and a weird spread to shots that lets you one-shot one enemy and then miss six point-blank shots on the next. The hitscan attacks are probably the biggest reason the game feels so weird, because there are literally no visual effects for your attacks. Every time you fire your slingshot, nothing actually happens. There's no projectile, no impact, and no reaction from enemies when they get hit. The only way you know you hit is when they fall asleep and on bigger enemies that can take dozens of invisible hits.
The same is true for the sheep and camels that spit invisible loogies at you, which can make it very challenging to avoid damage or even realize how much you're taking. And that's what's really remarkable about this title, that a family friendly bible game is actually
. You can certainly play on easy or super easy if you want to get through it but normal is going to have the good Lord's flock kicking your♥♥♥♥♥all over the boat. There are six chapters, each ending with a boss that will machine-gun spit you to death unless you snipe it around corners. Noah also has limited lives that earn him a full game over when they run out, but just losing one restarts the map with all of your accumulated weapons and items gone.
I'm not sure how many people are looking for a new coat of paint on their 20-year-old FPSes, but for anyone that is Super 3-D Noah's Ark is a fun and surprisingly challenging spin on a classic genre. There are around 30 levels chock full of enemies and secrets (and even secret levels!) so getting through the game once even on easy is going to take an hour or more. Playing on normal or (God forbid) hard is going to extend that playtime significantly as you get burned down by agitated ostriches. The only other warning I'll give is that if you've never played an old old FPS like Wolfenstein and you're susceptible to motion sickness, the weird way the flat ceilings and walls move might trigger it. Because of that I can only play it for 10 or 15 minutes at a time, but I'm still having fun sedating livestock with watermelons to the dome. Now we just need a Wolfenstein: The New Order style revival for this, because as far as I'm concerned it's just as deserving.

Ok, I loved this game when I got into it.....Then greed finally set in. Dev's go F**K yourselves and get your fingers out of your A****. This was great fun when I got into it. Everything was *reasonably* priced for a F2P game. If you wanted the nice stuff you were *enticed* to pay, but it wasn't impossible to grind, for a casual player even. It was a good balance. Mods for your guns were a bit steep, but do able. Then a big update came out. Now, standard issue...I REPEAT standard issue, *you taking notes dev's??* bolt action rifles are a HUGE grind now. I'm lucky I got my KAR98K with only having 5th ribbon in SA rifles, i'll never grind it to a scope. I dont even know what it takes now, poor new players. I have a bunch of stuff on my toons that i'm not suppose to have for a long time now. Thats saddening with the amount of time already put in.
Gameplay:
I agree with other reviews, up to level 3 is good fun, then you level up your "battle qualification". That's your learning curve. After that, you are literally thrown to the wolves. Before I get into this, there are two styles of play, STAGED BATTLES and the WAR. You have to lead targets etc., so you kind of get that immersion from it. In tanks, if you want a full 360 snap shot you have to physically leave the cab and pop your head out the hatch. You can pick off people that pop their heads out of tanks and actually can steal them, which is kinda exciting. My first experience in a tank was done in this fashion. Theres nothing more rewarding than following a tank in the bushes, waiting for them to need to look out of their iron beast and then the head shot. If you leave the tank they can spawn back into it. Two solutions are available. first is to steal it, second is to plant mines around it. Either way its a win. You can actually shoot people out of any vehicle and "hotwire" it as your own. The game has a couple differnt game modes, which are painfully similar. It is all objective/control point based. They do, on occassion, have battles which include all 3 factions, it's a complete gong show, but good, near mindless, destruction. Usually your team will have a try hard or two that will attempt to organize the monkey s**t fight in the zoo, but it usually doesn't help at all. The modes are basically attack and defense or "assault". Then there's a 3 capture point "skirmish" on smaller maps. A well organized team in a battle is a lot of fun, even if you aren't super powered (P2W style), you can follow, help capture points, and even spot enemies for your team, earning ribbons and xp still. There are 2 kinds of "main" battles modes, staged battles and war. You have to repair your weapons of war this includes: weapons, attachments, ammo, vehicles, their ammo, vehicle attachments. Your toons have a base salary that you get for each battle and will be rewarded more based on performance. I have had some battles where I have lost money. This game really is a game of patience, lemmings will be eradicated, with pejudice I might add. It's a war....if you don't know how to survive in these games by now, go play something more run n gun. There are, however, times for the run n gun tactic, but dont try it all the time.
STAGED BATTLES
These are relatively matched battles, but can still have the odds overwhelmingly one way, if the other team is full of P2W infantry, with all the different ribbons and classes and styles of play, you can only expect the match maker to do so much. All the assault teams are pre loaded by a bot "general" so they are fairly even IE: no heavy tanks for one side and only lights for the other, as you sometimes see in "WAR" mode. They also are usually infantry heavy battles, which is great for lowbies. These staged battles are your grinding grounds, you just have to put up with it if you want to progress.
WAR
The war or "real" mode of heroes and generals is the games true unsung gem. As you reach an officers level, you get command points and can decide where battles will begin in a huge world map. Your side needs to capture key cities to win the "war". You as a "general" allocate assault teams in a battle zone and actually have to communicate with other generals to form a group of assault teams that will stand a chance. As a "Hero" in the "War" you can choose a battle to enter on the world map, or you can join a battle in progress. You can only choose to be with Germany, USA or Russia for each war. Once you pick your faction, you have to wait until the war is over to select a new faction in the next war. Participation in the wars is OPTIONAL. I don't believe you get any extra xp from war battles either.
**WARNING**
These are the unbalanced battles....
Scout the assualt teams allocated before entering a battle....because you can. If theres heavy tank teams in there and you have a light tank and a diff level 5 toon, get ready for some punishment. It's not hard to find battles that are *relatively* decent battle.
Unless you are stubborn like me, paying about what is average for a good WW2 shooter ~$20 and buying into your play style, you will have a fairly decent experience.I got lucky and got some decent gear before they made it impossible to get for free. I love the different branches, but, again, grinding as an infantry is horrible, unless you bought into it. I have several toons now. I made a russian tanker right when they came out and now have the BT-7, before the new slew of price raises came in. I will probably never play enough to get the t-34 now. You can kind of sub class as an infantry, which gives you a slight draw to the game. You can be anti-tank or a driver or even a sniper without buying into the recon thing. Infantry can be fun, if theres not a mess of people with LMG's and scoped bolt action rifles. I never got into the planes, but have heard good things about them.
CONCLUSION
Gameplay 6/10
F2P P2W balance 1/10
Progression without money 0/10

Okay, initially, I really enjoyed this game, but...As time went on, now the novelty has worn off, I will say that I'm cooling on this game pretty rapidly. The game is still pretty good - A very fast-paced bullethell dungeoncrawler sort of deal, but...There's flaws. Pretty big ones.
First off, the visuals. Again, Initially, I quite liked them...But soon after, I discovered that the vast majority of the visuals in this were taken from an asset pack with little to no alterations. Now, I'm all for using asset packs as a base, to get your project off the ground, but...At least tweak them a bit, ya know? It makes the game look a lot more cheaply constructed, and it DOES hurt the game.
Second...The difficulty curve is unfair, to say the least. I understand a game of this nature is meant to be difficult, yes, but as it stands now it's less of a difficulty curve and more of a difficulty wall when you reach a boss, a wall you need to smash through with your face. Now, yes, a game like this that you could get through on your first try without upgrading yourself would be lunacy, but at the same time, it can be critically disheartening if you can barely progress past the first boss. Maybe I just suck, but it's pretty harsh. There's also some issues that result in some very cheap deaths, such as some of the monsters doing far too much collision damage too quickly, and very limited feedback for when you're getting hit, meaning you can die very quickly without realising you're in danger.
However...I will still give this game a borderline positive review. It's still very playable, but these two things are pretty irksome. I understand there's probably more fixes to come, so...If they changed up the graphics and made the difficulty a bit less insane, I would find this game more approachable and easier to reccomend.
So, if anyone reads my review and wonders if they should try it or not - Put basically, It's alright, and honestly, I've paid far more for far worse games. Give the Demo a try if you're unsure.

sZone Online is a bit like a mix between DayZ, STALKER, and an MMORPG. It's environment mimicks that of the STALKER franchise. The gameplay is a bit similar to DayZ (though not exactly), and it has some heavy MMORPG aspects.
Many of the "poor" reviews I'm seeing on here are from a lack of understanding of the game.
First: Tips for newbies
1. Talk to Sour and Blacksmith. They will give you free weapons and some rewarding quests
2. Push N to hide other players
3. Push F to talk to NPCs. Translations have improved immensely. Be sure to read the quest dialogue. Often it gives you more info on what needs to be done then the journal
4. The area you first come to is the tutorial city.
5. The FPS has improved but large populations may change it
6. We have three servers. EU PvP, PvE, and US PvP. Their locations are obvious and each will determine your ping and what the majority of players speak in terms of language
7. When I played a lot about a year-year and a half ago, there was open world PvP. This caused a lot of problems. People would shut down entire towns with snipers and such, mass DM. As a result, it appears they've changed it. I will update this mroe as I learn the new system. There is also clan wars PvP and Arena PvP.
8. Clans can go to war with one another and capture territories on the second map you visit.
9. Yes there are anomalies and artifacts.
10. The game can be very difficult. Take your time. The key skills to doing well in this game is taking things slow, planning, accuracy, and socializing.
11. Push I to open inventory, U to open character, K to see your skills, and J to see your current quests
12. There are still some things in Russian. It has improved immensely, but it isn't uncommon to see something you don't understand.
13. To get out of the starter city the NPC named Duchonik (if that's how you spell) at the Police Station near the kindergarden gate will start a quest chain. Leaving via this way will side you with the military and their allies in terms of reputation you get. The reputation effects is minimal so you don't have to worry about this too much. The other way is to talk to Courier and do his chain at the north settlement in the city. This one sides more with the STALKERs/underground.
Overall I give the game a 8/10. They fixed a lot of issues with the pings, but graphics are still meh. The game is very challenging and time consuming. A lot of people have compared its design to something that of early 2000s MMOs, before the "WoW formula" became so frequent.
EDIT: UPDATED REVIEW to give better tips

A terrible game that ♥♥♥♥♥ on the legacy of something beautiful, 'The Fall' is more like 'The Fallen'.
It's a port of a mobile game, and not much has been changed to bring it to the PC. Seriously? I have to live with these terribly over-simplistic controls and rubbish graphics? This may fly on a the iPad, but not on my beautiful machine.
I did a Let's Play of this game, so you don't have to. Find part one here:

I find myself in a bizarre situation. On the one hand, Deus Ex: The Fall isn't all too terrible. On the other hand, there is no mention anywhere of this being an episodic game. You simply play for a little bit and then reach a "To Be Continued..." screen. It feels a bit cheap.
Cheap is easily the best word to describe this. Don't bother wasting $5 on this. I got it for around $2 and feel a little cheated. Graphics don't make a game, but holy crap is this a bit of a mess. Character models barely animate, there is clipping abound and performing takedowns almost always results in the world disappearing around you before forming back. I also got stuck in a box very early into the game.
As for the actual mechanics, there are a bunch of differences compared to Human Revolution, but the iOS origin of the game makes that understandable. What isn't so forgivable is that none of your keybindings show up on the screen. Everything is left as if you were still playing on an iPad. At least the tutorial voice recognizes your keyboard and mouse.
The level design is also entirely forgettable. This is pretty much a greatest hits of what the Deus Ex series has to offer. Nothing new ever happens. You hack terminals and computers, you stealth takedown enemies or blast them away and you crawl through vents. There is even a requisite nightclub, as if the first game made a permanent blueprint that can't be escaped.
I don't necessarily mind the chopped down areas, but there isn't much in the way of freedom. You definitely have choices in how you tackle the objectives at hand, but the AI is so shockingly stupid that you often wonder if stealth even matters. I often just ran straight at people and attacked them, barely taking a scratch.
The music is the standout feature here. The voice acting is hit and miss, but you can easily forget the characters are even talking when you hear the music. It may be a bit too short (the samples loop quite a bit), but it sounds far better than Human Revolutions did. It fits the tone of the game very well.
I also have a love/hate relationship with the store system. Instead of having to go to a merchant or even terminal, you simply buy what you want at any given moment. This turns moments where you get outnumbered or cornered by a robot into trivial affairs. I suppose trying to aim sucks on iPad, but it's flawless on PC.
So I could take the bad if there were at least a complete game here. As it stands, I feel like I only got half an experience. It wasn't devoid of fun, but you could spend your money a lot better. Human Revolution routinely goes on sale for $5 and you could even get the first two Deus Ex games in a pack for $5. Doing either option would be a much better investment then dealing with this drek.

Star Trek Online has been consistently high quality. I am a lifetime subscriber with no regrets. Expansions in this game are gratis. The new ships are not. If you treat the game like Pokemon, you can by the Legacy of Romulus or Delta Rising packs to get access to everything (and some exlusive perks), but you need not do this. Almost everything you want can be earned in game.
Lets be clear about the busines model though. You want F2P and refuse to pay anything? You will be punished by an endless grind for Dilithium to sell for Zen to buy the ship you want. Dilithum is capped at 8,000 refined per day. The average going rate has been around 160 Dil per Zen lately. At this rate, if you wanted a Zen ship worth 2500 Zen, you need to sell 400,000 Dil, or spend 50 days to earn it. Now you have your ship! Keep grinding that Dil so you can get the really good gear on it! Everything that is important costs Dil.
On the other side are Zen sellers. People who put $5 on their account and buy 80,000 Dil on demand. These are Cryptic's customers. I have seen a lot of complaints about this, or claims that is is Buy2Win. It's not a competition, and without a revenue stream there would be no game to play. Remeber that when you sell Dil, you are requesting other people subsidize your play time and the economy that controls this is regulated to Cryptics benefit.
One of the negatives of this game is the parent company. CBS has a strong hold on certain aspects of the game. Want to fly the NCC-1701 at endgame? Sorry, it's a 1st tier gesture that costs 500 Zen. Romulan T'liss Warbird? Same deal, no dice. You get this wonderful ship to start, but you have to use the T'varo from Enterprise, which is technically and "older" model. Want to play an android like Data? Flat no, the reason given is that Star Trek is about the human experience. The current Enterprise (NCC-1701-F) is actually captained by an Andorian these days...
So the big positive, if you chose to embrace it, is that STO is a "popcorn" type game. There are loads of content, but most of it has no impetus. Jump into a PvE queue and go. Jump into a system and do an away mission. It all earns you experience, energy credts, various faction marks, and of course Dilthium. Play one mission or play all night. There is no requirement for heavy investment of time like other MMOs.
Overall, I recommend the game. There are nits that you will see as well, but they grow over time. Many quality of life changes are in flux with each update, so the game is actually improving. If there is something that could be done right now to make it better, it would be to create daily seed missions that drive and reward people for the content they are currently missing by waiting for it to be spoon fed.

Ahh, The Evil Within, how I love you so...let me count the ways.  You're dark & gritty, bloody, violent, with just a dash of originality that you can call your own (four ways I guess....err.....mostly that many, but seriously, It's got more to offer than just that).
I've spent just over 70 hrs with this game and even after all that time I can say that I still love it; that I still love to play it + I can't wait for the DLC too (which finally begins releasing March 10th, or so I've heard).  For those not aware of this, The Evil Within is a Shinji Mikami joint so you know right off the bat that it's got something to offer as far as horror gaming goes, as he is the legendary creator of Resident Evil and 'Survival Horror'.  Yes, the Resident Evil series has greatly suffered over the years, having taken a major detour from the 'survival' aspect of the type of horror game that it was always supposed to be, but it has kinda made a comeback in recent years (*whispers*....kinda...).
That aside, The Evil Within, though not a flawless representation of what Shinji can do with a horror game, is still well made, it looks and plays good and even attempts to regain some of the lost suspense/survival aspects of earlier RE games.  Though there are definitely a number of action-oriented moments in this game, it does attempt to utilize elements of stealth by which to offset the action and create a sense of fear/suspense in the player.  It's not exactly a scary game, but it is most definitely trippy and can be creepy at times too, with a look and style + usage of traps and chainsaws vaguely similar to RE4, with subtle undertones of Splatter House to balance it out (the gore factor I mean, but some enemies may remind others of SH as well).
You utilize green gel to level up your stats/stock/weapons (you get the gel by defeating enemies and as a pickup throughout the game's various environments) and there are small keys hidden in statues that you use to unlock the morgue room drawers for ammo, green gel, etc. The morgue room is part of the asylum that you travel to by way of mirrors located throughout chapters and also between chapters (this is the 'trippy' aspect of the game that I mentioned earlier - the asylum acts as a sort of HUB world for the game; there are also collectibles to find there too, such as newspaper articles and missing persons posters + map pieces).
The enemies/bosses in the game are truly horrific, at least some of them are, and will often take multiple shots to weak points to take down, so be especially adept at aiming on the higher difficulty settings, or try to be anyway (otherwise you can try and level up your firepower to aid you in combat + there are some cool unlockable waepons as well, but I won't spoil any of that).  Don't even get me started on the spider-b*tch (that's what I like to call her; she's actually a representation of Ruvic's sister - Ruvic being the main bad guy in the game) and the Keeper.  Both these enemy/boss types will be encountered multiple times throughout the game (yeah, it's one of those games) but don't let that discourage you from playing it - it's still a great game that deserves to be played (especially considering that it's supposedly Shinji's last directorial effort in gaming).
Get it on sale if you can but it's still worth it at full price.

What a fantastic Zombie horde survival game...
If you are wondering what this game is...it is exactly like Left 4 Dead, as you and a group of other players will traverse across the stage, killing zombies, finding safe rooms, finding checkpoints, and at the end of each level there's some sort of boss.
I however, enjoy this game more than Left 4 Dead. There's no real plot or narrative besides Hitler unleashing his "Nazi Zombies", shortly dying after by his own creation, and you are set out to find the mysterious relics when which combines destroy all the zombies.
But... the game isn't focused on story at all, rather it focuses on pure gameplay, and fun. The level design is so gothic, and gruesome. The zombies are slow moving, and are pretty realistic as most only go down with headshots...
This is where the "Sniper Elite" part comes into play, as you are not able to mow down zombies with sub machines guns without running out of ammo. Therefor, you end up using your sniper A LOT, and must rely on your ability to get headshots at a distance, otherwise the zombie hords will overwhelm you.
Like other Sniper Elite games, when sniping zombies from a long-distance you will go into a "slow-mo" instant replay showing where the bullets hit, and how they break through the zombies insides. Unfortunetely.... this is only really shown in Single Player, considering the game has to slow down in order to show you the replay. In multiplayer it does happen, but is very quick, and often not as rewarding.
As for gameplay, this is a 3rd person shooter, but while aiming with the sniper you go into a first-person sniper scope. It's an interesting mechanic which isn't quite as good as Call of Duty's World at War / Black Ops Zombies, but it does the job quite nicely and is a more challenging game then the easy child's play game of Left 4 Dead.
----------------
The few downsides I saw were pretty minimal complaints...
- There's no power-ups
- Not many things to find or collect

Let me first say, this game is not for everyone. I'm saddened to see the "Mixed" rating for Recent reviews. This game is extremely niche and has some issues, some of which are serious. It's not perfect. Furthermore, the niche nature of the game I mentioned earlier will probably be extremely alienating to some people. As a disclaimer, I do not know much about the Warhammer universe (like, I don't even know if the futuristic and fantasy Warhammer universes are even connected.) I know NOTHING about Warhammer beyond bits and pieces of info I've picked up over my life, and this is the first Warhammer game I've ever purchased.
That said, this game is amazing, and I love it dearly. I wish I realized what a complete and total exact clone of Left 4 Dead this game is when it was released; and let's be clear here, the skeleton of this game is identical to Left 4 Dead. If you, like me, got into the super nerdy aspects of Left 4 Dead, like understanding the mechanics to a disgusting degree, figuring out how spawning works, using audio queues to best respond to your situation, etc... you will LOVE this game. This game actually *improves* on many of the design aspects of Left 4 Dead, and the intricate nature of how so many complicated mechanics work together is where the infinite replayability of these games comes from.
I may have 54 hours in this game as of this review, but I feel like I'm just scratching the surface. Yes, there are very few levels, just as there were in Left 4 Dead. If you plan to "play through" the game you will almost certainly feel ripped off, but this game is not intended to be played like that. This game is meant for us masochists which want to challenge *ourselves* and work towards that seemingly unattainable goal of mechanical mastery.
Keep in mind I'm very new to this game. Yes, 54 hours in this game means you are new. This game is absolutely brutal and on the higher difficulties does not forgive laziness at all. You must be on top of your game at all times. This kind of masochism appeals to me and I know it appeals to many others. If it does not appeal to you, turn away, because playing all the content on easy would be a very quick and unsatisfying experience. This isn't an adventure game. I have no idea what "genre" I'd call L4D, but this game is essentially L4D3, and it's so, so glorious.

This is a game that should be free to play with cosmetic transactions.
It does not feel like a game that should cost. Graphics are pretty decent, nothing amazing.  Performance is awful, sucks CPU power up. Even a high-end rig that dawrfs the recommended requirements can't keep a consistent 60FPS.
The worst offending part of it is however...this is Warhammer. WARHAMMER! The most important part of Warhammer games...is combat and satisfyingly meaty. Vermintide is not... The melee feels slightly worse than L4D's melee...and if you've played L4D, you know what I mean. Not very good at all. Weapons have no weight. There's no sense of impact.   Dark Messiah in 2006 understood first person melee combat better than this.
The melee combat is also exceedingly simple, like L4D, you have normal slash, and a push attack.  You can hold down the mouse for a "heavy" attack, but animation wise it's identical.  Just slower / does more damage. There's also a "block" button, but it's pathetic  Ranged weapons are slightly better, they have a sense of power, but once again sometimes you can't even tell if you hit an enemy.  I mean it, there's no indicator you've actually HIT a enemy, be it some kind of ping or change in crosshair, or visually. Enemies can be shot 50x and have no visual damage to them to indicate you've shot them. This is not ok in any game, let alone a WARHAMMER game.
Story wise...what story? There's less story here than L4D. It tells it's entire story in the opening cutscene, it's based off a book, so it expects you to know the source material. IF you don't...yeah.
Levels look great...but they lack depth. It's entirely linear. There's no alternate paths, no hidden secrets to find,  it's a corridor shooter like Call of Duty pretty much. All the events are scripted as well.  Far more so than even L4D.
It's all style, no substance. Right now I can buy the game for like...6$, and I won't. I could see myself having fun with it, sure...however there are too many issues with crashing, bugs making the game get stuck in general, co-op is really...eh. There's no sense of Teamwork like other shooters like this.  Everyone feels like bots.
You have 4 classes with the ability to change their melee weapon. About it. Comes off as sparse.  It does not feel at all what a Warhammer game should be like. It has it all on the surface, but nothing deep.
It's melee is even worse than Chivalry, and Chivalry is pretty bad in my opinion.
