Loads of action and loads of enemies... can get a bit repetitive though.
Overture has basic pixel-art graphics and a great soundtrack.
You can pick a character from 4 distinct groups and every group contains a few different hero types. After that you're thrown head fisrt into the action. You can move around a medium sized arena and your goal is to descend 10 floors and kill the final baddie. Combat is simple: hold LMB for your basic attack, which can be a quick slash or a stream of fireballs depending on who you chose to play as, and RMB is your hero's stronger ability, for instance the Druid can shapeshift or the Arsonist can randomly lay down flames that continually damage your enemy. There is also a sprint mechanic where you make your character follow the mouse cursor and it will give you a small speed boost as long you don't attack during the sprint.
Action can get a bit hectic, because sometimes there is so much going on screen: enemies, damage numbers, loot, fireballs. It can be a total mess at times, but it won't last longer than a few seconds, either you kill all enemies or the trample you. After the battlefield calms down you can pick up t3h ph4t l3wt left by the enemies. Items like armor to raise your defense, heal you or boost your attack power are all present here.
After you die (this will happen a lot) or beat the game (this takes some practice to do) you will be shown the result gravestone telling you how many enemies you've defeated and how much gold you were able to snatch. Gold can be used to unlock new character classes and permanently increase their attack power - you will need to do this to stand a chance at the later stages of the game.
Final verdict: A simple and hectic hack&slash that can get a bit repetitive, but overall a nice time killer. :>

SUMMARY: A seemingly simple, brutally hard, speed roguelike that has unexpected depth and unlockables as you play.  A fast, twitchy grab-the-gold, kill-the-monster, go-as-deep-as-you-can game great for people looking for that experience.  Has a lot to offer, but takes some patience.
Overture is the classic, stereotypical dungeon crawler/roguelike boiled down to its basic - go into a dungeon as a given class, slaughter monsters, level up, grab treasure, live as long as you can.   It's for fun, fast, short-term play - though you may be surprised how long you may play it.
You pick a class, which has two different attack abilities, and wander across a randomly geneated field, battling monsters of many kinds by using your various abilities.  The monsters themselves have different abilities, though most are cannon fodder - but watch out, some more powerful versions (who have titles or are different sizes) and special monsters may surprise you.
Monsters and various chests, jars, and barrels will drop treasure.  Most of this is gold and healing and mana potions, but the occasional piece of equipment drops as well.  The equipment often has little game-changing rules and additions that can make a different and require some thought.  You may even find NPCs who join you - until the inevitable onslaughts kill them off.
Each level has a boss monster guarding a stairwell, which leads in turn to a REAL boss monster.  Defeat these much more difficult opponents and you get a bonus to mana or health, a chance to buy random equipment, and then move on to the next level.
The game at first seems overly simple and overly hard, but rewards retrying.  Classes are different - radically different.  You can learn strategies for different enemies.  Gold and scrolls (which can become gold) that you recover can unlock new classes and level up ones you already have.  There's a lot to the game, its just often concealed beneath the frenzy and the randomness.
The game's biggest flaws are erratic difficulty and limited documentation - made more painful due to the randomness.  It takes patience to get into it enough to really enjoy it.  More polishing and documentation would definitely help.
Do I reccomend it?  Like many games, the question is "is it your thing."  It's not something everyone must play - it is something for people who like dungeon crawlers and action, and want a "hardcore casual" game that's challenging, but can also be picked up and put down.  In the latter case, Overture delivers.

For fans of games like RotMG... sort of.
The sprites and effects are nice, if uninspired. I've seen them used in dozens of games and I can't help but be tired of them at this point. I understand it's a sprite pack, and there is a reason this one is so popular, and that reason is why you should consider using something else.
Damage numbers are inflated to the point of irony right off the bat. The numbers cover the screen in a way that feedback is difficult to deliver on things such as damage dealt, whom it is dealt to, and who is on the verge of death. In the midst of combat it is hard to tell who is actually about to die: you or the dozens of enemies around you.
Having the camera so close to the player certainly doesn't help either. The fast running is a neat mechanic, and is utilized fine in boss fights, but in any other scenario the camera is unable to keep up with the character, making it feel like a gimmick. If the camera were to lead in front of the player as he ran rather than slog behind, this wouldn't be a complaint.
Upgrades and class unlocks are, as far as first-impressions go, pointless. There is no real progression - all classes cost the same to unlock, are all available from the start, and all "tiers" do the same thing as far as I know (a flat damage boost, maybe some other stats are raised). The only real differences between the classes is the sprites used, accompanied by a small change to the attack used, though they all basically function identically, filling the screen with massive damage numbers and not enough feedback to the player. Compared to games such as the obvious Realm of the Mad God (c. not 2014-15), this is extremely lackluster.
Overall, disappointing with some challenge. Fun to look at for a little while, but nothing to consider a favorite for any genre - and especially not as a roguelike. Would be worth it if it were cheaper, but with how shallow the progression is I wouldn't consider a purchase at this moment.

The Evil Within is a beautiful survival horror game. Although the game has many issuses and flaws, it is still one hell of a ride.
Most of the issues have to deal with are main protagonist, Sebastian Castellanos, who is pretty bland and boring. He isn't an interesting character at all, the same can be said for most of the characters. The story does not have a lot of character development, most of the notes you find are interesting and give a good look into Sebastian's back story but that is all there is. The main antagonist Ruvik is probably the most interesting character of the bunch. The game also suffers from texture pop-in during cutscenes.
Overall the game is wonderful it is scary and fun. The game may start off slow, but when it picks up it gets really good. The Evil Within is a horror game that survival horror fans will love, and I think it is one of the best survial horror games in a while.

Is the Evil within scary? At times its terrifying, all of the time its intense.
You dont see clearly and you dont feel sane, anxiety ensues. The dark broooding atmosphere weighs heavy as you trudge through blood soaked corridors wondering what could of caused those long deep claw marks that stain the very walls of this claustraphobic never ending hallway. A trickle of light filters through from a room up ahead, you can sense something truly evil lurks within, you know to progress you have to enter, an ammo check seems pointless, health is low and vision is limited, the previous enemy proved too much and the need for respite and care is great. The silence here pulls you down, you know that deep crimson stain you see in the centre of the empty space is where the claw marks end.....As you investigate further, heart beating vision blurry silence all consuming, all hell breaks loose, what ensues is an intense chase away from what can only be described as a twisted morphing of hair claws and blood soaked flesh. The screams are deafening the sound of clattering claws draws nearer as you scramble for the nearest door, you look back as you begin to lose your breath, fearing the worst. The creature is gone, but you know it will return and you know that next time it wont give up.
Its intense and its captivating and The Evil within presents the player with many similar moments throughout its rather difficult and long campaign. The story develops slowly and fleshes out the individual tales of characters such as the one described above, you begin to piece together the fragments, the story made for some interesting concepts that touched upon Freudian ego and the develpment of psychosis. In terms of gameplay its similar to that of Resi 4, the camera angle can become a bit too limited resuting in some unfair moments as your FOV is almost cut in half. Enemies can be bullet sponges and their attacks can cause instant death which results in some frustrating repetition of some difficult twitch response sections later on in the game. Visually it holds up well, background textures are ugly as sin but character and enemy models remain full of textures even though its heavy on the film grain.
All in all The Evil within was enjoyable, intense gameplay with some creepy scares here and there coupled with an atmosphere dripping in surreal heaviness, a strange story thats left quite open to interpretation and a long singleplayer story mode thats missing from a lot of similar games. I highly recommend this game if you can look past its difficulty spikes and sometimes unfair sections, what you get is a game that encapsulates survival horror thats often been missing since Resi 4.

This game is a mixed bag because the gameplay is awesome but the story is lacking. However, it did scratch the survival horror itch that I have been looking for and is a great additional to this genre.
Gameplay: The gameplay is very reminiscent of Resident Evil 4, which is a very good thing. The developer’s did add stealth gameplay to the formula but I rarely found myself using it, besides avoiding the traps and disarming the bombs. The RPG like upgrade system is a very welcome site to this genre that I love so. This game also brings back the classical survival horror gameplay elements like low ammo, traps from RE4, lack of health packs, and the trial and error. The classical gameplay may be frustrating at some moments, but still a welcome site for me. As a side note, the game does award you for exploration and is a must if you want to gain more ammo and health.
Graphics: I loved the grittiness of the graphics for this game. It doesn’t seem as polished as current games but I believe it was intentional to set the atmosphere they wanted. I didn’t care for the “cinematic” black bars, but fortunately on the PC you can avoid that. The atmosphere of this game was fantastic, from the environments to the great enemy models.
Story:  This is where “The Evil Within” falters for me. The story is broken apart and not very engaging. It raises so many questions that is doesn’t successfully answer at the conclusion of the game. The voice acting and writing is also very weak. However, thinking back, the original Resident Evil had the same problems, but with the advancement in story telling in games, it just does not cut it anymore.
Conclusion: If you are a person that enjoyed Resident Evil 1 and 4, like me, then play this game. Just do not expect any advancement in mechanics or storytelling. Also, as a word of caution for newcomers to this genre, the difficulty is high and can sometimes be frustrating with a lot of built-in trial and error. If you can power through it then it will provide a great 10 to 15 hour experience. In the end, I recommended this game to all my survival horror nuts and newcomers interested in a true survival horror experience.

Buying this was a painful reminder to always check reviews before getting something. It's actually a ported Android game, and I guess it's fine if you want something to play on your tablet. But as a PC game, especially a Deus Ex game, it's a joke.
The UI is big and weird, and not just in the usual console port way. It's really strange and awkward to use with a mouse. (It's probably more or less the original made-for touch-screens interface)
The tutorial forces me to do very specific things, like attaching a silencer to a certain weapon. So much for player choice.
While the art style definitely looks like DX:HR, the level design is much simpler, the rooms are smaller, more blocky and your choice of non-obvious approaches usually boils down to a single alternative air-vent route.
Combat doesn't feel that great, you basically have the same cover system as in DX:HR, but it didn't work as well, can't quite say why exactly, it just isn't as satisfying. And the AI is really wonky and stupid.
I can't say much about the story, since I didn't play that much, but it certainly wasn't interesting enough to keep me playing despite of the lackluster gameplay.
Finally, my GTX 980 didn't even go above 35° C when playing, which tells you everything you need to know about this game's graphics.
Fantastic start... Can't wait for more progress on this game.

If you came to this game expecting something like Human Revolution, you may find yourself dissapointed. However, I think this game is still recomendable for those of us die-hard Deus Ex fans. Although a much shorter (and simpler) game, it's still, in my opinion, a good game.
The graphics are inferior to those of Human Revolution, but that should be obvious, considering that this game originated as a mobile game. Even then, they managed to capture the aesthetic of HR, with all its golden glory. As far as the environment goes, the city of Panama is an interesting location to explore, although it's much smaller in scale than the hubs of DEHR.
The gameplay is also simplified. You don't need to search around for people to buy guns and/or Praxis kits from; you can do it whenever you please from the pause menu, and you also can't sell your weapons (but it doesn't matter, as money and bought weapons carry over to new playthroughs). The AI feels a bit dumb, as they'll quickly lose interest in you if you stay under cover for a short time; add to that the fact that bodies dissappear, and it makes for a much more "casual" Deus Ex experience. Even then, it's enjoyable.
Finally, the story, in my opinion, is worthy of a Deus Ex game. It already starts with the main character trying to uncover a conspiracy, only to find about an even bigger conspiracy, and getting involved in it. The only downside, though, is that it ends on a cliffhanger. It seems that they intended to make this game episodic, but they abandoned that idea (probably due to the bad reception it got).
Still, it's worth a shot in my opinion, I recommend it.

The real horror in this game were the striking similarities it shared with my own life. My growing madness, my hatred of rats, my unfinished opus magnum, my enjoyment of a good drink. Not to mention when ever I walk through a door it always leads somewhere else on the way back.
The game plays like spending 2 hours in a haunted house. While it's no Mc cready manor the atmosphere is worth playing for alone.You wont leave broken and crying but will be taken by the enthralling concept of the painter gone mad. The game attempts to scare players with haunted props and occasionally a monster. However it's hard to be frightened once you look closer and realize the monster and set dressings are made of animatronics and plastic. Since you can't actually be killed and your fate is predetermined you are more of a carnival patron wandering down a set route until your ticket time expires and you're asked to leave.
This doesn't mean the game is bad though, as the ambiance, tone and atmosphere are all very  engaging, enough to keep you immersed and intrigued. The game is surreal utilizing madness/psychedelic visions rather than traditional monster cliches (for the most part). The game looks good and appropriately creepy with it's period decor. While the audio is also strong I'm still not entirely sold on the voice acting. Seeming a little predictable when read out to us, I feel it can slightly hurt the overall mood. The idea being mystery may remain more eerie.The concept it's self of horror revolving around paintings is interesting and well done. Capturing how unsettling these old masters works can be.
With a few more game play elements or perhaps puzzles this experience could be enhanced. As it is now though the game still deserves a play through by fans of surreal horror.

After playing the demo, I really felt like this was going to be another Amnesia or Penumbra (which I've been craving for a while now...)  Much to my dismay it turned out to be a Resident Evil clone.  And by that I mean, it's basically a large addon for the RE games.  After playing through it once, I read up and learned that it was made by the creator of RE.  So go figure, I should've researched it better.  That doesn't take away the fun.  Although it wasn't the game I wanted it to be, it was still very enjoyable.  I'm working on my 4th playthrough right now (on the hardest difficulty) and I don't plan on stopping until I get all the achievements.  So if that can stand as a testament as to how fun it is, then so be it.
The first play through took me about 16 hours.  That's not how long the game lasts, mind you.  It's how long it takes to find all the collectibles, keys, tapes, and unlockables.  There were also several moments of fear where I simply could not progress because I was shaking too much.  I started the second play through to finish finding the last couple things I missed and to upgrade all of my stuff.  It's impossible to fully upgrade everything with one playthrough, there just isn't enough green goo to allow that.
The second playthrough took me about 4 hours, allowing me to fullly upgrade, find the last of the collectibles, and nab the <5 hour achievement.  (THAT'S how long the game ACTUALLY takes to play).
So if you want to be scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  This isn't your game.  If you want to be jolted.  This is your game.  If you love RE games, then you'll love this one.  Do like me and wait for it to go on sale and enjoy the next 20 hours.  After getting this last playthrough, I'll probably never touch it again.
Initial Playthrough 7 / 10
After 3.5 playthroughs    4.5/10

This game is a mixed bag because the gameplay is awesome but the story is lacking. However, it did scratch the survival horror itch that I have been looking for and is a great additional to this genre.
Gameplay: The gameplay is very reminiscent of Resident Evil 4, which is a very good thing. The developer’s did add stealth gameplay to the formula but I rarely found myself using it, besides avoiding the traps and disarming the bombs. The RPG like upgrade system is a very welcome site to this genre that I love so. This game also brings back the classical survival horror gameplay elements like low ammo, traps from RE4, lack of health packs, and the trial and error. The classical gameplay may be frustrating at some moments, but still a welcome site for me. As a side note, the game does award you for exploration and is a must if you want to gain more ammo and health.
Graphics: I loved the grittiness of the graphics for this game. It doesn’t seem as polished as current games but I believe it was intentional to set the atmosphere they wanted. I didn’t care for the “cinematic” black bars, but fortunately on the PC you can avoid that. The atmosphere of this game was fantastic, from the environments to the great enemy models.
Story:  This is where “The Evil Within” falters for me. The story is broken apart and not very engaging. It raises so many questions that is doesn’t successfully answer at the conclusion of the game. The voice acting and writing is also very weak. However, thinking back, the original Resident Evil had the same problems, but with the advancement in story telling in games, it just does not cut it anymore.
Conclusion: If you are a person that enjoyed Resident Evil 1 and 4, like me, then play this game. Just do not expect any advancement in mechanics or storytelling. Also, as a word of caution for newcomers to this genre, the difficulty is high and can sometimes be frustrating with a lot of built-in trial and error. If you can power through it then it will provide a great 10 to 15 hour experience. In the end, I recommended this game to all my survival horror nuts and newcomers interested in a true survival horror experience.

Having played this game for almost four years, I think I can safely say that I know this game inside out. The game is being run by 30 something amateur developers who have absolutely zero gaming sense. They might know how to code but they have never played any FPS games in their life as is evident by the state of the game. More on that later.
Basically the way this game differentiates itself from other WWII games is that it has a RTS map combined with the FPS shooter. Every battle you play makes a difference on the global RTS map. A good concept with poor execution.
Now coming to state of the game. The game is absolutely broken. If you are a serious gamer who really wants to enjoy the game by playing it properly, there is no way you can do anything, especially as germans. Please keep in mind that my review is based on Clan vs Clan battles, that is when both the team have equal skills. Allow me to explain.
1. R T S    M A P
The RTS map is completely broken with different exploits and features that make up for a poor gaming experience. You won't really understand this part unless you play the game. Auto resolve, Para blocks, Alt accounts are some of the exploits to name.
2. S P A W N     P O I N T S
The FPS part of the game is pretty much impossible to win when attacking. The spawn points are placed in ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ positions which always favor the defenders. When playing a clan vs clan match, there is absolutely no way for the attackers to win the game. Ofcourse when you queue on an FPS battle with your entire clan and you face a team of noobs you can destroy them in 5 minutes but whats the fun in that.
3. N O    C A P    O N    S P E C I A L    C L A S S E S
A free 2 play game attracts a lot of kids who just want to be a recon or a tanker. Problem is that this game does not have any caps on special classes. The game is to be played by capturing points, that is to advance along the lines. To do that you need infantry mostly and a couple of tanks, planes and recons. With no caps on special classes, this game usually has all planes, tanks or recons with a few infantry most of the time. This completely breaks the entire FPS part of the game since you can't really cap points by playing tanks and recons, but since majority of the players are kids, all they care about is to snipe with their scopes or shell HE with their tanks/planes. They are least bothered about winning the game.
4. W E A P O N    I M B A L A N C E
The game has been suffering from weapon imbalance ever since it was introduced to the general public. For the last year or so there are no competitive guns for the german faction. Call it asymterical balance or whatever, the gameplay is completely broken because of weapon imbalance. For teams with equal skill players ( clan vs clan ) there is almost no way for the german faction to win Assaults against other factions. Combine that with the bad spawn points described above and you have a completely broken game that no sane person can play. This is what one of company's representative says about a starter SMG compared to a high end Machine gun. You be the judge.
5. G A M E     E N G I N E
Game is being developed on RETOX, a game engine that was custom made by the company. Needless to say it sucks. It comes no where near to what modern engines. Because of this the game is extrememly poorly optimized and even the high end systems can barely run the game with 100 FPS. The gaming engine is also a bottleneck for a lot technical things like map design and so on so forth.
These are some of the major problems in the game. The game has a lot of bugs and exploits that would take forever to mention. Now coming on to the development team.
The developers have ZERO gaming experience. They have never played any games in their life and have no idea what they are doing. They did hire some veteran players to be part of the support but i wouldn't really call them developers since they have no say/input in the game development.
Its a free to play game, with kids coming in, spending 40-50 bucks and then leaving. This is what keeps the game/company alive. That is why to end my review, I think HeroesAndGenerals is what i like to call as "Legal Scammers"

Okay, after 16 hours of this game, I'm ready to tell you to play. I read the "pay to win" reviews feeling dubious, but I went ahead and jumped in. First off, you do NOT have to pay to win. Yes, it takes time. It indeed took me these 16 hours to get to Rank 5 (the first rank where you can join the overall war that counts). Along the way, I upgraded my M1 Carbine to the max and bought myself a submachine gun with upgrades, still with credits to spare. No real cash. I suspect that those who cry "P2W" are the types who expect to advance to the highest level before reaching the bottom of their first bag of Cheetos. I enjoy a game that takes time and patience to advance, get weapons and win. Playing intelligently gets more XP than running around like a moron throwing grenades everywhere. Seriously, get low, don't move, one shot one kill.
On the downside, once I joined "the war," there were far fewer players. Queue times were much longer and battles were not even filled 50%. The community also went downhill. There was a lot more of the typical BS chatter that is often seen in PvPs. It was disappointing. The community in the lower level skirmishes was far more mature and the battles more exciting. I'll be sticking with those until more players reach level 5. I hope the developpers lower the requirement to get to the war, since it'd be a lot more fun if it was full of players.

Hotline Miami 1 was awesome and refreshing - the difficulty was set at a nice level, making the game challeging, it had good level desing, introducing new mechanics, masks and weapons as you progress trough the game. It was brilliant, and I loved it and I had high hopes for the sequel. Unfortunaly, it's bad... almost everything that was good in the first game was changed to be bad in the sequel. First of all the liberty - in HM1 you could swap masks as you liked, to try to find the playstyle you liked the most. In HM2:WN you can't choose your mask, instead you have you beat every level with a character and rules forced by the creator of the game - in this level you can't kill anybody, in a other one you have to go meele, in another one you can't drop your weapon and have to collect ammo, from ammo boxes, etc ... It's super annoying, because additional rules to the levels could be like optional, or on an extra difficulty, as an extra challenge, for those, who like it. Because personally for me, it's no fun, to have to beat a level with meele only, while all the ennemies have guns. No fun at all, very frustrating. The second worst part of the game, is the level desings - 90% of the levels are huge rooms with glass windows everywhere! So a lot of the times you don't really know from which side you gonna get shot. In HM1 the windows were introduced in the few last levels, here in HM2 you get them in every damn level. The story and music are good, as in the first game. But due to the negative elements of the game, I'm not gonna finish it, dropping, after trying to clear a unfun, unfair, badly designed level. In HM1 I enjoyed the challenge, but HM2 is not challenging, it's just stupidly frustrating. If you liked HM1, don't try the sequel, if you haven't played the original, you can try it out I guess ... but you're better with part 1.

It starts out simple enough but as you progress it starts to get more complicated as you need to plan who pairs up best to produce a baby with the best genes. Super 3D Noah's Ark is an all right game!  I heard of this in 1995 and thought it was a joke, but playing it for the first time in 2016, on Linux with the steam controller, I admit it is not bad at all!  The game is just like
, but instead you play as Noah, trying to put the animals to sleep on the Ark.
Aside from the regular elements you would expect to find in this G-Rated game, like different food shooters, animals and bosses, keys and secret passageways, it also has quiz scrolls which will really test your understanding about Noah.  So be sure to study before hand if you want to get health & food from them!
On the down side, the small animal cast gets repetative, and the boss battles are a bit fleeting.  Also, some of the animals are very powerful in close range, and are often placed where you are not expecting them (like right around a corner, or behind a door), so you can expect to die - a lot.  If it wasn't for the save game feature I would have given up already.  There are a lots of achievements to get, but some are very difficult to get, like beating the game 100% in hard without saving (if you can do that, maybe you should consider changing your name to Noah)!
But overall I enjoyed the game, and had a few hours of fun exploring the ark!
7/10

*On the other hand I really enjoyed the variety of jump-scares. It seemed no one was the same as another. There was obviously a lot of creativity in their design.
*I also liked how the environment resembled a twisted version of the reality that the story is trying to portray at any given point.
tl,dr: Boring jump-scare gameplay only made interesting my the variety of events and environmental sets

Overall great game. As long as you don't go into PvP, you'll have a blast. Also, I ran a field test with me as the guinea pig. If you're poor, you're less inclined to pay for stuff. And it feels rewarding when you get stuff without coughing up a dime. For example, I have a constitution-class cruiser (alliterations, yay) at lv. 12 because there are milestones. All the P2W negative reviews are either people who are raging from PvP or people who spent all their money trying to get a fancy new spaceship. This is also one of the few games where a hotbar system actually WORKS. Sure, there are plenty games with hotbars that function, but this one actually feels natural, unlike WoW's "spam 1 to see generic sword swinging animation" tactic. The reason this one works so well is because of the layout of a starship. There are buttons all over the place, so why the hell wouldn't you press buttons to do stuff? The ground combat, though enjoyable, is rather clunky and buggy, but that doesn't necessarily ruin the experience. The missions are layed out like an actual Star Trek series, consisting of beaming down to unknown planets, scanning the area, saving the planets, and hailing Starfleet. The combat is obviously based off of the JJ Abrams movies, as you can tell by the nonstop action. But this game is worth investing your time in, as long as you sink your hours in instead of your wallet. Overall 8.5/10

I haven't played this game for too long, as thus haven't gotten very far, but I believe I've grasped how it plays.
This is a light-rogue, hack n' slash, with minimal RPG touches. If you've played them, it will probably remind you of Hero Siege and maybe Quest of Dungeons.
The controls for this game are very easy, specially since there are only five actions you can take:
list]

There aren't many options to customise this, but they're really not necessary anyway.
That said, although it's easy to get the hand of the controls, winning/ not dying? Not so easy.
The game doesn't have true permadeath, you get to keep the money of your runs and use this to unlock other character classes and upgrade them.
It can be a bit slow at first as you get familiar with the classes and the game. As far as I've gotten it seems progress is slow too for a while (I haven't made it further than the second floor). Luckily though, the floor is randomly generated, so at leats you're not stuck with the same layout/design each time.
As I've mentioned above, there are many classes: a total of 24 divided into 4 subgroups of Warriors, Rogues, Mages, and Shamans. Each have their small differences which are fun to discover.
Seeing the trailer or the screenshots in the store page the game might seem very messy. Once you start playing though, it's not so hard to know what's going on. It might still get a bit confusing if you're playing a ranged character and you get yourself in the middle of a mob, but it's not so crazy.
To help with your questing, different types of NPCs can be freed. These NPCs follow you around and help beat monsters up. They die easily though.
The game has a nice pixel art from Oryx Design Lab (thus why it reminds me of Quest of Dungeons so much) which you might have seen in other games. It's a nice pack and it's fun to see how it's used here if you've played other games with the same one.
Awesome bit music that keeps you exited while hacking everything.
As of the date of this review the game is only available for windows.
However! It seems like it works perfectly with wine :)
Even though the game has left early-access, the development pace is still very fast, with many updates being released. It's great to see a development team that listens to players and keep working on the product even after it could hold its own.
This is a great buy if you enjoy fast paced rogue-likes. You can play this taking advantage of the upgrade system to make advancing easier, but you can also ignore it if you enjoy permadeath experiences.
Each game doesn't take long, so it's a great game to play when you don't want to/ can't spend too long on it.

The premise of the game is simple, but fun. You have 24 different classes to chose from, each with their own pros and cons. Some of the differences can be subtle, so try out every class to see what works best for you or try to master them all!
The addition of the running mechanic adds another level of unique gameplay. If you stop attacking and move towards your mouse cursor, your character will run faster. You will have to switch between offense and defense to survive and conquer each level. You need to constantly pay attention to where your mouse is positioned instead of mindlessly holding down the mouse and targeting enemies, or you won't get very far.
The developer is very active on the forums and frequently updates the game based on player suggestions. There's definitely a lot of potential with this game and I can see future enhancements that will expand and improve on the game.

Okay, after 16 hours of this game, I'm ready to tell you to play. I read the "pay to win" reviews feeling dubious, but I went ahead and jumped in. First off, you do NOT have to pay to win. Yes, it takes time. It indeed took me these 16 hours to get to Rank 5 (the first rank where you can join the overall war that counts). Along the way, I upgraded my M1 Carbine to the max and bought myself a submachine gun with upgrades, still with credits to spare. No real cash. I suspect that those who cry "P2W" are the types who expect to advance to the highest level before reaching the bottom of their first bag of Cheetos. I enjoy a game that takes time and patience to advance, get weapons and win. Playing intelligently gets more XP than running around like a moron throwing grenades everywhere. Seriously, get low, don't move, one shot one kill.
On the downside, once I joined "the war," there were far fewer players. Queue times were much longer and battles were not even filled 50%. The community also went downhill. There was a lot more of the typical BS chatter that is often seen in PvPs. It was disappointing. The community in the lower level skirmishes was far more mature and the battles more exciting. I'll be sticking with those until more players reach level 5. I hope the developpers lower the requirement to get to the war, since it'd be a lot more fun if it was full of players.

I've played way too much of this game. Most of which has been spent in the level editor, but I have yet to make a campaign I'm proud enough of to publish, but when the time comes... So, I love this game. Maybe it's my obsession with Tarantino, but the whole "telling a story out of order" thing appeals to me a lot. It was a little weird at first having this game take place before/during/after the first Hotline Miami Game. I'll give a quick rundown of all the characters, with as little spoilers as possible.
First character you meet is the Pig Butcher: He only has one actual level and takes the spot of the game tutorial, but his level is really interesting. He blurs the lines between what's a movie (not a spoiler, you learn his parts are a movie in the tutorial) and what isn't. He's a great character.
Next is Corey: She is one of four (or five) fans. They're all nutjobs who practically worship Jacket (from the first game) and take out a bunch of kids just because they're in gangs, (they don't know Jacket's motivations and about the phone calls). She has a USELESS roll dodge, meaning that when you press space, she does a stupid ♥♥♥♥ing roll on the ground. It's not as bad as I make it out to be, but it is pretty useless in my eyes. When rolling, she's impervious to bullets. But when she gets back up, she usually get's shot, which is why she's only really good for rolling across distances. She wears a zebra mask, and a Miami Dolphins jacket.
Next is our good, handsome friend Manny Pardo (that's my profile picture): He's a dirty cop who get's his sick kicks out of killing a bunch of kids just because they're in gangs. He uses his powerful badge to murder and get away with it. The people he murders aren't innocent but he doesn't let anyone find out.
Next is Evan Wright, the writer: He is a writer. His motives are to write a book about Jacket, leading him to some crazy places. He "fights" his way through a mafia building to interview the leader of the gang, named Petrov. Evan is friends with Manny, and Manny owes him a lot for something that happened in their past. It isn't made entirely clear what that is exactly, but you get a pretty good idea towards the end of the game. Also, Evan doesn't kill anybody, he just knocks them out, leading to some pretty sweet takedowns. He doesn't use guns or knives, and he can take the magazines out of guns to disarm them. You actually CAN kill people with Evan, but it takes a little while. After two kills, he goes ♥♥♥♥ing berzerk, and you won't like him when he's angry. Mainly because he throws off his jacket and you get to see his glimmering biceps. No homo.
After Evan is Tony: He uses the familiar and sexy killing punches from the first game with the Tony mask, but this time with a twist. He can't use weapons. At all. All he has are his fists. He wears a black shirt and they Tony mask from the first game, but it's weird and bloody. It's never actually stated how he gets it, but it looks cool, nonetheless. And he's also another fan of Jacket. He, Corey and the three other fans hang out in a cool bar place.
After him is the Henchman: He works for the new boss of the Russian mafia, who I'll get into later. He wears the classic white jacket with a blue shirt, and has a silenced pistol. I hate his level, it's really annoying and there's too much open space, leading to a lot of cheap kills.
Next is Alex & Ash: That's right, two people for the price of one! Why? Because you get to play as both of them at the same time. They're both twin brother and sister. Alex, the girl has a chainsaw and Ash, the guy has a pistol, or whatever gun you find on the ground. Left click to use the chainsaw, right click to shoot the gun. Ash follows Alex. They're both two of the last fans. They hang out with Corey and Mark at the bar. They both wear matching swan masks with a 1 and a 2 on them so you can tell them apart when they talk. They also wear football pads, and Alex uses a backpack. Playing as them is action packed and awesome.
Next is The Soldier, Nicke, Beard or whatever the hell you want to call him, he goes by a few names: He's a... familiar face from the first game, and you get to fight Communists in the Russian-American "Cold War" in 1985. His levels explain a lot of questions you might've had about the mysterious cashier in Hotline Miami 1. His levels aren't my cup of tea, a lot of them are too open and lead to cheap deaths. Cool character, but his levels often have bad design. ESPECIALLY THE LAST ONE!!!! But I digress.
After him is the final fan, Mark: Not much to him, he wears a bear mask and starts out with two ♥♥♥♥ing machine guns in each of his hands. M&B: Warband is truly a masterpiece. This game epitomizes the medieval open world genre. The amount of things you can do means you are never bored. Some things I've seen in M&B that no other game I've played offers include:
-Nobles are never static, they are constantly joining new factions which means a hostile lord could defect to a friendly faction and become your bro. In addtion, if you capture an enemy noble you can ransom him back to his kingdom for a decent sum of money.
-Control of villages, castles, and cities gives you a steady stream of money from the taxes, rents, and tarriffs. You will also lose money from soldier's wages and tax loss, and depending on the type of fief(s) you hold you will either gain or lose money from this feature.
-You can get married to the daughters of nobles, if you are a male. If you are a female, you can marry the nobles themselves. This has several benefits including increased reputation your spouse's father, brother, mother, etc...unfortunately you cannot have children in this game.
-You can join a faction or make your own. You can also capture nobles of other factions and recruit them to your own, or persuade friendly nobles to support your cause. If you make your own faction you can also declare war and make peace with other kingdoms at will. Not only that, other kingdoms will declare war or make peace with you depending on your current status with them (i.e. if you attack a caravan belonging to a certain kingdom, they will likely declare war on you, but if they lose too much ground in a war then said kingdom will offer you a truce.)
And that's just what I can think of off my head. There are countless other features in this game that no other offers and I think that's what makes M&B a true work of art. This jewel is easily worth twice or three times what you pay for it. If there was a such thing as a flawless game this would take the cake, but sadly no game can be perfect.

Niche is a Great game, not only is it fun and challenging it also can teach you.
Niche is "composed" of 2 aspects genetics and survival. The genetics part is what really brings the fun :) there are as of this review 73 different genes (Though some are similar) and 18 gene slots. Most genes (57) change the appearance of the creature and the non cosmetic ones give creatures various abilities to help thier survival. But not all genes are helpful some such as no paw, hemophilia and blind eyes hinder your creatures and now for the most fun part  breeding. Breeding is essentiall for survival but you must choose your pairs wisely because you don't want double immunity creatures running around.
Now for the survival, Each creature needs 1 food at the end of each day so you're going to need to balance the amount of creatures you have so you don't starve. This is where your genes come in Strength allows you to hunt prey and defend your self from carnivores, collecting allows you to gather berries, digging for roots, cracking for nuts and shells and fishing for well fish (All food when collected is the same). As i have already mentioned you need to defend your self from other creatures. Depending on which island you are on their will be differentt threats, on most islands their is the carnivore the "medium" predator, on jungle and mountain there is the apes and balance bear which are 'Hard" predators, but you don't just need to defend you self from predators, rouge males will breed from your females (not good) blue birds will steal unprotected children and dodomingos will steal nests.

I enjoyed
.  This game gets a lot of flak from people who (for some reason) expected it to be up to par with
.  But you must remember
was one of the best games ever made; of course a cheaper, more simple, smaller-scale game that was originally developed for mobile devices isn't going to be on the same level as
!
was going to be a “hamburger” from the inception of development to the very end.  I understand that there is a desire for more
games of “steak” quality, and I share that desire.  But I don’t see why anyone should hate this game for not being something it was never supposed to be in the first place.
I greatly enjoyed my playthrough of this game and I think if you can understand and accept the game for what it is, and get it for a price you feel comfortable with: you will enjoy it too— especially if you are a fan of the genre or the

It was toned down, sure, but I could still feel the
atmosphere as I played.  I liked the story.  It was simple, easy to follow.  The game is only 5-ish hours long to beat, (maybe a little longer if you 100% it, which can be done on one playthrough).  Also the game is easy.  Whether you are sneaky or Rambo, the combat scenarios are mostly small and easy; and the RPG elements are toned down as well, (i.e.: there are not that many abilities, and you can access the shop from anywhere in the game).
All together, the pieces fit nicely into a small package of a game.  There are some trivial decisions to be made, and a few alternate paths to choose from. When one thinks of Deus Ex, they think of multiple choice avenues to virtually every task they come up against. They think of smart storytelling that makes you want to keep playing. They think of all the unique situations that a play style gives. Well, don’t expect any of that here folks.
Coming off the heels of Human Revolution, you would probably think it would play and look the same, if not better in every regard, but come on, we all know it’s a port of a mobile/tablet game so we can’t be expecting miracles, but the effort made by the developers to improve on the build and make it more PC friendly is comical.
Let us start with the visuals. The game itself does indeed lend its art style from Human Revolution, although heavily watered down. The models of everything, from cars, NPC’s, buildings, you name it, are horribly rough edged, and don’t look much better than the original Deus Ex… which was released in the year 2000!
The textures fair no better, sporting their low resolution sickness all over the place. It extends further though, as the UI, which again, is almost identical to HR, is poorly done, and is quite obviously up-scaled from a very low resolution, which results in that pixel edge look… nasty.
Other SFX such as explosions and the sort have as much visual punch as a wet teabag. In fact, the only models in the game that even have a decent model and texture to them are some of the weapons. They’re obviously ripped directly from HR and watered down to match the rest of the game.
Now don’t get me wrong! Visuals don’t make a game, I mean look at how well the original Deus Ex holds up, even today, but that has other features, such as great mechanics and story.
The sound is no better, with most voice actors doing horrible jobs, on what sounds like very low grade microphones. The ambient sounds and soundtrack are similar to HR, and probably sourced from that also, so at least we’re good on that front.
Putting that all aside, we come to the meat and potatoes of any game, THE GAMEPLAY! So then… the shambles of this becomes apparent from the start. Yet again it ports over Human Revolutions animations and pastes them onto the dreadful models. So you can expect most of the same features, such as cover and rolling from it, sneaking but OH NO WAIT! You can’t jump. For some reason Panama doesn’t stock jumping augs, and apparently has super gravity as you can’t even jump an inch, or even sprint for that matter! I don’t need to explain how much of a game breaking issue that is to a Deus Ex game.
We do get practically every augmentation Jenson received, besides the aforementioned jumping augments, so you’ll be very familiar on this front at least. Oh, what’s that? No merchants in the hubs? No no no! Instead, we have a store that we can access on the go, at anywhere at any time. Obviously a remnant from the mobile version where players could dump their real money into the game to get items faster, and is extremely game breaking. You can just buy more painkillers mid fight and be fine, essentially making you invincible for all intents and purposes. Oh, and did I mention you don’t have an inventory screen and seem to able to carry everything?
Maybe you’re like me. A man who was simply thirsty for a bit more Deus Ex and bought the game on sale in spite of all the bad tales I heard, because hey, it must have a story right aside from all the horrible gameplay? WRONG! The story is pathetically boring and simplistic that actually ends up with a “To be continued” screen, and guess what?! That will never come as the idea was obviously abandoned after its massive flop.
In short, I don’t think it’s worth it even for the most hardcore of Deus Ex fans. Do yourself a favour and replay the original or Human Revolution until we get that sequel to HR that is on the horizon. Unless of course, you like torture, then I’m afraid you did ask for this…

There is a subset of gamers that really intrigues me: the type that slaves away hunched over their monitors, doing the same repetitive task over and over, with only the faintest glimmer of hope for a reward at the end of their trials. I’ve never much been into games that require excessive grinding, or for the  player to invest a lot of their time for that shiny trinket that is only marginally better than the previous one, but each to their own I suppose. So, when Overture landed in my inbox I wasn’t exactly overcome with joy, but I wasn’t filled with trepidation either.
Overture is reminiscent of Realm of the Mad God, Diablo and even, to an extent, The  Binding of Isaac. It sticks you in the middle of a vast, randomly generated dungeon with hundreds of bad guys and tasks you with fighting your way out, and that’s pretty much a wrap for the game’s main features. You’ll do all the usual Action RPG things, like collecting better gear and upping your stats, but, ultimately, not much changes as a result of that. Yes, you will be fighting horde after horde of bad guys, and bosses, over and over again, but that isn’t necessarily a bad thing. My dislike for repetitious games aside, Overture is a well designed, smart game that will give a certain crowd of gamers with hours of action.
While the game is certainly a one trick pony, there are lots of ways you can approach it. With 4 different classes and 24 different characters, each with their own attacks, there’s something here for every type of player. So, whether you want to be a warrior right in among the action with blood dripping from your blade, or an archer taking potshots from a safe distance, you’ll find a character to suit your tastes.
Once you have chosen a class you are slung straight into the action, but not before you’ve seen the handy control scheme tutorial. Playing the game is as simple as using the left mouse button to attack and the right mouse button to special attack. If you find yourself in a pinch you can hot tail it out of there by moving toward your mouse cursor, which will send you off at great speed. There’s a bit of a knack to mastering Overture‘s “hit and run” style of gameplay, but once you have you’ll be tearing up countless undead, blobs and other indescribable evil doers.
Gameplay is simple and formulaic, and you’ll wander through each floor looking to pick a fight with scores of different mobs at the same time, and the odd elite as well. You’ll occasionally come across a mini boss which are harder to kill than normal mobs, before having to take on a much more difficult boss.
You’ll be accruing experience and levelling up as you kill enemies, increasing your stats ever so slightly, whilst bolstering them further with various pieces of armour you’ll receive from chests and enemies. You’ll also gather companions  that you’ve freed from the clutches of the enemy, and they’ll fight alongside you.
If Overture was a candy bar it would be the most sugary, mouth-watering bar on the market, the kind that dilates pupils and causes synapses to fire uncontrollably. Its action is swift and meaty, with just enough danger to keep you on your toes. It also rewards even the slightest amount of skill with lashings of blood and a hail of gold coins, that is sure to intensify the “candy bar” effect I mentioned above.
One thing I don’t understand though is why it features no local coop, though, Overture is  the perfect game for playing on the couch with a buddy. I’ll call it an oversight and not a missed opportunity, in the hope that Black Shell Games adds this feature in later.
While Overture hasn’t made me a total convert, it has, at the very least, allowed me to understand the appeal of difficult grindy games, and that’s a beat I can dance to.

I will preface this by saying that I was given this for free on RAOG on reddit. I'm not sure if this makes me more or less qualified to write a review. On one hand, I don't have buyer's bias which would make me feel obliged to think it was good, but on the other hand, I got it for free, which might make me obliged to write a good review. But I'm going to be honest.
It's a time-waster, and I love it. This is one of those games that you could pop in and pop out of. Whenever I needed to decompress after a lot of studying, I would just open up this game and play as a cleric (my favorite class as of right now). There are a lot of classes and a lot of subclasses that really make the game feel unique. You probably could find one that would fit your playstyle.
One of my gripes with this game is that it was kind of odd how I came to learn about many things. For example, it took me a long time to figure out that you could right-click to attack and even longer to learn that there was a limited magic system. It also took me a while to figure out that you could equip stuff you found on the ground.
You'd say I'm just stupid for not figuring this out when there are indicators that you could do that stuff. But there's so much other stuff happening on the screen that it sometimes just gets lost on you. I'm not saying make a sign in bright pink neon, but maybe just a little optional tutorial for noobs like me. That's why this isn't lowering my score of the game.
There are numerous other sources to actually learn about the more in-depth stuff about the game to see if you'd want it. But this is a Steam review, so you're probably looking at a bunch of other ones on here. That's why this isn't all-inclusive. But I believe that it is worth it at the point it's at right now. I would still be fine if there were no more updates at all to this.

This game is not without it's faults. The missions can be a little buggy, the quest destinations (or where you go to get your rewards) can be vague, and the ground combat is a bit clunky. But the space combat and customizing your ship is where this game really shines. And there's more than just combat, some of my favorite ground missions just involve saving scientists from a fire in their research facility, or even investigating an abandoned facility and sealing atmosphere leaks; so much like real episodes of Star Trek. You'll find yourself spending a lot of time just flying your ship around aimlessly because it's just so fluid and relaxing. If you want to blow up spaceships, scan for resources and craft items to sell on the market, carry out diplomatic missions, or just explore a massive galaxy and numerous systems within, you can find lots to occupy your time and enjoy.
And now you can play as Klingons and Romulans, so that's neat too.
The game is free, but if you find yourself enjoying it I can see spending some cash on getting your dream ship, some great crew-members, or your favorite uniforms. The developers certainly deserve some cash as while the game isn't perfect there's lots of Trek-universe stuff in it that fans of the series, casual or hardcore, will enjoy.

Star Trek Online, what do we expect. It's an MMO, and it's not pay to win, but it has that evil nature of subconciously forcing you to pay real money for it just to get fancy stuff quicker, similarly to WoT (I fell for it on WoT, not here though). The game is, to put it straight and bluntly, a grindfest. Initially, it may appear fun and promising, but everything you do ends up being a mindless grindfest. With every new patch, Cryptic introduces a new way to grind new stuff for new shallow content. Pluses are the fact that the devs stick to canon lore (might be something for die-hard trekkies) and the nice space battles. Ground battles are totoal rubbish. Avoid.
All in all I'd say that there's a lot of content in Star Trek Online, there's just not much depth to any of it, and that's what makes this an increasingly boring and repetitive game for me.

Ive been seeing a lot of bad reviews lately about this game and most are right, but also very wrong.
The newest and biggest complaint that has emerged was the "Pay-to-Win" aspect of the game, which it really isnt, pay to win is when you hand over real currency to get an advantage over other players, which in this case yes, they get new weapons and parts, but there still is no real advantage in sight, no matter how much another player pays for the game, you're still going to be able to destroy them with your stock loadout, if you're good.
Another thing about the PTW matter is that with this game, if a player is paying, he is paying A LOT, gold and "premium" time are very expensive and is around 200$+ a year, so you cant complain because only thousands, out of a 5 million player range, actually play to win.
the last complaint is the grind, and thats really the only downfall to this game, but not all is lost.
Level 1: you're having fun and figuring out the game
Level 2: you're still having fun, but the grind already makes itself clear
Level 3: be ready for the long haul
Level 4: you're guns are upgraded, you have new guns, and even a jeep by now, maybe more, but the game is getting sour and the grind is long and hard from here
Level 5: You're having fun again, you can drive a tank, perticipate in more than just staged battles, you're guns are fairly upgraded and now youre making decent cash by level, the xp grind is still going to be the kicker
Level 6 and up: You're unlocking and buying new things every week, by now you have a few friends and are a good shot, it will take a long time to progress, but you have the income and unlocks to deal with it, after this its a smooth, but long sail.

Where to start? Mechanically, the game is adequate. It looks alright, performs well enough (although not great), and most things work as expected. From here, things go down hill.
The story starts out non-existent and ends somewhere between there and non-sensical. The game jumps all over the place (literally), and the story makes pretty much no sense (even after the credits roll).
There was not a single point in the game where I felt like it was a 'horror' game, and most of the attempts at horror just come off as cheesey schlock. "Survival" is another tag attached to this game, and I think that's also a bit of a stretch.
The above would all be forgivable if the rest of the game was actually fun, though. There are good moments in the game, but there are also a slew of awful moments in between those far too rare good ones. Checkpoints are sporadic, as is the difficulty. So you'll go through entire chapters with a save every 5 minutes and never be in danger, and on another level you'll end up replaying a 20 minute section over and over because of a (literally) randomly spawning enemy that instagibs you if he touches you. Fun.
Overall, I would not recommend this game. There are so many other games that this one is trying to emulate that do it better. Go play Dead Space instead.

Plagued with awful design choices, technical mishaps and crashes, and a practically non-existent plot (or a plot that might as well not exist). Anything and everything in this game can be an instant death trap, even with all health upgrades. The game has an incredibly frustrating habit of changing the rules or adding new mechanics and then instantly killing the player for his lack of clairvoyance.
Unfortunately, this is aggravated by the lengthy pre-scripted, inescapable death animations and the awful checkpoint system which ensures that you get set back as far back as half an hour before the point that killed you. Only about half the time that I died was I completely sure of what had killed me, or had any idea of what to do to escape death the second time around.
Ammo is extremely limited; more times than not you'll have more enemies to fight than bullets, and the shooting controls are finnicky and unresponsive, making sure you waste ammo on near misses. Enemies also display no evidence of taking damage or how close they are to death, so you won't know how effective you're being until the enemy simply explodes.
The boss fights are the absolute worst. The bosses all have a ridiculous amount of health and all use instant death attacks, full health upgrades or no; Some of them are invincible and require special strategies to defeat, not that it's really possible to tell that they're invincible until you're out of ammo. Boss characters are shamelessly reused multiple times with absolutely no alterations to their mechanics as well. And the final boss doesn't even count; literally a gun turret and a rocket launcher fall out of the god damn sky and you're told to just go to town.
There's no story worth talking about here. You get some half-baked ideas about shared consciousness that goes nowhere, characters that hit their one-note personalities and never grow or change in any conceivable way, a plot concerning a conspiracy and the main character's dead daughter that goes nowhere, plot elements that are introduced, fleshed out, and then promptly abandoned, a main villain who's so cartoonishly evil and overpowered that it's impossible to take him seriously, and in the end, nothing gets accomplished, nobody learns anything, and absolutely no part of the story gets explained or receives any kind of closure whatsoever. To ensure it's as confusing as possible, every location is isolated from the other ones, and there's no clear goal or objective, and the game has no continuity whatsoever.
I don't even mind that it wants to be an action game or a Jason film instead of something that's actually scary, but since it's marketed as a horror game, let me be absolutely clear; There is absolutely nothing in this game that is the least bit frightening. This is just any regular action shooter, just covered in giblets and grotesque imagery. Because that's all you need to do horror. Just give a big guy a chainsaw and everyone will♥♥♥♥♥♥their pants.
At it's best, the game actually threatens to be entertaining. Some of the gunplay sections can be satisfying when the shooting controls feel like cooperating and you actually have ammo. Enemy heads explode when killed, which never gets old. The crossbow adds an element of strategy and depth to the fights. That's when the game really shines; when you're given a large open level, lots of ammo, and a number of enemies and just told to dispatch them however you like. But then you run straight into an instant kill trap that you had no chance of seeing coming because it had never been introduced before this point and indeed will probably never show up again.
I don't hate the Evil Within, but my experience with the game was largely negative because of the poorly designed mechanics and narrative. There are parts of the game that are fun, but every time you start to have fun it feels like the game punishes you for it.
Basically, if you read the entire review and still feel like that's your cup of tea, go ahead. This game is for you. Otherwise, it's a buggy mess of a game, and your money would be better spent elsewhere.

Let me start  of on a negative note: The Evil Within's voice acting is laughably bad. Granted, the original Japanese voice work could very well be a nuanced, or at the very least, passable affair. Not being a Japanese language speaker, this is sadly a perspective I'll never be privy to.
That said, Evil Within's [english language] voice work is almost a non-issue, as the piece's tonal strengths and atmosphere are masterfully delivered through a slavish devotion to aural and visual craftsmanship. The lighting is incredibly dynamic, shifting and warping organically. The same can be said about EW's soundscape; whether it be the nerve-rattling soundtrack or near unbearable haunts of silence, the game's phonic presence lends itself perfectly to the nightmarish journey at hand.
Gameplay-wise, anyone familiar with the likes of Resident Evil 4 and beyond will be right at home. Shinji Mikami and Co. once again struck a near perfect balance between keeping the game's mechanics tight and enjoyable, while never giving the player enough breathing room to ever feel comfortable or overpowered. Resource management is crucial, especially on the harder difficulties.
I found the game optimization reasonable (infuriating launch-day shortfalls notwithstanding). Rigged with 2 Nvidia 680M's and an Intel i7 3940xm (3.9ghz OC'ed), the game ran fairly smooth at 30fps at Ultra settings. However, removing the letterbox, which adds an additional 30% of screen real estate to the GPU's workload, caused noticable lag spikes. I recommend anyone facing performance inconsistencies to utilize  Nvidia Inspector and its extensive array of customization options and game profiles.
Highly recommend to any fan of survival horror gameplay with an action-centric slant. A small measure of RPG-based character modification also adds to the game's tension, encouraging the player to trail off the beaten path, in hopes of collecting the ever precious "Green Gel" (the game's version of upgrade currency).

I'm a big fan of the original DX and I enjoyed the follow up, Invisible War. Human Revolution had some good ideas and great atmosphere. This heeling title has nothing going for it.
The Stealth play is not fun: no distractions to divert your enemies; unconcious bodies automatically clear themselves away; shaving the walls and rolling between boxes is all you are expected to do.
The Guns don't measure up either: the plasma projectiles look horrendous, like they are pasted from the original doom; no arc in trajectories; the guns don't feel like they are firing; and I question terminal physics calculations that prescribe three taps from every gun.
The takedown system barely mimics Human Revolution: allowing the player to attack advancing, alerted enemies from behind cover and then returning them back to cover seems a little too forgiving; to add insult to injury you have to watch the same disjointed takedown animation over and over again.
Looting is the worst: no inventory, just a shop with counters for items you've already picked up; enemies invariably drop credits and a gun (converted to bullets); I got more from raking bins than I did from cracking safes; and I shouldn't have to shuffle around to find the 'sweet spot' to pick an item up.
The level surroundings have no depth and cheapness lingers: areas are boxily subdivided and mostly alleyways. The writing is uniform and bland. Voice acting delivery often feels cold and hurried. And who approved Robot Aunty's voice for the tutorial?
This game wasn't worth the very low sale price.

Let me start with this. Ignore the majority of the unhelpful negative reviews!
This game seems like it was an incredible game for Mobile, and it is still a good game on PC.
The gameplay is so close to Deus Ex: Human Revolution that it felt like I was playing some kind of DLC or expansion to DX:HR(which is a good thing)! There was some changes to the gameplay, as you would expect as it was originally a mobile game, but overall the gameplay was entertaining. The most disappointing part, however, was the fact that bodies disappear, so you can not hide them to stop enemies finding them. Instead, guards have about 5 seconds to have a chance at noticing body and after that they are unable to.
The story was quite interesting and entertaining. I am however disappointed in the game as it ends with a "To be continued..." and yet it seems the devs thought, "Ah, you know what? Screw it!". Perhaps the game didn't take off very well (the ridiculous amount of over the top criticizing reviews seem to back that up), or/and the devs just cancelled it. Or, maybe we are going to have to wait a ridiculous amount of years to continue it (which is very unlikely. It has most likely been cancelled, which is a shame as it was great fun while it lasted).
The graphics are decent. If they were like this on mobile, then they did a fantastic job. The game seems to run incredibly well on high settings, so I thinks it safe to assume that most modern PC and perhaps even Laptops could run it (yet to try my old laptop yet, but I may).
The sound and voice acting is fairly good. The sounds are mostly recycled from DX:HR, any new ones aren't fantastic. However, the voice acting on the other hand, is fairly good. The majority of named characters are voiced at a good standard, however the un-named character are mostly voiced poorly. Ben Saxons voice actor sounds quite bad at the very beggining, however, he soon sounds better.
Oh, and there is only one save file... Yeah... Only one... That's pretty much the only negative thing I have to say about this though, and it's not that much of an issue.
Overall, I give this a 7/10.
Pros:
Almost completely mirrors the gameplay of Human Revolution, and therefore feels like an expansion rather than a new game (which is a good thing!).
Awesome main character (like every other Deus Ex game).
Interesting story.
Decent Graphics.
Mostly, good quality voice acting.
Stays true to the Deus Ex franchise.
Cons:
Not much new. Now I know it was a mobile game, but they could have got some slightly new stuff.
New sounds are quite naff.
Unfinished story/disappointing cliff hanger. And it doesn't look like it's going to continue anytime soon.
One save file. Now that is just annoying!!! D:< xD
Anyway, like me, you should ignore all the bad reviews and give it a shot yourself! I bought the entire Deus Ex collection and this was the first one I played (I have of course played some of the other Deus Ex games in the past (DX1 and DX:HR)), because I wanted to try it for myself. Give it a shot! You, hopefully, won't regret it. (Although, I'd get it on sale if I were you, it's definitely not worth £8.00. Mainly because the story is unfinished.)

The atmosphere is spot on for this game. It has been a long, long time since a game (or movie) has made me more than nervous. The scares are subtle (and not so subtle) and does what horror does best, subvert expectations. The music is spot on to match the mood while the sound effects themselves (squeaking doors, weight shifting on wood, etc) are more than enough to get the heart racing.
The gameplay however is little more than a walking simulator. However, this does not detract from the experience at all. The amount of stuff I missed on my first playthrough was astounding and I found out a certain someone can do a certain something to you twice before the elevator thing. Yes I am being obscure on purpose. As of right now, there are two more pieces of the puzzle missing. I will update this review when the last two are added. I have high hopes for this game.
One slight recommendation if the devs see this: Don't show much of the Other. Keep it more blurry. Best fear is hidden within ambiguity.

well myfirst game;
-Started in th savanna/plains
-Adam and Eve bred produce baby
-Lots of wonderers with short lifespans. Oh look two babies! ¬_¬
-4 carnivores and the death of Adam and Eve later
-Well I've got 4 nests, 4 breeding females and some berries. I'm forced to grab cactus berries whenevera carnivoreome along.
-How am I managing to keep the immunity genes alive? breeding the hell out of everyone!  I manage to keep hold of both = genes, the triangle, circle and + one. with 5 genes, I had a choice of pack mates.  I nevr saw any other gene and honstly, the way the first 4 carnivores tore through my pack at the start, I on't think I really had time to consider things.
-All I have is spitsnot and claws.
-next thing I know... 6 nests and 30+ members.
Okay so I learn early on the secret was to focus less on keeping traits I wanted and more about breeding for the sake of immunity genes. There were times I took inbreeding risks for the sake of maintaing a circle or + sign one. I had female constantly in the nest breeding.
So I also took some notes from nature and how animals behave.  I kept the young in the centre of the pack protected by the adults and slowly moved the access adults out.  By keepingthe young in the centre not only did I have a circle of protection to them, but I also had a breeding stock at hand near nests.  As one partner died I moved a baby with a gene the other partner didn't hve into breed. I never had less then 12 babies in the centre at all times.  I always took breeding from them and pushed out the unwanted members to keep the gene pool fresh.
As I said, the big weakness was genetics for survival... I lost the berry paw really fast, and the big nose. I had a rams hend but lost it within 1 generation.  The poison fangs, however, survived because of Eve and Adam's soul off spring survived.  Otherwise I had a army of spitsnouts.  I managed to load up a berry paw and bring it back into the mix later but tht was when I had 20 individuals.
I know some advise making paths in the grass but I foun it stronger as a move to slowly expand the terroritory one bit at a time.  This meant the carnivores and bunnies had nowhere to hide and made sur the back areas of area arond nests was safely exposed. I also made sure no one in the outter areas of the pack was alone without at lest 2 back up pack members.
I do like the random nature of the breeding and exploring... Even my best plans had flaws.  I nearly lost a immunity gene.  But once you have 4 nests down and a decent amount of pack members and berries to pick, the game becomes easier even if you mess up.
Edit:
The island migration update changed a lot of things, but there are some conclusions I've come to.
1- Eventually you'll come to an island where instead of the carnivores hunting you, you hunt them.  They produce 10 food and there are few bushes to raid and sometimes trees.  So you need to turn focus away from running and berry collecting and towards double claws and ram horms/antlers.
2-At this point, I realised you can only have x amount of females on nest, so taking a note out of Lions I sent the etra females off to scout.  Yes, horny males were a problem, but I wasn't breeding from the ones sent off.
3-I surrounded each nest with a harem of males.  The males gave a genetic selection for the nest sitting female.  They doubled as shielding the females on nests from horny males.
4-hunting females went out solo, they were often fresh out of the nest with ram or antlers and double claws. They scout slowly the island and found and killed carnivores while slowly unveiling the grasses.
5-expansion was slow, I could only breed when a carnivore was downed.  At this point the spawn rate was high on them so they were appearing almost every other turn.  Later on as the double claw and antlers became common, I was able to slowly push out, get to other nests, hunt down the carnivores more effectly and things sped up.
6-The trick on slow epansionw as to never have more then one or two scouts, even if they were slow double claws, they could slowly cut way the map.  Patience was rewarding.
7-Trees were often more valuable then bushes.  while I would sit one female gathering the acorns, bushes were just cut down while the girls were hunting.
8-If your lucky, you may get a double bush near a nest.  Carnivore high spawn rates means even then a double berry paw is dangerous.  Your creature is vunerable.  It becomes a high risk, especially as often its not worth it unless it rains.
9-So about the females who are moved away from the nests.  Okay so there was always 4-6 females not breeding I could not do anything with.  Occasionally a horny male would come along and a baby would result.  This is a gamble.  I clustered them together to ATTRACT the males. Sometimes the males gave a hidden trait among their rubbish genetics, like a immunity gene.  I know some hate these guys, but often their a blessing in disguise.  Early on, when you move onto a new island sometimes things are cruel.  I traveled to island 3 with 8 young and strong individuals but their numbers fell.  I was lucky to find 3 nests within a few squares of each other.  But I ran out of food looking for food.  So I ended up with a shallow gene pool in immunity genes - until a horny male blessed one female with both toxic body AND a new immunity gene.  I had to breed out their crap genetics, but I think thats the idea.
10- about 50% of the island unveiled leaves a lot of dark areas for carnivores to spawn.  cut that grass ASAP to get finding them easy to do.  Without grass they lack the element of surprise and can't ambush you.  By 100% of the map unveiled, they are exposed, weak and this makes them just sitting ducks even for slow double claw paws.
11-you don't always have to have plenty of food to migrate if you've made the right breeding.  The first migration to island 3 I had 24 food.  The result was I bred rarely.  5 of my guys had to be sacrficed for the greater good of the pack.  They were the first scouts. Their efforts unveiled the areas that made carnivores easy to find.  Their deaths weren't in vein.  Sometimes, you have to choose between the death of a few pack members like this.  But neverless, it is possible to get migration through on less then 40 food and prosper.
Basically, the game pushes you more and more to become less "hunter/gather" and more "hunter" it seems later on in the current migration update.  The most valuable traits right now are toxic body, poison fang, ram horns, antlers, double claw paws, Lean body (edit; sorryI left this one out).  Speed and gather paws are almost useless. You have to bait and wait for the right things to come to the nests, be it prey or mates.
