I'm not even sure where to start with this game since, as I've played it, it's not much of a game but rather a hurried, and horried, mishmash of poorly laid out plot with a veneer of "mystery".
I'm well aware that this game is rather dated as it's directly from 2008 and has been ported onto steam but I can't help but cringe at the beginning sequence which has horrendous graphics, terribly cliched imagary, and some cringe worthy voice acting (none of which gets better over time). But I overlooked that in favor of giving this game a fair shake. I should have trusted my gut from the start and stopped playing.
After the intro lets up you find yourself in control of Nigel Danvers of whom the hilariously corny "villain" and "hired goon" spoke of earlier. You, as Nigel, have very little option but to speak with the 'Station Master' on the platform where you'll be spoken to like a right moron and given quite unhelpful information about where you are and a jolly shot in the mouth because, guess what, you're stranded here because apparently no one at the train station told you that you weren't going to be able to reach your destination, which was very much not where you ended up, because the train, apparently, doesn't go further due to seasonal flooding...which is something you'd expect to be informed of when you bought your ticket to begin with. [Plot hole or just lazy writing? My vote is on extremely lazy writing.]
But not to worry, Mr. Danvers! There's a little town within walking distance across a marsh and through a very dank, dark, and quite unsafe cave!
When you do reach the town you're going to spend a terribly long time just clicking on random things that have absolutely no value to you whatsoever, having inane (and poorly voiced) conversations with random people, and being condecended to by just about everyone in town who knows exactly who you are, why you're here, and seem to have gotten their dialoge from a Vague & Mysterious'  2 for 1 special.
Twenty minutes in and I was no only completely bored but actively wishing I could set Mr. Danvers and/or the town on fire so there would actually be SOMETHING to get emotional over; this game does very little to endear you to the supposed protagonist nor the townsfolk of which you're forced to ineract with. It's all rather a tedious experience.
This is NOT a game for anyone that's looking for an engrossing dark mystery. This isn't even a game for anyone looking to waste time with. It's just a mess.
I wouldn't recommend it to anyone for any reason but I do actively encourage people to form their own opinion...just please watch youtube videos of gameplay or something first because it's not something you should waste your money on even if it's currently (during the winter sale) cheap.

A psychological horror game /walking simulator.
It is sometimes detrimental to compare one game to another, but this reminds of a mash up of Gone Home and Amnesia:dark descent. Player is guided through the labyrinthine corridors and rooms of the protaganists home/mind, discovering clues and objects that go some way to explain the unfolding of events. Unrelentlessy claustrophobic each twist and turn brings BOO scares, morphing architecture and paintings and surreal imagery.
So is it any good? In its current Early Access state, answer is a reserved Yes.
Some of the scenes are chilling haunting and genuinely surprising. Where the game is subtle is where it mosts succeeds; was that a human shadow flitting accross the corridor? a figure through the rain lashed window pane illuminated by lightning? The atmosphere is well managed, there is no escape from the tension and the dread of turning round opening a door or turning a corner is all pervasive.
On the downside, there are far too many jump scares that ,yes, scare the beejezus outta you, but quickly become the norm, and start to feel a little cheap in consequence.
There were some "events" I surely missed because the game did not attract my attention to the occurence, although the sound track indicated something had happened The story up to this point is underdeveloped, and although I felt in the most part immersed in the game this is despite of the story line rather than because of it.
Despite the usual old horror tropes that don't bring anything "new" to the game genre, if you don't mind jump scares and a linear gameplay, then give this one a go.

A Decent Deus Ex Game Held Back by a Terrible PC Port
Deus Ex: The Fall is a decent Deus Ex game, if you can look beyond the terribel PC port, poor graphics and and abysmal shooting mechanics, then you'll find an enjoyable but short singleplayer campaign. I clocked in around 6.8 hours for my first run, but I was looking for loot and doing sidequests, so if you rush its probably more like 3 hours. It's clear that the developers didn't bother to adapt the Ipad game to PC.
What the Game Does Wrong
The biggest problem with the game is the shooting, its terrible, if you're shooting something apart from the assault rifle your FOV will move up and down, creating a disorienting screen shake effect, this is most noticeable with the shotgun which could make someone nautious  with repeated use.
Scoped weapons are incredibly awkard to use too, instead of holding right mouse or mousewheel to look down your scope and  pressing left mouse to shoot, you hold left mouse to look down scope and release to shoot, its so akward that I never used a scoped weapon outside of the tutorial. There is no aim down sights, the gunplay feels flacid and unsatisfying.
Also in gunfights the AI is terrible, if they aren't standing in the open shooting at you, they are taking cover at the wrong wall leaving them exposed to you. All these issues means make  you want to avoid gunplay because of the screen effect and the akwardness of the scoped weapons, and poor AI.
Aside from the gunplay, gameplay dumbed down for Ipad is left unchanged, smaller leves, there is no jump buttion, only jumping over predetermined locations, no sprint, you cannot move objects around, bodies dissapear into particles so you can't move bodies, there is no inventory screen instead there is a shop/inventory screen where you can buy anything at any time  so you can buy items in the middle of a firefight.
The graphics and PC port are also terrible, there is limited pc options and the port lacks many important essentials. For example there are no save slots, only one save slot that is used for autosave, thankfully there is quicksave which works just fine. The graphics are poor to, textures are very poor quality for 2014, animations are awkward, especially the taking cover animation.
What the Game Does Well
While the game's levels are alot smaller compared to Human Revolution, they are open-ended enough to be fun to sneak around, the hub area is also good theres quite a bit of loot hidded, althought the lack of jump means its not as fun as Human Revolution's hubs. There's about 6 sidequests to do, all of them add some secondary objectives to your main missions.
Overall the sneaking is well executed too, I never noticed moments where I felt I should have been seen but wasn't or vice versa, and the routes you go to avoid guards a fun to find. I played through the game ghost style and there wasn't any area outside the tutorial where I felt the game was pushing me towards combat.
Augmentations are largely unscathed, they basically got all the useful augmentations from Human Revolution and put them in there's a new augmentation called 'stealth run' but it feels akward using it on PC, its something was clearly designed for Ipad.
Story is interesting, the presmise is that there's a new alternative to Neuropozine, however it looks like there's something suspicious with the drug. Unfortunately there's no real resolution to this plot as it ends on a cliffhanger, as there's meant to be an episode 2, but I won't hold my breath for episode 2. The voice acting is not great, it ranges from horrendous to okay.
Reccomendation
If you play Deus Ex for its shooting, then you should avoid this game, however if you play for the stealth gameplay then the you will probably enjoy the game, the stealth is well executed and there's always a way to complete the ojectives stealthily.
If you do play Deus Ex for the stealth, I would reccomend picking up the game during a sale, I got my copy for $3 and I felt I got my money's worth.
If you're new to the Deus Ex series I'd reccomend you get the original or Human Revolution Director's Cut instead of this, they have much better mechanics and depth compared to this game. I think only hardcore Deus Ex  fans will be willing to overlook the poor PC port, graphics and design decisions in this game.

An all around good game in many ways. First off you have three factions, all with at least a few races in each. Both ground and space combat are solid however space combat is easily the better of the two. There is of course the Federation, the Klingons, and the newest faction which are the Romulans.
The Romulans have a story of liberation and resistance against a nearly rogue sect of the now shattered Romulan Star Empire. You fly warbirds which at each new rank grant you a new ability only usable on warbirds. All of them can cloak and a later version can even split into two.
The downfall of the Romulans in my eye is that they have no great massive ship of their own. I find the Ha'apax Advanced Warbird a bit lacking in that department. And even though you are in fact forced to join either the Federation or Klingons you cannot actually gain access to their T4 and higher ships. So I must recommend a mightier faction, one of glory and honor. The Klingon Empire.
The Klingon story is far more diverse and even includes a small portion of the Romulan story, even including the Romulan end mission around lv32. The story ranges from house rivalries and betrayals to the return of Klingon enemies from ancient lore among other interesting developments. The Klingons are a faction with many mighty ships designed for head-on combat that have hull strength only rivaled by ships you'd have to spend $150 opening gambling boxes to get your hands on. And this does not even diminish their offensive capabilities as their greatest ship is a carrier armed just as well as any warship.
The Fedration offers little that can compare to the might of the Klingon Empire. Their ships seem to be designed around a doctrine of agility as many of their ships are far smaller but probably just as effective in combat if used properly.
There is also a system for crew missions, where you deploy your crew to go do things like sacking a colony, bribery, espionage, fighting in tournaments, trade agreements, asteroid mining for arguably the most valuable currency dilithium, among other tasks. These all net rewards which vary by the rarity of the mission, its difficulty, who's on it, and of course what the mission is in the first place determines the base set of rewards. You can even send one of your crew to be executed for incompetence as a Klingon, which even though its useless is just great to have sitting there as an option.
The visuals are good, the game hasn't crashed once for me, the UI is customizable.
All in all, a great MMO.

Here's my First impressions, Demonstration, and Review video:
Okay.. the graphics in this game might turn some people away.  Don't let the graphics fool you and this game is the perfect example of the wise old saying  "Don't judge a book by its cover"
This game is an action packed rogue style dungeon hunter where no two games are exactly the same due to the procedurally generated levels.  There are tons of mobs, mid-level bosees, and each level has a gigantic mega boss that can be pretty difficult if you aren't prepared to dodge a massive assault of elemental damage thrown at you.
This game is challenging right from the first level you'll start at, and while it is a very easy game to learn, mastering it requires good hand-eye coordinationand practice.  It never feels "too tough" to conquer however, and you always seem to have that feeling like if you had only moved here or done that, you might have won.  So you try again, eager to defeat the evil forces the next time!  What I am saying is that this game is challenging enough to keep you focused and alert, while at the same time rewarding you heavily for your success for however long you live with massive piles of loot, gold, and virtual goodies.
You only have a single life, and once your health runs out, your game is over.  The good thing is that you can release NPCs who will follow you around and shoot at whatever it is you are shooting at to assist you along your journey, and they will help you until their very last breath.  There are also loads of health potions dropped and found in barrels, chests, and other breakables to keep you alive and going.
This game mixes old school classic arcade goodness with gameplay similar to Asteroids, Galaga, and Centipede but with much more responsiveness and action then any of those golden oldies could have ever have been able to do.  This game offers relentless exploration of dungeon levels  that are filled with fantasy RPG baddies, massive loot, and non-stop choatic action.
I would pay three times the regular asking price of this game and still feel that I got a good value for my gaming dollar, but with a regular price tag of only $4.99 you simply cannot go wrong.  On sale, this game is a no-brainer, and I give this game one of my very rare "MUST BUY" ratings.  The price paid versus the solid gaming fun you'll receive in return is nothing but pure 'win'.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Niche is a unique strategy game where the goal is to breed your animals & make your tribe stronger through genetic mutation. This game feels like a turn based style with charming graphics & adds a good concept, Genetics! Something we all should of learned in biology class.
You start next to a bush, a nest & 2 animals. The interface is easy. Click on the animal. It tells you what its name is, its gender, its abilities & its genes. These genes will help you when breeding. If you'd want to name them, you can't! Some of the names I've come across are dumb. VanVanVan is one of them. The white line that's above your animals name is their LIFEBAR. If your animal gets sick, gets attacked, you starve it or your animal eats berries from a thorn bush, you'll shorten your animals life & the damage shows up as a red bar.
The game gives you an unfinished tutorial  that doesn't include the controls. Took me 5 hours to discover how to turn the camera Q & E. Zoom is R & F. On the bottom right side of your screen you'll see a DNA icon. This was never explained but i call it PLAYING GOD. You get a chance to add 2 genes to your animals & put them on the 10% & 30%. If you mix & match some genes, a green color will appear saying you can unlock a new gene. Eventually one of your offspring will make a new gene.
The animals have action pendants on their chests. You can preform 3 actions per day for each. Each stage of life is different. Babies only have 1 action, teens have 2 & adults have 3. There are 4 different actions you can preform. Gathering, Moving, Making Love & Attacking. You need to spend FOOD POINTS for each action. These are located at the bottom right of your screen with a apple icon. You will also find new animals to breed within the bushes that will generate in Niche so your tribe can avoid having incest.  For the actions, you can attack a carnivore to shorten its life & try to kill it for its meat before it kills you, gather the meat afterwords from your kill (you can kill bunnies too), you can gather berries, you can attack the bush for more berries but the bush never regenerates, you can make love & move your animal. The next day button is located on the bottom right side.
In the Ability section of each animal, there will be different abilities. The ones to note are Speed, Strength & Collecting. The number next to the ability will determine how much you can move, how much attack power you'll do & how much food you can collect. Not every animal will have speed, strength or collecting. If your animal only has collecting & not strength, that means it can only collect berries. It can't attack. Attackers can't gather either. Some of your animals will be able to have both of these abilities.
GENES! Please take the time to look at each one of your animals genes. I found out if your animal has white eyes, they're blind & will not be able to go out & explore on their own. If there are no other animals around them, the spaces will begin to go dark the further out your blind animal goes, preventing it from traveling to spaces you've previously discovered or want to discover.
Overall this game is great to play & they'll be adding new features like a water feature where you can probably swim in the future to different islands but developers please take notes. If you can't have a decent tutorial explaining the gameplay, the controls, how genes work, then your players will find this game too difficult to understand & stop without seeing its full potential. So I Recommend it in its early stages because i can see this game going far. If you want to support it, buy it.

(Time recorded on Steam does not reflect actual time played. I completed the game in full prior to the Steam release.)
The Lost Crown is the pinnacle of modern adventure games, without question. The length alone is simply staggering, clocking in at around 30 hours(maybe a bit less now dialogue skipping is in). Unlike most of the genre you can't simply breeze through it in an evening of playing.
Unfortunately as with many indie games, sometimes the limited budget shows through. Character models are sub par for today, though fortunately the backgrounds are stunning as they are photographic and wonderfully done. Voice acting is perhaps the weakest aspect of the game, with the inexperience of the actors being plain as day--a problem shared by many of Boakes's games unfortunately.
Storywise, it is hard to touch the depth of Boakes's writing. He puts more dialogue and written material into his games than most AAA even dream of. And while the ending of the Lost Crown certainly leaves much open, that is understandable as it is only the start of the series(which is itself a spin-off of Dark Fall).
For fans of the adventure genre, supernatural mysteries, or horror games there are few titles that I could recommend more.

Creepiness level: a couple of very mild jumpscares, some gore and animal cruelty, a whole lot of suspense and oppressive atmosphere. Most of the spooky stuff is conveyed through hints in dialogue and text fragments, as well as through environment and sound design, so there's not a lot of on-screen violence or anything.
Difficulty level: I think there are only two timed puzzle/action sequences, you can take your time with everything else, and you can't die in this game. The slow pacing and easy point-and-click mechanics are perfect for anyone with slow reflexes or coordination problems. People have complained about Nigel's slow walking - the Steam version allows double-clicking for faster screen transitions, which minimizes the time spent just watching Nigel trudge around. It's still not a game for fans of fast-paced action, but personally I found myself deliberately slow-walking through many scenes, to better immerse myself in the atmosphere.
Only minus point for tiny cursor and no hotkey for highlighting interactable items - in some scenes I had to check a walkthrough to see if there was another item a couple of pixels apart from items I'd already clicked through (and there usually was). The directional arrows are also sometimes confusing.
As a completist gamer I'm also grumpy about the problems with the Steam achievements. I spent a lot of time trying to unlock everything, but had to give it up as a lost cause (there was nothing more I could try short of playing the entire game through in German, which apparently fixes the achievement bugs).
I've previously played Jonathan Boakes's Dark Fall trilogy, and while I enjoyed those, The Lost Crown is superior both visually and in maintaining a consistent atmosphere. By now I've come to the conclusion that as a writer, Boakes excels in creating mysteries you want to keep following through, and that makes the games very addictive. He's not good at endings, though. All four games of his I've played so far have ended in a way that's abrupt and anticlimactic. But that used to bother me more than it does now - the endings are unimportant compared to the interconnected worldbuilding underlying his games. The layers of mythology, science and science fiction, different time periods and recurring themes really start to pay off once you've played several of his games. I'm looking forward to Boakes's future projects and to finding out more about the mysterious Hadden Industries.

This has got to be the strangest point and click game i have ever played. It is really enjoyable if you get over its flaws early on but there are things that deserve criticism.
The first thing that will strike you about the game is the unique art style. I like it. It is largely black and white but has splashes of colour that become more frequent when the overall 'mood' of the game gets better and then drops to total monochrome when things get bad.
The second thing that will strike you is that the voice acting (assuming English language version) is completely insane. I don't think this is deliberate but I have not played all the related games so maybe I'm missing something. Seriously the voice acting is so bad it eventually becomes totally hilarious.
Assuming you see the funny side of the acting quality, there is a lot to like about the game. The overally plot is a bit average but some of the subplots are really good fun to play through with plenty of moments to make you jump. I think the art is really pretty and the ghosthunting side of things builds some serious tension.
I'm glad I bought it for the art and the subplots and the well pitched creepiness and tension.

Once you jump over the starting "nothing really to do, or can't do logical things (like approach/talk to at least two out of four people you meet) for double-digits sceens" hurdle in the beginning, it becomes a a rather fun game. You get pulled into a rather misterious and intriguing story, getting fed hints by tiny snippets but left guessing for more.
Then, when you get the tools of the trade, it gets even better, if you don't count that the first few encounters are railroading you in totally un-obvious ways, like audial clue not just not giving you audial results, but not even allowing you to attempt to get them, and vice versa. This quickly passes, though, and it gets really fun.
... If you manage to forget the main character's main and only motivation being obsession with finding some treasure he didn't even know existed the day before. But he still delves into ghosthunting with passion.
... Then, half the game through, you are suddenly forced to lose all interest in hunting the supernatural outside the two main ghost stories and little threads. Suddenly, your equipment doesn't react a all to a full-fledged pocket of ghostly life,  letting you take it for real, and even when you learn that these people are LONG dead, the ONLY reaction is kinda "hmm". Another such pocket, again, doesn't show any reaction from your equipment, but you are shown to recognize it as such and even acknowledge by telling so to ghosts involved -- but don't (and can't) do♥♥♥♥♥♥ Just interact with them as if it's absolutely normal.
And then you stumble onto the real mood killers. Suddenly, the story flips over from being on the edge of supernatural to full fledged antique precursor spaceship visit (not literally, but it feels that way -- advanced technology, airlocks, elevators, etc, which would be at home in Assassin's Creed series).
The pinecone on top (those who played the game to the above point will understand the pun) was some little details like game designers making a puzzle based on Moon phases, but totally having no first idea about them. Waning Moon in England, it being located in Northern Hemisphere, looks like (, not like ), which is waxing Moon.
And as I already mentioned tangentially, there are too many side stories which are, for absolutely unexplicable reason, not followed and dealt with in an absolutely nonsensical way.
A few game-breaking bugs (thankfully, random) like getting stuck with no actions available and not even an option to load a game or even quit besides terminating the process don't help.
So... Overall, it would have been good game. IF.
Be warned. You're in for a MAJOR change in style and genre about mid-game.

STO has come a long way. I played it for a couple months long before it went free-to-play, and since F2P it's only gotten better. Unlike some other MMOs, this one actually encourages you to play with other people. You get bonuses for working together, you gain benefit from being part of a fleet, and drop-in/drop-out co-op missions are really well-done.
Aside from that, the ground game now is no longer just a placeholder, Klingons actually have content, and Romulans have just been introduced as a third faction. But not really. You can play a Romulan, but once you're done with the intro content you choose to ally yoursef with either the Federation or the Klingon Empire.
Because the game never tells you, I will. Whichever faction you choose as a Romulan, you will be able to buy their ships, go to their "members only" locations (Earth and Qo'nos, for example), and unlock uniform options to make yourself look more like them. As a Fed Romulan, you don't start playing through all the Fed episodes. You start playing through the Romulan episodes and occassionally get help from the Federation or fight Klingons.
Anywho. The space-flight model is worthless from a technical standpoint, but nonetheless fun to play in. The enormous design flaw is that it's not really free-flight. There's a definite "up" and "down," and you can't actually fly in those two absolute directions. You can only turn up or down so far until the game says "that's all you get." In theory, that's a huge problem. In practice, it rarely becomes an issue.
If you like Star Trek, here is some. Playing an episode of STO is really remarkably like watching an episode of Deep Space 9 or Next Generation. The flavor of Trek is all here, and the storytelling is really quite well-done.
THIS GAME IS NOT PAY-TO-WIN. Buying things from the in-game microtrans store absolutely can increase your enjoyment of the game, but it won't help you be better at the game (maybe a little, but not to the extent that someone having bought nothing can't compete with someone who owns everyting in the store). I've taken two characters to end-game, never bought anything with real money and been perfectly happy.
UPDATE:
Still good. Just started playing again with the release of Delta Rising, and I'm loving the new stuff. Msotly I've just seen the new content so far, but it's cool. The acting is MUCH better than that turd Michael Dorn dropped a little while ago when he did a Worf episde (srsly, can't say enough how disappointed I was that he phoned that in), and the new missions and episodes are fun.
That's one thing that STO has always had over most other MMOs. The quests aren't all just fetch or kill quests. In fact, it's pretty rare to have a "kill 100 borg" quest. Playing through an episode of STO really is like watching an episode of TNG.
Even the daily quests are fun! When the Deferi missions first came out, I did them every day with two different characters. Not because I needed the loot (which was nice), but because the missions were varied enough that it was fun to do them every day.
Now there are too many dailies for me to even contemplate doing them all every day, but that's good! that means that when I get tired of the New Romulus missions, I'll stop doing them and move on to the Nukara dailies.
And the ocassional limited edition rewards? Always very cool. Not always very useful, but always very cool. As a Tactical Officer, I don't get a lot of use out of my Obelisk Carrier (the thing turns like a dead whale), but it is super nifty.

I thought long and hard about whether or not to give this a thumb down/negative rating because I hate kicking independant developers and this isn't actually a bad game but a flawed one. However, since there are (at time of writing) so many reviews and comments heaping praise on this game (and even calling it a masterpiece), I figured a negative rating would probably get more people to read this review and consider some of the poorer aspects of this game before buying it.
FIRSTLY LET ME ACKNOWLEDGE THE GAME'S FINER POINTS. The artistic design is excellent. The stylistic grey and white with splashes of colour is a great device for delineating supernatural vs ordinary events. It makes use of the night vision camera all the more spectacular. The setting of an isolated english town steeped in history and pagan beliefs is very good too. In fact, as a premise for a game the whole thing sounds perfect; explore a spooky town with ghostbusting gadgets, solving mysteries and vanquishing evil. What could go wrong? A fair amount, it turns out.
For a start, it's slow. Painfully, bloody slow - even for a point and click. You can double click for quicker movement but it doesn't work everywhere and you have to sit there and watch the player character, Nigel, slowly glide across the screen or perform an animation at a slugs pace. Meanwhile, you're sitting there grinding your teeth in frustration. It also takes a while to get the ghost-hunter gadgets so I reckon a lot of people may probably give up before the game gets interesting.
Oh, have I mentioned that Nigel comes across as being stupid. Well, he does. He just seems to react (or not react at all) to things so strangely. He's like those characters in horror movies that trip over things that aren't there and you're kind of glad when they get killed. He's also voiced poorly (by the game's creator) so his response to characters, ghosts and events in the game can be so odd and jarring that he is quite unlikeable. For example, there are a couple of times in the latter part of the game when pebbles are hurled by ghosts at his head and hit the camera - absolutely no response! I wanted Nigel to die. I really did.
The game also isn't scary/spooky enough. There are one or two genuinely creepy moments and a couple of jump scares but that's about it so it really shouldn't be described as a horror title.
Look, I don't want to completely trash this game and dissuade people from playing it. I repeat, it's not bad, just flawed. Just take my criticisms under consideration. If you're ok with slow games and/or love point and click adventures, then grab this game. Maybe wait for a sale!???
One last thing; some STEAM ACHIEVEMENTS are buggered (they certainly didn't unlock for me) and according to the discussion forums, you may need to tamper with the game files to get them to unlock.
UPDATE: For whateverer reason, this review seems to float at the top of postings and has garnered a few critiques of it's own. Some people seem to superficially misunderstand the first paragraph here as a petulant or contrarian stance against positive reviews of tLC. To be clear, I wrote that WHOLE first paragraph to openly outline my bias and to address the fact that STEAM ONLY ALLOWS BINARY POSTIONS OF THUMB UP OR DOWN. It's that simple.
I stand by my brief review in almost every respect. It's not terrible but it's not great. The flaws tend to drag the game down the further it goes on. A few people won't mind this but most will! Adventure-game fans will probably love tLC but I can't give it a general endorsement of thumbs up.

I have a somewhat complicated relationship with "point-and-click" games...a part of me definitely wants to like them, but they in return stubbornly refuse to like ME.  I'm not quite sure what it is.  Partly, I know, it's that they tend to be a tad pedantic with the puzzle-solving and/or just a little too ♥♥♥♥ing "clever" for the dumb-arsed likes of me, but another part of it is...I'm not sure, but I suspect there's something about the whole interface which just doesn't resonate for the most part.  With few exceptions, I'm also not that terribly fond of turn-based strategy games, so perhaps it's something to do with the unnaturally "static" natures of such games.  I won't deny for a second that most of my favourite games tend to be fairly "cinematic" in nature, and if an equivalent term could be applied to these point-and-clickers, the word "literary" perhaps springs to mind.  Certainly less visceral and "immediate" in their audio-visual thrills; perhaps even requiring a bit more "imagination" on the player's behalf, rather than just serving it all up on a silver platter to be easily consumed.

The Lost Crown is certainly anything but an "action-packed" or "fast-moving" game, at least as far as I've played it.  In fact, I think it would be safe to say that unless you find its storyline as compelling and immersive as some evidently have, it downright PLODS.  Perhaps it's very "English" in that way, I'm not sure.  Which isn't necessarily a bad thing...it's certainly preferable to a Michael Bay movie, a phenomenon which is comparatively very "American", in the worst possible way.  Maybe that's the thing with point-and-click games for me...I WANT to like them, because they represent an ideal which I would like to support; that of INTELLIGENCE and TASTE, in favour of just making♥♥♥♥♥♥BLOW UP.  But...and I hate to say this, and I'm sure some of you will hate me for saying this...but maybe...just maybe...video games, to some extent, NEED to be about more primal things like, well, "blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up".  Again, I'm not sure.  Or maybe I just feel that if you're going to indulge in what is, just like a movie, a fundamentally "audio-visual" medium, perhaps you need to take full advantage of the strengths of said medium and create a predominantly audio-visual experience.  Which, all things considered, point-and-click games basically DON'T.

Some people hate these games for being so "old-school" and "retro", and basically believe the medium should have died out a good decade or two ago.  Other people LOVE these games for PRECISELY THE SAME REASONS.  I guess I'm somewhere in between, and while I appreciate the great lengths The Lost Crown has gone to to evoke an interesting atmosphere and tell a quite possibly interesting yarn - I love a great ghost story, no doubt about that - unfortunately the glacial pacing and pedantic talk-to-everyone-and-examine-absolutely-everything gameplay left me a little uninspired.  And let's not forget the main protagonist, who may look a bit like Simon Pegg but is entirely bereft of said man's charm; he's an insufferably rude, borderline belligerent♥♥♥♥♥♥ truth be told.  I found myself constantly bemused that the other characters didn't just slap him in the face and walk the other way, the condescending little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!  Which isn't to say that I found many of the other characters terribly charming either...eccentric, yes, but not much else.  It's all just a bit...odd, and...awkward.  There's no doubt Mr Jonathan Boakes is an interesting and talented game-maker, but if he's responsible for the dialogue and/or any of the voice acting in this game, he should probably learn to be just a tad less stubbornly "independent" in his future endeavours.

None of which is to say that The Lost Crown isn't successful in being something very different and even somewhat intriguing, it's just...well, I'm only a few hours in, almost ♥♥♥♥-all has happened, and apparently the game lasts a good thirty-plus hours and has plans of being sequelized, so...sigh...I'm gonna have to opt out for now, perhaps wait 'til I age another decade or two, then come back to it in the hopes that I will have "slowed-down" enough to better appreciate the paint-peeling pace which it seems so determined to maintain.  On the other hand, should Mr Boakes ever choose to widen his horizons/lower his standards and make a full-blown "survival horror" (read: action/adventure) game, I'm there with bells on.  This just wasn't the game for me, I'm afraid.  I will, however, heartily recommend it to anyone with far more patience than I apparently possess...just don't expect a non-stop-thrills/rollercoaster-ride of a game - quite the opposite, really - and you may find much to love.  Each to their own, no accounting for tastes, etc etc, ad nauseam...

Verdict: 7/10.

This game is absolute garbage. I had expected them to polish it by loading the content into the PC engine to make it less clunky than the tablet version, but they did not. It's a straight port and it's absolutely terrible piece of garbage that's not even worth buying at 75% off.
The story and content are fine, they just need to be repackaged into the full Deus Ex: Human Revolution engine for the PC. Anything less is a disgrace and does not belong on Steam, merely the appstore for iPhail.

The graphics... let's be nice and call them "retro".  Texture quality and model complexity are extremely crude for a 2014 release.  This isn't a problem on a mobile device's tiny screen, but on PC you get a clear view of just how crappy everything looks.
Animations are very stiff.  Everyone looks like they crawled out of the deepest abyss of the uncanny valley.  Lips do not sync with dialogue.  At one point you visit a nightclub (because, by law, every work of cyberpunk must have a nightclub), where you can see dancers whose moves make Commander Shepard look like Fred Astair.
Dialogue is full of cheese and cliches.  Voice acting is a mixed bag of terrible.  Main characters have this flat, dramatic voice to emphasize how serious everything is.  Panamanian NPC's, meanwhile, take it the opposite direction and talk like Speedy Gonzales.  I don't mean to say that's racist, but it is kinda silly given the game's intended tone.
I think most of the major bugs were patched out by the time I played the game, but takedowns have some occasional animation errors.  Sometimes all surfaces will disappear and the animation will play out in an endless sky, as if the game briefly genre shifted to shonen anime.  Once I beat up a guy's floating gun while he stood back looking bewildered.
There are no shops in this game.  Rather, for a modest fee, you can instantly teleport any weapons, health packs, and other supplies you may need to your location through the inventory menu!  Who knew hiding from bloodthirsty mercenaries would be so convenient?  Unfortunately, the inventory screen does not stock the cyborg drug you're looking to score.  Too bad.
I think the achievement for non-lethal runs is bugged.  I tried not to kill security guards, but I did gun down several mercenaries and gang members.  Look, achievement, I know those aren't very nice people, but they're still people.  You should acknowledge when I murder them.
In conclusion, I would not recommend paying full price for
.  However, if you can get it cheap, this game is a laugh and a half.  I enjoyed my time playing it, and if you like so-bad-it's-good games, I think you will too.

All those limitations of a tablet are present in the PC version.  However, my biggest complaint is that about 4 hours into the game (including side quests), you are hit with "to be continued."  Now, I would not mind this except nowhere in any description before/during/after purchase was it mentioned that this is only "part 1".  DLC is fine, but normally it augments an already complete game (such as Deus Ex: Missing Link), and not a requirment for completing.  I will not recommend until a complete game is available.

This is a very fun, intense action game. Like most other reviews say, this game is very much like Left4Dead. While there are differences, it's close to where, if you didn't know better, you could innocently assume they were made by the same people.
Like Left4Dead, you place in teams of 4 against swarms of weak enemies that you can easily slaughter with both ranged and melee weaponry, there are special kinds of enemies meant to act as mini bosses or to otherwise 'pin' your character.
The action is never dull, and unlike Left4Dead, each character has their own class, ranged weapon, melee weapon, and set of skills. It has a simpole RPG leveling up system, as well as the ability to use Loot Dice to unlock more unique weapons for your preferred character.
The setting is a dark, unique medieval fantasy, and as such the charcters and weapons more or less represent that.
The graphics are gorgeous, and can be scaled up or down depending on your PC.
The AI in this game are very lackluster, though, so playing with friends is highly recomended, though skilled players should have no problem playing with computer-controlled teammates.
One thing I dislike about this game is the lack of an ability to play offline, though that may be added in the future.
Overall:
9/10

I'm only marginally concerned with managing a kingdom, and Medieval II: Total War this ain't, though I have hopes for something of that ultimate scope in the future. I'm here to cut ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
Battle is rad. Currently I'm cruising around with a group of about 115, 10 of whom are heroes.
The fight begins and your troops charge the enemy by default. You hit a quick sequence of keys ordering your cavalry to follow you, screening your force behind a hill to prevent archer fire. Meanwhile, your infantry and ranged units are still closing head-on with the enemy.
By the time the ranged units begin to exchange fire your cavalry force has formed up behind the edge of the hill to the rear of the enemy. You crest the ridge and charge as your infantry close to melee distance. Blows begin at the front line followed almost immediately by impact of the cavalry charge from the opposite direction.
This is a good time to tell your archers to stop firing if you haven't already, as chances are that on these settings, a good third of the opposition will be cut down in the initial attack, leaving far more of your troops likely to take an arrow to the knee than anybody else's.
Being that your superior tactics have scattered the totally inept enemy, you can hit the backspace key to bring up a little minimap displaying the locations of soldiers, and chase down the stragglers before they escape. Riding at full speed and delivering a two-handed axe blow to the skull of a fleeing peasant should really cause like brutally graphic decapitations and such, but we can only hope for such innovations in the future.
All-in-all, Mount & Blade: Warband is a gratifying experience with a few flaws that tarnish its epicness. Definitely worth the few bucks they often charge for it-and more if you've got the cash and you don't want to wait. I'm waiting to see if all the bugs get worked out in the Viking expansion. I really want to try it- but not if it's a mess.

Let us compare the orginal and the sequel:
Hotline Miami: Mysterious plot; gory, breakneck violence; killer soundtrack; choose your style.
Hotline Miami 2: Confusing plot; plodding and frustrating cover based shooting; medicore soundtrack; no variety or choice in play style.
Too much glass means that enemies can see you coming from off screen, and surprise! everyone has guns. It just becomes an endless slog of peek-a-boo in the end, and there's no fun in that.
I guess that's the biggest problem with this game: It's just not fun. It feels like a chore to finish, and I have no desire to replay it at all.

When I played the original Hotline Miami back in December of 2012, I felt like I was playing DOOM for the first time. Both games resort to brutal violence using a variety of weapons combined with a perfect soundtrack. Where DOOM was a FPS, Hotline Miami was top-down twin-stick shooter using pixel graphics. Back then Pixel art style was a novelty, not as abundant as it is now right now.
What amazed me was how the game made violence and gore look and feel powerful, despite the obvious limitations of the pixel graphics. The original game proved that a powerful art style can evoke more emotions over better graphics. So what about Hotline Miami 2? How much can anyone push this type of game forward when the limitations are so steep?
With Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number, the developer Dennaton Games tweaked the core formula of the shooter here and there to make the experience feel almost as fresh as the first game. For starters, the game now jumps back and forth between multiple characters. This has two implications: narrative and gameplay. Now the developers can flesh out the story from multiple angles, allowing them to tell a story which otherwise would have been impossible if there was only a single character to revolve around. This also opens up to different variations of the basic shooting style everyone who played the original are familiar by now. For example, some characters have secondary ability to dodge, some can pull out a knife, while some situations actually allow you to control two characters at the same time, backing each other up. These tweaks when combined with some enemies who are vulnerable to only a certain type of weaponry or attack, forces players to re-think their strategy constantly instead of resorting back to the same tried and trusted approach players of the first game would take.
A recent updated brought mod and level creator to the game. Ensuring this game will be played for years to come with the help of the clever world builders out there.
Most of the changes and additions to the original Hotline Miami formula worked well, however some don’t work so well or cause some problems. One of them is how the game constantly shifts perspective, as well as time. This makes it a lot harder to keep track of the story and piece it together. I understood it on a basic level, however I failed to connect a lot of the dots together.
Another big issue with the game is the camera. Now, the original Miami had this issue too but it was not too annoying as the maps were fairly simple and not very large. However, with this game, the maps are much larger, have complicated layout and have different types of enemies thrown into them. This would have made a good challenge, if only you could see half the stuff happening in front of you. Even after using the extended view by pressing Shift constantly, it does not really help much. So what happens is you carefully plan out a string of tactical takedowns and out of nowhere a bullet to your skull resets the entire scene. The bullet came from a direction which is impossible to scout ahead. Now had it worked both days I would have understood, however the enemies during these times have the eye of an eagle. This caused a lot of frustrations for me, especially at the tail end of the game.
Another issue to note is cover. Due to the nature of graphics, it was sometimes very hard for me to understand what was an actual cover and what was just a prop which wouldn’t stop bullets in anyway.
In conclusion the game is still incredibly fun to play, especially when you go into a combat high with a killstreak backed by the amazing soundtrack (of which there are plenty by the way). Sadly, a lot of the novelty is worn out since the original and some of the design decisions work against the game. If you want more of the same, seeking bigger challenge and okay with playing through some of the frustrating elements I talked about, then I definitely can recommend this game. Otherwise, I believe the original is still a better designed experience of the two.

If anyone is familiar with the director of this game, shinji mikami, you would do well to curb your enthusiasm with this title. Before I go into details, it's a solid  7 out of 10. The story is relatively interesting, however the protaganist and people directly associated with him seem flat personality wise, with or without regards to their occupations. There are a few puzzles and navigation scenes that are actually fun, and replay value is good for 3-8 times depending on how much of a completionist you are. The sound design is very effective, however what little musical scoring there is doesn't seem to add much impact when it does appear. The bosses in this game have great visual design, but the execution of the encounters are poor. There are alternate ways to deal with most of the bosses, but most of them come to you through trial and error, not any observation of the environment or the enemy itself. The three styles of playing through most of the areas (Shooting, using traps, stealth) don't often actually present you with much indication as to if you can actually go through with it. For example, there are areas where stealth is plausible, but the arangement of the enemies or environment don't give you hints or lend credence to the idea that you CAN go through someplace playing a certain way. The gunplay is rather clunky, in that the crosshair tends to move a bit stiffly, and the camera while aiming is only effective in corridors, a result of the camera being too close most of the time. The game is still littered with bugs after several months, such as the match mechanic not triggering half the time, enemies detecting you through walls while sneaking, and in very tight quarters sometimes your weapons will not do any damage. If you don't want any information about the ending so you can experience it yourself skip the rest of this, not spoiling anything, just don't want the ending to be hyped or de-hyped. The ending of this game because of the lore that has built up around you, is utterly inconclusive. I don't know if someone dropped the ball behind the scenes, or if this is some production/marketing scam to aggressively hook people into buying the dlc, but needing to buy an extention to finish a story, is absurd. You could draw paralells to Mass Effect 3, but that ending had a conclusion, it wasn't presented in the way everyone wanted, but there was ultimately resolution. Evil Within did not deliver on my expectations at all. The first playthrough was fun for story purposes, but most of the enjoyment dips greatly after the first ride. I really, really wanted to like this game, and I'm sure others feel the same way, but with the production value this game seems to have, it just falls short.

Niche - a genetics survival game gives you the task of survival through the exploitation of Genetics. A very cool concept. You start with 2 creatures with a series of special traits between them and you begin creating offspring. You need to gather food to allow you to explore the map, find food, find more creatures to potentially breed desired traits with and also protect yourself from predators. Each creature has a limited life span effected by time, illness and damage. Better breeding by avoiding incest and pairing good traits will limit your chances of breeding sickly or likely to become ill offspring.
Its a game of incredibly careful balance, you have to monitor the size of your group as food is shared but also keep numbers high enough to you don't run out of males or females with desired traits to ensure your survival.
It's a cool game with a great concept. It is very early but the base work of this game shows a very great idea I think. Defiantly worth keeping your eye on if it interests you.

Since I seem not to quite get my point across and after some discussion in the comments on this thing I figured I should rephrase this and add some things that were requested of me including my own thought on the game. Perhaps I've been to clinical about this.
TL;DR of this review:
- If you want to support a game with a lot of potential, I do reconmend this game. Even if at the moment of this review it is rather barebones
- As stated in on the early acess dropdown of the shop page, it is in alpha and you have done about everything you can after playing for about 5 hours. First off, I'd like to state that I was really excited for this game. I got it as soon as I could buy it and I've played for a little more then 2 hours.
GAMEPLAY
In a nutshell this game gives you two creatures to start with. Adam and Eve. These creatures are the basis of your pack of creatures. It's up to you to maintain the population, make sure you don't breed in genetical flaws that hinder your creatures (usualy caused by inbreeding) and make sure your creatures don't starve in the process.
The mechanics are simple. Adult creatures get 3 actions every day. These actions require food points. In order to act, you need food, in order to find food, you need to explore. Things like movement, attacking, harvesting, exploring and mating all take up an action. its up to the player to balance this and not to have their population starve.
MY 5 CENTS
I enjoy this game and I think it has a lot of potential for growth as more mechanics get added to it. While I've done everything that is to be done in about 3 to 5 hours of gameplay it has been a fun experience. Though I will probably wait untill the next update to play more of it. At this point it starts to feel a little same-ish and repetative, but thats to be expected with the limitted amount of features.
There's currently some issues with starting in the savanah area as most berry bushes have thorns making it rather hard to gather enough food to do much. But I've found it can be somewhat mittigated by finding prey warrens to harvest.
Also my pets freak out over the sounds and get all excited, thats really entertaining too.
RECOMMENDATIONS
If you want to support the developer then feel free to buy the game at full price. It certainly has potential.
Right now the game feels a little bare bones and at its current price I really can't reconmend it to players who are looking for a more full experience. Maybe the finished product will be worth it in the end, but as it stands it almost feels like I'm playing the demo to a larger game.

I just missed out on the kick starter and now own the game. It is a great game however would be better if it integrated a score system. For example how many days you survived before losing your species, or how far you expanded your area, etc. Just so you can follow a goal. This is Early Access however and it is very promising.

I'm going to keep this short, since it appears that I share the views of many who have played this sad excuse for a game.
I went into this not expecting much and was STILL disappointed. For those of you that don't already know, it's only the first 'part' of the game, though nowhere does it say this on the store page. Since it was a port for tablets, some of the control conversions were wonky and there is NO way to change them. Sometimes I would be stuck in cover when I wanted to move (Causing me to die multiple times), and during hacking the STOP! Worm software wouldn't always take effect. It wasn't just a once or twice thing, it happened consistently throughtout the game. Also, you only have one save slot. I repeat: ONE.
Other things that bothered me was the lack of depth in the gameplay, and felt like a bad attempt at being able to do what you could in DE:HR. For example, it made absolutely NO difference if the camera saw you. Alarms didn't sound. It wouldn't call guards or robots. Once you realize this you stop worrying about cameras at all.  It didn't even stop me from getting the 'smooth operator' experience at the end of a quest. So, what is the point?
There were a few things that I liked, such as the ability to buy 'bundles' at a cheaper price and being able to disarm proximity mines. The story itself was intruiging, and the main characters were interesting. I WANTED to care about them, but we got so little interactions with them that it became difficult after the first few scenes. It was frustrating to see a game with so much potential to flop so miserably, especially after how much I loved Human Revolution.
All-in-all, I wouldn't bother with it. If you REALLY want to ignore my advice (and the advice of almost everyone else as far as I can tell) at least wait to get it when it's on sale for extremely cheap, so that way you don't feel so ripped off.

If you liked any other Deus Ex games, please don't buy this one. Rather than having in-depth gameplay like the other ones, this game dumbs it down, leaving you unsatisfied.
Since I looks like the previous game's graphics and gameplay, you might be thinking "Like human revolution with guns 10/10" but you would be dead wrong. The game clocks in at around 3-4 hours. I know it's supposed to be episodic, but for a Deus Ex game, 4 hours really isn't enough to expand on anything. It's almost like a Deus Ex demo, because all other three games were so long and had so much stuff to do.
Length shouldn't bother too many people, but everything else will. The game has been made insultingly easy. You have an in-game menu that allows you to buy anything you want. Seriously. It makes the game so easy because you can stop at any time to buy yourself a new gun or some ammo. There are not multiple paths through things anymore. There's usually one or two ways to approach something, no matter what it is. The graphics smell like mobile port, but that's because it IS a mobile port. Many models look very ugly. The voice acting for the main character is not great either.
All in all, there's really not much to enjoy. For 10 dollars, you could buy yourself the original Deus Ex, or even Invisible War, the second Deus Ex game which now looks like Jesus compared to the Fall. Unless you are mad about Deus Ex and need to play every game, don't buy it.

Chilling atmosphere combined with a gripping tale. This game is a rare breed cast out among the denizens of horror games that are created. It's possibly one of the best ones I've ever played.
It's a story you experience rather than a game you "play". I loved the game, and I think it's a fantastic start to a foundation that seems set to deliver a certain experience rather than a free flowing run-away and survive type game. So, if you are looking for an Outlast type game, this isn't your game.
The story is good, and that's what makes this kind of thing okay. I would harp on the gameplay if the story sucked, but it's well put together, has narrative action, and displays a unique sense of regret from the protagonist. It's not just a go here and you will see what happened type game.
It, is all, just a delve into the psyche, where death is not something that is particularly an end to a means. Going crazy? Yes, definitely possible. But Death is just something that wouldn't happen in a game like this, where you are traipsing through the mind of a sycophant, rather than through an actual haunted house.
The jump scares were seldom, so you'd never know when to expect them. The only flaw with the game was optimization of the graphics; I was getting random frame skips on a Titan X, but they were extremely rare, so it's not that big of a deal.
I highly recommend this.
UPDATE: They seem to have fixed the stutter problems, so it runs as smooth as a peach now.

Pros:
Satisfying combat feel
When you hit a rat♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the face, it just feels right. The way their model reacts to the swing is just perfect, you really feel the weight of the swing when using a hammer for example. Rat's will be send flying/toppling over left and right as you whirlwind yourself through a horde. Melee combat has been implemented incredibly well.
Graphically impressive
At max settings, the game looks incredible. The engine is, however, not optimized incredibly well. So even with a decent setup, you might not be able to run the game at max. But no worries, because even at low settings the game looks just fine. It won't be as beautiful, but it won't ruin your ratslaying experience.
Very fun with friends
If you have some friends to play with, this is the game for you. The game heavily promotes team play ( although it is possible to roll through a stage solo, if you #gitgud) and there will be plenty of hilarious situations playing with your buds.
Good way to make friends( for me at least)
I've so far made two good friends in this game whom I speak with on almost a daily basis, and not just about vermintide. One of them actually lives a couple hours away from me, so we hang out now sometimes.
The develepors are very engaged with the community and are easy to contact
The devs are constantly looking at all the forums, I've even got the community manager on my friends list and if I ask him something he answers right away. Thanks to this they take a lot of feedback into account.
LOOOOOOOT
There is loot, which I think is neat if you like to see your character improve. But getting your equipment exactly the way you want is no easy task. The loot system is rather quaint in a way. Nonetheless it won't take long untill you've gotten most of the weapon types. BUT: if you get too fixated on aquiring loot, you'll find yourself getting angry over unfavorable rng and grinding the same stage over and over again. A lot of negative reviews seem to be due to the grindy nature of optimal loot aquisition, which is true. But I like to see loot as more of a neat extra than as a main goal. Probably due to that, I've personally never gotten angry over loot, and I've played the same pair of stages 200 times more than the other ones. But somehow they're still fun to play, it doesn't feel like I'm grinding.
Replayability
You keep discovering little tactics to employ in each of the levels, and the levels never get old. One thing factoring into this is the dynamic spawning system. No two playthroughs are ever the same. And when playing a different character or a different weapon it completely changes your playstyle. Or perhaps you want to channel your inner sonic and go fast and do a speedrun, very much possible although difficult.
High skill cap
At first the game might seem unfair because enemies are hitting you left and right. But soon enough you'll kinda get the hang of blocking and dodging. A while after you'll be able to solo and entire horde. Again later you'll be keeping a horde at bay while kiting an ogre and killing two specials. You see where this is going. There is a lot of room for improvement in the game, it is not at all impossible to finish a stage without getting hit once.
Very cheap
The game is very cheap for what you're getting, below 30 euro's, that's a steal. If you're on a budget though; don't buy the dlc. Comparitively they give much less content for money than the main game. But if you're really into the game don't feel bad for buying em, I did and I've got no regrets. Also if you don't own the dlc but you have someone on your friendslist who does, you can still join his game and play the new maps.
Free dlc
Usually for every paid dlc, fatshark also releases a free one, containing something like a new gamemode, or a new map.
Cons
Small team of dev's, changes might take a while
The develepor (Fatshark) is not a very big company. Because of this they don't have the manpower to instantly take care of business. If a bug is discovered, it might take a month or two to get it fixed. Or when the fanbase pleads for something like pvp or dedicated servers it's impossible for them to instantly comply, although they've made it very clear that they are thinking about such plans for the future.
Working out some of the kinks
The game still has a few bugs, and now and again a new one surfaces. Though I think of most of them as what we normally call 'Bethesda polish', meaning that most of the time when one of those bugs happen and an enemy gunner slides around the map, a patrol of 10 gets trapped in a tiny shed or the stairs disappear causing you to be able to walk beneath the map it's just hilarious.
No versus
If you're looking for something competative this is not for you. You can of course try to get the highest scores in a stage, or race someone to the end, but there is no dedicated gamemode
Not intended as a single player
If you're planning to play by yourself, the bot's are adept enough to help you through easy, normal and most of hardmode. But the final 2 difficulties are best played with people. Although I'd recommend you play the game with people anyway.( They could all be played with bot's but that requires a certain degree of skill)
All in all a solid game. If you're into the warhammer universe this might be something for you to look at. Same goes for left4dead fans that are into melee combat.

If you've been on the internet for quite a while you'll probably know about this game. If for some reason you don't know about this game, It was covered by AVGN in one of his early episodes. If you don't know who AVGN is, please just google it, you owe it to yourself. The rest of this (rather short) review is going to assume you've already seen the AVGN video.
So yeah, this game is wolfenstein, everybody already knew that, it plays exactly like wolfenstein, the only differences is that there are animals instead of nazis, most of the textures have been replaced and one new powerup asks questions regarding the story of Noah's ark. Nothing really all that new or special. There is slightly different music to the SNES version, due to it being in MIDI format, so it sounds "nicer" than it's SNES couterpart.
One thing I was suprised about was that the company that made the SNES version (Wisdom Tree) is still actually in operation, the copyright on this game is actually 2014. I suppose some things never truely die.
The gameplay is fine, if a bit akward for modern gamers. The Wolfenstein engine has not aged that well in terms of control. There is no mouse control, period. You use left and right to look left and right, and press up to shoot. wasd does what it normally does and space is the use key.
Beyond this there's not much else to say. I suppose you could say that this game is actually the first total conversion mod in existence, so if for some reason you happen to be a collector in the modding genre, you can pick up this peice of history for cheap. For everyone else, this is essentially a joke gift (which is something I think even wisdom tree realises). So if your friend already owns a copy of Bad Ratz, you can nab them this little gem.

Hotline Miami 2 is a confusing, disorienting game that makes you feel less than sane after playing it. It's also so ♥♥♥♥ing hard it'll make you want to break something.
If you haven't played the original Hotline Miami, don't jump to this one. You'll be extremely lost, so go play that first.
So how does it compare to Hotline Miami?
Well;
- Better soundtrack (due in large part to the massive number of tracks)
- Better characters (much more characterization this time around, and everyone's memorable)
- Level by level design is worse (Each given level is much larger than the original, which sounds good but in practice means you're often killed by offscreen enemies,
- Much more levels and much more replayability
- WAY harder. Often in less than fair ways. This will make the first Hotline Miami seem like a cake walk, I'm serious.
As for the story, it's both better and worse. The biggest flaw is that the story is told out of order. I understand why; to make it more disorienting and confusing. However, this means the story will be near incomprehensible without reading timelines and♥♥♥♥♥♥on the internet, and that's the furthest thing from immersive. It makes it hard to get in to the plot, and overall, Dennaton failed to make it work the same way most devs fail to make it work. Telling a story out of order just breaks it. There is no sense for a beginning, middle or end, and up until the ending I was wondering what the *goal* of the characters even was. It felt like a story in which nothing was happening, and even now that I understand it, it still pretty much feels like that's the case.
The ending will smack you in the face out of nowhere and the whole thing is so abrupt it almost feels like a "♥♥♥♥ you" from the devs. And yet, it's still one of the most compelling endings and storylines I've seen in a game. I've watched it over and over and legit have trouble stopping myself from thinking about it.
If you liked the first Hotline Miami for it's gameplay, I think you'll be happy with this one too. They've taken care of the 'Hotline Miami but more of it' aspect several times over, especially now that there's a level editor on top of a hard mode. If you liked the first for it's story, you'll probably have mixed feelings like me.
Overall, the first game was tighter, shorter and sweeter. The sequel is bigger, but that comes with some stretch marks and some things lost as it usually does. I would recommend it. In spite of its shortcomings, it might even be my preference.

Truly beautiful game when it comes to graphics. It certainly doesn't look like a indie game. Movement feels fluid and it makes opening and closing doors and drawers strangely satisfying. And there's a lot of doors and drawers to mess with. I would have wished there to be more stuff to explore in the cabinets and such. Hopefully the developers will add more content to them.
The game feels very polished already with it's visuals, sounds and music, which is great by the way. The slight weakness is, at the moment, the story and how it's been presented. I would like the developers flesh out the characters a bit more. For me a good horror story requires having somekind of connection with the characters. Since it seem like the game deals very serious matters, it would be a shame to leave their meaning to fade away because the story will not make me "feel". I would like the developers to consentrate more on the character building and less on the jump scares. There's a lot jump scares in the game and, unfortunately, their impact started to diminish pretty fast for me. This is my experience and I understand that others may feel differently. I have nothing against jump scares in general, but there should always be substance in the story to support them. This game has a very good start having the visuals reflect the thoughts and obsessions of the main character. What I want, I guess, is more backstory. It's not an easy task, because there is a fine line between building a story and having to reveal too much.
All things considered, I enjoyed playing this game and suggest others to give it a try. I have high hopes that it will continue to build up into a great game it deserves to be.

By this standard, the game feels like a very basic Dungeons & Dragons game. They even put the four basic classes in the start-up lineup.
I played the co-op and single player modes. Co-op play is an overall fun, arcade-style go at the adventure. The "lite" story campaign feels more like a linear stand-up arcade game, so you just sort of go with it as you would any other arcade game. Co-op was quite a bit easier with 2 players, so I have a feeling that the game didn't scale in difficulty with more players.
Graphics are dated by today's standards. They suffice for a game that will most likely be relegated to the "Heavy Sale" category for Steam sales promos. One thing that bugged me was the grunting noises all the NPCs made for talking sounds. I would have preferred silence or a tone as the dialogue unfolded. Then again, the story wasn't all that compelling. There are camera issues as well - which, while annoying, aren't gamebreaking.
Pros:
Decent co-op (fast paced and minimally bogged down with the RPG element)
Has both action and RPG elements, neither sacrificed more than the other
Plays fast and is a good boredom buster
Cons:
Graphics aren't kind on the eyes
NPCs grunt-speak
Weapons & armor are yawners
Camera is possessed by gremlins
Overall: C+

Camouflage is absent in the current version, making hunting difficult.  You'll also want to selectively breed your most genetically advantageous pairs- developing a tribe with no front paws is entirely possible, and a really bad idea.
The genetics system is not yet fleshed out, but the idea of unlocking new mutations over generations is already addicting, and will become more so with expanded content.  Arguably, the price is a little steep for what's currently there, but I'm impressed enough to be confident in the investment.
