Niche,
a survival, management, strategy game with relaxing gameplay.
I kind of enjoy my 70 minutes of gameplay in this game and would continue to play again later.
You have to build a colony of animal and survive as long as you can. In order to do that you will have to find foods, breed your colony, protect your pack from carnivors, explore the island. While the gameplay looks simple, however there is more indepth gameplay you will eventually learn by yourself as you are playing, and it is not that hard to learn the game.
If you are new to the game, look at the right bottom and click the "?" mark to have a quick start.
-THE PACK-
With 2 starter of animal (Adam and Eve), you should get them married and get a new pup to expand the pack. When expanding the pack you could later on find new species which gives better features to you (more eye sight, more attack power, more movement, more food gathering ability, etc). By finding these animals with new genes you could get better features for each animal in which will help further in your gameplay.
-THE FOOD-
For every action of each animal (move, gather food, attack), you will need one food. If you make action without having food you will deplete your health (in which will shorten your animal lifespan). You can collect foods by: finding bushes (1 to 6 berries), killing rabbits (2 foods), or killing carnivores (10 foods). Beware that some bushes has torn and would hurt your animal if you collect it. As foods are scarce, sometimes you will need to move around to find new bushes. Rain will refill all bushes again.
-AGE-
The animals have 4 stage. Newborn (no action), kid (1 actions), teens (2 actions), adult (3 actions). I am not sure how many nights for each animal to reach adult stage. However once you reach adult stage, each animal would get old and died eventually once the age meter has been full. Every time you hurt your animal, you will shorten the lifespan. Finding animals in the wild would have random stage of age, which sometimes they are already too old and will die in a couple nights.
-EXPLORE-
You will eventually have to explore the island. By exploring you could find new food source, new nest, new animals, rabbit holes, rabbit, somekind of stone (i dunno what the stone for. prob just blocking the way), and eventually a carnivores. When exploring, keep your eyes on the moving grasses. If there is moving grass, you could find new pack, rabbit (foods), and carnivore (uh oh, nightmare).
-MOVEMENT-
Animals with higher movement points could move further. Be aware animals with low eye sight would be trouble some to move around by itself (you have to clear the path before moving). It is best to stay with animals with lower eye sight to help them moving around. Moving in pack would also help for faster movement, you could create some kind of movement chain for further movement. Clearing the path will help movement for your animals.
-SURVIVING-
Survival is not easy. Sometimes it is better to sacrifice some animals in order to survive the whole pack from danger. I sometimes leave 1 animal near food resource while moving the others. Sometimes when carnivore come I would use 1 animal for lure and run away. For thorny bushes, I use the old animals to collect them. Be aware that some animals could get sick, make sure to seperate them from pack or it will spread.
-LAST WORDS-
As i mentioned above, i really enjoy the game. Survival is hard. Yes, sometimes you will find it very hard to find food source. I even sacrifices 9 out of 10 animals to find another food source, in the end with this 1 last animal I could find another new pack and food sources.
Should you buy this game?
If you like to play survival game, with management style, yes you should buy it. It is fun. It is challenging. Is it hard? Depends, but the hardship what makes the game fun. In the end it is up to you how will you make your pack survive.

Niche is a seemingly simple game; you start with two animals and you breed them together in order to survive. As you progress through the game and explore different areas, you pick up other animals with different traits that you can breed into your family in order to increase their chances of survival. However, the game is way more complex than it comes off; you can mutate genes into your family, and you can choose to focus on either berry collection, or combat, each with their own strengths and weaknesses.
Berry bushes (and cacti) contain berries that your tribe will eat, and each time you perform an action, you eat one unit of food. Occassionally rabbits will pop out (don't even bother chasing them, wait for them to come to you), and you can kill those for food. Rustling bushes will alert you to either a rabbit, another animal to add to your tribe, or a carnivore, which basically looks like some terrifying were-bear (let me tell you, when these things pop out of the bushes and scare the sh** outta you, you're gonna hate them too).
Overall, I like the game. It's addictive, and it's challenging without being stressful. I have yet to discover a way to rename my animals, which would really help in distinguishing who is from what family to avoid inbreeding (which creates sickness). I think a better and more obvious tutorial would certainly benefit the game as well. All in all though, I do reccommend it, and it's a lot of fun.

This is a very interesting and unique take on a survival and strategy. You control a pack of animals and your aim of the game is to survive. No advancing to tribal stage or any direct form of civilization. Just you, your creatures, and all the elements that mother nature has to offer. It's a little hard at first, I had to start a new game a couple of times to spawn at a good location. Your creatures will breed, change, grow, die, and repeat. They only have 3 actions that they can perform on a single day. Each action cost 1 food, so food management is key in this game. You can alter your creatures genes in two ways that I've found. Either by breeding two different creatures with desired genes together (be careful of incest though), or by pulling up a menu of genes that have at this moment in time, two slots. One slot has a 30% chance of occuring in ofspring, and the other has a 10% chance. It's still missing some feature that will be added later on. Such as jungle, swamp, and water genes, as well as ancient genes and the ability to breed hybrids. This game despite being an early access is pretty solid and plays very well, and I'm very eager to see where they take it!

Super 3-D Noah's Ark. Now if that isn't a title that sells itself, I don't know what is.
S3DNA is a Wolfenstein 3D clone, and before I say anything more, I feel like I should start with:
. In fact, it's pretty decent. If you like Wolfenstein 3D, that is. And I do! Very much.
All the animals on the ark have grown roudy. As Noah, it's up to you to feed them all (or as many as you have to until you've beaten the six bosses, anyways) so that they'll go to sleep. In order to streamline this process, you'll be shooting the feed at their faces using various slingshots and what-have-you. Basically, what we have here, is a kid-friendly Wolfenstein 3D.
Now, you've probably mostly all seen the Angry Video Game Nerd's review of the original Super Nintendo game. The one that came in a jank bootleg cartridge that required you to plug another game into the top of it because Nintendo never gave the game their approval. If you haven't, here you go:
(skip to 13:17 for S3DNA). What you've seen or will see there is a low-resolution, low-framerate game which doesn't really look like a lot of fun.
The Steam version is not a straight port.
This baby has been given a nice spitshine for its new release. It seems that, rather than the original company bringing it over, a fan actually sought and received permission to put this port together and release it for us. The game looks good! I mean, well. It
like a Wolfenstein 3D clone. And, being on a wooden ship, the environments are mostly brown, though there are more colorful areas here and there. But it looks about as good as all that could look.
The game runs smoothly, and it seems some work has been put into making it acceptable for PC gamers. There are loads of options which I'm certain wouldn't have been in the original. Controls, audio... I wasn't even expecting display options, but they're there. There are
options for the automap.
The level design is also surprisingly competent! The narrow, twisty mazes got annoying towards the middle, but overall it's decent classic shooter fare for anyone who finished Wolf3D and Spear of Destiny and want more, but don't want all the fancy big city modern complications of Doom or Duke Nukem 3D. Or for those people who want a shooter, but also want to answer questions about the Bible and aren't allowed to play anything violent!

This is not a review of Super 3-D Noah's Ark. Instead, it's a juxtoposition of Id/Bethesda's attitude to their classic games on Steam and Piko/WisdomTree/ECWolf. Put frankly, Id and Bethesda don't care about their older properties. Classic Id games like Doom and Wolfenstein 3D have terrible terrible Steam versions not even on par with some console ports. The Steam ports of both are as phoned in as possible, clearly put up just to have them listed on Steam. To make matters worse, they were the first studio to get away with this. Back when there was very little on Steam but Bethesda and Valve properties, Id set the standard for bad ports with these games.
Some background for the unfamiliar, Id Software's engines are among the most free and meticulously documented engines in mainstream gaming. Id, from the beginning, has consistently released the source code to its engines a few years after it stopped making games with each of them. What this means, is that both the Doom and Wolfenstein 3D engines are available as source code, allowing gamers to create versions of the engines that support new platforms, are more stable, and allowing for new features. So this seems like an easy fix right? Go to github, grab the latest stable build of ECWolf or GZDoom and plugin the proprietary files. You end up with a version of both games that runs on Windows, OSX, Linux, iPhone, Android, PSP, DS, PS3, PS2, Xbox 360, Xbox et al.
Bethesda and Id didn't do this. They simply released 20 year old windows executables with no patches or bugfixes. These versions are known to be problematic on modern windows, so .bat files and dosbox are also included, which run an even older version of the game. Whatever version you run, it won't support your resolution or graphics card, I hope you enjoy playing these games without a mouse, in software mode, at a crippled or overly sped up framerate, at 480p 4:3, stretched to 16:9 with no way to unstretch it other than changing your monitor settings. No DirectX. No OpenGL. These games don't even know if you have a GPU or not.
And then you have Wisdom Tree, the ECWolf devs, and Piko Interactive. Through a licensing collaboration, advanced Noah's Ark specific features were backported to ECWolf by hand. Thanks to relying on the ECWolf source port, the game supports modern hardware, comes defaulted with controls that make sense, supports OpenGL, runs on OSX and Linux, consistently hits 60fps, and runs and looks like butter. Best of all, all of this works without ruining the artstyle or menus of the original game. This is a brillaint port job, and makes Id and Bethesda look like elitist hacks who hate their communities.
The only reason I can think of for Bethesda's arrogance is toxic proprietary software elitism. Put simply, Bethesda doesn't respect the work that Id has done on these free engines, nor the work by the community, and thinks their terrible dosbox ports better because they aren't maintained by hobbyists. This is a disgusting outdated view, even Microsoft doesn't operate this way anymore, leaving only the games industry to wallow in greed and judgement of its own customers. Worst of all, buying these games on steam is about the only legal way to get the data files needed to run them in a modern engine, so Doom fans will continue to buy them to support Id. This is depressing and unethical, and bethesda should really do something to fix it. My advice is that if you buy them, make sure to leave a negative review.
Bravo to Wisdom Tree though for their honesty and open-minded attitude towards Source Ports, though I guess I shouldn't be surprised, Wisdom Tree has been protesting lockouts and licensing for decades.

I've seen a lot of complaints about 30fps and borders but I started playing this after that was fixed and it runs smooth, pretty solid 60fps for me (half decent i7, GTX770, 10GB Ram) at 1080p with everything maxed out.
I really like this game, a lot of people seem to moan about the field of view and clunky controls but that is by design, it's on purpose - so it's a bit of a daft moan really.  You feel clumsy and vulnerable and you can't really see too much of what's going on around you and that's kind of the point.  It's much less frustrating in this game than it was in Resient Evil 4 becuase at least here you can move and shoot and there are nowhere near as many enemies coming at you at the same time.
Atmosphere wise this is the closest a game has come I think to feeling like Saw or Texas Chainsaw Massacre.  A brutal nightmare that you can't wake up from, SIlent Hill is obviously an influence too.
Ths game is hard, but in a good way - every time you are faced with a seemingly impenetrable enemy or group of enemies there's always a smarter way to apprach them than shooting your way out which makes each encounter feel more like a puzzle to be solved rather than a battle to be won.
It doesn't fall into the cliche of providing an endless amount of locked doors and doors locked from the other side either, so whilst the overall path is linear the contained hubs of the levels are not, providing lots of creative opportunities to approach them in many different ways.
It doesn't do tension as well as Alien Isolation and it doesn't make you feel as uncomfortable as silent hill but it delivers in jump scares and vile, disgusiting gore.
If you are a gamer and a horror fan this is definitely worth 20 hours of your time.

I will concentrate on what I personally think are the most pertinent facts regarding your decision to buy TEW or not:
The Good: If you liked RE4, you might like TEW too - gameplay-wise, both feel very similar. Main differences are that, in TEW, the melee is toned down quite a bit and a crouch-stealth mechanic is added. TEW has very good graphics in terms of atmosphere and lighting. Levels are long and varied with only little reuse of stuff, so it never feels repetitive. Bosses are well designed and the boss fights challenging and interesting. Story is kinda Lynchian (and so not everyone's cup of tea), but kept me interested until the end - I got to say I really, really liked this game.
The Bad: The port is optimized poorly. Only with the best GPUs you will get 60fps. With midrange GPUs you might fall well below 30fps easily even on the lowest settings, leading to a clunky feel of control. (It *is* possible though to up the framerate somewhat using certain tricks - after alot of fiddling I myself play TEW with a Geforce GT 540M with acceptable results.) Please consider this before buying.

UPDATE: I think this might be of additional interest to you. I have a rather lowend rig: I7 quadcore @2Ghz with a by now totally outdated Geforce GT 540M (yes, it's a laptop). Still I can run the game with 30fps and without stutter or hitching using the following settings:
- I keep the letterbox enabled (ups framerate).
- I lowered the resolution to 1280p.
- I use the 30fps cap without vsync (vsync wouldn't really work in this game, but it would cause input lag on potatoes anyway!).
- I turned off all ingame graphic enhancements like bloom, motion blur, AA etc - I just kept shadows on medium as on low they are too blocky.
- I turned off postprocessing with the launcher command r_skipglare 1. This improved framerate quite a bit. It does not in fact turn off all effects, don't worry! Especially lighting is still great. Game gets a "warmer" overall hue, though.
*************
UPDATE 2: In the meantime, I switched to a much more powerful rig using a Geforce GTX 980M. Game is running smoothly on max settings and HD resolution, but there still are a few situations where 60 fps cannot be held. My verdict that the game is lacking in the optimization department still stands.
Regarding the game itself, I found that it really begins to shine in nightmare mode. Here, not only are the enemies harder and more aware, the enemy placement itself is often different. Nightmare mode forces the player to carefully pick strategies and utilize the whole of the environment - this becomes very obvious in chapter 2 already. I feel that this is how the game was actually meant to be played.
I'd also like to recommend using "Flawless Widescreen" with "The Evil Within". It allows you to adjust the FOV to your liking. It is also working with the DLC. Speaking of which: The first two are excellent additions, elaborating on the stealth mechanics as well as the story. I personally didn't like the third DLC which is a first person melee/boss rush mode which - in my opinion - doesn't quite fit.

Let us compare the orginal and the sequel:
Hotline Miami: Mysterious plot; gory, breakneck violence; killer soundtrack; choose your style.
Hotline Miami 2: Confusing plot; plodding and frustrating cover based shooting; medicore soundtrack; no variety or choice in play style.
Too much glass means that enemies can see you coming from off screen, and surprise! everyone has guns. It just becomes an endless slog of peek-a-boo in the end, and there's no fun in that.
I guess that's the biggest problem with this game: It's just not fun. It feels like a chore to finish, and I have no desire to replay it at all.

When I played the original Hotline Miami back in December of 2012, I felt like I was playing DOOM for the first time. Both games resort to brutal violence using a variety of weapons combined with a perfect soundtrack. Where DOOM was a FPS, Hotline Miami was top-down twin-stick shooter using pixel graphics. Back then Pixel art style was a novelty, not as abundant as it is now right now.
What amazed me was how the game made violence and gore look and feel powerful, despite the obvious limitations of the pixel graphics. The original game proved that a powerful art style can evoke more emotions over better graphics. So what about Hotline Miami 2? How much can anyone push this type of game forward when the limitations are so steep?
With Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number, the developer Dennaton Games tweaked the core formula of the shooter here and there to make the experience feel almost as fresh as the first game. For starters, the game now jumps back and forth between multiple characters. This has two implications: narrative and gameplay. Now the developers can flesh out the story from multiple angles, allowing them to tell a story which otherwise would have been impossible if there was only a single character to revolve around. This also opens up to different variations of the basic shooting style everyone who played the original are familiar by now. For example, some characters have secondary ability to dodge, some can pull out a knife, while some situations actually allow you to control two characters at the same time, backing each other up. These tweaks when combined with some enemies who are vulnerable to only a certain type of weaponry or attack, forces players to re-think their strategy constantly instead of resorting back to the same tried and trusted approach players of the first game would take.
A recent updated brought mod and level creator to the game. Ensuring this game will be played for years to come with the help of the clever world builders out there.
Most of the changes and additions to the original Hotline Miami formula worked well, however some don’t work so well or cause some problems. One of them is how the game constantly shifts perspective, as well as time. This makes it a lot harder to keep track of the story and piece it together. I understood it on a basic level, however I failed to connect a lot of the dots together.
Another big issue with the game is the camera. Now, the original Miami had this issue too but it was not too annoying as the maps were fairly simple and not very large. However, with this game, the maps are much larger, have complicated layout and have different types of enemies thrown into them. This would have made a good challenge, if only you could see half the stuff happening in front of you. Even after using the extended view by pressing Shift constantly, it does not really help much. So what happens is you carefully plan out a string of tactical takedowns and out of nowhere a bullet to your skull resets the entire scene. The bullet came from a direction which is impossible to scout ahead. Now had it worked both days I would have understood, however the enemies during these times have the eye of an eagle. This caused a lot of frustrations for me, especially at the tail end of the game.
Another issue to note is cover. Due to the nature of graphics, it was sometimes very hard for me to understand what was an actual cover and what was just a prop which wouldn’t stop bullets in anyway.
In conclusion the game is still incredibly fun to play, especially when you go into a combat high with a killstreak backed by the amazing soundtrack (of which there are plenty by the way). Sadly, a lot of the novelty is worn out since the original and some of the design decisions work against the game. If you want more of the same, seeking bigger challenge and okay with playing through some of the frustrating elements I talked about, then I definitely can recommend this game. Otherwise, I believe the original is still a better designed experience of the two.

Best World War 2 (WW2) Game Ever!
World War II was one of the bloodiest wars in human history. Millions took part in the fighting, and sadly, millions died. Unsurprisingly, there are lots of amazing stories from the conflict, though some are more well known than others. New stories surface constantly, such as the recently uncovered encounter of Charlie Brown and Franz Stigler. Here are 10 stories that are less well known but no less amazing.On June 2, 1944, just before D-Day, driver Benjamin Gimbert and his fireman, James Nightall, were in charge of a freight train delivering bombs to the USAF in White Colne, Essex, UK. As they approached the village of Soham in Cambridgeshire, Benjamin realized that the wagon coupled directly behind the locomotive was on fire. That’s never a good thing, but this fire was particularly dangerous, given that the train was carrying tons of explosives.He stopped the train, and James came down from the footplate to uncouple the blazing wagon. Only 128 meters (420 ft) from the station in Soham, they attempted to ditch the wagon in the open countryside before the bombs exploded. They failed, and seven minutes after Benjamin originally saw the fire, the wagon exploded. It flattened the station building, damaged 600 others, threw Benjamin almost 200 meters (about 600 ft) away, and killed two other railway workers who had stayed to stop another train that was headed for the wagon’s path of destruction.Despite the crater the explosion created that was 6 meters (20 ft) deep, the track was up and running again by that evening. Both Benjamin and James were awarded the George Cross, the highest award for non-combat bravery in the British and Commonwealth. Their actions are commemorated with two different plaques in Soham.After the disastrous campaign in France in 1940, the remnants of the British Expeditionary Force and the Free French Forces found themselves critically short of vehicles, ammunition, and other equipment. This led to the formation of the well-known Home Guard, but Winston Churchill also ordered the creation of a secret, underground army that was known simply as the Auxiliary Units. They remained secret until the 1990s.Its 3,500 members were recruited mainly from the civilian population and trained in a variety of tasks, including stealth killing, explosives, unarmed combat, and sabotage. To avoid suspicion, they were assigned to Home Guard units. Despite the shortage, they were equipped with the best weapons available, including Thompson submachine guns and PIAT anti-tank rockets. They were also given silenced pistols and rifles, sticky bombs, and single-shot cartridges that could penetrate steel at almost 100 meters (over 300 ft). Their operation bases were built 4.5 meters (15 ft) underground and held 6–8 men each, plus all of their equipment and weeks’ worth of supplies.In the event of an invasion, the plan was to attack German communication lines, railways, airfields, fuel and supply dumps, and senior German officers. Perhaps most chillingly of all, they had orders to kill any British person collaborating with the occupying German forces. One advantage of the units was that the German army would not expect organized resistance so soon after an invasion. The fatality of such a mission was certain, but luckily, the Auxiliary Units never went into action, although many of its men joined other units after it disbanded.

Right. So. Hum. Sniper Elite : Nazi Zombie Army 2. The title alone reads like the gaming equivalent of Sharknado. It probably should be the gaming equivalent of Sharknado, going so far off the hysterically ridiculous scale that it actually warps around to awesome. Let's start with what this game is not - It is not in any way to be taken seriously, it is not to be played with the kind of serious approach that one might use for say, Call of Duty. That's not to say it's easy or anything, quite the opposite, but to get the most out of this game, you need to stop, put your brain in neutral, and only then, run the game.
The opening cutscene, using the ingame engine no less, provides a rather amusing explanation to how Hitler ended up meeting his maker at the hands of the very zombies he released in a sort of last ditch attempt to protect his empire. Yes, I actually had to watch the intro twice, the first time I was too busy laughing to make much sense of it all, but it's nice to know that the developers in this case played him almost as Ren from Ren and Stimpy. I near expected him to scream "YOU STUPID EEEEEDIOT" before pummeling his lieutenant with the mcguffin.
We're talking pure B movie brilliance, it's wrong in every possible way and yet the mixture somehow results in being entertaining, and that extends to the game. These zombies are not the L4D rushing mobs of screaming gnashing teeth, but rather the zombies of old. Slow, shambling, numerous. A slow and ever advancing wave of undead flesh, many of which are still decked in their uniforms and wearing helmets - this element is important, the gun modelling has been lifted from Sniper Elite V2 and as a result, deflections from indirect hits can and will happen. Additionally simply riddling a corpse with bullets isn't a total guarantee that they will stay down, more often than not they'll resurrect a short while after and require re-killing. The only solution, as with any good/terrible zombie trope is to shoot them in the head.
Unlike Sniper Elite V2's unforgiving and often po-faced approach, this one allows you to go nuts with the entire toolbox, not bother with all the stealth malarkey and go right in for the bangbangs. The result is a significantly better game, playing to the strengths of the V2 engine, complete with wonderful moments where you see your bullet go through an X-rayed version of a zombie, causing havoc as it tumbles. Grenades, tripwires, all of the fun things are yours to use and abuse, and the result is -glorious-. Carnage and havoc and a bodycount closer to the somme  - and that's just the first level.
The only real criticism is that the enemies don't change much, though the inclusion of kamikaze grenade holders and the odd Stormtrooper wielding a LMG do add some solid spice to proceedings, but let's be clear, you'll be shooting zombies. You need to like shooting zombies, a lot. This game hinges around that concept, see. It's in the Title. Nazi Zombie Army. There is an Army, of Nazi Zombies. You will be killing them. If that's not you're thing, you're in the wrong place.
Seriously, one point I need to highlight. The options menu. This game delivers. In every possible way, if you want graphics customisation ohhhh boy does it deliver. Every possible option, slider and checkbox in the history of GPU tweaking exists here. Same for just about everything else, if you can change it, there's an option for it. Suffice to say, the game can be made to run on a massive spectrum of systems and will scale up to some amazing levels of pretty at the high end, whilst still managing to look good even on modest budget systems. This game set the standard for the Trilogy, and that didn't disappoint either.
The game looks fantastic, runs and scales well, and delivers on a wonderful B-movie supernatural experience. If you go in expecting that, you'll get what you paid for, and it will definitely give you your moneys worth. In shambling, stupefying, and groan inducing entertainment.
However...
With the trilogy out, this now becomes something of a museum piece. The trilogy is now the place where all the cool kids are. This review will be held as a reference. But from now on, Sniper Nazi Zombie Army Trilogy is where people should be headed.
Verdict :

This is my first time reviewing a game and due to my love of genetics I may be a little biased so I recommend watching lets plays or even trying out the early version demo they provide to see if it is the game for you. I Also have 15 or more additonal hours of playtime from demos and kicstarter betas. With that said I shall now say I defitely recomend the game and encourage those intersted in it to get it to help the devlopment team. This game has tons of potential and the dev team defitely is attentive to the community and encourages us to provide some ideas to further with its devlopment. The base work which we get to play now is defitely playable and entertaining there is still some UI problems but I am sure that will be addressed sooner or latter. Then the list of things to come is defitely exciting. The game may seem hard at first and seem impossible to get your group to survive but once you get the hang of it soon you can start selective breeding and trying to mutate genes so you can get desired looks and attributes. With selective breeding after getting the few you want you can choose new ones to mutate in another group this way you can make different groups that specialize at berry picking, fighting or hunting, and exploring great distances to expand your visible territory. As it develops I be sure to update this review with more info.
The creatures have four stages of life infant (1 day without parent sitting in nest), kid (3 days), teen (5 days), and adult (20 something days) If they get hurt while still newborns they die instantly otherwise they get one day taken off life span for everytime they get hurt. Right now there is no way to heal the damage but a couple of future genes healing spit and healing purr may be able to remove some red so they can last a little longer if they were hurt. Things that can hurt is moving or performing any action unless it is gathering food without any food availble in your storage. Picking berries off a cactus no gene exist yet that protects you from the thorns nor can you even get strong enough yet to cut it down. Then getting attack by a carnivore can also cause damage although you can breed for fighters that can basically one shot the carnivores so eventually they are no longer a threat. When it comes to food you can get berries from bushes which repleshies once a day if there is no drought going on and fully restorses when it first rains after it has not been raining. The bushes have 4 - 6 berries each and depending on your creatures paw traits they can collect either none to up to 4 berries per action. Carnivors that you kill then when you gther their meat don't need berry collecting paws to gather meat will give you 10 food while rabbits give you 3 food. Fishing and moles will be options in the near future as additonal sources of food. Other things that are incoming are aquatic genes which will let you travel to little islands and fish, able to make sterile hybrids with the carnivores, and a family tree as well as additonal things to look forward to.
For additional information this is a good place to look and reading updates there is also helpful

-As of November 21st of 2015, this review is woefully outdated. Be aware-
Actually one of the more decent MMOs I've played. Strangely compelling.
Even so, there basically is no endgame. Well, actually, there is, but the endgame really is just there for the sake of itself. You grind missions to get better gear to grind missions faster to get even better gear to grind the missions even faster, ad nauseum.
Levelling up to endgame is fun but fast, and is really only there for the sake of getting you used to endgame, which the game still doesn't do extremely well. Skills in particular can be confusing to level.
All in all it's a solid game with solid mechanics though, most of the powergaming bits can be ignored for the sake of its core gameplay, which is blowing the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everything in a spectacular fashion. Not very up and coming of a Starfleet officer, I think, but as a Klingon or Romulan is definitely fitting.
As for the IP, STO uses the Star Trek universe to its advantage and makes fans of the series feel right at home, while not alienating people who've never watched an episode of Trek in their lives. Even so, the aforementioned tonal contrast between the Starfleet of the shows and movies and the more Imperium of Man-style gung-ho militaristic Starfleet of this game can be jarring but still doesn't ruin the experience (for me at least).
As for the Pay2Win question, Star Trek Online is one of the better examples I have seen of the F2P monetization model. Everything the game gives you for free is more than viable for every single PVE confrontation in the game. Even so, getting the very good stuff is still free. Explaining STO's currencies and economy takes a while, but basically it goes like this:
-Energy Credits are the GP of Star Trek Online. They're gained mainly from selling random loot you don't end up needing. They can be used at NPC vendors and the player exchange, which sells everything from high quality equipment to rare ships usually only acquirable from Lock Boxes or the Lobi Crystal Consortium (more on those later)
-There's this stuff called Dilithium. It takes dedicated effort to grind for the unusable version, which is then converted to the usable version at a rate of 8000 daily. Dilithium is used to do pretty much everything endgame.
-Zen is the paid currency. You buy it for $1.00/100 Zen. You buy advanced ships and other helpful sundries with it.
-You can exchange Dilithium for Zen. Players buy Zen and want your Dilithium because they don't want to grind it themselves. You want their Zen because you don't want to buy it. You put your Dilithium up and offer it for Zen, and someone grabs it. Or vice versa. The economy of Dilithium/Zen exchange rates are dictated by supply and demand.
-Lock Boxes (basically Mann Co. Supply Crates) can be opened with Master Keys, giving you a random goodie (sometimes an extremely good ship) and some Lobi Crystals. Lobi Crystals are bound to your account, but can be used to buy things on the Lobi Crystal Consortium, things like desirable equipment, advanced consumables, and even good ships. Master Keys are bought from the cash shop, which you can get the currency for by exchanging the grindable currency.
Again, everything in the game can be gotten for free. If you have enough time you can have the best equipment in the entire game without ever paying a cent.
All in all, Star Trek Online is one of the better examples I've seen of an MMO doing things right. It had a rocky start, but has grown into a great game. I definitely recommend trying it, even if you don't really like Star Trek.

A truly fantastic video game, who's full potential is lost amongst a miasma of corporate-publisher bulls**t, extremely low quality testing and 'questionable' design decisions.
For every one thing this game does right, there are 10 things it did wrong looming in the shadows, ready to jump out and ruin the experience. It's visually impressive with an amazing atmosphere, but it runs like crap. It can be set to 60FPS, but it's made immediately clear that it was never meant to do that, resulting in nasty screen tear and other visual issues. It's more than happy to crash on you and save points are few and far between for most of the game. A mild checkpoint system kicks in eventually, all too late I might add. The characters look good and have fine animations, but the dialogue between them is stiff and unnatural. Nobody asks important questions like "What's going on here?". Spoiler:
, one example among many I assure you.
If you can get past the performance and character issues, then the Publisher issues kick in. It seems that this game was going to be much closer to Silent Hill and less like Resident Evil. This is demonstrated for most of the early game, I'd say at least the first 5 chapters. But I imagine Bethesda coming to Tango Gameworks and saying "A game that is not 90% combat is not going to sell, so put more combat in the game", because that's exactly what happened. From chapter 6 until the end of the game is a non-stop rollarcoaster of very, very bad combat sections. Suddenly it becomes obvious that the game wasn't built with combat in mind. Aiming a gun causes the camera to zoom in by a ridiculous amount, making aiming genuinely difficult in a game consisting mostly of tight and narrow levels. Melee is utterly useless, you've probably heard enough about that from others by now. Almost every boss in the game is a one-hit-kill to you if they get into range (I am not exaggerating, the bosses in this game are perhaps the worst bosses I've ever seen), and just like Resident Evil 6, they just keep coming back over and over again removing any sense of satisfaction from defeating them. To top this off, some of the weapons really get brokenly powerful if upgraded right. The Crossbow has bolts that can be upgraded to do 240% more damage per shot to enemies and cause them to catch fire, or stun every enemy in a room and leave them vulnerable to be stealth-killed (A single button) for up to 16 seconds. Yes, 16 seconds. This ammo can be manufactured by the player at will too. Please keep in mind, this is supposed to be a Survival Horror game, by a company well versed in this genre.
But enough about the combat, carrying on with the Publisher bulls**t, some of the most powerful equipment in the game is pre-order bonus only, such as Incendiary Bolts. While most of the bolts in the game need to be upgraded to be useful, the Incendiary Bolts are instant-kills against any enemies, including groups in range and are extremely powerful against most bosses in the game too. The story is never explained well either. This is something else I'm sure you've heard many people complaining about, such as the deeply unsatisfying ending, but it is true. Character's never discuss the important parts of the game, and the story as a whole is full of loopholes. It smacks of bad writing, until you realize that the story was left this way intentionally because it's going to be explained in the future DLC. That's right, they're pulling the EA Tactic, buy the game now and then pay more later for the privilege of being allowed to experience the full story.
Summary:
If you really like character-action games in horror settings, like Resident Evil 4 or the Dead Space series, then stick with what you already have. This game is not the next big RE4. It will not deliver what you want.
If you love Survival Horror games then The Evil Within is sure to disappoint. From its mounted-turret sections to its QTE's to its one-shot-kill recurring boss fights... It is just too crippled from it's performance and design issues and is just not satisfying to complete. Nothing happens in the end to make the struggle worth while.
If you love Shinji Mikami, like I do, and want to follow his work then Resident Evil Remake has just been released in the form of a HD Remastered version. Pick that up instead.
Thank you to all who supported my review and agreed with me, and to those who found the review helpful. I've re-read my review a few times, I've recently tried to play Evil Within again, and I have watched a Let's Play of Evil Within since finishing it myself. Nothing has changed in my opinion, and I still stand by what I have said in my review. Thanks to the LP I've watched I can also confirm that not only is the game crash-happy on PC, but also on PS4 as well (I didn't even know a PS4 could blue-screen crash, but apparently it can).
In other news, I've recently finished 2 of the 3 DLC packs for this game. The Assignment and The Consequence are quite a step up from the main game, they do more to explain the story and they are much shorter than the main game (Which I feel is a good thing), however they still suffer from many of the main games gameplay faults (Such as one-hit-kill bosses, single-use melee weapons, etc). I tried my best to play and finish the third DLC, The Executioner, but alas the game glitched out on me and I was unable to proceed. See what happened here, for those of you still saying the game has no technical issues -
I severely lack the motivation to try again.

Resident Evil 4 is one of my favourite games of all time. I've bought and completed it across 3 different systems - Gamecube, Wii and PC - and, as such, my expectations were set high for Shinji Mikami's spiritual return to an old classic. All I wanted was a competant modern day update of Res 4 and The Evil Within does not even deliver that.
On a purely mechanical level, this a porting disaster. I have no issues running recent games but Evil Within is just plain badly coded - I've had dozens of unexplained crashes and graphical artifact issues that persist despite turning all the setting down to low, updating drivers and tweaking the ini and launch options. Shots often fail to do any damage to enemies (incredibly irritating in a game with such a scarcity of ammo). The stealth sections are broken. The character models and animation actually looks worse than PS2 era games. Then they have the cheek to put all of this into a 40GB download! It's clear that Bethesda just plain didn't care.
The storyline is a mess that makes no sense. There's no craft put into generating the kind of creeping dread that the Japanese do best. Instead, this goes through a checklist of cliched imagery (aslylums, wheelchairs, spooky forests) and piles on gallons of blood and gore in a way that makes Saw seem subtle and nuanced. I actually enjoyed the hamminess of Resident Evil's dialogue but the Evil Within decides to play it serious and comes across as an even bigger joke. They were aiming for True Detective and ended up with Hammer Horror.
This is a sad blemish on an otherwise perfect creator's CV. I wouldn't even recommend it if it was under £5.

+++ Review date: Feb. 7th 2014 // Version "Battle Builder Public Beta" from Oct. 2nd 2013 +++
** Summary **
Ace of Spades is not only a superb game, it is predictably the first of a new subgenre of first person shooters that will bring gameplay strategy to a whole new level. I don't say this lightly. Its main innovation is that it allows heavy map modification in game. It's a delight to play. It is well balanced regarding classes, the graphics and art stle are not for ooh's and ahh's but appeal in a naive and amusing manner that doesn't require heavy graphics. There is a special kind of delight you get when you see a blockheaded man that looks like a Lego person with a gun teabagging his dead opponent. Oh, and the game awards points (although not many) to the teabagger. This adds to a light hearted, funny, yet violently competitive game experience. The user base is  immature to an extent, but within a very reasonable degree for an essentially online game suitable, regarding content, for children/young teens and anyone older. The community as about large enough to enjoy the most popular game types with large amounts of players within any regular western playing hours, but it's difficult to find the least popular game types, particularly at the odd hours. The game has no story/adventure mode or single player mode. There are no NPCs or bots in multiplayer games.
** Rating / Score **
I'd give it a solid 8.7/10. I highly recommend this game to anyone with an interest in First Person Shooters, even those who found the genre vaguely lacking in the past. Here's the breakdown.
** Who this game is for **
People who don't dislike first person shooters, players who have a knack for turn based or real time strategy, people who can enjoy a game with non high-end graphics and a retro art stle. People who don't mind a 100% online play game with no single player (besides the map editor), people who don't mind patches taking long to release, people who like lego, people who are constantly fighting and player killing in Minecraft and would like a faster pace.
** Who this game is not for **
People who don't like first person shooters, people who require realism and detail in graphics, people who want role playing game aspects in their first person shooters, people who want in-game levelling in their first person shooters, people who dislike children and teenagers to a large extent (i have found myself snapping and then apologizing to the most exasperating ones), people who require large communitites to play competitiviely regardless of daytime.
** The good **
Innovative, strategy-oriented, dynamic, fast paced, lots of creative and destructive chaos happening during gameplay, competitive, ruthless, funny, light in tone, decent user base, balanced, good for short bursts of fun with no story mode or single player. These aspects are accomplished masterfully in my opinion and justify the game completely, despite its sins.
** The bad **
Delightful as this game is, there is definitely room for improvement in the following aspects (i'm talking to you, Jagex). No single player practice against bots. This can make the game difficult to pick up for newbies. No story mode. No ability to create crude story mode quests through events and triggers in the map editor. Some gameplay aspects could use progress (such as inclusion of of more responsive/offensive infrastructure in the buildable set e.g. vehicles, traps) and the long time the community has taken to start playing custom maps in any widespread and meaningful way has seemed rather long. This is an indication of a small community that still needs growth. Maps are also, in most cases, torwards the large side, making  2 vs 2 player battles rather uneventful, yet recommendable for not so experienced players as they can be slower paced. During regular play hours finding 18 and less player games is usually possible within deathmatch mode, but not necessarily other game types. At least 8 are needed in a map for good fun in my opinion. Jagex has been slow in the past to release key patches. There was a large delay in a particular patch which basically made regular online play feasable. There was an issue where finding populated servers was very difficult.
** The Boil down **
The game is relatively cheap. At the time of writing this review it's around USD $15. If after reading this, you think you may be interested, i'd say give it a shot. Also, if you buy this game, all of your wildest dreams will come true. ;)
** Anything Else? **
Yes, if you would like to check a game that attempts something similar, look up Guncraft.
** The part where i stop writing **
Thank you very much for reading all the way down to here. If you're a skimmer you get partial credit. I hope you found my review useful! Happy gaming.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This is my first time reviewing a game and due to my love of genetics I may be a little biased so I recommend watching lets plays or even trying out the early version demo they provide to see if it is the game for you. I Also have 15 or more additonal hours of playtime from demos and kicstarter betas. With that said I shall now say I defitely recomend the game and encourage those intersted in it to get it to help the devlopment team. This game has tons of potential and the dev team defitely is attentive to the community and encourages us to provide some ideas to further with its devlopment. The base work which we get to play now is defitely playable and entertaining there is still some UI problems but I am sure that will be addressed sooner or latter. Then the list of things to come is defitely exciting. The game may seem hard at first and seem impossible to get your group to survive but once you get the hang of it soon you can start selective breeding and trying to mutate genes so you can get desired looks and attributes. With selective breeding after getting the few you want you can choose new ones to mutate in another group this way you can make different groups that specialize at berry picking, fighting or hunting, and exploring great distances to expand your visible territory. As it develops I be sure to update this review with more info.
The creatures have four stages of life infant (1 day without parent sitting in nest), kid (3 days), teen (5 days), and adult (20 something days) If they get hurt while still newborns they die instantly otherwise they get one day taken off life span for everytime they get hurt. Right now there is no way to heal the damage but a couple of future genes healing spit and healing purr may be able to remove some red so they can last a little longer if they were hurt. Things that can hurt is moving or performing any action unless it is gathering food without any food availble in your storage. Picking berries off a cactus no gene exist yet that protects you from the thorns nor can you even get strong enough yet to cut it down. Then getting attack by a carnivore can also cause damage although you can breed for fighters that can basically one shot the carnivores so eventually they are no longer a threat. When it comes to food you can get berries from bushes which repleshies once a day if there is no drought going on and fully restorses when it first rains after it has not been raining. The bushes have 4 - 6 berries each and depending on your creatures paw traits they can collect either none to up to 4 berries per action. Carnivors that you kill then when you gther their meat don't need berry collecting paws to gather meat will give you 10 food while rabbits give you 3 food. Fishing and moles will be options in the near future as additonal sources of food. Other things that are incoming are aquatic genes which will let you travel to little islands and fish, able to make sterile hybrids with the carnivores, and a family tree as well as additonal things to look forward to.
For additional information this is a good place to look and reading updates there is also helpful

I really, really wanted to post a positive review for that game. I play it regularly with my friends, and having some change from L4D2 is always welcome. The realisation is overall very well done, nice characters, nice gory feel, nice lore, nice level design, a couple bugs but that can be forgiven.
But the loot system, the ennemy spawn and poor AI make me cringe.
The loot system is definitely the worst of the three. You get to roll a dice
if you complete a mission, for a completely random item, then you can fuse them to try to get another weapon (random), or break some to make shards to improve (randomly) those you like... but all of this is completely random, forcing you to grind endlessly to have a somewhat acceptable item to start fighting with. We like to play in Nightmare with my friends for testing our skills, but most maps we can't even begin to take them on, for the lack of good weapons.
We've played L4D2 for two whole years because we loved challenging ourselves. We play Vermintide in hope of looting a weapon that doesn't suck. And a LOT of them suck.
For this reason, it only makes sense to play the first map, because it's the easiest one for loot. The rest are very pretty, but honestly nobody play them because it's not "worth" it.
And the ennemy spawn. It's terrible. You can do the whole first mission without meeting any Rat Ogre, and the finish is a piece of cake, and sometimes you get the ogre in the worst places, and a freaking dozen armored rats and specials on finish that wipe you in mere seconds. It's really not balanced, feels very random.
It's a shame, as I said I want to recommend it and I still play it, but every week the frustration of not getting any loot because a ♥♥♥♥♥on of specials fell on you makes me want to flip my desk.

Love Hate and Somewhere In-between... So I picked this game up for 20$ U.S. and figured if I absolutely hated it I've wasted that on worse. No Biggie, the idea is pretty awesome. If nothing else I have a time waster on my hands as I just like to tune into the little details and work everything out perfectly. The first 10-15 minutes of the game I had no clue what to do. "if you can call it a game".
It's more like a design program that lets you build some pretty neat stuff and thats where it ends. It is still in early access so im not getting my knickers in a wad about the 20$ and plan to stick with it to see where it will ultimately go. However it is seriously lacking in game content. There are no quests, no objectives, no rewards, no levels, no hunting or gathering materials. Absolutely nothing of that nature. It really doesnt matter if you build in flat or terrain the end goal is the same. Build whatever you want and pray it works. The mechanics of the game are pretty well summed up in the handbook so it's easy to figure everything out. I did notice that after leaving a game and coming back my house mechanics no longer worked properly. Which I spent hours working out the kinks of and tested continuosly to make sure they worked perfectly.=( There is no undo button so be prepared to get aggravated when you remove a piece and everything collapses around you. It also appears that some of the physics of it are a little off but I am sure they will work that out in later updates.  It would be nice to implement a shovel or something of that nature. So I could dig out a cellar or a dungeon for the massive castle I am currently working on, but thats just one idea of many that could be added to the game.

The only form of multiplayer I have seen is inviting your friends to play, which means they have to purchase the game and you have to invite them to your world. But Again when you finish building whatever you want to build the rest of the game is just asinine. Sure the fact that I made a house that transforms out of a big box is pretty awesome but after you see it a couple times it's like eh whats new. There is Quite a bit that could be done to improve this game and I am anxious to see what the devs. will do, but as of right now here are the pro's and con's.
Pros.
Build whatever with no restrictions
unlimited materials
Cons.
Runs more like a simulator than a game
No objectives.
No Rewards.
No Goals.
No Mobs.
Physics are off a bit.
No consequences.
As far as I can tell the Hammer is completely pointless.
So with the con's at the moment outweighing the pro's
ask yourself if you have wasted 20$ on worse and then make a decision hopefully with added content the game will fill out a bit and become something to hold your attention longer than the time it takes to build whatever is in your mind.
As The Game Stands Right Now I Would Not Suggest Dropping the 20$ but then again the more money the devs. make the more inclined they are to improve the overall product.
Regardless of what you choose to do have fun doing it!

To those who are complaining about this game:
"For 3-8 Players and an Audience of thousands!
The team behind the hit party games YOU DON’T KNOW JACK, Fibbage, and Drawful presents Quiplash, the laugh-a-minute battle of wits and wittiness! Use your phone or tablet to answer simple prompts like “Something you’d be surprised to see a donkey do” or “The worst soup flavor: Cream of _____.”
No rules, no correct answers! Say whatever you want!
Your answer is pitted against another player’s answer in a head-to-head clash of cleverness and comedy (or just “Which answer is least stupid?”). Other players – and even an Audience of people waiting to get in the next game – then vote for their favorite answer.
Quiplash is a go-to party game that everyone can play and enjoy!
NOTE: This game is a same-room multiplayer party game.
NOTE: This game is in English only."
Wait, what was that?
"NOTE: This game is a same-room multiplayer party game."
This is essentially a virtual board game. There is no online multiplayer, just like your box of Apples to Apples on the shelf. If you're more into solitary settings with gaming, you may listen to the negative reviews. If you have a group of friends who can come over with smart devices, You will enjoy it. If you love it, which is likely, go look at the JackBox Party Pack.

Absolutely one of the most entertaining party games I've ever played, and that is regardless of how "mature" the audience may be. While the game, among adults, can very quickly get a bit on the wild side I was pleasantly surprised how much my kids and their friends loved playing the game as well even without it getting racy.
Unlike Apples to Apples or Cards Against Humanity where you're forced to pick the best you have in your hand at the moment Quiplash puts you on the spot to flex your creative muscles on a deadline and the results are both intense and generally incredibly entertaining. I was absolutely shocked how great some of my kids' answers were once they got used to the game; everyone loves to play it and as a mental exercise it is great for getting those improvisational juices flowing.

Battle is rad. Currently I'm cruising around with a group of about 115, 10 of whom are heroes.
The fight begins and your troops charge the enemy by default. You hit a quick sequence of keys ordering your cavalry to follow you, screening your force behind a hill to prevent archer fire. Meanwhile, your infantry and ranged units are still closing head-on with the enemy.
By the time the ranged units begin to exchange fire your cavalry force has formed up behind the edge of the hill to the rear of the enemy. You crest the ridge and charge as your infantry close to melee distance. Blows begin at the front line followed almost immediately by impact of the cavalry charge from the opposite direction.
This is a good time to tell your archers to stop firing if you haven't already, as chances are that on these settings, a good third of the opposition will be cut down in the initial attack, leaving far more of your troops likely to take an arrow to the knee than anybody else's.
Being that your superior tactics have scattered the totally inept enemy, you can hit the backspace key to bring up a little minimap displaying the locations of soldiers, and chase down the stragglers before they escape. Riding at full speed and delivering a two-handed axe blow to the skull of a fleeing peasant should really cause like brutally graphic decapitations and such, but we can only hope for such innovations in the future.
All-in-all, Mount & Blade: Warband is a gratifying experience with a few flaws that tarnish its epicness. Definitely worth the few bucks they often charge for it-and more if you've got the cash and you don't want to wait. I'm waiting to see if all the bugs get worked out in the Viking expansion. I really want to try it- but not if it's a mess.

Lets be clear, Coppercube is intended to be simple and easy to use. This is a software for non programers, or those like me who prefer to focus on art and design, rather than typing tons of code. For this Coppercube is the best out there. Porting between PC, MacOS, WebGl, Android, and flash is near seamless. Most of the time its as simple as clicking the publish to option. There are tons of behaviors and actions to mix and match to do most things you will need, and their is a Javascript API if you want even more control. I've used quite a few game engines over the years (Multimedia Fusion, Gamemaker, 3DRad, Jamagic, Gamesalad) and none were as easy and fast to develop 3D applications than Coppercube.
BUT if you looking for a engine that supports cutting edge technologies, endless libraries of game resources, portability to every device on the market, and constant frequent updates, this may not be the engine for you. Coppercube is actively developed by one dev but he also has a handful of other tools he manages so updates are usually months apart. While small there is a community that shares custom actions, behaviors, and plugins for Coppercube. Keep in mind their are graphical limitations with this engine, so don't expect the same level of GFX as you would expect from Unreal, Cryengine, or Unity.
As with Standard vs Professional, the only real difference is that Standard limits you to 10 scenes, and there is no limit on Professional (professional also allows you to edit the source, but if you are able to do that you probably wouldn't need coppercube anyways). To be honest you really don't need more than 10, its not too hard out a system where you can reuse nodes to make larger scenes to reasonably stay within that limit. You can always upgrade later if you need it.
With that said I'm still happy with my decision with Coppercube. (I have the professional version) I have been developing a game on it since December 2016. Hopefully you find this review is useful.

I have enjoyed playing this game.  However, I can't recommend it.  It does deserve more than a joke review, so I'll give it that.
The good stuff:
- The graphics are nice, the character designs are good, the gore is phenomenal.  A lot of love and attention went into this stuff, and it's appreciated.  I especially like that instead of being idealized fantasy heroes, the characters are all a bunch of beat up, dirty, insane murderers.  It's a nice change of pace from your typical fantasy game.
- Nice weapon variety and the push mechanic is great.  Overall, the combat mechanics actually work pretty well.
- Some of the levels are quite good.
- You can pick up a sack of grain and score touchdowns while stiff-arming kids like Bo Jackson.
- The game is challenging, and the grimoire pickups serve as risk/reward enhancers, once you've learned where they are on each level.
- 4 player cooperative games of this sort are just plain fun.  It's a strong genre.
The bad stuff:
- The loot system is terrible.  Terrible.  Terrible.  I don't have words for how terrible it is, because it's so terrible.  At the end of each level, you roll for completely random items, with bonuses to your rolls based on whether or not you picked up tomes (which take up your health item slot) and grimoires (take up your boost potion slot and lower the party's health).   You then roll dice to see what kind of item you get, with better rolls giving you higher quality items.
Then you have to unlock item attributes by dismantling other items and using the shards to unlock the abilities.  Then you can reroll the item attributes by spending more shards.  Then you can try to improve the attribute % chance to activate by spending more shards.  All of this is totally random.  It's all dice, for everything.
So if you want to get a specific type of weapon with specific attributes, you have to keep grinding it out until you get the specific type of weapon you wanted, and then you're at the mercy of the RNG to keep grinding and dismantling until you can get the attributes you want, and then boost their percentages.  It's awful.  It's awful.  It's awful.
It's frustrating, and it gates difficulties off from individual players, which is the worst thing you can ever do in a 4 player cooperative game that people are playing with their friends.  The massive difference in efficiency between a character who has Bloodlust and Berserking/SwiftSlaying/Devastating Blow and one who doesn't isn't a matter of skill, it's a matter of grinding through the stupid loot system.
Oh, and there's not even an option to take something 'worse' than what you got.  You literally can't even choose to take the consolation prize when it turns out to be better than the grand prize.   How did anyone think this was a good system?
- The weapon balance and movesets are often curiously bad.  For instance, why did they even bother giving the soldier the single cudgel weapon?  Why would you ever bother with the Waywatcher's Shortbow?  I never see experienced players using these weapons, because they just plain stink.  Yet they're there in the loot table, and you can wind up getting them on a 'good' roll.
Oh, and why the heck do the shield combo weapons use a shield bash as the power attack?  What is the point?  The shield bash moves are terrible, and everyone hates them, and they don't make any sense in the first place.
- Enemy design is very hit and miss.  Rat Ogres spawn randomly in each level, and one of the first things you learn on Nightmare (where there is friendlyfire) is that if you run into a Rat Ogre in certain confined spaces, you just got plum screwed and you'd better hope for a lucky instakill proc (if you have that trait on your weapon!).    It's nonsensical.
- Some of the levels are just frustrating to play, and not fun.  For instance, in the White Rat mission you have to run barrels through these tiny, narrow chokepoint corridors where rats never, ever, ever stop spawning.  And if you take even one hit from a rat, the barrel catches fire.  I've beaten the mission, but there's a reason nobody ever wants to play it: because it sucks.
As a last point, the current pricing of this game is ridiculous.  $30.00 for a multiplayer coop game that only has a handful of missions and what is essentially a terrible F2P progression system, and they want $10.00 for a DLC that adds a couple more missions?  Nope.

A fan of co-op at all? Left 4 Dead? Warhammer? Smacking things over and over until they die? Then you're in a for a ride.
- 4 Player Co-op with drop-in/drop-out feature (except for the host).
- A fun vanilla campaign that lasts around 8 hours if you speed through it on Normal, each missions can take 20-40     minutes.
- Another 1.5-2 hours of (high quality) campaign from the latest DLC.
- Don't need new DLC to get the DLC weapons!
- Free, wave-based survival mode the devs added onto the base game with a previous update.
- 5 Unique characters that are each well-crafted, each have their own backstory and have interworking dialogue.
- Multiple possible weapons for each character, with a dizzying amount of special effect/"trait" combinations each one can have.
- The combat is responsive and feels powerful, even with the smallest daggers.
- The dodging mechanism is also responsive, you can learn to dodge different enemies' attacks if you're fast enough!
- Blocking/pushing actually works (is a must for mastering higher difficulties).
- Weapons are varied AND BALANCED across characters, doing differing levels (and types) of damage.
- Loot system/in-game currency is rewarding and varied, didn't get the same weapon in a row until many hours in.
- Difficulty levels really DO vary in difficulty, on Easy (1/5 difficulty) the rat-men will barely scratch you, but on Cataclysm (5/5) it only takes one wrong move and you're punished hard.
- Good in-mission inventory, allows for one melee weapon, one ranged weapon, and three types of consumables.
- Good post-mission inventory system, organises items for you effectively.
- Friendly AI equips whatever weapons/gear the host uses on that character.
- An item is ALWAYS obtained after each mission.
- Level of the item depends partially on level difficulty.
- Two items can be obtained at once if your chances are augmented through gear.
- Item acquisition based on a dice-roll.
- In-mission side-objectives increase quality of the dice, which increase overall chance of loot.
- Items can be traded in for in-game currency used to buy weapon upgrades/other weapons.
- Items are either weapons, trinkets (special gear), in-game currency or HATS!
- HAAAAAATS!
- Beautiful and haunting game, even on lower settings.
- Many options with helpful tooltips on which will impact your performance the most.
- You can set it so you can see 500 blood decals, 500! This meaning you can turn a horde of skaven into a bloody hallway and still get to take a messy screenshot after.
- Stable FPS/Well optimised.
- Sound design is done well, with character's voices not being too quiet or loud during the fight.
- Music is immersive and matches the mood.
- Each "special" skaven has a unique, identifiable sound.
- A select few missions are better/easier than others, making them a first-choice 100% of the time if people are gridning for items.
- Survival mode has long pre/post-wave waiting times.
- Even a momentary wobble in the host's internet will crash the mission and restart it (This has only happened to me twice, but it's annoying when you've already completed 80% of a mission.).
- Pushing negates your block for a short amount of time, you can be hit during this time before rats are actually pushed away, which can be quite annoying on higher difficulties.
- Due to the nature of item/object interaction with the player, you may sometimes need to reposition yourself to a different angle for a second to interact with it.
- If it consistently doesn't go your way, it can be very frustrating.
- Not budget PC friendly.
- FPS may dip slightly in large hordes at higher graphics settings.

Update since completion: Unfortunately I have to switch this to a negative review. The complaints are wide and vary, but I'll keep it short.
1) 'Zombies' with guns - it may as well be any other third person shooter game in this regard, once you put a gun in the zombie's hands, its no longer a survival horror game, its just a generic action game, with zombie models.
2) Repetition - There aren't many different enemies, and your way of approaching them doesn't vary.
3) Length - The repetition wouldn't be so bad, if it weren't so god damned long. Usually I prefer games that are long, but this game is just painfully long, the title drags, with the story barely being explained, with the same enemies being fed to you over and over.
4) The 'puzzles' don't require brainpower, just willingness to do the same stupid thing over and over. You need to be patient to complete this game, it's truly subpar.
TL;DR - Squandered potential. Not worth the money, or your time. It's hard saying this as a big fan of RE 1-3 // Silent Hill franchise, I really thought this would be a step in the right direction.

Noah, clenching a Super Feeder 5000 in a deathly-grasp, anxiously peers around the corner. “My Lord, why are there so many Godforsaken doors on this ark?” “NOAH, YOU ARE DRUNK, I INSTRUCTED YOU TO INSTALL ONLY
!” Noah then turns about-face, immediately catching corrosive buckshot with his despairing visage. The 950 year-old man throws himself upon the floor, rolling in agony as Carl the Camel, his perpetrator, begins to “be fruitful” with Noah’s convulsing body.
Fading in and out of conscientiousness, Noah realizes that he has been stripped of all his assets and is once again at the beginning of stage 3-5. “Fornicators! Thieves!” Noah shouts while shaking his maimed arm. Kneeling like the humble servant he is, the elderly man initiates in great and wholesome prayer, “Please almighty God, the animals aboard the ark have become increasingly unruly. I need your strength to assist me in my endeavor! I ask of you in all sincerity: LET ME PURGE THE BEASTS UPON THIS VESSEL!” Spontaneously, a BFF9000 (

Noah rises to his feet and charges audaciously into the silver key room. As the pneumatic door seals Noah inside, sounds of hitscan saliva and pellet-spam resonate from within; dolorous cries of both man and beast clash together in wicked melody.

Just one more bandage, one more food crate, one more extra life; any of the three could have circumvented Noah’s brutal demise, but this is how Lady Level-Design desired things to be.
Perhaps Noah should have considered save-scumming?
It’s too late for that now…

I've been a CopperCube user since version 1.x, as well as purchasing an upgrade to CopperCube 4.x several years later.  From the very beginning, CopperCube has offered fast prototyping, and I was quickly able to produce a 3d first person Flash game in the late 2000's which earned me enough to pay my rent for a few months.  I continue to use it for prototyping to this day.   Neko, the author of the program, is a veteran of 3d game engine development (he also created the Illricht engine) and he has been fantastic with support consistently for years, which has greatly impressed me!  I'm happy to see CopperCube 5.x on Steam.  You can prototype quickly using events and not need to touch code for some basic  game loops, but for larger projects coding is easy and straight forward, with a simple API and clear documentation.  I highly recommend it to anyone, both beginner and expert alike. If you are looking for an engine for fast prototyping or even full game production, especially for mobile and html5, then CopperCube is a fantastic value.

I really enjoy this software!  Coppercube may be more graphically limited than other engines out there; but if you only have integrated graphics like me you cannot run other engines, making Coppercube a great choice.  If you want to get serious with this program you will have import your own 3d models, however.  All in all, this programs compatibility with many 3d models, Java support, and many options for exportability makes it a top choice.

I have used many engines over the years for my hobby, and they all have their advantages and disadvantages. This engine allows you to very quickly get things up and running. This engine comes with a load of pre-built behaviours and actions that you can mix and match to create the logic for your game, but if you're like me you want to code your own, which you can also do using the very simple JavaScript API.
It's fair to say that this engine is not going to break any visual records, but it makes up for it in ease of use and flexibility. You can use this as a fast prototyping system for your game idea, or you can use it to create the game in its entirety. I would definitely recommend this engine, but would also strongly advise that you download the demo first, but please don't take the bundled graphics and games as "all it can do", so many companies release their engines with poor assets/content and it makes the engine look bad.

I am using CopperCube since the first version, and in short:
You can create wonderful 3D games with it, and create cool stuff relatively easily, but CopperCube won't hide the fact that game development is hard. This software great, but it is not for everyone: This is not a sandbox for moving existing assets together. It is like a 'real' development tool for beginner game developers without previous experience. To create games, you have to invest time and work, and CopperCube helps you to create your projects.
Games created run without extra costs out of the box on Windows, Mac OS X, on mobiles, and I think CopperCube has the best WebGL support out there. It also creates Flash websites, but I think Flash's days will be over soon. WebGL support in CopperCube is open source.
Negative is maybe that the graphics look not like a modern AAA-3D engine for PC, but still very nice on mobile or web. I think the devs also planned an update for that.
Bonus points for the many free upates, which usually also come with cool new features, like recently the realtime 3D water. Also, the features it has are quite many, from procedural tree generation to indoor room creation, terrain editing, scripting, VR, ect. There are also quite some free downloadable additions, and the community on the official forum is very friendly and helpful.
