Deus Ex: Human Revolution was one of my top games of the last console generation with it's innovative gameplay, memorable characters, and an all around excellent presentation. With it's prequel "The Fall" I expected a game with the same sort of quality  as Human Revolution, unfortunately this game is nothing more than a mobile port straight to PC.
---
The story in The Fall is a sequel to the story Deus Ex: Icarus Effect, a novel released around the same time as Human Revolution and providing a good side story for fans in the Deus Ex universe. In The Fall you play as Ben Saxon, an ex-military and ex-mercenary of The Tyrants (the three mercenaries from Human Revolution that shot up Sariff Industries) on the run with his friend Anna Kelso in Panama shortly after being betrayed by The Tyrants.
Throughout the (short) story you will play as Ben running around Panama doing the main story and side missions, talking to people around the city, and having the choice of going into gun combat or using stealth.
While Panama does not have the same detail and feel as Detroit in Human Revolution, it still feel's like being a part of the Deus Ex Universe and works okay.
---
- Fans of the series will enjoy revisiting the Deus Ex universe.
- The soundtrack is very good with new tracks and returning tracks from Human Revolution.
- The game has the same augmentation system from Human Revolution.
- No micro-transactions.
- The game has decent textures, anti-aliasing options, and ran on my cheap system at 60FPS.
- Has a new game+ mode.
- With a recent patch (most) controls are rebindable.
- Story and characters are weak.
- No harder difficulty options other than new game+ mode.
- The inventory system from Human Revolution is replaced with an inventory system with no ammo/item limits.
- Item/weapon dealers are non-existent in The Fall as you will buy everything through the inventory system.
- Selling items/weapons is not an option.
- When an enemy is knocked out or killed their bodies simply disappear rather than remain.
- The AI is not smart and tend to miss shots.
- Ben takes quite a bit of damage before dying making the game too easy.
- Only one save slot and quick save.
- Guns have almost no recoil (and this is before upgrading recoil reduction augments)
- While the game's environment look okay, character models looks atrocious with bad animations.
- Voice acting is also not great.
- The game is extremely easy and short, with no real need to replay other than wanting to earn achievements.
- and even more.
---
Throughout my entire playthrough the game was a disappointment and I spent a majority of the time comparing the game to Human Revolution, completing the game in 4-5 hours with a short TO BE CONTINUED ending. While I received my copy as a gift and only goes for $10 on Steam (even cheaper during sales) I cannot recommend this game to many people including Deus Ex fans.
If you are going to play this, expect a very mediocre to poor experience.

In a refreshing change from other games that purport to be 'difficult', and then feel like the 'easy' or 'normal' difficulty some of us older gamers grew up playing, Vermintide is actually difficult - sometimes unfairly so.  And that's a good thing, in my opinion.  The accomplishment of completion is more meaningful when there's an actual penalty (lost time, and poor rewards) for failure.  None of this "get a trophy for showing up" stuff, you have to actually play well in order to obtain your rewards.
This game has
best first-person melee combat of any game I've ever played; it's set in a universe that makes me nostalgic about childhood, and it the in-game character diaglogue's as they interact with each other are fantastic.
The mechanics of the game, being very much based on the Left For Dead franchise, absolutely punish you for failure to play as a team.  Sadly, many people still can't seem to understand that "play as a team" does NOT mean "run off on my own ahead of the party so that I can get the highest score on the meaningless leaderboards at the end of the match and I hate you jerks for not rescuing me after I got grabbed".
That being said, the vast majority of people I've played with - and I almost exclusively play in pickup groups - have been good people to game with.
Word of warning, if you are the type to be overly concerned with your loot reward then this may not be the game for you.  If you spent 20-40 minutes on a run that was enjoyable and a great experience, but getting sub-par loot through the random loot award at the end will completely ruin what was a great experience just moments before, then yeah, this may not be your cup of tea.
However, if you just like killing an endless horde of rats, gaming with a good group of people, and spending time in a very well done universe, then Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is for you.
edit: 5 months later, I still play this game almost every day.  The recent Quests and Contracts free DLC is very rewarding for casual gameplay of an hour or two here and there, and the substantially improved loot tables from patch 1.4.3 greatly improve the quality of loot that is obtained.

The game owes a lot to the L4D series, but the unique elements it adds really make the game shine. The best feature, in my opinion, is the different characters and weapon types you get to use, each of which lends itself to a different playstyle. Unfortunately, it can take some effort to figure out just what that style is, because the game's interface doesn't really give you enough information about your own capabilities. The game still feels unfinished in certain places, mostly in terms of flavor text and effect descriptions, but the gameplay is solid and obviously well developed.
The progression system is simple and enjoyable, the combat is fierce and fun, and the community is surprisingly positive and helpful. Striving for better loot and bigger achievements makes it fun to risk runs at higher difficulties, but players of any skill level can achieve slow but steady advancement on the easier modes.
The game has its share of bugs, though they've grown steadilly fewer as time has passed. Mostly it's standard errors, like characters falling through the level geometry or even flags failing to trigger. They've been an inconvenience on occasion, but only stopped me from completing a level once, several patches ago. Overall, I'd say that of the bugs I notice, 10% are frustrating, 10% are actually helpful, and 80% are just amusing.
Play this game if: You like intense arcade-style co-op games, you love the setting and atmosphere of Warhammer Fantasy, or you loved the melee fighting elements of L4D2.
Avoid this game if: You want deep and complex character customization, you're not a fan of random loot drops, you get frustrated in games where you die and have to restart the whole level.
Its like Left4Dead if Left4Dead's AI director was replaced by Stanley Kubrick.

Specifically on some of the bosses I had to fight with slimy tentacles and limbs. No map textures or anything like that. As far as everything else the game was smooth as butter with the 60fps cap at the highest settings and it NEVER once crashed on me. I did not meet the requirements even. (dual core i3 @ 3.8ghz r9 270 8g of ram). The system requirements are BS.
The GAMEPLAY was alot like re4 which was one of my favorite games btw so It didn't bother me too much. They could've come up with something new though TBH like any new game should.
FIGHTING the zombies was not as epic as I had imagined considering how scary they looked. The encounters were rather predictable and repetitive which consisted of: Melee back up avoid the counter attack/"flailing arms or weapons" then melee again repeat 5 or 6 times till their head magically explodes or just shoot them a couple of times as they walk up to you slowly. If they charge you take a few steps out the way.
The A.I wasn't that challenging as they would sometimes run up against picket fences and walls and the gun play itself wasn't very intense or as satisfying as RE4. You might shoot something every once in a while if you had ammo but rationing resources was kind of forced on you. The one thing I absoluted HATED about this game was the stamina feature. Anytime you run out of the few seconds of sprinting stamina you had, Instead of slowing down, he would pause for a few painfully long seconds which was a guaranteed instant death in a boss battle or chase scene. Like as if he was a winded morbidly obese person. This got on my nerves more than anything and I felt was complete BS. I get the reason for the stamina feature but you don't pause to catch your breath if you're being chased by a psycho chainsaw murderer WTF!
What I did really like about this game was the visuals. It was eye candy and it played very well. The level design was very convincing. Each room or hallway was very detailed and the lighting and overlays created a strong ominous atmosphere which at times put me on edge. Enough to make me apprehensive of going into certain rooms. The characters and monsters were some of the most aesthetically pleasing I have ever encountered.
With that being said I would recommend this game to a friend but not for full price.

Pros:
+Gradually opens up into something resembling a more modern Resident Evil 4.
+Interesting antagonist & story premise, once it eventually decides to slightly explain itself.
+RPG-like character-building encourages exploration & killing avoidable, difficult enemies
+Beautiful graphics in certain places
+Not necessarily scary for the most part, but maintains a consistently high level of tension throughout
Cons:
-Been there, done or seen an older version of that.
-You're in a forest village of sorts. Poof, now you're in a sewer with basically no explanation whatsoever as to how you got there. Better get used to a lack of context. It's really bothersome in that it makes it difficult to rationalize pushing forwards at times.
-Poorly told story. It has potential and a fair amount of depth to it, but you get drips of narrative at a time until well over halfway through the game and by then the vagueness that remains isn't at all justified. It's DLC baiting, really.
-Poorly fleshed-out characters. I still like 'em and all, but there could have been much more there. Not much to go on in the character development department, really.
-Enemy variety, or the lack thereof. 99% zombies of the typical weapon-wielding type.
-Poorly optimized for PC. Good luck keeping a consistent 60 FPS; my GTX 980 didn't manage it in places.
-FRUSTRATION. There's a Dark Souls level of difficulty to specific scenarios in the game, only you can generally blame poor design and a lack of timely checkpoints for your many deaths while dealing with
rather than your own mistakes.
-Gore isn't scary in and of itself, apparently. Even if you turn it up to 11 or 11,000 or beyond, as The Evil Within does.
In case this isn't TL;DR already:
Sprint time: 4.0 seconds. Early on you'll be surrounded by zombies, and this is what you've got to work with. Exceed those four seconds of slowly-recovering sprint time and your character will stop moving and gasp for air for *several* seconds, regardless of how imminent the nearest zombie's ax is to his head. Factor in the facts that melee attacks are nearly useless, you've very little ammunition (if any) and your character's aiming abilities are informed mostly by apparent alcoholism, and it's safe to say you're incredibly weak and vulnerable at the beginning of the game.
You'll gradually grow stronger, sure, but initially you're going to be looking at a lot of frustration due to protagonist Sebastian's generally not being an unrealistic badass. Unfortunately, this frustration will keep showing up later on in the game when you're facing certain poorly-designed bosses; there's no way to really kill
in a particular encounter, for example, and if anything the real offender here is the checkpoint system. You're guaranteed to die in certain scenarios at least a few times, and the checkpoint system has no apparent logic regarding when and where to kick in.

A quick review about how this game evolved since late 2012, when Jagex Games Studios took over the development of the game. This is not an objective review, but I will try to give as many details as possible.
Whelp, this was a great game.
I used to play that game during its beta and bought it on Steam. It used to be a really dynamic game with decent game modes, a decent balance and interesting features that allowed players to have a good time, until the developers strayed away from the original game. Now it is just a slow-paced, worthless mash up of Team Fortress 1 & Minecraft beta, except those were actually fun to play.
The basics of the game: in most game-modes, there are 4 classes:
•The Commando, who carries a rocket launcher or a minigun, the balanced guy
•The Sniper
•The Rocketeer/Engineer, who can use a jetpack and carries a SMG-like gun
•The Miner, who carries a shotgun and works on modifying the environment to benefit his team
Here is a quick list of examples explaining how the gameplay changed for the worst over the past 8 months.
•Dynamism is gone. The Rocketeer used to be able to fly across the map and actually do stuff. Now his job is to use a "jetpack", once every minute give or take, fly up for 2 seconds and wait for snipers to gun him down.
•Digging tunnels or just using your ability to change the environment is not worth it anymore. For one, snipers have been given a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ beam that gives away their position when they aim down the sights, making sneaking around just useless. Some would say it's to avoid camping, but there are other solutions that don't imply making one of the 4 usual classes useless, unless they go for close combat.
•The specific game modes that do not involve the 4 classes depicted a few lines ago have not evolved a bit and the Zombie one suffered from the nerfs on classes so much it isn't even nearly half as interesting as is used to be.
•The community keeps being ignored and slowly decays (hence a series of awful changes to the game). Today, January 26th 2014, across the United States, Europe and Australia, less than 30% of servers overall had any players playing. It took Jagex a single year to destroy a community of 2 million players?
To sum up, Ace of Spades is now a shadow of what it used to be, and a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥map editor will not save this game from its terrible evolution

The game itself is mostly a PTW type of game. The weapons are pretty hard to get, expect to grind ofr about a week or so just to get maybe at most an LMG. The games are mostly littered with tankers and its not like you can keep grabbing the free AT launcher, Panzerfaust 60 from the spawn area, get to the middle of the map and shoot the tank. Most of the times, it takes two shot not one shot, so you better have a buddy with you, else the tank will  traverse and kill you. Even if you did buy some AT equipment such as the Bazooka or AT grenades, they cost a hell load of gaming credits for starters if you decide to go anti tank for an entire game.
Levelling up is not too hard, if you know how to play FPS shooters and know how to lead your target, you should be just fine, in fact pretty good. The key is to slow down and aim, dont run and spray. Semi auto rifles are most of the times, really annoying esspecially when youère using a bolt action. Whats more annoying are the SMGs and/ or LMGs. Full auto weapons. People just run up to you, zig zagging pattern and spray you away. I really think bolt action rifles should be getting more damage out put per round and they should lower the damage on some particular full auto weapons like the PPsh. maybe the STG.
So here are my points, it an ok game, though its going down the PTW path as long as you stay calm and play along. When someone kills you or you're on a long death streak. Stay cool about it, its just a game. Tanks in matches are a serious problem since not much people really want to buy AT equipment and go head to head with the metal beasts. All the tankers have to do is cap the points while inside their metal monsters and done. they win. Of course you can take the panzerfaust 60 and fight them, but it requires two hits to kill a tank. Even if you some how do get a buddy to follow you around with another AT launcher and kill the tanker in his tank. All that player has to do is just spawn another tank and you have to repeat the process. I think they perhaps should tone down the costs to refill your AT equipment if this continues. Full auto weapons are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ but if you know how to keep headshotting people or pimp your gun to maximum damage output let it be a one shot or something, you should be fine, though the grinding....
In all, I say this is a pretty goood game to try out and keep playing. Theres a healthy selection of vehicles for you the choose from, good weapons once you grind them out. And trust me, grinding the BAR is taking me long enough, but i know i wont be disappointed once i get it. Lots of interesting weapons and really puts you into that WWII experience. Tanks are a problem, but as long as you know how to deal with them, you'll be fine. I'm gonna give the game a rating of 8.5 out of ten stars.

In all seriousness, "Layers of Fear" is an extremely interesting and immersive experience about an painter falling deeper and deeper into madness. I cannot reccomend this game more than enough because of its nuances and subtle story telling, all of which you do not really have to read to experience the full potential of how psychologically scary this game is. This is rarely a "BOO!" scare typre of game, but when jumpscares do occur, the game truly earns a fright from the player, by extensively building  atmosphere and tension. This game deviates expectations when it comes to scares, and I love it. If there is a downside to this game, it is because it may need a little bit of optimizing (which is probably because it uses the Unity engine) and that there is really no ending yet because of Early Access. Overall though, this game has many unique ideas thrown into one creepy atmosphere and almost made me have to buy a new pair of pants. If you liked PT, you will absolutely adore "Layers of Fear"

Free-To-Play games are often limited unless you're willing to put money into them, which makes the whole "free" part pointless.  Star Trek Online doesn't do that. It is possible to play the entire game through without paying a dime. There are several in-game currencies that can be used to buy things you might need, so spending real-world cash is unnecessary.
The game itself is very true to the Star Trek mythos. The ship models are nicely done, ship combat is similar to the Starfleet Battles game from the early 2000s, three dimensional but it shows you things you need to know, like shield strength.
Ground combat is similar to most MMOs, essentially point-and-shoot. This isn't bad. The streamlined nature of the system allows you to concentrate on what you're killing and let your NPC team do what they do.
If there is a single downside to this game it's that there's no manual available, at least on Steam, and that's a shame because this game is deep enough that a manual would be extremely useful.
If you're looking for a Sci Fi MMO that's FTP, STO is for you.

I've played this game for over a year and it's been pretty fun.
The game features iconic ships from the various Star Trek movies and series, as well as ships that were designed by the game developers. The types of ships are broken down into groups that include escorts, cruisers, and science vessels and these ships can be captained by players of any profession.
The professions are pretty much broken down into something commonly seen in most MMOs, Tactical (Damage), Engineering (Tank), Science (Healing).
Almost everything is customizable on the ships, player characters and the bridge officers. For ships, there are options to change a ship's appearance, mount various weapons, shields, engines, deflector arrays, and warp cores (singularity cores for Romulans). Player characters can choose many types of uniforms, weapons, body armor, personal shields, and equipment. Bridge officers have these options as well but are limited to a degree, such as the selection of uniforms and only being able to carry one weapon unlike the player who can carry two.
As of the time of this review, there are three factions players can choose from, Federation, Klingon Empire, and Romulan. All three factions have their own story campaigns with various enemies to fight in space and on the ground with your away team and the Romulan players will have the option to ally themselves with either the Federation or Klingons as they advance in the campaign.
Of course, as with most MMOs, there is a grind aspect to the game as players finish the story campaign and go into end-game or max level content. The end-game content will allow players to earn powerful top level equipment sets which are designed to fight specific enemies such as the Borg and Tholians. These equipment sets can be used to fight other enemies as well.
There are also guilds in the game, usually referred to as fleets. A relatively new feature introduced in the game is the fleet starbases in which fleet members can contribute to projects to upgrade various facilities to gain access to even more powerful weapons and equipment. I'm currently in a fleet right now founded by Mike (aka Law) from the SWAT 4 clan |SOG|. The fleet is called Starfleet Special Weapons and Tactics (SSWAT) and it is a small fleet at the moment but we accept players who are willing to play tactically as a team and of course have fun :)
Overall, it's a fun game to play and you can easily end up playing for hours at a time.

The Evil Within is a new original survival horror game, developed by the minds behind the original Resident Evil games and the genius of Shinji Mikami. The game seeks to provide players with an 'old school' survival horror game; complete with chills, scarce ammunition and challenging enemy encounters. I'm pretty happy to say I really enjoyed this game despite a few missteps.
The story has the player controlling a detective named Sebastian Castellanos; Sebastian and his team are called in to Beacon Mental Hospital to investigate the scene of a gruesome mass murder, and from then on, a whole lot of horrific supernatural shenanigans occurs. It's worth noting that the story is pretty confusing and was certainly not easy to follow; the characters are also somewhat dull, so if you play this game, I wouldn't really advise doing so for the narrative.
Gameplay is the real heart and soul of The Evil Within, and oh my, what great gameplay it is! The game handles like a fresher version of Resident Evil 4 in nearly every way; third-person camera angle with similar over the shoulder aiming. Ammo is incredibly scarce, and just like in Resident Evil 4, the zombie-like enemies will amble and shuffle towards you while you attempt to pull off a frantic headshot. There are a few boss fights thrown in throughout the game, all of which were stressful and challenging. There are also a few neat mechanics; for example, the upgrade system has Sebastian collecting vials of green gel, which can be used back at the hospital ward to upgrade his various skills and attributes. Additionally, the player can also burn the corpses of downed enemies in order to ensure that they don't rise from the grave as well as providing you with valulable resources. Just like in Resident Evil 4, you'll navigate mansions, villages, as well as the modern day city, hospital wards and abandoned facilities. Due to the supernatural nature of the game, you'll be thrown from one area to the next without context, which I didn't really mind since I was mainly in this game for the intense gameplay. I wouldn't say this game was 'terrifying', however I will say that the enemy encounters were very stressful and the game really doesn't skimp out on gore and incredibly intense enemy encounters. The Evil Within makes a nice compromise between horror and action, with only occassional dips into ridiculousness. In short; this is a very similar experience to Resident Evil 4 with a whole lot of refinements. If you liked that, you'll love The Evil Within.
Technically, the game succeeds both in audio and visuals. Ambient sound effects are very creepy, and set you on edge before enemy encounters, along with the various 'gross' sound effects that make the gore so visceral. The graphics aren't exactly groundbreaking, but they look nice enough. There's many detailed environments to be found here, and the lighting effects are also quite nice.
My only other real gripe with this game apart from the mediocre narrative is the PC optimisation; this game runs quite badly on most systems, even after the multiple patches. The devs were kind enough to remove the black bars and the 30 FPS cap, which was a very welcome addition.
In conclusion, The Evil Within is an excellent survival horror experience that will please any super fans of the older Resident Evil games. The folks over at Tango and Bethesda have managed to craft an intense and unique horror experience despite missteps with the story and PC optimisation. Highly recommended.

When it comes to the story of this game, it seems rather fitting and somewhat appealing for a Deus Ex game when you read about it. Unfortunately, actually playing the game seems to show that it’s the exact opposite; with a storyline that’s difficult to follow without losing interest along the way, as well as boring dialogue and rather uninteresting characters, you’ll honestly have a hard time following what’s going on. The conversations between NPCs, whether they be related to side missions or the main story, are drawn out quite a bit with some unnecessary information that could’ve been easily skipped. On top of that, the game seems to rely more on literally telling you everything it can about one particular moment in the game, instead of letting you find the information yourself along the way. This kind of breaks away from the norm people expect from the Deus Ex series, which takes away from digging up necessary information and replaces it with extended dialogue that could very well make the player lose interest in the game.
In terms of visual quality, this game is a bit mixed in terms of quality, but ultimately comes off as a bit sub-par for a PC title. Deus Ex: The Fall runs on the Unity engine, demanding very little to play on its highest quality and allowing players with a low-end system the ability to play this game without worry. The Fall also makes use of the assets from Deus Ex: Human Revolution, giving it a more fitting appearance for a Deus Ex title. However, this is about as far as the game goes in terms of positive remarks on its appearance; although the environments look good, the lack of shaders seen in the game tends to take away from them, leading to a somewhat dull appearance when comparing it to Human Revolution. Male and female NPCs are also very low quality and seem like something you’d expect from an older game, and are extremely limited in terms of variation; at most, you’ll see one or two models that look different from each other based on gender alone, while every other NPC will literally be using the same model and a maybe variations of the same textures. There’s also the matter of the weapon models having noticeable smoothing related issues that give them a lower quality appearance when compared to what you see in Human Revolution.
The sound quality isn’t exactly the best either, but there isn’t much to say about it since a majority of the sounds used in Human Revolution were re-used for The Fall. Although most of the ambient and weapon sounds seem to be taken directly from Human Revolution, some of the sounds you’ll come across sound really poor in quality when compared to others you hear throughout the game. The voice acting itself is also not that great either, with little to no emotion being present whenever someone is speaking and making it seem like the actors themselves weren’t even interested in their lines. There’s also no variation between voices used for generic NPCs like there was in Human Revolution. There’s also a couple of issues with the sound where certain audio clips seem generally out of sync, such as when you speak with NPCs and they end up doing a sort of puppet-style chatter movement. There’s also no pauses between lines in conversations, so everything seems like a rushed conversation whenever you talk to someone else.
In terms of gameplay, this game is just a horrible mess of unbalanced combat, poor controls, and buggy AI. Not only were the controls for the PC and controller setups rather buggy and unpolished, you also don’t have the option to re-map your bindings to something more fitting to your own style of gameplay. The combat system was also rather clunky and unbearable at times. The AI used by enemy NPCs was also a bit lacking in terms of being intelligent, considering that you can literally walk right up to an enemy and shoot them a couple times before they or their allies even noticed you. The game’s difficulty is also heavily unbalanced, being a bit too easy in areas where the difficulty would need to be increased and being overly difficult in areas where it shouldn’t be difficult at all. The Fall makes very little use of the available weapon models from Human Revolution, only using a select few and re-purposing them with very minor tweaks to provide a larger “selection” of the exact same weapons with slightly different stats; considering that you can go through the entire game with two of the cheapest weapons available and not have to worry about running out of ammo, this system is highly unnecessary and rather pointless. There are also various points in the game where certain functions or prompts won’t appear where they are needed, such as when you are hacking a computer or door panel and need an auto-unlock device; the prompt simply doesn’t show for the item that’s needed, and you’re pretty much forced to either hack certain devices manually or find ways to slow down the security system when hacking. This can be very aggravating at times, especially when it involves important parts of the game. For example, you supposedly only need one AUD (Auto-Unlocking Device) to open a security panel or have access to a computer without having to manually hack a device; I ended up having to mod the game to create a debug mode just to give myself a bunch of AUDs, and I still couldn't use any of them until I completely restarted the game. The only positive thing I found in terms of the gameplay was that the inventory system was re-vamped, removing the need to play “inventory Tetris” and just buying or equipping whatever weapons/items you need at the time. While it does partially take away from the feel one would expect from the iconic inventory system that’s been used since the first Deus Ex, it does provide a bit more relief in terms of how much of a single item you can have stored away for later use.
Overall, Deus Ex: The Fall was a rather shoddy port of an already sub-par mobile game. The visual quality is decent enough to still look good on a low-end system, but there’s a large amount of room for improvement on the PC version. The sound quality is also nothing special due to the re-used assets from Human Revolution, and also suffered from rather low quality more often than it should be. The gameplay itself is just atrocious, having more problems than it honestly should and just being a pain to work with without taking some time to calm down mid-play. In all honesty, this isn’t a game worth buying for the PC; if you’re really wanting to spend ten dollars on a game, it really would be in your best interest to spend it on something else.

You won't even know half of the story if you don't take the time to look for the little notes, clues, and details that only come from taking it slow and soaking in all of the details. This game is RICH with details, and delivers a story in a compelling, and frightening way.
If you buy this game don't do it with the intent to see how fast you can beat it, do it for the experience. And do it with the expectation for it to scare your pants off at the same time, I think taking it slow and absorbing the details delivers a more intense gameplay anyways.
Anyways, I gotta say, I loved this game!

I've started playing this game since it became open beta (that's going to be over 5 years ago), with quite long break due to stuff and things. Picked it back up again over 3 years ago, then played it pretty much non-stop almost until now. Don't get fooled with 5k+ hours played on record, my real playtime is far, FAR bigger than Steam shows. In reality it's probably more than 10k hours. I was able to, thankfully, switch back to standalone client. Which I was very glad about - Steam client is pretty glitchy on its own, Steam achievements still don't work, and on top of already existing bugs in game, it's teeth clenching combination. Steam players would often notice cluster♥♥♥♥ of corrupted sprites (which wouldn't happen on standalone client), nearly after every update they were blocked from the game, and forced to wait extra few hours for Ankama to sort out the issue. Steam players couldn't purchase ogrines or even write on forum without unnecessary mental gymnastics, Steam packs that are treated as DLCs often caused plethora of issues that could've been evaded, but instead they were ignored unless some players made noise about them on public forum.
Creators are infamous for neglecting international community, and focusing mostly on feedback from their French players. Earlier I could've blamed this on language barriers, yet, there were many cases in which they ignored even French players and disregarded entire feedback they've received, did their own thing anyway, and sometimes implemented very, very tiny and meaningless changes to new, often half-made, features in a "we care but not really lol" manner just because game forum got flooded with posts in which people literally begged them to look into the mess they've pushed onto live servers (notable examples: recently added Power of Will mechanic about which players have been complaining for about month already, and earlier pop-up ads - YES, in-game POP-UP ADS you'd rather expect in a mobile game that's a Farmville clone - advertising boosters, after sea of complaints they made them a bit less intrusive, yet, player without active booster will get royally fed up anyway - they looked far worse than that, trust me - the only difference is that they don't appear every 5 minutes if one performs a particular action, but once in 24 hours).  Customer support could've been way better - I had to wait about month for them to solve reports I sent to them. They won't solve all tickets the way you would wish them to, so if for example, your account's info got compromised, then you're out of luck. A bit more curious player, if they will know where to look, will find, for example, very negative reviews written by their own ex-workers on situation in that place. Always mentioning the same issues, over and over.
New content is usually added in half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥state, or postponed into infinity and beyond. There is a beta server - which sometimes is available to all players, sometimes only Chosen Ones with Active Booster will have the blessing to test out new content. After about month of testing new content is pushed onto live servers. Often with so many bugs players end up wondering how the hell all of those managed to get overlooked. Many changes - mostly ones players probably would immediately try to veto - aren't even tested out first on beta, but pushed immediately onto live servers.
Professions are boring, obligatory, grinding HELL. People who leveled all professions to 130 and more are rare. Really, really rare. If it wasn't for my friends' support I would end up eating both of my hands, my laptop, entire desk, and then myself out of sheer frustration, because amount of required mats is just ridiculous, and two professions out of 14 (back then 16!), namely chef and leatherdealer are the worst ones to level up. Whilst former isn't much of a necessity, second one is, since it's used to craft and upgrade some pieces of your gear. Professions aren't a way to get your gear upgraded faster at cost of some materials, unlike in other MMOs. It's the
way to have your stuff upgraded. Upgrading single item gets progressively harder and more demanding for materials. Whilst at the beginning items are somewhat easy to upgrade, at the end-game levels upgrading single item of the worst quality (you won't see that item dropped in better quality!) becomes a challenge, and a full time job if you play several characters at the same time. Thanks to Secure Crafting feature you don't HAVE to level up your professions just for your own use, you can just find someone to craft you stuff without having them scam you. Yet, as I said - they're rare. Many end-game players I knew have left because of that particular reason (and several more). Yes, surprise surprise, rumors are real! Playerbase is tiny, and still dropping. It was the most noticeable after implementation of Moon Island, with dungeons that favoured ranged classes over close-combat characters (by which I mean - bosses with ohko attacks that made even sturdier bruisers evaporate, yet required tank'n'spank strategy - melee damage dealer needed a specific party combination and strategy not everyone agreed to - it was easier to use 4 archers, tank, and healbot). New content in form of Zinit Mountain looks better compared to it, but you need booster pack to access it - it has several areas of various level range, including end-game content. Which is already can of worms on its own. Pretty nasty one at it. With p2w flavor.
I haven't probably covered everything that I've seen after playing the game for such long time. I don't think I've got enough energy for this nor actually remember ALL of issues. I may continuously edit the review to add up more onto "why you should go play something else" pile. But I guess you get the idea. This one isn't worth your time and energy, unless you want to play it until mid-level content, or if you really, really hate yourself. I'm not even writing this review with joy or any other feeling of positive nature. I was stubborn enough to keep on going despite all signs that the game is going down the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I loved it since it scratched that "itch" I didn't even know I had. I adored it, it gave me inspiration to draw more often, and it pains me so, so much to see it in such state. It will still take a special spot in my heart, and I really do hope that at some point a damn miracle will happen, and this game - which has LOADS of potential and charm, but suffers from worse-than-mediocre idea execution, and culpable attitude of creators towards their customers - will shine once again. Preferably before it's too late to save it.

I finished the very short alpha of Layers of Fear. It has the potential to be a great horror game, although at the moment it lacks a lot of direction as your character becomes lost in the mind-bending, psychedelic shifting house. You collect artifacts and clues to your former life, while working on a slowly morphing painting. However, your character's motivations and goals are somewhat muddled - and as I progressed I felt more like a passive observer to the horrors around me, as if I was being shuttled through a haunted house, than a player with any actual agency.
Good SFX, great game sequences with unique scares, and an intriguing beginning to a story (A painter who goes mad, with a potential schizophrenic wife). It all just needs a more cohesive story, with a more clearly defined goal, some tighter level design, and more player agency.

When you play this... journey, you're getting more than just nonstop action. You're also getting the untold stories of Noah's adventures on his Ark. As you seed your way through hordes of animals, just remember that this is true. This all happened. You are playing a part of history, my friends, and I want you all to know it. While you force feed food down the throats of goats, I want you all to take a moment to stop and think about what you're doing... want to know what you're doing? You're continuing the legacy of the great Noah from Genesis (the Bible one, not the Sega one).

Despite being labeled as "family-friendly", this game is brutal, you constantly run out of ammo and often end up lost. Every animal on the ark is out for you, and sometimes you get ambushed from the sides. One of the main goals is to put them to sleep, and it doesn't really matter how you do it. One of the weapons is a steel slingshot that shoots coconut sized projectiles, but I guess the animals are alright with that. My only qualm is that sometimes the levels can have poorly placed enemies, and unless you know beforehand what to do, you're in trouble, cause those goats hit HARD. Oh well, at least the announcer is a pretty nice guy, he exclaims "WOW" every time you clear a mission with bonus objectives.
Overall it's classic Wolfenstein gameplay, with new enemies and designs that are surprisingly worth your time.

After reading a mixed bag of critics for this highly anticipated title, I took the opportunity of a sale to pick it up for 20 euro and I wasn't the least disappointed. First of all, most of the technical issues described in former critics have been fixed. The game is stable, textures are okay (with one exception towards the end of the game) and the infamous black bars can be opted out from in the settings.
The Evil Within is a challenging, athmospheric game with good gameplay, nice visuals and varied settings, including a mental hospital, a village, sewers (yes, what's a game without sewrs?), a crumbling, modern city, an old mansion, a farm, some surreal lanscapes and many more. It's like a potpourri of survival horror sceneries and I personally never got bored of wondering what would come next. Ennemies are okay. Some people deplored bad AI but what do they expect from zombies and monsters? These guys aren't supposed to be very smart, are they? You really have to manage your scarce ammunition and search every corner for stuff to help you on your way through the incessant nightmare the main protagonist is going through and, allthough the guy is a total badass with neves of steel, the feeling of weekness never fades. There are a few very challenging boss fights and a couple of annoying ennemies, allthough they didn't annoy me so much personally.
All in all, I suggest very much to download the demo and see for yourself. That's what I did and I was instantly hooked.
Don't expect this to be a game for you if you're only satisfied with games that give you all the shooting power you want in order to mow through hordes of ennemies. This is not the game for you. On the other hand, if like me you enjoy a game like Alien: Isolation or Half life mixed with oldschool Resident Evil, you might enjoy this game as much as I did.

These characters all carry their own statistics, likes, and dislikes. It's this combination of effects that makes it imperative that you choose your fellow adventurers wisely. Maybe that Drow elf has a dislike for frat boys and won't work well with your Party Bard. Or perhaps the Bard dislikes Gnomes, and so you should avoid swiping right on any of the short folk.
You'll take these heroes and go on adventures, overcoming obstacles and snatching treasure up. A series of adventures leads you from a small village where you start, to a climatic confrontation with some dark evil. It's basically D&D with a cute skin.
The game itself has a lot of content, but mechanically it's not too varied. You're basically looking to matchup heroes as closely as you can, spend your upgrades to ensure they work together and read their responses to guess who would be the best to overcome a challenge.
As an example, I had come across some Orcs. Each of the heroes has a statement about Orcs, giving you hints at how to complete the challenge. My party Bard wanted to party with the orcs ("These bros throw the best parties, break out the kegs!") and I selected him to attempt the challenge. They partied and we succeeded!
Because of the random combination of elements that goes into creating characters, foes, and events, I can see a lot of possibility for future expansion so any repetition that bothered me across my time playing has obvious points the developers can inflate the game at to remove these repeating patterns.
The game has a unique art style, serviceable sound, and solid gameplay mechanics. But each of these things falls flat when it comes to repetition. The art they have is great, but you end up seeing the same portraits over and over. The sound works, but there isn't enough of it for variety. The gameplay is fun, but you'll come across the same match-ups and foes over and over.
In short, for 5 bucks you'll get more than an hour or so out of it. Maybe you'll like it enough to keep playing or maybe you'll dislike it. But it'll be worth the money, if you were to compare it to watching a movie or buying an album.

In order to complete an adventure you must create a party that can work well together by having compatible classes, likes/dislikes, and alignments. However, some people lie, in some cases lie about everything about themselves, and from what I can tell there is no real tell if someone is a liar before it is reveled. If there is, I wasn't able to figure it out in about two hours of gameplace and the fact that there's no help screens or tooltips may make it so that I'm just missing something.
Also, once a liar is found out you are stuck with them. There's no way, as far as I figured out, to eject them from the party once revealed. If a person you took on reveals that he hates everything about everyone in your party you are left helpless as you watch morale plummet because of that one liar in your midst and, at the end of the adventure, the party's current morale plays a key role in determining if your party is success chance.
Add to this some technical problems as well; the game crashed a few times on me, including twice when I was trying to record it for my video (link below) and the fact that it keeps resetting its volume settings on start up just adds to my aggravation with the game. Plus, the game is a bit on the expensive side for what it is at the end of the day.
I do hope that Questr improves during the early access process but right now I have no choice but the swipe left.

Alright.
I have spent around 2 hours playing it (it is now 8th September). I have bought it after watching one episode of some random youtuber. I wasn't sure about it, especially that it's an Early Access (we all know what that has been like a lot of times) and because it's a single-player game.
After watching the first episode I was hooked. The game looked really well, rooms were full of small details, graphics looked amazingly well done. So I decided to buy it and give it a try - after all, there is still a huge drought after Amnesia or Outlast, both of which took horror games to another level in my opinion, mostly due to the fact that Amnesia was such a success and an incredible experience for me.
Now, I started the game, rushed through first 5-10 minutes because I knew everything there after watching the video (though I still picked up all notes and stuff to read them myself). There has been a lot of improvements and details added that made that first few minutes more scary. That's a huge plus, seeing that the developers don't rush to finish the game but instead, they improve every piece that has been arleady released and slowly progress through the story releasing updates. This is one of the first things that hit me.
The fact that they actually DO listen to other people such as *spoiler ahead*
makes me very exciting and I want to see the ending to this story.
These 2 hours has been incredible experience. Story is absolutely amazing, mysterious and it keeps me wonder what will I unveil next, considering that I've arleady had experienced so many confusing and plot twisting moments. Game is still not finished (by now I have finished only half of it) and it seems that every time you make a big discovery, it takes you more and more time to get to another one so we can assume it will be much longer than it is now.
People that like art and are somewhat knowledgable will find many famous paintings, but, not only this game consists of famous painters' art, you actually experience your character's art. In fact, going deeper and deeper into the story, you create your own painting which seems to unveil the truth at the very end, which makes me very exciting. The fact that you can't see yourself in the mirrors (you can see you character, but it is very blurry) is making me wonder what is actually going on.
Overall, I DO recommend this game. This is an amazing piece of art, not only in terms of graphics, but also in terms of story, atmosphere, music or details included in every place. The fact that you can't fight or run doesn't make this game less scary. It might be less intense or adrenaline-packed than Amnesia or Outlast (second one especially) but it tells a great story along with some good horror experiences.
As long as you're not looking for something to run away from or fight with, you will be pleasantly surprised that the game that is still in the Early Access offers so much and is so polished and amazing.

Pros/Cons first, then some other stuff.
Pros:
-Varied classes with a decent selection of weapons, even if a good chunk are "shared".
-Fast paced gameplay. Some maps are just basically finales of L4D2, and about as long.
-Loot! Everyone likes getting stuff.
Cons:
-Maps are short. Like, really short mostly, which makes the lack of save points/safehouses fine generally, except for when you get the one or two long maps. Or hosts migrate. Or the game crashes.
-Classes "share" weapons, without actually sharing them. This means you could get a 1H axe for the witch hunter, but your soldier CAN'T use it. This factors into the point below.
-Loot! Unlike L4D2 which is based on a little luck and a good amount of skill, now it's based on getting the perfect weapon to drop, with the perfect traits (i.e. heal on hit), or a trinket that heals everyone a slight amount when you heal. The only way to get loot is either"
A: finish a mission. Higher the difficulty and more grimoires and tomes you collect, the better loot you get. Maybe.
B: Level up. Very slowly. Each level gets you one weapon.
C: Spend crafting mats (gained through either extremely high levels, salvaging weapons, or The Last Stand mode.)
D: Fuse 5 weapons of the same quaility to get one weapon of a higher quality.
-Modding? HA! For a game that tries really hard to be L4D2, it doesn't have any mod support, or plans for it last I checked.

Personal Story:
>Make it to wave 29 on TLS, unlocking all the difficulties for that map
>We all die finally
>Host leaves, host migration kicks in.
>All rewards, unlocks, and experience are lost
Note, this was like, the 3rd or 4th time this has happened.
Now, that happens with any map. There are no checkpoints. No safe rooms. Nothing. No matter how far you get in a mission you had BETTER finish it or you get jack all (except exp, you get like, 10% of that)
Oh and farming? Hope you like farming! That's all there is to do once you finish ~13 maps w/o DLC, half of which are basically the finale of dead center, except half of the time whe you get it, the "gas cans" start exploding, meaning you have to go ALL the way back to it and grab another.
If you get this game ~50%, it's probably worth it. Otherwise, I'd pass. Left 4 Dead 2 is $20, and is a million times the game that this is.

I do have a problem, though. So recently, my brother let me play this game on his super beefy gaming computer. The game ran like a dream; 75 fps running it on Extreme (this game's version of Ultra). The game was immersive and atmospheric. There were no bugs whatsoever, and it was fantasticly fun.

I remember just trying to survive the avalanche of Third-Person shooters in 2008 after the success of Gears Of War and Resident Evil 4. Every game was now including currency systems and cover-based shooting it became hard to find anything that truly stood out.
Dark Sector was a game I passed by, and I really should have given it a chance! A buddy of mine picked it up and just wouldn't stop raving about the gameplay and the gore, but more importantly, how hard as hell it was!
Now, almost 10 years later, I decided to romp through it in it's entirety. And to be perfectly honest, I missed one hell of a ride. But hey, better late then never!
Story wise, the game doesn't give much of a crap. I'm not kidding, you barely get to know your main character other then he did a "Really bad thing" a few years ago and was basically sent to die on a mission that essentially boiled down to the CIA throwing a garbage bag at the homeless man on the outskirts of town so he would ♥♥♥♥ off. Hell, the guy the main character pops in the first level was actually the father of the ex-love interest you meet midway through. The games excuse was that all the context was in the manual but we don't have the luxury of such a thing with most steam games.
Thankfully, the gameplay makes up for it by turning into a limb-lopping extravaganza!
The main selling point of the game is the "Glaive", an organic shuriken that can be wielded with any secondary weapon and can slice through Russian limbs like butter. While ammo is very plentiful the fastest and most enjoyable method of killing the denizens of this Eastern European hellhole is by throwing your glaive into a crowd and watching the blood and severed arms soar to the heavens. Along the way you will also unlock extra powers but you will also learn to use environmental elements to yoru advantage and giving your glaive a temporary boost in both combat and solving puzzles.
Hell, you can even guide your glaive personally as it rips through the air in slomo! Playing this game honestly put me back into the baggy pants and unkept hair of a 13 year old instead of the comfortably fitting t-shirt and dangerously receding hairline of a 25 year old man who thought gore couldn't wow him anymore.
Difficulty wise, it's going to kick your♥♥♥♥♥ I played this like a Gears of War clone but after dying more times then I could count, I started playing like a gun-totting ninja, the way Dark Sector is meant to be played. Scoring quick headshots and darting around fire while seeking out elemental hazards to gain a temporary edge in order to reach the end of the level is key here. It's a great example of a game rewarding frantic and aggressive combat and punishing those who cower in a corner to hide as the game throws vastly quick and superior creatures at our hapless anti-hero.
However, as much as the gameplay shines, it does have some pretty nasty cons.
For one, the controls can be a bit finicky. It was clearly designed with a controller in mind so dodging attacks and even sprinting is more of a hastle then it should be, nor do weird AI bugs and strange navigation glitches help much when the going gets tough. Checkpoints themselves can be rather unforgiving and some damage output is just insanely unbalanced in some portions of the game. There is also ingame achievements that BLOCK a good majority of the screen during combat crunches and twice in the game, movement slows to a staggering crawl as the game forces the player to jump into this big lumbering dog-mech that slowly dog-paddles across segments that could have been traversed in a minute on foot.
I also had to do extra leg-work just getting the game to run on my current rig. Not hard for me but certainly head-scratching for those used to picking up games and playing.
Beyond those cons, I still REALLY enjoyed my time with Dark Sector. It's a great example of a game that excels on gameplay even if it has a plethora of cons that might otherwise weigh it down. Give her a go, it's an underrated gem!
Also, it's set in the Warframe universe, so a few of my Warframe buddies suddenly got super-excited about this game when they learned that nugget of truth. The noise one of them made when the Tenno grabbed my rocket midair in the first level probably wasn't human...

The good: the glaive with aftertouch to change the trajectory is fun, it's quite something different than shooting straight or in arcs.
The bad: PC port fail: resolution doesn't match up with the screen, you can't select which upgrades to apply on your weapons (no keybindings for it) which forces you to either sell them or apply them in order, there's a dead zone with keys that aren't available to bind with.
The ugly: the level 7 boss is dodge or die. Which wouldn't be so bad if it weren't invisible and attacking from behind. So I chose neither dodge nor die. I chose quit.

The Rant: They should not have promised survival horror when what the delivered was an action game with not enough ammo and constant boss fights. You never had to search an area for a key or puzzle pieces like silent hill, or RE . The game is inconsistent with itself. An example is seeing two shotgun shells next to the box of ammo yet recieving one shell. What is the green goo? Was it a technical challenge to explain it? Why are the enimies so flamable? Why bother burning them at all, when they dont get back up anyway. If the game could have been more like the first chanisaw guy area, snaking the key off the table and outsmarting him, then battling an injury inflicted by him giving weight to the gravity of the situation. That is what we wanted. Having to oursmart a scary boss, not shooting them over and over. Having to use your brain a little rather than easly running past enimies or being forced to kill them all before the door opens to the next area. After all that scourng for info, and exploring, and I am no closer to knowing what the hell is going on after fininshing the whole game. I reccomend the game because it is alot of content, but I am not happy about being sold false hope. Resident evil remake is TRUE survival horror as I have played through the GameCube version already. Priorities are so messed up in AAA games now, you guys should know that the public will call you out on your bs, so call a game what it is. End Rant

I enjoyed this game immensely. I went into it understanding that it came from the original director of the Resident Evil franchise, but not expecting to play the "lost" Resident Evil. The truth is, this game should stand alone and not be compared to other survival horror franchises. Does it take some notes from Silent Hill? Yes. But, that's OK. I don't know why it would be considered a bad thing. I must say though, Shinji Mikami did a fair amount of "hat tips" to his original work on Resident Evil, in this game. I found it both nostalgic and a very considerate gift to his original fanbase. Is it short? If you're basing it on your adventures in the D.C. Wastleand and Tamriel, then yeah, it is. Those games are meant to be played for hours and hours and hours. I beat this game in just under a day's worth of time (not all at once, mind you). The chapters are set-up at appropriate intervals so that you are both left with a sense of a cliff-hanger, but not putting you in a position of being forced to play the next chapter to get your fill.
For reals, just play the game and enjoy it. It's pretty amazing and wicked fun. Don't let a bunch of wannabe game reviewers convince you of their beliefs.

Vermintide is basically a L4D2 clone with warhammer skins, grindy rpg elements and great visuals. In a nutshell, that explains everything you need to know about this game and on its face, those things are enough to make it a great game. Digging deeper, this game features several characters who all play significantly different, from the bright wizard to the dwarf ranger to the witch hunter. Every character has their own weapon types and operates differently, allowing you to change up playstyles depending on who's in the party. It supports up to 4 players at once and people can drop in and out of games on the fly, where bots will take over if someone leaves (just like L4D). The game has a good number of levels and combat wise, it's just like L4D with weaker regular enemies, and stronger special enemies like the ratling gunner and rat ogres which require a coordinated effort to take down and prevent from killing your party. The combat itself is meaty and works well and requires people to play their roles effectively to get through, as the game is quite a bit harder than Left 4 Dead.
The part of this game that really annoys me however is the loot. Unlike L4D, Vermintide has a loot system which requires many, many hours of grinding and has only recently been (slightly) improved. You tend to get nothing, or at least next to nothing for failing levels and the loot is random at the end of a mission, giving you a dice roll to decide what loot you get. Nothing is awarded during missions, and the crafting is expensive and slow to reward.
Overall, Vermintide is a fantastic game that deserves to be tried, but the developers really need to fix the loot system. The general consensus is that most of the people who really enjoyed the game quit because it's so unrewarding and generally feels like it takes forever to get anything, or requires exploiting glitches or bugs in the levels repeatedly to make headway. With that in mind, I still recommend it if you have friends to play with or if you don't mind finding strangers to join you in killing rats.

I'm not opposed to the idea behind it, a mini-series that focuses on side-characters from the novel; a sort of microcosm of Deus Ex HR's gameplay in an episodic format. The execution of this idea in The Fall leaves much to be desired, partially due to problems with the game itself, but mostly due to the pains of being an obviously rushed port.
To the devs' credit, it does hit some HR beats. You have a hub location (Panama City Slums/Boardwalk/Downtown), with plenty of storage units and gates to hack, a few side-quests (though they are gated by story progress), buildings with hackable doors and safes, man-sized vent systems to serve as alternate paths, upgrade points and PRAXIS kits, stealth takedowns, tons of goodies lying around in or on trashcans/desks/safes, and the persuasion system returns at certain points (and thankfully, the CASIE mod is not an insta-win button this time, just a way to score some extra items/info).
And that leads us to the rub. Imagine, for a moment, if there was a painting you enjoyed so much that you commissioned a different artist to make a painting with a similar style and feeling, with one stipulation: the artist can never look at the original painting, they can only use your written description. Even if the finished painting resembles the original painting's style from a distance, when placed upon closer inspection, several flaws will surface.
There are a variety of upgradable weapons, but the balance feels weird (e.g. headshots from the base pistol are not one-hit kills, which means that the silenced pistol isn't a useful stealth weapon until you apply a damage upgrade). You can still choose to go in stealthily or burst in guns blazing, but the small area sizes with few enemies makes the faster Rambo option much more viable (the Pacifist achievement is bugged, as it unlocks even if you kill people in the campaign). Plus, the AI is as dumb as a doorstop; civilians don't react if you takedown a guard right in front of them; in a firefight, guards will either stay in place or walk towards your position. There are computers to hack, but almost all of them are unlock codes for doors and safes; outside of two memorable e-mails (one being from a certain person in the novel, and another referencing FF27), it's a wasted opportunity for world-building.
The story starts off somewhat interesting (Ben's flashback to his last mission with the Tyrants), then it devolves into what's essentially busywork, as Ben Saxon puts the conspiracy-fighting on hold to go to Panama City and try to find a source of Neuropozyne for himself and Anna Kelso. Naturally, he stumbles onto a conspiracy (because conspiracies are as common as Starbucks in the world of Deus Ex). Things do get somewhat interesting again due to a twist. Unfortunately, the game doesn't go into much effort to build the characters of Ben/Anna/Janus, nor does it provide much of a look at the Tyrants, with the exception of Jaron Namir. It also doesn't give much background on these characters outside of a rough outline established by a few audio logs; leaving much of their origins in the novel.
If it were just those problems, I'd probably excuse it, but as I said before, a bevy of porting problems indicate that this was a rushed port. The UI is largely the same as the mobile version, and while I can see how it would have worked on a touchscreen, it's clunky and unintuitive with a mouse and keyboard. Switching items/grenades/weapons are mainly accomplished by holding their designated key and picking the desired item with the mouse. It pauses the game, but it feels like an unnecessary step. I guess you can use the number bar, but, unlike HR, there's no constant reminder of what each number activates. That's a problem throughout the whole UI: It doesn't generally show key or button prompts, just action prompts. You might end up checking the key bindings infographic quite often.
Then there's the graphics, which weren't scaled up for the PC release, so you'll frequently notice blurry textures, simple geometry, and many low-res character models. The only character models that are detailed decently enough are the Belltower guards, the Riot Cops, and the characters that are important to the storyline (though Ben has a dead-eyed stare when his shades aren't on). Despite the low-res graphics, I still experienced some framerate drops at random times.
There are a few other notable problems with the port; a few bugs (there's a bundle of four barrels in the drug den with a Pocket Secretary on it, I'd fall through the floor and die if I took cover on it and grabbed the PS), only one save slot (saved at area changes and quick saves; I could feasibly see someone saving in an unwinnable position), the single-mouse-button shooting controls (on the crossbow, holding LMB will aim down the scope; on other weapons, it'll just fire multiple times). Perhaps the most annoying thing is when two objects are very close to each other (e.g. credits in a netphone slot); you have your crosshair on one object (the credits) and the game activates the other object (the netphone) when you hit the use key, until you find the correct position/angle to stand at.
Oh, and as for that buggered-up recoil that you've probably seen in gifs, they've fixed that problem. Now the recoil is just a slight screen shake; the difference is immediately obvious as soon as you fire a gun.
It's a sideways-thumb kind of game (leaning heavily towards thumbs down due to the rushed-port problems); not that good, but not so terrible that I'd want to actively warn people off of it. If you got into the Humble Bundle early (back when the BTA was $5-6), then it might be worth upgrading to check it out. Not so much at the current BTA price unless HB adds some big bonuses on Tuesday.

If you're a fan of Deus Ex Human Revolution then you'll probably like this game - it continues in the same theme and style of the original quite well. I enjoyed playing this almost as much as DE:HR.
The Fall brings a lot of the good gameplay aspects from Human Revolution, from incremental augments to weapon upgrades, stealth vs assault, lethal vs nonlethal. Weaponry and upgrades can now be purchased from the pause menu which is both useful if a little jarring. Side quests also appear, as does the free roam across the city.
IF you're a person who requires a game to be 'well made' then this is a little less for you. While it's nice that this game was made for desktop and mobile at the same time it does show through - the animations aren't as good as its predecessor, I found a lot of the sounds didn't play, and some of the controls are a little problematic. I don't want to dwell too much on the downsides, but you might run into a little bit of difficulty in places if you don't have a controller.
My biggest complaint of all is the sudden ending, the game asks if you want to travel to Australia, a quick cutscene ensues and that's it. It's not a long game (think the original Portal in terms of length) but to be fair it is priced appropriately, get it on sale and it's worth a few hours entertainment.

It's tough with steam reviews since the only options they give you is either "recommended" or "not recommended" which doesn't allow for nuance.
As someone who loved the original game, Hotline Miami 2 is not a bad game by any means, but it's also not a great game either. It's a "recommended only for certain people" verdict from me.
Pros
- Smooth and (mostly) responsive gameplay.
- Excellent soundtrack, probably the strongest part of the game.
- Has many references to the original game's story which is nice for fans of the series.
- Decent diversity in number of locations you visit.
Cons
- The storyline tries very hard to feel deep and controversial, but it's paper thin and generally incoherent. This is especially a shame considering the first game, while not a literary masterpiece, had a generally coherent and interesting storyline. It tries to tell too many narratives, but ultimately just feels hollow. You will likely not care about any of the protagonists or antagonists as they all blend in together in their violence.
- The "explicit" sexual scenes really add nothing to the storyline. It feels like the developer added it just to be controversial. It didn't bother me, and you can skip it, but it felt completely unncessary.
- The game feels "buggy" or at least inconsistent at many points, eg: the range for melee weapons seems random at times. Also sometimes enemies become invulnerable when they enter doorways, and god help you if a bunch of enemies run into a swinging door, all hell breaks loose. The game is also very RNG based, which can be good or bad depending on your view.
- The sequel switches to very heavily gun focused gameplay. There are lots of hallways that make melee almost always suicidal. The only way around this is to "bait" enemies into corners and then mash them with your weapon. This gets old quick, and I wish there was more variety in the strategies you could employ.
- The windows, oh my god, the windows. Apparently in the late 80's and early 90's, Miami city adopted ordinances which led to the construction of 5 billion windows inside every building. Be prepared to be shot through countless windows.
- The game's difficulty just feels cheap generally. I beat it in 8 hours, but content wise, there's probably 1/2 of that, which is artificially inflated by amount of times you'll have to die. Most of it is just trial, error, and frustration as you constantly get killed by gun wielding enemies at the far edge of the map, or attack dogs that spawn behind you.
- Because of the above points, you will generally spend most of the game holding the shift button to peek around the edge of your screen and hope that a shotgun enemy doesn't blast you from a hidden location.
- The difficulty is also very inconsistent. Some levels feel fun and challenging, while others just become a chore as you mow down dozens and dozens of gun wielding enemies.
- A lot of the masks or weapons you unlock are really underwhelming, and this is a missed opportunity for gameplay variety.
Verdict: Ultimately, I beat the game and felt like I got my money's worth. However, certain levels and stretches of the game felt like an absolute chore to get through, and I found myself just hoping it would end already. The storyline wasn't satisfying to me either (despite a cool last level).
Pick this game up if it's on sale and you're a big fan of the original. Otherwise, you can probably safely skip this, you won't miss out on much.
TLDR: Semi-recommended. Decent game but not great, and not as good as the first.

Ace of Spades is a FPS game that offers two "distinct" gameplay features:
1. A shooter, one with classes of your choosing and unique weapons that are given for each class. Missile launcher, shot gun, grenades, ext...
2. An art style and gameplay clearly taken from Minecraft. You're able to build your bunkers, mine into enemy towers and otherwise prepare strategies with your forces to take out the other team.
And while the gameplay does have these things, all of them are used to the bare minimum, unfortunately. Specific character classes are imitations from Team Fortress 2, and are pretty unbalanced... Snipers have the ability to fire killing blows from one edge of the map to the other; the General has the only fire power worth using in close range combat. Not that these are necessarily bad things, as with most FPSs it does take time to get that good with a sniper and even more time to learn how to outmaneuver him with your General/Sniper. But once you have, what's the point of using the engineer and the miner who are essentially useless?
And that's where the other problem comes in. With uneven classes, the miner and engineer are basically used for the "building" part of the game. But there isn't really such a thing. You can create instant shields and build a bridge, but there's always a way around it and no real reason to ever create those things to begin with besides a little cover fire. That's because the individual blocks can be destroyed by bullets or missiles pretty easily. You can destroy structures, but all buildings have the same resiliency, so any weapon will break through barriers in their own time. Even the uniquely structured maps (which don’t look half bad), are all basically made out of the same material for you to destroy. Each map probably won’t get used to the full extent that it should.
If there’s anything I liked about the game, I will say that multiplayer is easy to get into and takes only seconds to link up with friends or online players. And it is fun to play for those first few rounds, but only because I enjoyed the company I was with, which made the game more amusing than it actually is.
Summary:
Ace of Spades is a Minecraft/TF2 combination with average shooter play, and very limited sandbox functions. (Though I have yet to try out the battle builder feature) It's not really worth the time... Go play TF2 (which is free) or Minecraft (with tougher gameplay) instead.
Usually I would write something concerning the art and soundtrack, but neither is outstanding in any way.

Dark Sector is a near future third-person shooter in which you play spec-ops CIA agent Hayden Tenno. Tenno is sent to the virus infected, fictional Eastern Bloc country of Lasria to "eliminate a target." While there he is exposed to a biological compound which mutates his arm, giving him the ability to create and hurl a 3-bladed glaive-like weapon. This weapon acts as a boomerang, can damage and dismember enemies as well as capture various elements for greater effects. After his mutation Hayden sets out to halt the spread of the virus and destroy those who infected him. Here are my thoughts on Dark Sector;
Pros
+ Gorgeous graphics.
+ Dark storyline.
+ Phenomenal musical score and ambient soundscape.
+ Challenging but not frustratingly impossible boss battles.
+ The glaive is truly an awesome weapon. The developers perfected its use in the game.
+ Brutal and gory combat, especially with the glaive.
+ Many horror scares in the game.
Cons
- No patch was ever released.
- Some load up problems, although they're easily fixed with a restart.
- Inventory and upgrade system could use some tweaks and a bit more explanation
- Money for upgrades is rather scarce.
- No jumping or crouching, just a Gears of War style dash and cover system. The dashing can be a bit disorienting if you're not used to it.
- Reoccurring sound distortion where static/wind noises would be amplified and constant completely overpowering all other sounds in the game. This issue is constant and will not fix itself even on a restart of the game. The only way I figured out how to fix it was by resetting the sound controls to default.
- No stealth gameplay or mechanics.
- Story became rather secondary.
- Enemy types are rather limited and constant Waves of them can become a bit tiresome.

Gameplay:
Paced like a stealth game, plays like an cover shooter without sticking to cover (edit: apparently you *can* stick to cover, the game just fails to mention this, the dodge roll and grenade controls in the first level tutorial messages, because of great game design). The gimmick is two-fold:
#1. You are some kind of infected anime mutant, who can throw a boomerang blade a la Xena's chakram, and can't hold non-handguns for too long because of "infection detectors", which combust the guns after about a minute.
Graphics:
Grey. The game is, depending on the locale and time of day, different hues of monotone gray. Detail level is on par with multiplatform games of the era.
Story:
It's a combination of all the worst tropes: things start in medias res, there's an "X years later" timejump, a ton of hamfisted exposition, etc. etc.
The "low down":
I don't mind the slightly dated graphics, the protagonists horrible potato head is actually pretty funny, but the game is just a slog. 3rd person shooters have iterated since the naughties, and Dark Sector constantly manages to remind you of this. I've only played about 40 minutes, which is apparently just ~5%-10% of the whole experience, but I just got so bored I couldn't bring myself to continue. I'd watch a Let's Play of this, if it was heavily edited down to speed things along.
Aparently the developers recent release, Warframe, lifts some names and aesthetics, and most positive reviews on Steam seem to recommend it because of this. I haven't played Warframe after the beta, and did not make the connection, nor did learning about the link make me any more interested in giving Dark Sector another go.

Visually intriguing, demonstrates some interesting concepts and executes really slickly - extremely lavish environments and  FX potentially belie origins as a tech demo but otherwise worth price of entry for those interested in visual/atmosphere design in games for sure.
MAJOR negative is the narrative, which is conveyed in blunt fashion thru narrated clips attached to objects of interest and primarily concerns super ableist/gross elaborations on the nature of "Madness" (Summarized the message is essentially "mentally ill people are terrifying") and piles on schlocky and exploitative references to self harm and suicide w no real understanding of the weight of these topics or sensitive portrayal thereof. You can do this stuff in games, you just can't do it like this and expect it to be taken seriously - using mental illness as a prop to create a Spooky Setup is super crass and smacks of amateur and ignorant approaches to narrative design.
In short - I can't recommend this game to anyone who wants to engage w it on more than a visual or technical level - there's a lot of talent on show here and as an exercise in genuinely inventive and compelling set pieces, I had a lot of fun with it. But unless the narrative is heavily revised before release I don't want to encourage this kind of boogeyman approach to portrayal of mental illness.
