The Evil Within is Shinji Mikami's new playground for survival horror, and though it has its stumbles, it is nonetheless a triumphant return to the survival horror genre.
First of all, the letterboxes in the game are both distracting and obstructing. They cripple your field of vision and disable you from gathering your surroundings properly. Thankfully Bethesda gave the option to disable the letterboxes. The Evil Within does look great though, the atmosphere throughout the game is always appropriate and helps immerse the player.
In terms of gameplay, The Evil Within does an excellent job of building tension by placing you in uncomfortable situations and forcing you to make your best judgment to overcome obstacles. Every resource in the game seems deliberately placed, giving you just enough to survive. The budgeting of resources causes the player to think more about how to overcome obstacles with maximum efficiency and adds alot of choices and depth to the gameplay. During your encounters with the Laura and The Keeper, the game does a poor job of communicating what course of action you should take to survive and I found myself dying alot in trial and error. The game also had too few segments which required stealth, and the game becomes heavily action oriented after chapter 10.
I actually found the story in The Evil Within to be fairly interesting despite it's painfully boring characters. It did a good job keeping me invested to the very end, though admittedly the ending could've been executed better. Nonetheless, a horrific world created from the network of psychopathic minds is an intensely interesting idea, and is the perfect playground for Mikami's horrific imagination. The premise of the game is especially interesting when you take the time to identify what memory or mental defect concieved each monster you face in the game.
There is plenty of room for improvement in The Evil Within, and I hope Tango Gameworks takes some of the low points into consideration. I think there is great potential in this new title, and I'm looking forward to future installments.
8/10

This game has a long history of urban legend. It was originally rumoured to have been made due to id Software employees being disgruntled at Nintendo for censoring the SNES Wolfenstein 3D, and handing the source code to Wisdom Tree, but this rumour has turned out to be untrue. Wisdom Tree legally liscensed the engine from id Software, in a boringly normal way. Even though the rumours were nothing more than urban legend, I still was interested in seeing this oddity for myself.
I bought it for curiosity's sake as an AVGN fan, and found it's actually not as bad as I expected. It's just a Wolfenstein 3D mod with some decent levels and a strange premise. I've seen worse. If you can get past the odd aesthetics of the game, then you might as well give it a try, considering that the dev who ported this oddity is the developer for ECWolf, a great source port of Wolfenstein 3D, (which this game happens to run on) as well as a developer for ZDoom. I don't mind throwing a few bucks to support Blzut3, considering his work on ECWolf and ZDoom, both of which are great source ports.
If you are concerned about the religious theme of the game, don't worry, it's pretty much just windowdressing. I'm an Atheist, and the game doesnt bother me. It's not trying to push an agenda or anything, it's just Wolfenstein 3D where you go around shooting nazi animals. The game was pretty much created to sell FPS games to overprotective parents. I view it as a novelty game, and nothing more than an odd modification of Wolf3D.

Like the movie Edge of Tomorrow but you're the one who has to keep repeating the same events over and over until you get everything right.
Has A LOT of potential but is mired in flaky and counter-immersive mechanics.   About every other level amounts to being chased by an enemy you can't kill from checkpoint to checkpoint, and saves are agonizingly few.  You may think this sounds like a fun challenge on the order of Dark Souls, but in actuality you're tied to a very linear path with pre-determined events.  Furthermore, the actions you take don't always work the same across playthroughs.  For example, a certain "long haired bloody woman" sometimes spawns further away from her "typical" spawn point than intended, meaning your fastest-but-riskiest means of killing her suddenly becomes a deathtrap for you.
Additionally, progress seems almost neglibible as none of the major enemies ever actually stays dead.  Not one!  Granted, you can "kill" some of them temporarily (usually at a tremendous cost of ammunition) but the effect doesn't generally last beyond a single checkpoint (and please note that checkpoint doesn't always mean save point).  Mechanically this is meaningless, but psychologically it means you ultimately never seem to make visible progress.  Instead you fight the same opponents over and over again, always being unable to kill them either within invidual encounters or across the game at large.  This is immensely discouraging.
The net effect of these flaws is that the whole thing feels like a glorified puzzle game rather than a skill-dependent shooter, an exercise that can (and often has to be) solved by trial and error; and the horror is rapidly displaced by frustration and tedium after having to repeat the same cinematics and actions eighteen times in a row.
For point of reference, I've played every Resident Evil game, most of the Silent Hill games, and all of the Dead Space games.  They've all had their ups and downs, but none of them has ticked me off as consistently as this without delivering some measure of fright, tension, or laughter.
Ultimately I want to support this game, but the truth is that I repeatedly find myself turning it off in frustration.

If I had to give this review a title, I'd call it Opportunity Lost.
The Evil Within struggles very hard to be a true successor to Resident Evil 4. It builds upon RE4's basis and improves it with an almost Silent Hill-esque insanity setting, a little bit of the new horror era features and everything Mikami wanted to put into RE4 but couldn't for whatever reasons.
And I tried really, really hard to appreciate it for what it is or, at the very least, for what it tries to be. However the game ends up blatantly mimmicking other projects and failing to recreate their features in a satisfying way - be they features from fellow horror games,, simple monster shooters or Mikami's own creations. I still don't understand why.
The starting chapter introduces you to what looks like a genuinely creepy and thrilling setting, but as a fan of Outlast I couldn't help but notice the fact that I've done it all before. All of it. Imagining the rest of the game would be like Outlast with weapons, I move on only to realize how misinformative the intro sequence is.
As the adventure went on, I noticed familiar elements from RE4 in terms of gameplay, Alan Wake in terms of atmosphere (at least in the forest) and The Last of Us in terms of controls, don't ask why.
Point is, the game constantly feels like it's trying to be its own thing while being something else, and ends up being much less than the sum of its parts. The chaotic story and the seemingly brain numb protagonist don't help. Sure, RE characters were cheesy as hell, but for some reason you cared about them. Detective Drunken Voice from EW on the other hand - not so much. I almost felt liberated at one point when I got killed, as if giving me a justification to stop playing.
Keep in mind that I've only played for 3 hours and there's still a lot to this game, but even throughout these 3 hours I got bored a lot. It's not scary. It may be a good atmospheric adventure with monsters though, if you're into that sort of thing.
I wouldn't say it's a blatantly bad game, because on paper it isn't. I'd even go as far as saying you should try it. Just know what to expect from it and be prepared to be bored if you were expecting psychological horror and not a lot of blood and guts.
Otherwise I'd recommend you to stay away from it and treat yourself to a nice big Jill Sandwich in the RE1 remake.

This game is proof that history repeats itself.
The original Deus Ex, an excellent game which won Game of the Year, was followed by Deus Ex: Invisible War. A game that wasn't bad, but which was rushed, and which really didn't live up to the first game. The mechanics and storyline were just a little bit worse, is all.
Fast forward to Deus Ex: Human Revolution. A prequel to the original, and an absolutely FANTASTIC game. And now we have this game, The Fall. It really wasn't bad; I'm not going to give it a thumbs down by any means. Hell, I just played through it in a day. I could hardly put it down. But it just didn't live up to the standard set by Human Revolution. It felt extremely rushed (the game isn't even finished yet, more content has yet to be released for the second part), with very few mechanics changed and those that were seeming a bit clunky and off. Especially irritating was the lack of a jump (what is this, The Stanley Parable?). The plot was engaging, but the few choices the player had were essentially meaningless to the ending.
If you're a hardcore Deus Ex fan like myself, then you might as well get this game. If it's on sale, and you liked Human Revolution, you might as well get this game. If you haven't played any other Deus Ex games, don't get this game! It does not stand alone! If you're looking for something different from Human Revolution, don't get this game! If you are expecting a full-blown game, and not just a 3-hour mini-game to tide us over while the real next game in the Deus Ex series is being worked on, don't bother getting this game.

That update has FINALLY come out, and it couldn't be any more clear that this is a scam. What's the big change?... a simple UI overhaul. under [Windows_Config,/Types/Config]
add
Graphics.DisplayAspectRatio=FullScreen4x3

News Tycoon is the wrong execution of the right idea. The news industry is a fascinating concept to explore, given then industry's social-engineering, black-propaganda and other aspects. News Tycoon gently touches on this this, with various entites offering incentives, often large cash payments, to spin articles in their favor. However, the game is very much in an incomplete and partly broken state, and it doesn't appear that the developers are very interested in correcting even the simplest flaws, despite their critical impact. As of the writing of this review, the last response to a bug report was in April of 2017. To make matters worse, they've been advised of and acknowledged easily remedied flaws, such as mispelling "Korea" as "Corea," but they've yet to correct the problem.
Major flaws include such things as the player being unable to sort topics by relevance. The option to sort be relevance is available, but not all topics are displayed when doing so. In fact, only a very small percentage is. This means that as your staff grows, you can either micromanage everyone, choosing each topic for them, or you can allow them to choose their own topics, but the relevance will be random. This is comparable to India declaring war on China tomorrow, and newspapers printing articles on increasing electricity prices and the sale of a spoon manufacturer, but never an article on anything relevant to the war, or relevant to the reader at all. The "relevance" of your paper will plummet, as will your revenue and subscribers. The bugged relevance sorting is probably an easy fix, but the developers can't be bothered with correcting that bug, nor any other.
While the relevance issue is a glaring flaw which forces the player to tediously micromanage their journalists, or suffer poor ratings and sales, a variety of smaller issues will also be immediately obvious. There's little variety in the subjects available. You'll be writing the same articles over and over again. You might be surprised how often America's president decides to fire the entire government on New Years Day, how often that same president resigns, or how often NASA announces a mission to Mars. There's also very few topics available in general. Whatever subject your journalists specializes in, they'll run out of subjects to report on often. There's an entire world of "economics," "politics" and so forth taking place, but your staff is oblivious, and you'll have to invest massive sums of money, maxing-out your news organization's ability to discover news, just to ensure a single journalist in any subject will be aware of enough events to consistently have something to write about on their assigned subject, and even then he/she will still have to write about some other random topic fairly regularly. Apparently your journalists have never heard of the internet, and apparently the game's developers have never heard of newswires like Reuters or AFP.
A game on this topic could be fascinating, and thus this game has potential. The developers are however investing no effort what-so-ever. News Tycoon looks dead. To make matters worse, the developers have disabled Steam Workshop, so even if the community wished to correct the game's problems, it can't be done in any practical fashion. Not that there is a community. Until the developers start developing again, if that day ever comes, and until, at a bare minimum, the developers correct the easy-to-fix autosearch/relevance bug, I don't recommend this game. As of this moment, News Tycoon appears to be abandoned, incomplete and broken.
Lastly, even if the developers begin developing again, and even if the relevance/autosearch bug is corrected, I can't recommend this game at any price greater than $4.99, especially considering Steam Workshop has been disabled. That limits the game's potential, and also suggests the developers intend to intentionally leave things out so that they can sell them to you later as DLC.

tldr:
pros
-The UI is simple and quick to master
-Some ability to automate reports
-News articles have entertaining titles
cons
-no real tutorial or guides
-readers have no clear quality requirements.  Producing a paper with the same number of articles of the ssame average quality with the same reader base may add several readers or lose several
-Quests are buggy or poorly presented, sometimes failing to recognize that writing 5 "economics" notes qualifies as 5 notes about "the economy"
News Tycoon is a relatively simple game with some relatively basic problems.  The basic objective of the game is the same as most simulator / tycoon games; build a customer base and balance expenses against profit.  With no tutorial or manual, and a seemingly arbitrary determination of the quality of your paper, your ability to grow your reader base will be extremely limited, and the game therefore extremely frustrating.

I confess: I was excited, as much as anyone, prior to the game's release, bought it, was immediately dissappointed, then excited, disappointed again (slightly less, however, than the previous dissapointment), and now have arrived at place that is firmly grounded in reality...or at the very least, a place of compromise.  This utterly changed the experience for me, in a very positive way.
The game required a lot of setting adjustments, more than usual, before I felt comfortable playing it.  This isn't a complaint mind you, since every game requires at least a little, but in my case, a lot of trial and error was in order.  Again, not a complaint.
The controls and feel-of-play was the source of initial frustration; mostly because I stubbornly fought the game tooth and nail, playing against it, rather than on its own terms.  Sadly, this tactic failed.  Once I accepted the game's functionality for what it was, and not what it could have been, the game and I got along very nicely.  You can get spoiled by some of the smooth-as-glass mechanics and controls of certain games.  Evil Within's controls can sometimes feel deliberately clunky, inaccurate or shockingly unresponsive.  This apparently is by design, which in my opinion, is okay, and once I adjusted my play-style to accomodate this aspect of the game, it created a much more enjoyable experience overall.  But, I will admit, it doesn't take long to realize that the ackward controls do not enhance the terror, they only amplify the frustration.  To the game's defense, however, all of the enemies, including the boses, are stricken with the same mobility-ailments that you are afflicted with, giving the combat encounters a sense of fairness.  And I became more, and more accepting of this the further into the game I played.  *Be forewarned: you will die countless times.  At one point, I had to stop because I reached a stress limit, and, to calm my nerves, elected to play, Dark Souls for a bit.  This game can be brutal.  You will die over, and over again...and many of those deaths will not be your fault.
Lastly, I enjoyed the game a whole lot more when I chose to thoroughly search levels for anything and everything that could be found, resisting the urge to run through the game.  In fact, this aspect of the gameplay is why I'm recommending this game.  Alien: Isolation, I felt, failed on this point, whereas, Evil Within succeeded.  Yes, I died many times in both games, but I felt more rewarded and a greater sense of progression with Evil Within.
Frustrating-fun at its best.  I would rate the overall experience a solid 8.7 / 10; a high mark for a solid horror game.  This is the closest thing to actually being in a real horror movie that you will ever experience.

is a 1-4 player cooperative game in the style of Left 4 Dead. The action is unequivocally fast-paced and sticking together is vital for avoiding the team dying a quick death. It was clearly built with a primary motive of supplying replay value, but it of course depends largely on your investment in the atmosphere, mechanics, and loot system.
I'll note here that I know very little of Warhammer fantasy but still enjoyed the game and the setting, and also that I bought the game pre-release.
Some DLC was released for the game but the developers seem to have taken measures to avoid it splitting up the playerbase too much. You do not necessarily need to purchase the DLC in order to play the DLC.
Sigmar's Blessing and Last Stand were just free updates to the game. The first was to improve the loot system and the second adds a survival mode with one free survival map (based on a section of a regular map).
The Schlusselschloss DLC was a second survival mode map (this time unique). You can play it without paying for it by selecting 'Last Stand' and then selecting to play a 'Random' level or by having a friend with the DLC invite you to the game.
The Drachenfels DLC adds three more regular maps, and again a friend can invite you to the game even if you don't own the DLC yourself (you're still fighting Skaven and it's largely more of the same, to some people's dismay).
it's a fun game for people who like frantic cooperative gameplay. It's fairly easy to get into but also requires you to learn and evolve in order to tackle the higher difficulties. And it's essentially a multiplayer game. Attention to detail and loot progress mean replayability is the focus.

Originally released on the Super Nintendo in 1995, 20 years later here with are with a steam release. Was it worth the wait? Well, if you love retro games and grew up playing Wolfenstein/Spear of Destiny/Ken's Labyrinth and the bunch of other spinoffs/mods.
Gone is the simple dosbox and rom option (free extra in game folder), instead you are treated to the full makeover that older games deserve. Including modern OS support, mouse support, gamepad support, resolutions and screen ratios that scale up to 4k along with steam achievements and cloud support. It's like comparing the classic release of shadow warrior/duke nukem with the redux editions, night and day.
Wisdom Tree have a history of christian based games on a range of platforms. Many of them were quite good but not often sold in stores, Bible Adventures was a personal favorite. Friends constantly wanted to 'borrow' my copies and you certainly didn't need to be religious to enjoy them. Very family friendly games as well. Animals are not killed but merely put to 'sleep' and weapons are slingshots that shoot food at that animals.

So what this is is an old Wolfenstein 3D total conversion that was originally released as an unlicensed SNES cart. I guess there was a DOS version too because it's included with this version. I don't know if the updated version is based on an existing Wolf3D source port (it seems like it might be ECWolf) but whatever it is, it's pretty fantastic. It's got full controller support that's better than what you see in most modern games. It offers full control remapping and you can input custom names on your saved games using a controller (most games struggle with this very basic feature). A wide range of 4:3 and 16:9 resolutions are on tap (4k+ included) with proper aspect ratio scaling options.
As for the game itself, I haven't yet played enough to speak to the overall quality of its gameplay mechanics, but I'll say this: The first kind of enemy you encounter in Super 3-D Noah's Ark is an angry goat that charges at you in a zig-zag pattern, so it's wilier than a Nazi at least. For that reason alone it seems to be about on par with the game it's based on, one that remains to this day a highlight of the early FPS era. There are no quicktime events.
Super 3-D Noah's Ark is a quality product that performs better than recent AAA release Batman: Arkham Knight in every regard and is well worth the $5 they're asking for it. This isn't an ironic review and frankly if you think it is then that's on you. Try to shed your defenses for one second and accept that this weird 20 year old Bible game could actually be pretty good, ya dingus.
You can knock goats, sheep, and even a goddamn bear unconscious with a slingshot as an old man. 10/10. Nobody screws with Noah, not even Chuck Norris.

I have always been a huge Star Trek fan since as long as I can remember. I remember vividly my dad going out of his way to purchase me all of the model ships and I'd create my own fleets and adventures across the galaxy. Meeting new lifeforms and new civilizations of my own - essentially living out all those amazing moments from the TV series I adore. As I've "grown" (in age but still childish at heart) toys have given way to the more accepted choice of roleplay - videogames.
There has never really before been a game to capture the essence of what is Star Trek. Mostly generic shooters with nothing more to add than space combat, Star Trek games fall short of capturing the dreams of aspiring captains. Star Trek online however is differant. It adds something new to the mix. Storylines, player driven content and at last a ship that you can actually call your very own.
The gameplay is very solid. Essentially a game designed with two modes - Space and ground exploration/combat. You level up your ship, captain and crew respectivly giving them differant abilities and strategies to aid you as you visit distant galaxies. There is a multitude of Episode missions that allow you to progress through the story as well as hundreds of differant paths for you to take your character in. If you want to be a diplomat, there are missions and a level system in place for that. Or if you want to be a spy, or a research scientist, trader - ANYTHING, you will have a place in the star trek universe.
There are two factions to play through thus far. Each with their own storylines, cultures, ships, territory and fleets (guilds in other MMOS) and there is enough content in each to have you playing for well over a year to fully flesh out your character. There have been some complaints and not without foundation that the game was very generic and bland. While this was true the first year and a half of the games life, this has vastly changed in the latter half of this games lifespan so far. Remember this game is an ongoing project released well before schedule because the fans demanded it released. so bare with the constant updates.
If you can forgive this games minor flaws and see it's charm you will find you will invest months of playtime into this game. Personally I find the opposing faction, the KDF more accessable gameplay style.
In fairness - if you don't like Star Trek then you wont like this game. It has enjoyable gameplay features you will like however, but if you ARE a fan of Star Trek then you will Cherish what this game is and what it will become

Cryptic does a nice job with the grapics not just in space but also on planets that you visit and explore making them rich, full, and beautiful. There is so much to do and see. Go on an exploration tour of an unexplored part of the galaxy. Manage your crew in real time with tasks and missions that complete even when you are logged off. Join up with MACO and commit yourself to the front line of the Borg invasion to earn unique items and equipment. Speaking of equipment, there are all sorts of devices and weapon types to choose from and, with the exception of kits which are linked to your classes powers, you are not limited in what you can use. The skill system is simple and straight forward while still allowing for experienced players to specialize their character in a number of different areas including damage, survival, healing, or even disruption and support. And best of all, it's completely free to play.
Even if you are not a Star Trek fan, this game is fun, fast, friendly and best of all free!!

Think of Scrap Mechanic as a graphically polished Minecraft with a few degrees in mechanical engineering. If you like building a variety of simple to complex structures and vehicles, this game is for you. Several different locomotive resources (regular engines, electric engines, thrusters, etc.) can be combined with a variety of materials with different weight and bearings. Add in buttons, switches, controllers (that can program bearings to move at set angles) and some interesting glitches to further flesh out building more than just a car with 4 wheels.
The only big issue currently is that, being in alpha, they're still working on optimization. I have a high-end rig so I don't have any problems running the game unless I flood it with thrusters and other things, but your milage may vary.
Mind you, this is just in alpha and yet I've had an amazing time with the game already for the few hours I put into it. The full game promises more and I can't wait to see what it'll be like!

As of late, I've been on a cheesy movie kick. Movies like Commando, The Last Starfighter, and Universal Soldier. Action movies that take themselves deadly serious, but are over the top hilarious, and feel kind of kitchy. After marathoning these beautiful pieces of garbage, I asked myself: Are there any games like this?
Dark Sector is one such game. Dark sector is a game trying so hard to be serious and dark, yet made by a team so inexperienced and unfamiliar with the Unreal Engine, that it often trips on it's own shoelaces. This game has UI-resolution issues, floaty character movement, not nearly enough ammo drops, no online (only LAN matches, which is a tribute to this game's age), special abilites that are either overpowered or completely useless, and lackluster special effects.
But the game is trying so gosh darn hard to be a dark gritty sci-fi action tale, it's absolutely adorable. If the game acknowledged how cheesy and stupid it was, I wouldn't shy away from describing it as a second rate...no, third-rate MGS3 clone. Imagine if MGS3 was made by a much less talented team, was much less ambitious, and yet at the same time, just a bit more morbid. This is the kind of game you lump in with games like Legendary, Ride to Hell, and Rogue Warrior. Games so bad, you absolutely have to experience them at least once. Wait for a sale, as $10.00 is double the price of what it's worth, but give it a shot. The game is begging for your approval.

I normally hate turn based games and MMOs, but I found Wakfu to be rather enjoyable. Lots of variation between the different classes, and different ways to play each class too. It's super fun when you find a guild to play with.
I'd say it's not really worth spending money on because it's poorly managed, but it's easily worth someone's time investment to just dip their feet in and experience most of what this game has to offer.
However, this game also has some pretty blatant issues, and I'm a firm believer that the best to to figure out if you'd like to try out a game is to acknowledge it's issues beforehand and to considered whether you'll be able to tolerate them or not.
-There's technical issues such as it running on Java(which has memory leaks), and each patch brings more bugs. The recent patch had a bug to make a certain class invincible.
-There's a massive population issue where you'll pretty much have to solo unless you join a guild. And good luck finding someone to PVP with. Mid-late game dungeons will pretty much require multiple players, or even a full team.
-There's overall poor design choices such as the politics system which allow an individual to lock down all of a nation's resources just for the heck of it. Or allowing players to activate PVP against others so long as they're not 50 levels above themselves; so a level 200 player could attack and hinder the progression of level 25s all they want with no consequences.
-There's glaring balancing issues, some classes are just significantly stronger in PVE and PVP such as Sacrier, whereas some are near useless in both like Sram. There are also dungeons where melee classes are useless, or ranged classes are a lot less effectve.
-Quests are few and far apart, most of your levelling will have to come from repeatedly grinding monsters.
-There's very little to do apart from grinding for exp. Most motivation one has to play this game would come from group activities.
-Due to this being a relatively older game, player-set prices on the marketboard suffer from quite a bit of inflation.
-Newer classes and zones are locked behind a paywall. A zone(the only decent endgame one) is still locked behind a paywall despite being released about 9 months ago.
-The puns and excessive use of parodies make the game lose a bit of it's professional feeling and sense of it being an RPG. It got super tiresome for me. Most item's flavor text is also gibberish or jokes too.
And worst of all, players can not participate in the Christmas event unless they have spent real money on this game! For shame, Aknama! How dare you hold Santa hostage from players for ransom money!

They seriously need to up their PR game. Weekly updates would be awesome. Even short ones, just a few sentences saying they added new graphics to 2 buildings and tested 3 new contracts. Whatever. Anything to let us know that work is still being done. Something that will keep us even mildly interested. And make the game look less like just another Early Access that went down the drain of development hell.
In the end, like I said, it has potential. It's current state is playable (at least, i've been able to launch satellites, but that's it), but is so very barebones right now. I hope to someday change this to a yes and go get it recommendation, but at this rate, it's going to be a while.
UPDATE: They've finally released their long awaited "Apollo Update". The game looks quite a bit better. There's quite a bit more to do. It's seems to not be abandoned just yet. There's a lot that still needs work. Many of the buildings don't have a GUI or any use really yet outside of required for research. It looks like you can build the buildings, research the technologies and build sapcey things. One significant point to note, the amount of spacey things you can build is ridiculous. This was obviously the meat of the update (along with the graphics and GUI). The number of satellites, rockets, pieces of equipment are extensive. You can go all the way to building a fully sustainable Mars Base on the planet of Mars, it looks like. The one thing I wish they had put into this release was the contracts idea with the NSaAO, but that's not in there yet.
I won't change this to recommended quite yet, but the game is playable, with all the research and pieces you need to build a Mars Base it looks like. If this game is something you want or are looking forward to, I would consider getting your hopes up. I'll probably change this to a yes once they get the contract system up and running so that you can have an effective, money-making space enterprise. I'm feeling much more positive about this game now.

The concept is good but the game does not go deep enough. Workers do not take breaks and the day never ends. The sky changes and worker attribute drop over time, but there is no recovery or rest. Either there are not enough random populated stories or the posting of them have a random relevance ratio that doesn't work. Settings for the worker to make selections of stories do not always work and workers continue to make the same mistakes regardless of their level. Without any constant personal attributes or recovery / rest periods each day, no real sense can be made about their performance. The workspaces do not seem to have any real benefit either. What is comfort suppose to do for a worker? I could go on but the list is far to long. This is suppose to be a newspaper, but this game only deals with recording and producing it. Where are the people these stories are about and who are the people developing them? There are writers, photographers, proofreaders, copy, and editors, not to mention all the other things in the paper like cartoons, ads, and classifieds. The revenue stream from a paper is quite complex and even without the other media streams that are not within the game, a newspaper is a rich project to make a game the subject of to start. Get to work or dump the project.

Anyway, my biggest complaint is you cannot keep readers. You can lose all your readership with one bad issue. And you cannot really help it because you will automate your staff and if there is no celebrity news available, they just do another genre and boom, your readership dwindles.
It's hard to make money, seriously. You need the larger building to hire more than one other person and have a rest area, but then that $5,000 a month rent comes and just eats up anything you have made plus more. You can do these 'quests' to pay the bills, but guess what publishing a couple of notes a bout economics does to your readership levels.

You ever thought about how the world is going to end? Nuclear war, giant meteor, zombie apocalypse?
Well as it turns out, it’s rats! Big, giant, ugly rats… with mini-guns.
You and your group of misfits are caught right in the middle of it and the only option is to work together, decapitate rats and do whatever the local pub’s landlord tells you to do.
Vermintide is a lot of fun. The combat system is fluid and works well in 1st person. With a hack and slash I personally favour 3rd person mode but is helped by game options that can tweak your field of view. You don’t need to hit the enemy right in the middle of your crosshair, instead it simulates well the force and range of a mighty slash and thrust with your weapon of choice.
The combat is fast paced and often manic when pushing back hordes (and I do mean hordes) of stinky sewer rats. Team work is key and each character has their unique playstyle and abilities to help and counter certain enemies or situations.
There’s no real backstory for the characters at the start of the game (although a google search will find great backstories) but through hilarious and well written and voice acted interactions during the game, you start to see who these people are and how they ended up in the sewer storm that is the city of Ubersreik.
There is a nice crafting and loot system for you to personalise and upgrade your warriors, including new blades and blunderbuss’ or a new hat with an even bigger feather! Trust me, in the game the big feather makes sense.
The enemies are also well rounded and varied, from slave rats with daggers, to mini-gun wielding psycho rats and even giant rat ogres! The game system also slightly randomises encounters, so when you replay a level (which you will) don’t expect it to happen the way it did before.
The game is tough, it’s the end of the world after all and there are no auto saves or checkpoints during missions, meaning if you fail, it’s right back to the start like the good old gaming days of old! The missions themselves aren’t long but you will probably make several attempts before actually completing one. Checkpoints would be a nice addition as you will fail a few times and going back to the beginning does start to create level fatigue. I tend to dip in and out of Vermintide for small gaming sessions with friends, rather than a whole weekend of rat-slaying chaos!
Ultimately, this is a multiplayer game with a 4 human/dwarf/elf/wizard/crazy person team. That’s not to say you can’t play on your own, the AI isn’t bad although obviously it’s not as good (or sometimes as bad) as human players. The ability for players to hot join games is great, optional feature.
Although I’ve played solo, the game really shines when I’m playing with friends. Holding your ground, screams of panic, calling for help and cursing as you run crying from a rat ogre!
If you want a fun, manic and wonderfully detailed world with great characters to run around in with friends, then Vermintide is for you.

I went into Super 3D Noah's Ark expecting a Christian-themed joke of a game, but instead I got a solid Wolfenstein 3D clone.
First off: This port is excellent. Noah's Ark has been entirely remade from scratch in ECWolf, a source port of the original Wolfenstein 3D engine. As such, Super 3D Noah's Ark has a lot of modern amenities that you wouldn't expect of a 20 year old DOS game: Native compatibility with modern OSes (no DOSbox), support for 16:9 resolutions, non-buggy mouselook functionality, even extra fluff like achievements. The developers did a better job at modernizing this game than iD did with Doom or Wolfenstein; no half-assing at all.
The game itself is basically Wolfenstein 3D with a biblical coat of paint. If you enjoyed Wolfenstein 3D's gameplay, you'd probably enjoy this as well. The levels are all original, and pretty decently designed. There's a larger selection of weapons over vanilla Wolf3D: In addition to your "pistol" and "machine guns" (various slingshots which you use to propel animal feed), you have projectile weapons which function similarly to the rocket launcher and flamethrower from the SNES version of Wolfenstein. Gameplay is fluid and satisfying, and the game never drops below 60FPS.
If you're a fan of Wolf3D (or just want to experience a bizarre piece of video game history), this game is worth picking up.

I've heard some nasty things about Deus Ex: The Fall, so I booted it up cautiously. I'm a fan of Icarus Effect, the prequel novel to Human Revolution which this game pulls its characters and plot from, and I ventured into this game with the understanding that I may or may not get burned. What I found was a game that really wasn't all that bad, for being an iOS port job.
The most immediate thing you'll notice is the inferior graphics when compared to Human Revolution. This is natural for a straight port of a tablet/phone game, and doesn't really bother me. In fact, I consider it a plus, as the game actually runs very well with my integrated Intel setup. You'll then notice the widely varying quality of voicework, "eh" models, and stiff animations. The protagonist seems fidgety in conversation, but his entire upper body fidgets in a way that makes it seem as though his neck can't move, resulting in him turning his chest and head at the same time to look left and right and left and right and never at the person that he's talking to.
This is the sort of thing that you'll notice the game over. Everything's a little downgraded from Human Revolution, but not so downgraded as to ruin the game. There are certainly a number of faults, some of which I will be going over, but despite it all, the game
still fun to play. If you just want a little more Human Revolution and you've already played The Missing Link, then The Fall can do an alright enough job of filling that void for six or so hours.
Actually, on that note, let's just go ahead and address the length. I don't know what's going on with these people who complain that the game's so short because they beat it in two or four hours. You'd honestly have to be sprinting from objective to objective and ignoring all of the side quests for that to happen on your first playthrough. My first time through I explored the world, stealthed my way through everything, and did every sidequest available. Took me around nine hours. I'm not saying you'll definitely get nine, but expect at least six or seven if your goal is to enjoy the game, and not to reach the ending as quickly as possible.
The Fall is definitely easier than Human Revolution. Enemies don't spot you as easily, you can do takedowns and hack things while in cover and without poking your head out, and there aren't really enough consequences for being seen. If there are no enemies within the immediate vicinity, there's literally no reason to avoid being spotted by a camera. There aren't even any achievements for staying out of sight. Bodies disappear after a few seconds of being dead or unconscious. Other enemies can still see them for those few seconds, but once they fizzle out you're in the clear. Sneaking up on enemies and executing a takedown is still rewarding, it's just a little cheaper. And getting shot is certainly dangerous and something to be avoided. In fact, in close quarters, I've found that enemies can sometimes (and by sometimes I mean kind of embarrassingly often, in my case) shoot you for a one-hit kill.
There's no difficulty select in The Fall. You just start the game and go. Once you finish it, you can start again in new game+ with a tougher difficulty, but it turns out that that just means that the enemies have more health. The enemies are found in the same numbers, and they aren't any more aware of their surroundings. They just take a fat ton of shots to kill, which, if you're stealthing, should never even be a factor.
You can also go anywhere as soon as you get to the hub area. Anywhere at all that's accessible from that hub. There are no plot significant reasons keeping you from wandering into a place where you don't need to go yet, and murdering everything inside. In fact, the final minutes of the game can be made easier if you head through the area ahead of time and hack things and shut stuff down awhile.
There are visual glitches. The mouse tends to linger onscreen for a bit too long after closing anything that makes it appear, like ebooks and computer screens. Takedown animations have the worst of it, though. But as this doesn't really affect the gameplay and you'll be watching the same couple animations over and over again anyways, I find it more amusing than annoying.
Shooting is mostly from the hip-ish, which isn't as big of a problem as it sounds. You just have to get used to aiming better. Or, you know, forego guns and knock people out. Grenades aren't fun to aim, though. I usually save before throwing one because I know I'll probably miss once or twice.
Also, I don't entirely understand one major mechanic of hacking, which is that sometimes I can hack a node that's been taken over by the red node's creeping influence, but other times I can't. I wasn't able to figure out what decides this before I had enough praxis points in hacking that I never had to cross the problem again, anyways.
Apparently there were microtransactions in the iOS version, but those have thankfully been removed, here (unlike, say, Halo: Spartan Assault which hates you and wants you to know it). The persistent store still remains, and you can buy items at anytime with in-game currency, rather than finding a character in the hub to buy from. This can make things easier when you're low on snacks or booze (which I actually usually was, as I found it fun to drink ten bottles of beer and then pretend the audio was funky because I was having war flashbacks), but if you're smart you won't need to buy anything other than extra praxis kits because why be a human with a gun when you can be an invisible superhuman with the ability to shiskebab two low-paid hotel guards with families at the same time?
Deus Ex: The Fall can be fun if you're not expecting another Human Revolution DLC. It's lower quality in most aspects, but it's still worth a play. There's less detail than you might hope, but there was honestly
than I had expected, considering its original platform. The levels don't feel empty, things proceed quickly and can be as actiony as you'd like them to be. Unlike, say, Halo: Spartan Assault, where everything is slow and boring and levels are like three minutes long with twelve enemies to kill. It has a few social battles, it has some variety in action locations, and the writing and plot aren't awful (though the voice acting sometimes is). I do personally think that the game might have been better suited to being mission-based, rather than having a Human Revolution-styled hub. It's neat, but if you're going to make this mobile, I'd just like to jump in and out of some stealth, you know?
Also, I feel like I should mention that this is not a complete story. It ends on a to be continued, which is a bit of a bummer as I doubt whether we'll ever actually see another installment (which would have taken us to Australia, where I've been wanting to go in one of these ever since first reading about the Australian War in Icarus Effect).
Deus Ex: The Fall is decent enough. If you can find it for $2.50, or maybe even $5 if you're feeling adventurous, it'll work off its debt. And for the love of J.C. Denton, don't buy Halo: Spartan Assault. That's $3 I'll never get back.

I don't hate this game.
I bought it, at a discount, fully aware that it was an iOS port. As such, I was not surprised that the areas in the game were not as expansive and sprawling as those found in Deus Ex: Human Revolution, nor was I surprised that the graphics weren't as good as those in HR either (there is a noticeable difference in quality between character models for the protagonist and important NPCs versus background NPCs and generic enemies).
It's got a lot things in it that made HR great: atmospheric music, cool cybernetic upgrades (albeit less choices than those found in HR), multiple solutions to problems presented to the player, as well as opportunities for exploration.
Personally I found the voice acting for the main character, Ben Saxon, to be superior to that of Adam Jensen in Human Revolution, whose actor I found gave a flat performance with a voice that sounded like a cross between Keanu Reeves and Christian Bale's growly Batman voice.
Even if you're paying full price for this game, at $9.99, what you get is pretty decent, even if it is a little short at only 6 hours. This game is best played with a gamepad, like an XBox 360 controller.

mele/open door: Space
Pick up ammo: Z
Take cover: LeftCtrl
Throw glaive/AfterThrow ability: C
Grenade: Q
Etc. I quickly realized how bad they were and remapped them to much more sensible buttons of course (Glaive to middle mouse button for example).

The lords had assembeled at Praven. They had just finished a campaign and were at one of Harlaus's many bountiful feasts. They had little to worry about, seeing as the Sarranids were waging successful warfare against the Rhodoks and Khergits to the south and west. The Swadians had gained more lands under the newest campaign, in which Count Delinard and Harlaus divided up forces and lead groups of nobles about the Vaegir countryside, and took the area from Reyvadin to Khudan. The rest of the already weakened and disorganised Vaegirs were easy pickings for the newfound ally of Swadia, the Nords. The Lords still had one pressing issue: Who would own Ayyike, the village to the south of Khudan? It was hard to tell, as it laid between Dramug Castle and the City of Reyvadin. Harlaus himself had taken Reyvadin, Delinard, the Marshall, Dramug Castle. It was hard to decide, so Harlaus decided to hold a vote instead of the seeminly unusually heated debates about the fiefdom of the village. There were 20 Swadian Lords. They all voted. It was a 50-50 tie. 10 Delinard, 10 Harlaus. Lady Sonadel, Daughter of Grainwad and Wife of Lord Prescan, the new Swadian Lord after Haringoth died of old age, read them all off. The room in Praven fell silent. Not a noise could be heard in the royal hall. Some of the lords and ladies felt anguish, knowing that more needless arguments were to come over this. Harlaus knew what would happen, and decided to put an end to it. But there was one pressing issue - Harlaus, wise as he was on the inside, was a total ♥♥♥♥wad socially. Harlaus pondered at thoughts then and there, before deciding on one. Harlaus, in front of all Swadian Nobility, walked over to the table where the votes were counted in two boxes. He gathered all the Delinard-leaning votes, and placed them into a neat pile on the table. He stepped onto a stool, and then the table from that. Harlaus undid his belt, and dropped his pants and undergarments, before unleasing a torrent of Swadian Royal♥♥♥♥♥♥on the votes. The room fell silent. Harlaus, whilst still urinating on the votes, stared down Lady Sonadel, then Count Delinard in the eye. Tears began streaming from Lady Sonadel's delicate eyes, landing from her cheeks onto her fur coat. "After consulting with the peers of the realm, King Harlaus has decided to confer Ayyike on King Harlaus." Harlaus stepped down from the table, still naked from the waist below, and picked up the votes with his bare hands, Harlaus walked over to a nearby lantern, urine dripping from his hands, and dropped the votes in. A quick "Hsss!" was emitted from the urine turning to steam and the votes burning, and Harlaus wiped his hands on Delinard's beard. Mount & Blade Warband (or just M&B) is a fantastic game, and I would recomend it to anyone who is looking for a singleplayer game who is looking to kill a few hours. I think this game is like Minecraft in the extent that it is a game you open and spend tens of hours on easily, then just drop it, you find other stuff to do. I always keep this game (and the previous version) installed because I know one day I'll be bored and find the game you can open and spend tens of hours on easily.
There are a couple of drawbacks. This game's graphics are not the most beautiful. In fact, I would call them pretty bad when compared to AAA games. Some of the quest are generic and tedious, such as going across the land to find cattle for a village, or every village having the same issues.
With that asside, the game can be suprisingly complex if you get into it. There is no story, rather it is a free-roaming experience with combat as a main function, but you could be level one and have piles of Denars (currency) laying around. Trading is another route one may choose, but the combat is where the magic happens. The graphics, while being pretty weak, and nice enough to appreciate while you get imersed. There are stats such as renown where citiziens, lords, and kings know of your deeds, and honor, where people respect you as a gentleman or a fair lady. It adds a whole level to the roleplaying in this game. Since it is all about what you do, it is very easy to make your own story any enjoy every minute of it.
There is a bit of controvercy, however, that I admire. Mount and Blade as a whole tries to stick to historical values and ideas, such as honor, and dissapointingly, gender roles. I admire it because it adresses the fact that women were expected to stay away from adventure (as you'll notice with gaining royalty), even despised if they acomplished everything notable. It tends to leave the player to stick to a male character for a easier gameplay experience, but it does encourage you to think about the society you are playing in. I am dissapointed that this has occured in our history (as most may be) but the creators have gained my respect for it's inclusion in this open world, as it makes you think a little bit.
Overall, I recomend this game. I love it, and I always fall back to it. There are so many things to do, and the limit is what you set it to be. You can find a variety of modpacks for this game either online or in Steam's Workshop, so if you ever need to spice things up just throw on a Lord of the Rings mod, or maybe a Game of Thrones version.

Layers of Fear is a very different horror experience. Instead of focusing on jump scares using monsters it uses it's own unique horror. It actually does this very well and I have to say it's probably the most scared I have ever been at a horror game.
The horror this game focuses on is a psychedelic kind of horror. While exploring the house you will experience changing scenery and corridors without you even looking. You often find when turning around that you are now in a completely different room to where you was before. What this does is it creates a fear of turning around. Literally one of my biggest fears while playing was turning around because you never have any idea what you are gonna find. I also never found myself looking behind the curtains as such by seeing the walls change myself.
They then obviously had to include jump scares. This is more often than not done by ways of paintings. They often dissolve or mold into something else more scary. These jump scares I find rather unique and I loved them. But then the game also throws in a lot of cheap jump scares. These include things like pots being thrown at a wall and slamming doors. Although they definitely did scare me I find them rather boring and uninspired. I just felt like they needed something to fill the time spent exploring.
The game also features a story. It tells a rather disturbing story of a man and his wife which I won't spoil. I'll just say you may cringe listening to some of it. It is told in a kinda "gone home" style. This means by picking up items you will learn more about the story. Some is through reading extracts and others you will hear the main character reminiscing about the past. I will also add here that the actor is incredible with his voice work. Some people may be put off by this way of story telling but to me, having loved gone home, I also loved this storytelling choice.
The story is also open to interpretation I believe. Soemtimes the game is rather vague in these story extracts. It's probably quite meaningfully doing this so you can yourself interpret the story how you want. The game doesn't always tell the story in a logical order of events. This story isn't complete yet so i can't say how I feel about an ending.
Layers of fear does seem to have a goal. You are seemingly building up a painting. We don't yet know what the painting will represent but it is definitely looking disturbing. To build this painting you will have to find items around the house to paint with. These aren't your regular painting items and you end up finding stuff like bones to paint with. Yep quite disturbing.
One thing people may dislike is that Layers of Fear is an almost entirely linear experience. For the first kind of 10 minutes of the game you are able to freely explore the house. After this you are locked into the games linear routes. If you don't like linear games then this isn't for you.
A problem I have is that sometimes the experience didn't seem to quite flow. I mean sometimes the soundtrack didn't flow into each other and the events seemed to just be random without any real meaning to why they were happening. I think going forward this game needs to try and make events link together to make it slightly more fun and horrifying.
The big problem I have with Layers of Fear comes later in the game. Notice how earlier I was saying I loved the unique way of horror they use and how they don't use monsters. Well this isn't entirely true. Near to the end of the current experience a monster is introduced. The monster seems to become the heart of the experience from there on. I think they should really consider removing this monster and crafting more of the unique horror experience in it's place instead. It may be scary but I don't think it really has a place in this game.
Graphics wise I had no problems whatsoever. The art style isn't unique by any means but what it does with the art style is definitely unique. Performance was Ok. It varied between 30-60 fps on my mid range system. It could probably do with some optimization.
Overall Layers of Fear really freaked me out and is the most scared I think i've ever been at a horror game. It's unique version of horror is what really makes it stand out. It took me just over 90 minutes to complete it in it's current entirety which may be a little short. However the price point is really cheap at £6.99 so I think it's worth it. I definitely look forward to play more of it but I hope they consider some of the changes I proposed.
Disclaimer: I was provided a review key for free by the developer to make this review.

The Evil Within is without a doubt the best survival horror game I've played in years. Shinji Mikami, the creator of Resident Evil, 2, and 4 has come back to create a game that returns to the roots of survival horror. The atmosphere is enthralling, it's so thick and dirty that you feel as if you can reach out and grab it. Level design is reminiscent of Resident Evil 4 where there are large areas filled with explorable buildings and rooms. There's rarely a straight path for you to follow as you are freely allowed to explore your surroundings looking for scarce ammunition, currency, and health syringes. The gameplay is just as satisfying as it was in RE4, if you pull off a headshot you are rewarded with an extremely violent head explosion, just as gory as it was to do in RE4. There are quite a few jump scares but what really sells this as a horror game is how intense the combat can feel. You are never without concern for your ammunition and when it comes down to pulling the trigger you need to be certain that you will make the shot, as missing a shot feels worse than taking an axe to the face. The level design and pacing is also extremely excellent, the environment changes up frequent enough to make the game feel fresh, it also helps that the visuals are gorgeous, especially running on ultra. Playing The Evil Within you are really able to see Mikami's creative efforts poured into this game, the enemy design is terrifying, there are quite a few enemy types that will stand out as an icon for this game, if not the survival horror genre as a whole. Enemy animations are also very well done, they move fast, slow, duck from incoming fire, fling themselves about and do anything to throw off your aim unlike RE4 where you could just line up a headshot relatively easily. The story is the game's weakest point, but that's not to say it isn't interesting. Survival horror games usually sacrifice plot to create an immersive and terrifying world. The acting also isn't the greatest, but look at Leon's one liners in Resident Evil 4. Overall The Evil Within has been the best survival horror experience I've had in a video game since Resident Evil 4. At times it can be action heavy but with extreme pressure on the player. If you decide to pick this up take your time with it, immerse yourself in the thick atmosphere and haunting sound design. If you can get past theatre-esque bars on the bottom and top of your screen to add a cinematic feel and the zoomed in aim added only to increase intensity you will find an absolutely beautiful survival horror game soaked in blood.
Good game that rewards exploration and puts you up against a variety of enemies, combat system is a little clunky but overall absolutly worth playing through.

Completely overrated, in my opinion. I am a fan of horror games, in particular the Silent Hill style that is written all over Evil Within, but let me be brief and list the shortcomings that didn't make this game work for me.
1) The engine: the controls and precision of strikes/shooting in fights is a real shame. Given that it is a checkpoint game where you have to replay extended stretches of it if you get killed, it is extremely annoying when I get killed regularly because of the controls. In the fights, there is no sense in the way the protagonist acts. He can't use the knife that he carries in melee, only in stealth. He finds himself with his back to an enemy _all the time_ after punching or shooting. The camera angle in the fights doesn't make any sense either, with the enemies frequently ending up in your blind zone when they come close. And yep, you can stuff an enemy with bullets, then lose sight of him, and next moment he stubs you to death with one swift motion or cuts you in pieces. The whole fight dynamics were not making any sense to me. And like I said, when applied to boss fights, I had enough of playing for 5-10 minutes after a checkpoint to collect a weapon or ammo, get to the boss, do precisely what I need to do (say, shoot a bolt), see the camera losing the angle, furiously rotate the protagonist to get hold of the boss, get cut into pieces in the next second, replay 5-10 minutes after the checkpoint, rinse and repeat. Senseless.
2) The story, with all the pretense of the Silent Hill genre, does not grip.
3) I haven't experienced any game killing bugs, but had a few minor ones that just puzzled me. Like, I would start the game, load a checkpoint, and suddenly all game controls are empty. I can't move. Luckily, it's very easy to reset the controls to default, but the question is, what the hell has just happened? Why does it happen? Or take the intentional gameplay controls that are not intuitive and have to be googled up (such as, you press space to "examine" and can't find how to turn it off until you google up that you need to press "c"). Like, what has just happened? Why is it designed this way?
It's merely an ok pastime game if you got it on a major discount. I would be frustrated if I bought in presale and/or at the full price. The trailer was cinematic, that was all to it.

I had a very hard time making up my mind whether I should buy this game or not. I had heard that it's a bit of a mixed bag, and I've had friends warn me away, but on the other hand I absolutely love anything Warhammer related, and the trailer looked bad♥♥♥♥♥ Thankfully it happened to not only be on sale, but also to offer a free-play weekend and I got to experience it.
My conclusion after 15 hours of gameplat is that I really enjoy it! The setting, atmosphere, lore, characters and conversation are pretty much perfect. You really feel like a hero striving against great odds to help the human resistance defeat the invading vermin hordes.
That being said, the game is not perfect. I sincerely hope that some polish will be added in later patchs (for example, there's no indication that you're speaking when you press the VOIP button, and sometimes an enemy attacking you will be visible to other party members, but not yourself, which is very annoying, but also very rare, thankfully)
There's gear obtaining and upgrading mechanics to motivate you to put a little bit of extra effort in coaming the ruins for loot, and the classes balance each other beautifully.
Like all team based games you will sometimes have trouble finding skilled team members, but this plagues all such games.
Overall, I would recommend it to those who like the warhammer universe, with the addendum that you should probably get it on a >40% sale like I did. For $30 even if I only play it for 15 more hours it's still worth it ($1/hr is not bad for the entertainment I've gotten out of it).

Aight, this review will be a bit mixed.
First, if you are fan of horror games like the first Dead Space, Amnesia etc., you will be very happy with this one. This game is fricking creepy. It really is. Especially first three or four chapters your heartbeat will be really frantic (Laura!!!), and even in the late game it still can suprise you with something extraordinary and new. You will know since very beginning this is game made by Japanese guys - they are true masters of horror.
Atmosphere is brilliant, it is phantasmagoric ride till the end. Shortage or ammo, medkits and other useful stuff makes the game tense and sometimes a bit frustrating, but in a good way - like Dark Souls for example. Story is good, the ending is satisfying, combat is entertaining and frantic, graphics is great and music and sounds are just a cherry on the cake which complete whole aspects into the perfection. Almost...
Yeah. Everything above sounds great, right? It would be, but it is not.
Because this is by far one of the WORST PC ports ever. Really.
Refresh rate locked to 30 fps or 60 with VSYNC only? Really? No other choice like 60 fps WITHOUT VSYNC? Because this game is not HW friendly - even on my GTX980 it drops under 60 fps quite often and with forced VSYNC it stutters.
Ofc, you can use engine command to force different refresh rate, but jeeez, the fact I am an IT guy does not mean that everybody else is  an IT guy too.
Keyboard/mouse setting is a fricking joke. Sometimes it is almost impossible to change any key, especially those you have to scroll down to, because the game from no known reason still changes some other key which is not even seen on the screen. And even if you change all the keys after half an hour struggle, it sometimes just vaporizes away when you restart the game. Sometimes it don't load correct schema for fast choice keys (btw, these keys cannot be changed via standard GUI). And even if you change your settings via config file edit (which I strongly recommend), game itself resets this config file from no reason time to time and you have to reset it again - again, I strongly recommend to set config file as read only.
I do not have problem with gamepad, I usually play games of this kind with one, but this game is a way easier during the combat when you use some more precise method of aiming - which the mouse with no doubts is. But if you don't have more advanced mouse which lets you to set keystrokes for mouse buttons, you are screwed. Yes. This game does not support mouse buttons except left and right ones. No middle mouse button, no mousewheel, no side buttons. Jeeez.
Really, if you are not a geek and if you don't know how to workaround stuff, you will be desperate in no time.
Anyway, even if technical aspect of this port is another portion of horror emotions, in the end I still recommend this game. But I don't want to see any of these elementar issues in a sequel - if there will be any - and I hope there will be - because game itself is one of the best action horror games I ever played.

Good, difficult horror game, but not for full price.
There is a good job done on tension and strange/freaky/intense things happening.
I think of myself as someone that doesnt normally scare easy and that being said.... This is one of the few games that has actually made be jump and make my heart skip a beat. The only other games I've played that have done that are Dead Space 2 and Resident Evil 2.  However, that was only a fraction of time compared to the overall gameplay.  Other people may find it more or less scary.
Something I need to point out is that I personally I don’t like "helpless horror" like Amnesia, I'd rather fight back in some way.  This means the game has to have a balance between giving you power and taking it away.  The Evil Within does a pretty good job at this.
It's a tid bit of a rage simulator granted I didn’t play on the easiest mode.   To me, this gives you more accomplishment after you clear an area.  Your character is quite weak; profoundly at the beginning and the baddies will still rip you up late game if you are not on your toes.   Most of the time they are just another part of the puzzle so to speak.  They're just another obstacle that you need to use your head to get around like everything else in this game.  Even the main Antagonist in this game in not really something that instills large amounts of fear or hate into your heart.  Although the story does give him a good amount of back story. He's a sadistic madman that needs to bite the dust for sure, but most of the time you just deal with him which isnt too difficult so long as your Ego can handle a death screen every now and then.
The controls feel solid and I think the game handles better than RE4, RE5, and even RE6 and RE: Revelations.  They add a sprint feature which some horror fans seem to hate for some reason, but its a much needed lifeline in this game instead of a cheap escape.   If you don’t level it up you will have a VERY bad time.  If you run in guns blazing OR cowering in fear without changing your strategy you will have a very bad time.  You're going to have to think a bit, try different things, and not get too angry if it doesn’t work out.
The biggest gripe I have with the game is that it seems like they had to shorten quite a few aspects of it for some reason... not sure if they were crunching on deadline or if they just couldnt make up their minds about somethings.
For starters the gameplay isnt that long for a triple A game.  You can probably beat it in 15 hours or so.  New Game+ is available, but you'll probably blow through that even quicker because your character will be more leveled up (which I enjoy because you can put the pain on the bad guys much easier, but they will still mess you up if you are being stupid).
Oddly enough there are a few automatic rifle welding "zombies" in this game just like there are in RE5 and RE6 despite some people venting their angst about them. They are quite annoying and may have been better had they been left out or tweaked.  For some reason Sebastian doesn’t have the ability to aim while crouching or shoot from behind cover very well. Fortunately there's not too many of them.
I wish there was an online co-op for some part of the game. Most or at least some of the story would be ok if it was a "drop in co-op optional, but not required" game.    A horde or mini-level mode(s) with co-op or multiplayer capability would be fun too and really push the value of the game up in my opinion.   I know some horror fans like to play alone, but I like to jump in with my friends and doing so doesn’t have to sabotage a game.
The voice acting was a wash.  Some of the actors seem like they are doing an ok job just reading really bad lines.  I got the impression that some of the dialog may have been lost in translation (perhaps intentionally)  because it reminded me of earlier Resident Evil games.
The story is good, but could be much better.  There's quite a bit that could have been elaborated on in regards to the past of the characters, not just Sebastian, but the game never gets too deep with the narrative except for a few people.  Much of the story is left open to interpretation and opinion.   I would like to point out that the game does brush over some deep aspects of the human psyche that sent a tingle up my spine.  I really wish they would elaborate on because it would have made more sense out of the story/game while pulling the player in even further.
All in all its a good game, but could have been much better.  Especially for AAA game that would be full price for a while.

A classic SNES game that is too rare to find comes to Steam at long last. When I first saw the greenlight page of this game, that meant it should deserve a second chance. Sure everyone has their own tastes to this game, but trust me, I know.
The game itself is very fun. I recommend this game if you remember a wonderful (even if it was unlicensed in the past) classical gem such as Super 3-D Noah's Ark.

Let's just get some things out of the way first. Yes, it is a Wolfenstein 3D engine game with Noah themed visuals but, almost everything else has something interesting about it.
The levels are, as you expect like Wolfenstein 3D's with mazelike design. The secrets in this game are somewhat easier to find due to most of them having some sort of marking or obvious decoration design.
The animals (enemies) look to be reskinned Nazis but..... I find the animals to be worse than Nazis sometimes with their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t shooting around corners skills.
The weapons in the game seem to function like their Wolfenstein 3D counterpart but there are two more weapons that are not featured in the original Wolfenstein 3D which would be more akin to a rocket launcher.
To end with, I do recommend this game if you want to spice up the Wolfenstein 3D formula with variation in enemy and weapon design. I am in no way a religious man and I often get the questions on the scrolls wrong in-game but a manual is included which has the answers in these scrolls if you want to cheat and not brush up on your bible study ;)

Step 1: Give the source code of Wolfenstein 3D to the developer Wisdom Tree,
Step 2: Replace the Nazis with animals, (Even though it makes no sense to have more then two of each animal)
Step 3: Replace the pictures of Hitler with pictures of Noah,
Step 4: Replace the guns with animal food
All because the devs of Wolfenstein wanted to be a rebel against Nintendo. And then you have the really obscure Super 3D Noah's ark, the game with (In my opinion) the best develment story ever.
Why it's randomly on Steam after twenty years? I don't know.

PLEASE NOTE: I work for the developer and recieved this copy for bug testing, this does not change how I view the game however, it should be noted.
I like NT, it's a nice game to sit back and spend 1-2 hours unwinding, there are a few quirky systems and spelling errors  but all in all an enjoyable experience.
Gameplay revolves around your employees, you pick a proofreader (or multiple) and a journalist (or multiple) then assign them a story (which you can manually select or have your employees search for a story themselves on a regular basis) I like also that you can assign the same person to both tasks (which is usually what I do with my CEO at first until I have quite a few subs and capital under my belt)
I think the best part of this game is the news headlines and events, recently I went over and helped tidy up the news headlines to make them more English friendly. After seeing the true number of different things that can pop up ingame I have to say that this is probably NT best and most worked on feature (as it should be as imho seeing the same 2 healines over and over would hurt the game). I hope that others will play long enough to enjoy the feature
The worst part of this game, for me personally, is most likely the hard to read articles (not only grammer wise, but vision wise) I was born with a eye disability which makes some texts hard to see (usually small size text, white on white, etc.) and having to squint is a constant annoyance.
I think all in all the gameplay is good, for a tycoon game anyways. Although this game will need work (I have heard a few people say they experience some bugs, however I havn't hit any that I have noticed (though most of my playtime is on a prerelease build to view what the game would look like))
TL:DR
It's a good game, with a good idea that I haven't seen before. I think with improvements to the English side of things (which is what I play obviously) and a few tweeks here and there this game could become a great tycoon game, until then though 8/10 is the best I can give it.

This game doesn't really teach you to build a circuit. It's more of a brute force game. From a programming point-of-view, I think that the output of the osillioscope is just keyed to the combination and does not actually simulate the output; The reason being that the resistor, diode, capacitor, and inductors all have fixed values.
A true electronic simulator would be Multism or a free-version would be LTSpice.
Electronics Circuits Simulator, if you liked circuit warz you will likely enjoy this game.

Disclaimer: At the time of writing this review, I haven't completly finished the game.
Jump, Step, Step is an entertaining game with cute graphics. But don't let the first impression fool you, this game gets really challenging after the first few stages.
The concept is similar to games such as Lightbot. You control a little robot (called Bob) stranded in a world full of dangerous cliffs, spikes and breaking stones. You'll have to program Bob by clicking together a chain of commands. Bob will faithfully execute your defined commands. If he doesn't reach the goal, you'll lose a life (in form of a battery). If you have no lives left, you'll have to start over at a checkpoint.
As you progress in the game, the stages will become harder and you'll gradually unlock more complex commands. You'll have to think of clever ways to help Bob reach the goal. In the later levels, you'll inevitable fail a few times before you get the right idea and you have to start over at a checkpoint.
Unfortunately, there's no ingame indication when you have reached a checkpoint and sometimes the placement of the checkpoints is annoying because they're too far away from where you failed. The translation of the dialogues is okay, tough not perfect (I accidentally lost an early save because of a misleading german translation of the menu option "clear saved game").
Despite of it's minor shortcomings, the game is definitly worth the price and the right choice for everybody who likes to program and/or puzzle! Even experienced programmers will get their money's worth with this game!
