Replica puts you in the role of a snitch for the state's security, whether you cooperate or rebel is up to you.
The gameplay is simple: You are given a phone of a suspect and your task is to find as much information concerning the suspect as you can, instructed by an official in order to get your "get out of jail free card".
The game presents this opportunity in an authentic way, without much explanations you are given a phone and your first task is to gain access by using the revealed information. After that you are being granted the access to snoop around the privacy of the suspect, by reading their messages, seeing their photos and checking their apps. With that a government official orders you to pry in deeper to find more valuable information.
The setting feels natural and authentic, it feels like accessing an actual phone, the only concern I'd have would be the lack of interaction, though this applies to the short length of the game. However it offers you multiple endings based on your decisions, which gives you multiple ways to play around with it. The artstyle contains quite an impressive pixelart style, made to look naturalistic, which puts you in a rather gloomy, dark environment with a calm and dim soundtrack. All in all the artstyle, music and setting are playing well together with subject you're being confronted with: The life in a police state.
It's undeniable that the game has put its focus on trying to convey a political message, just like the famous example of "Papers Please", which the game was presumably inspired on. Using methods like the gloomy environment you're being put it and the statements each person in the game makes, the game is trying to criticize police states and questions topics like data security, surveillance and the intrusion into your privacy by the government.
The game certainly isn't long, but offers quite a few, but not too many details.
For those who expect a well-made short game which confronts you with a political subject, similar to Papers Please, I can recommend the game for its relatively low price. Due to its length and lack of gameplay it isn't the same experience, but it's absolutely worth it for those who are interested.

A wonderful slow-economy real-time-strategy game. Its economies are much slower and much more detailed than the likes of Age of Empires or Rise of Nations. You play a tribe of Vikings and build up farms, industries, and weaponsmiths so you can trade and build and army to conquer your foes. It takes time, but the time it takes is enjoyable, and not as much of a scramble as faster RTS games.

Cultures - Northland is one of those games I used to play quite a bit when I was far younger - back then, I got the game as a free extra to a gaming magazine. Now, I recently bought the game for the sake of nostalgia to be able to try it out again. While I kind of enjoyed the experience, mostly due to the nostalgia factor... if I am to be objective, I cannot really recommend the game due to its dated mechanics and numerous flaws.
Northland is a city builder game with some RTS elements to it, but at its heart it's a city builder game, so I'll focus on that aspect. You control a group of vikings (often the hero Bjarni, a swordfighter and the main character of the campaign, although there are free-play scenarios you can play as well) who have to set up shop in the unspoiled nature and fulfill various objectives. Depending on the mission, this can be "collect X resources" or "defeat an enemy faction" or "find an NPC that you have to talk to". You have to chop wood, mine clay and stone, and move up the tech tree to build up an increasingly sophisticated civilization. At first, it's actually quite a bit of joy to watch the adorable little vikings move around, do their work, talk to each other, and so on. The graphics are definitely quite good for their age, allowing for a nice atmospheric, if campy experience.
So far, so good. But one doesn't have to play much to see the numerous niggling problems of the game. The vikings are notoriously dumb and you need to erect a tight network of signposts to let them even find their way around their own village, but even then, often they will fail to find a critical resource they need. Sometimes an iron miner might be unable to find the iron vein right in front of their noses (NPCs seem to have problems with rough terrain), at other times the flour might be too far away from the bakery (despite not seeming to be too far at all). Many features are extremely finicky. You cannot transport resources en masse from the mill to the bakery, for example, at least not straight away. You have to either let the baker do it himself, carrying flour bags one by one, or assign a carrier to do so, who will still only carry them one by one. Then, after a carrier gains enough experience to become a merchant, you can have the merchant use a hand cart or ox cart (which are both quite far up another branch of the tech tree) to transport goods, but the mechanics to do so are still non-intuitive. Vikings who extract raw resources will put them on the ground, those who work in a workshop will amass their finished goods there. One would think that you could, for example, decide to carry all the bricks, stone slabs and marble in the town to a centrally located warehouse, but in practice, this is also extremely cumbersome. It seems impossible to "lock" goods out of a warehouse, so a carrier assigned to the warehouse will ferry random goods into there, while a carrier assigned to the stonemasonry will not know to carry the finished goods away. You need to manually task merchants to transport those exact goods - again, a very frustrating process that cannot really be automated. The lack of automation and other user-friendliness features will often have you scratching your head or yelling at the screen, depending on your temperament, thinking "What are these idiots doing? Is there any way to make them act sensibly?" The answer is usually no, or at least not very obvious, as the tutorial only teaches the very basics and leaves out quite a few important tricks that you have to learn as you go. And worse yet, while a lot of things cannot be automated, often even manual intervention is not enough to fix idiocy. I've encountered some of my iron miners half-starved to death because they couldn't notice the iron vein in front of them, but also didn't want to eat for some reason despite having a berry bush next to them and lots of fresh bread farther away in the town bakery. Ordering him to eat didn't help either, however, and it took quite a bit of trial and error to figure out how to make this unviable specimen survive.
Of the RTS elements, I'll speak less. You can train soldiers and equip them with weapons, armor, shoes to help them move faster, and potions to restore their health, stamina and nourishment. This is a ton of micromanagement, and unfortunately it's necessary since not stocking them up with nourishment and stamina potions just leads to even more micromanagement and frustration as soldiers fall asleep in the middle of battles, and not stocking them up with health potions means they die like flies (replenishing your townsfolk is done by ordering your married women to have children of  a sex of your choosing, but this takes some time). The combat AI is not too good, but fortunately, it isn't too good with your enemies either. Or, rather, unfortunately, since this means it's not much of a challenge. During the campaign and the combat-oriented scenarios, enemies usually just stand still and wait for you to engage them. If you kill them, they either won't replenish at all, or only to a very modest degree.
This also means that the campaign isn't that much fun as you basically have to build the same town over and over again in every scenario (the same resources are always available, only with a slightly different layout every time, and you pretty much always go through the same motions when you build a new town). Either you have to gather an arbitrary amount of resources, or you have to defeat an enemy force that, as I mentioned before, does not replenish much or at all, and it's only a matter of time. The enemy is never a threat to your town unless you accidentally lure the whole stack back to your town prematurely. Later, there are fixed-force missions which tend to have even more boredom and even less challenge.
Verdict: avoid. If you want cheap older city-building games with a historical theme, then Tropico 4, or even titles like Poseidon, Caesar, Pharaoh should be more to your fancy. Northland is just an exercise in frustration to get into and does not offer much in the way of replayability. If you've built up your town once, you've seen it all.

Ace of Spades is really a mixed bag. I, and many didn't like the news that the previously free to play multiplayer had been taken over and "redefined" by Jagex, the developer behind Runescape.
AOS is a first-person shooter game with classes similary to the game Team Fortress 2. The classes have diffrent weapons and equipment that you can use to your advantage. The game main selling point is that the maps is entirely destructable and buildable and while it's certainly fun, I feel like it's hasn't been though out properly.
Let me explain: The class Rocketeer is a character that have a jetpack attached to him. It tries to balanced itself with that you can shoot and explode the jetpack or it can overheat and explode if used to much. The problem is that building for example a defensive fort for your intel in a capture the flag gamemode, a rocketeer can just fly in with no problem.
The community isn't all that great either, being that it has seen episodes of hackers, griefers and overall people cursing eachother out.
The thing what saves it though, you may ask?
The classic capture the flag. It is like the free game you played before. Just the rifle and grenades and your shovel. This encourage teamplay. Building and maintaining a fort to defend your intel and try to breach your enemies ones. Having a few friends and trying to strategize and plot a plan for victory.
However that's just my 2 cents. A decent shooter with watered down with features that hasn't been well planned out.
I wish they could add the 2 other WWII weapons and a few other Classic gamemodes for the old school AOS players. Still get a recommendation, but only on deep sales.

"Not quite Deus Ex: The Fail, but still leaves a lot to be desired"
This game has received a lot of hate from fans of the Deus Ex series, as it was originally a game made only for mobile devices, and when it did finally get a PC port from the developers, it has not gotten much praise from the fans, for both the quality of the port and the core game. While I don't hate it, it still has a number of problems that make it the worst in the series.
Story
As a follow up to the book, this could already lead to some confusion for players, but it can be played without reading that first. The game starts off with you on a mission as part of a Black Ops team sent to assassinate one of the people responsible for the deaths of your previous squad mates. Not long after though, you find the circumstances resulting in their deaths were not what you have been told, and result in you going into hiding. The rest of the game has you doing various missions in order to get medication to help deal with your augmentations. The story itself doesn't really hook the player unfortunately, and has little of interest other than showing characters you might recognize from previous games.
Presentation
Graphics could be better. While not awful, and almost certainly better than what would have been used for the smaller mobile device screens, textures still aren't great, and even the fact that it was a port isn't an excuse, after seeing how nice some of the HD ports for 3DS and Vita games can look. Going in to the characters themselves, while they don't look great, most are at least okay. But then you have a few which I'll call goblins with their poorly constructed bodies and hideous faces. It was quite surprising considering the rest were at least decent.
Audio is alright. All of the music and sound effects seem to have been taken Human Revolution, so chances are you will notice familiar tunes. Voice acting is also of decent quality. Your ears won't be bleeding while you play through this game at least.
Controls
These have been considered a major flaw of the game. While the gamepad mapping is fine, anyone who has a problem with the default keyboard and mouse layout is out of luck, as there is no options for changing how it is set up. So if you are the kind of player who likes to set up custom layouts for your fancy keyboards, feel free to avoid this game. I played through the game on a gamepad, which uses an almost identical layout as the previous game, with only a couple of changes. However, even with a gamepad, things were not all perfect, as controls during the hacking minigame are fiddly, resulting in me moving to my mouse during those parts.
Gameplay
Now onto the meat of the review, and where more of the flaws shall be revealed. At heart, this plays very much like Human Revolution. You can talk, sneak, shoot and hack just like you did while playing as Adam Jensen, but now that you are Ben Saxon, a few things had to change, some of them minor while others are major changes to how the game works. For one, Ben can't jump at all. This limits some of your options, and levels reflect this lack. You won't ever see a hard to reach vent that might just need a few stacked boxes, not in this game. Not that you have the option to stack boxes at all. Yeah, you have very few chances to manipulate the locations in this game. You can break down a few walls and move a few heavy crates out of the way but little else. No more being really inventive in your choices as a sneaky character. Not that it matters much. The locations are small in scope anyway, most of the game consisting of a single hub of maps. You can do a bit of exploration, but there just isn't that much do look around. Just a few vents to sneak through, a few locks to hack open and a few crates and walls standing in the way.
The next change is a big one, this being the inventory. In The Fall, there is no limit what so ever to what you can carry. You can carry more weapons than there are enemies in the area. No more having to make a hard choice about which weapon to take with you, just bring them all. Your inventory in this game also acts as an in game shop, allowing you to purchase whatever item you might need as long as you have the credits. While I get annoyed at being forced to leave behind loot in the older games, this ruins any need for planning out your gear to maximize your chances or ensure you can carry the best selling items out of a level. Anything you need is yours with the push of a button and is sitting in your pouch of holding when you need it. On the bright side, at least the PC port doesn't include the option to pay for in game currency to make this even easier. We really don't need micro transactions here.
Now onto the AI and interaction with them. Yes, I have bad news here as well. Most NPCs are brain dead idiots who will mostly ignore you. Unless an NPC is marked as an enemy on your map, they will did very little other than panic if a fight happens near by, only to forget it seconds later. After how great the previous games were with their AI from friendly and neutral NPCs, this is what I'd consider the biggest failing of this game. It used to be that walking into the women's toilets would get them to yell for security. Here, they will calmly talk to you. Hostile AI will still react to you in a matter of ways, depending on your current actions and location, but this will never be the match of any other game in the series. Even the hostile AI are easy to deal with, and the fact that non combatants won't even warn them really tones down the difficulty.
Lifespan
After all of the problems I dropped on you during the previous section of my review, I have one more to mention. This game is short as it is currently incomplete. It seems the mobile game was designed to have episodic content, and nothing beyond the opening mission and first city at this time. You will beat it in a matter of hours, and unless you want to do New Game Plus to further power up your character and earn any missing achievements. Not really much incentive to play a second time unfortunately.
Closing
So there you have it. While it is most certainly a Deus Ex game, much of what made the series great just didn't make it to the game, resulting in a title with little challenge and little reward, though still playable in the end. My recommendation is to wait for a heavy discount, and perhaps some news on an (unlikely to happen) update to the campaign. It certainly doesn't offer enough to be worth your money at this point. I paid $3 and still feel it could have been better for what I've spent, given that Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Director's Cut can be had on Steam for as low as $5 itself.
6 / 10

this is a pc port of a very convincing mobile (android/ios) deus ex game. "mobile" being the very key word here with port leaving something to be desired around the control scheme. obviously its setting and much of the game mechanics is copied or adopted from deus ex: human revolution (dxhr). story is also closely related.
a playthrough will take 4-5 hours on average and around twice as much for a completionist/achievement hunter. for a deus ex fan or someone who liked dxhr, this game definitely contains a good amount of fun.
let us start with the good - this is a faithful deus ex game. gameplay is close to dxhr with most of its good sides still very much present. several approaches to any situation (combat, hacking, sneaking, maybe talking), hacking minigame has remained practically the same, getting additional augmentations with praxis (either purchased kits or level ups from gained exp).
setting, graphics, writing, background is also same as dxhr, maybe visuals being even a bit more yellow this time. naturally, you will find several tie-ins to dxhr (and some to other deus ex games) in conversations, e-mails and logs.
fortunately, dx: the fall has not gone the way of linear progression. with the exception of introduction/tutorial, the hub area with the linked locations can be freely roamed and pre-cleared if you wish. some areas get repopulated at quest triggers but there are only a couple that seemed to do that.
story is not bad in itself but considerably more shallow than expected. could have been used to give a bit more background to the tyrants but the overall theme remains with the daily struggles of fugitives and almost sidequest-level main questline. also, there are several references to part 1 and game ands with transition to what would seem to be another hub area so it is safe to say this was meant to be a first episode in an episodic game.
graphically, it looks like you would expect from a decent mobile game today - so in pc terms it looks only slightly better than the original deus ex from 2000. however, due to the setting still being excellent the visuals still work ok for a budged-priced game and naturally it works just fine with any remotely modern pc.
unfortunately, its mobile roots do bring negative aspects to the game. i think a list is a good way for this so here goes - design decisions that are ok in a mobile game but are questionable or simply out of place for a pc game in 2014:
- there is no jumping
- levels are small and clearly compartmentalized so that low-powered hardware would not have trouble rendering the levels.
- while dxhr ai was not groundbreaking, it was decent. the one in this game is not. most (of the limited few of) npc-s are completely static and the ones moving around are patrolling on limited trajectories. there are reactions to player actions (ex: hacking) but these are extremely limited in both range and function.
- the world has no physics. an example: there is still an augmentation for lifting heavy things but these specific heavy crates are acting like glorified doors.
- hacking does seem to be slightly modified, no hacking enemy-controlled nodes any more. this is annoying in some cases. available hacking layouts are very limited and will start very obviously repeating already about 25% into the game.
this leads us to the real problem with the game - who in the world thought such a lazy port would be a good idea? porting the control scheme from touchscreen to mouse and keyboard (or gamepad for that matter) has gone very awry somewhere along the line. i do not even know where to start so i will just make another list:
- menu items and ingame  buttons have a horrible delay. basically, they  need a second after appearing to start functioning. there is an indication at the buttons for when they are pressed but the indications are slight and you will find yourself often clicking on the button and wondering if it did work or if you were too quick.
- looking around with mouse is very choppy and not due to fps but due to something inherently wrong with the look controls.
- using keys is often uncomfortable. couple examples - space does not make you stand up from crouch as in most games. if a container is being looted and there is nothing in there, the dialog can be closed only by pressing esc or moving mouse to ok button.
- one savegame system is a crappy decision today but ok. but when saving from the menu while in game, the notification about game being saved is nowhere to be seen. it is logged in the game (that is covered by the menu) and a mild sound is played. that is it, and this is definitely not ok.
- usable item highlighting is not reliable. in addition to some items not being highlighted (ex: drawers), highlighting simply does not work at some angles.
- use prompt on screen can be a mess when there are several usable items. ex: person and computer next to each other both get use prompts highlighted and you can not be sure which one is activated when pressing e. it is probably due to prompts being separately clickable on touchscreen but leaving this in when porting is inexcusable.
- minor, but annoying gripe - mousewheel scroll in logs, books and e-mails scrolls by 5-6 lines, which is a lot. keys and scrollbar do not work, dragging the text does. again, nobody cared to change the behaviour that was ok on touchscreen.

This is a great game, little retro, but great
The core gameplay itself offers a lot of creativity. You get to create a backstory for your character, and it affects what your initial stats are. Then you get to literally go to any nation. It offers great replayabilty to figure out which combo works just right for you. The starting scenario is pretty much the same though, you get ambushed by someone on the conveiently empty streets and only after you kill him a random store clerk just runs up to you. You then a get a mission to hunt bandits who captured the merchants brother. it's the same everytime and I wish that it offered a more random experience. After that you get to run out in the wilderness and recruit people from nearby villages. Each nation's soldiers have a unique troop skill tree and really makes you strive to get every single troop type into your army. The travel system works as you and your army are moving across the landscape, consuming food, and other resources. You can enounter bandits, villagers, and other armies as you go and sometimes it's fun meeting people, but bandit raids can get pretty annoying. As you go from village to village you can sell/buy stuff and values differ depending on where you are. You can always get the latest values from travelling caravans that go all over the place. As you continue meeting lords you can join a nation as a vassal and work your way up to a full lord. It takes a long time, and a lot of commitment and when you acheive your goal it really feels like an accomplishment. It works realtime with randomized events, like battles and diplomacy being issues. A lot of times lords and vassals will change sides or desert their armies. It just adds to the completely random event system in the game. Ingame exploring is great, seeing the entirety of the continent. You can even find training camps which are pretty useful to xp grind. As you explore you can find many different side-quests/missions. So in summary, great replayability, and many different paths to take.
The game has an inbuilt cheat system that can be used to advance gameplay.  It's useful if you want to skip the beginner stuff, but it's better if you don't and keep the challenge that the game offers.
Graphics-wise, it doesn't really matter. The game looks and is old, but it doesn't take away the fun gameplay that's offered.

Likes:
Combat, character variety, sound quality, graphics.  Multiplayer is easy to join/create.
Dislikes:
Loot system is firmly in the camp of needing to endlessly grind for any significant improvement.
Entitled gamer gripe:
"Free Weekend" was not actually a free weekend, but a # of hours countdown.  So if you activated it on Thurs night because you were excited to try it out (like I did), and tried to play on Sunday, you're outta luck.

I think some reviews are being too harsh.  The game has its problems, and it can be a grind, and the population is failing a little, but it's still a pretty solid package.  Most negative reviews seem to be along the lines of;
"Well I used to play this a lot, but it has gotten repetitive, and there isn't enough content, too much grind, etc."
These complaints seem to stem from the fact that this game's genre can be a little misleading.  There's loot and some progression, which means that a lot of people are going to get autistic about this game, treat it like an MMO, grind for 100 hours of game time, and then complain that all the grind has gotten them no where.
If you play with the "I need to get more loot" mentality in focus, you're probably not going to have as much fun.  Loot is there to complement your growth in skill to help you beat the harder difficulties, which can be extremely challanging.  It shouldn't be your goal post, and the fact that it is for a lot of people in the community is the game's biggest detractor.
Don't be like those tools who have Horn of Magnus (one of the first missions) down to a science and play it over and over for the easy loot.  Play this game in short bursts with some friends, or even with people you find online, and you'll find it a very enjoyable take on the Left4Dead formula.  It lacks the diverse game modes that kept L4D fresh for so long, but the setting is really enjoyable and the gameplay is satisfying and leaves enough room for you to develop your own strategies to tackle the harder difficulties.

[Maybe, but probably not]
The art style is just amazing, I really liked the anime and in general I just love 'French Anime' art like Wakfu and Maliki
Turn based combat, plenty of casual things to do with a relaxed feel, nice music, unique classes and mobs
The story feels like it's too far in the background whilst playing, very little wiki resources, videos and guides written in English, a cheap subscription is recommended for many tasks and the game feels very slow to start
Customer support and some potentially game-breaking bugs
There's a huge comedic feel throughout playing the game that is built into the story and many characters
Firstly, I played and really liked Dofus. So Wakfu is one of those games that I know I would love just by looking at it, which is rare for me. However in practise the game falls short of enjoyable for quite a few reasons. First and foremost you're basically dropped into a game that has a very unique class and combat system with loads of little unique stats and mechanics that you need to learn. In Wakfu *character build* is incredibly important and there are not many English resources on what builds are viable. Asking on the Reddit sub just got me advice to use Google Translate on the French Wakfu forums... ugh. Secondly, given the kind of game that it is, most people I found were just afking to try and sell things in their afk shops and the UI is small and hard to read (and cannot be changed). In short, it's just overwhelmingly slow, confusing and complicated for new people to get into.
Due to being a free game it uses a cash shop and I personally feel there's too many items that give huge bonuses to people whom are willing to pay for them. Free transport, extra exp and money and dungeon uses; are just some of the huge buffs you get with a subscription, but these buffs are cut into 'packages' which need to be purchased separately and useful ones are separated which is very annoying. Finally an incredibly buggy patcher and the fact that the game cannot correctly log Steam Achievements combine with everything else to make this an unenjoyable experience. It took me 10 days just to get Ankama support to reply to my ticket about why the patcher wouldn't finish patching (it always crashed at the end). So initially I spent a couple of hours a day for 3 days getting the patcher working, and got an unhelpful response from Ankama 7 days after that.
Wakfu has all the potential to be a great game but it needs quite a few quality of life improvements. Namely the ability to change the size and layout of the game UI, a more clear indication of your direction in the game (questing and advancement), a patcher that actually does its job and a support team that is more responsive and helpful. Finally it also really needs more love from the English speaking community, the game needs more English guides, videos and more people who have a large follower-base to support and recommend it. Sadly it doesn't look like any of this will be happening any time soon. My fingers are crossed in the hopes that the next game from Ankama ticks all the boxes.

I guess I could say, it felt like instead of playing a 'scary video game' I was playing through somebodies nightmare. But.. i'm also a kind of person who is able to really immerse myself in a video game.
This is an early access review, and the game has left me hungry for more. I could see this revolutionizing horror games. This game is truly unique and I would highly reccomend it to everyone who loves a good scare (or hates it, but presses on anyway).

Ace of Spades started out as a good game.
The four unique classes all had some way of being useful, if you were just smart enough to figure them out. I remember for a long time being in constant fear when ever I hopped on a server of randomly falling over dead because of stealthy marksman, or having the ground fall out from under my feet so that I can land on a bomb in case the fall wasn't enough to take me out. There was even a chance that if someone sat still too long, a Miner would sneak up on you and smite you where you stood. The rocketeer (engineer for the new players) was hated for his ability to quickly get ouf out of a slippery situation. There were some unique game modes that each provided a new experience every time you played. The game was balanced. The game was hard. The game was fun.
But of course it didn't last.
It all started back in late spring, with what I refer to as "The Great NERF." Jagex published the game, and when they took over development they did what they normally do: listen to the complaints of the people who die because they can't figure out how to play properly. The game lost its balance when the sniper had a beam attached to it. No more suspense about "where are the Marksmen hiding?" Then, miner's weapons were decreased in power so that someone sitting around doing nothing would have a chance to fight back when he's attacked. The rocketeer was changed to the engineer and had his jetpack and glide pack removed from the game entirely. No more escapes. now that class is useless with nothing but the weak SMG to fight with. Then, last but not least: They buffed the commando. The commando class was originally no better or worse than anyone else. He could either hold the rocket launcher or the minigun. The minigun, while a powerful and reliable weapon, formerly took forever to charge. Now, not only does the minigun charge faster, the commando can carry it and a rocket launcher at the same time!
Everything that made the game fun and challenging was removed. The balanced characters all shifted in favor of the Commando.
But it doesn't end there!
After The Great Nerf, there was yet one more infuriating change: The St. Valentine's Day Massacre DLC. Back when I bought the game, it was listed as DLC. Several of my friends bought it and I felt like I was being left out on soemthing important based off of what they told me. Then, not too long ago, it was patched into everyone's game! There was nothing offered to the people who had already purchased the DLC. I was excited to play it, but it didn't matter because there weren't enough fans left who were brave enough to try out the more challenging game modes.
Unless you are a 12-year-old, don't buy it

At first this game may seem like Left 4 Warhammer, and it is... kinda. Unlike L4D, there is a progression system and it requires a good bit of grinding. You can't pick this game up and expect to jump straight into higher difficulties, because lower tier weapons simply don't do enough damage. Also unlike L4D, characters each have their own playstyle, and must coordinate with their loadouts with the team to be truly effective.
Much like L4D, it's a lot of fun, but it's very reliant on teammates. THIS GAME IS MEANT FOR CO-OP. Yes, you can play solo, yes you can play with pubbies, but where this game truly shines in a coordinated team who knows each other. I realize not everyone has that opportunity, but you should try for it at least once. Speaking of which, the AI is pretty bad. I don't recommend trying to play solo, as for the most part the AI will just wander ahead and get killed, often even ignoring useful items. The Devs have improved the AI since earlier in the game, but they're still got a ways to go.
The other thing the game is reliant on is the loot system. I love it, but it's definitely unpleasantly heavy on the RNG at the moment. Random selection of which items are in the pool, random slection of which character they're for, random chance of getting bonus die, random chance of what you roll... means sometimes you'll end up getting blue items for a character you don't even play on a full 2 Grim / 3 Tome / 2 Bonus run on Cata. That's incredibly frustrating. Fortunately, the Devs have said they're going to be improving this system, and right now I trust them to, which is a rare thing.
Lastly, I want to touch on the fact that the map design in wonderful, and tons of fun. The maps all feel different, and the challenges have a healthy amount of variation. The amount of detail in the Inn alone has entertained me a great deal while waiting for games. Every nook and cranny feels intentional. If you're a Warhammer fan, you can pick of plenty of references to the lore. The new Drachenfels maps especially shine, and have the best torch mechanics I've ever seen in a game.
Fatshark seems to be very responsive to the community in this game, and they're not screwing the playerbase in DLC costs. The most recent patch fixed a HUGE amount of crashes and bugs, covering almost all of my technical complaints about the game. The Devs very actively take suggestions and communicate with players on the Vermintide subreddit, which is something I appreciate greatly.
The game is reasonable priced, with the whole kitten caboodle coming in at under $50 (at full price). Including sales, you can get the game and all DLC for under $30. If Devs are going to continue to shove DLC down our throats, (because people keep buying it), that's the way I'd like to see it done. And this isn't just Horse Armor either, the DLC is a lot of fun. Last Stand mode gives you a great way to earn tokens to get around some of the loot rolling, and the new Drachenfels adds some of the most interesting levels I've seen in a game in a while. Most importantly, it doesn't split up the community because people who haven't bought the DLC can still play it, as long as the host has it.
Overall, the game runs great. YOU WILL NEED TO TURN DOWN SETTINGS. In my experience, and that of my friends, the auto-detect doesn't seem to work very well and leaves players with a lot of FPS hiccups, especially when there's a bright wizard. The fire effects and the ragdolls eat up a lot of resources, so in intense waves weaker machines will struggle.
Up until recently, rats could stab through floors and walls. That was awful. They fixed it. Thank god.
There are no dedicated servers. Keep that in mind, because it's a big deal. I think they added host migration in the most recent update, but I'm honestly not certain so I'm assuming I heard wrong (I usually host and have good internet, so I've not dealt with it yet). That could go either way, but the fact that it wasn't in the game from the start was a problem.
There are a lot of other random, minor bugs. Nothing game breaking that I've experienced, but things like duplicated potions falling through levels are annoying.
For the record, I'm playing on an i5-3570k, an AMD R9 390, with 16GB of RAM. Zero performance issues.

This is a great game and if you are interested in challenging platformer/shooters you need to pick it up.
Pros:
-very cheap price
-lots of content, there are 56 levels strewn across 8 worlds.  Every level has 3gems to collect and a time trial.  Each world ends in a boss fight.
- the worlds have a nice variety, sure you have the token ice level seen in every platformer but you also get cool levels like the moon and prehistoric times each with their own unique flair and obstacles
-lots of characters to unlock.  Characters are unlocked by collecting gems and completing challenges, the character selection is pretty cool and lets you play as all manner of things from a cowboy dog to a banana peel and other silly things
-each character has different abilities, they are not just pallete swaps.  Choosing the right character can make certain levels much easier and it is really fun to figure out the best tool for the job.
-good boss fights
-cool dash mechanic, there is a dash button and you can dash in mid air as many times as you like.  Mastering the timing of your dash and how you control your jumps is integral to success.
-tight controls
-challenging but not cheap.  The challenge in this game is just right, you will die but it is not hair pullingly frustrating either.
Cons:
- no real joystick support.  Not a problem if you use joy2key but native support would be nice
-the music and sound effects are generally pretty weak
Overall for $3 you cannot go wrong with this game and if you have any interest in this style of difficult game you definitely should pick it up.

Would have been so much better if the arrow keys moved, Z jumps, X shoots, and SHIFT dashes. Or at the very least an option to remap the controls would have been super nice! Also, this doesn't affect my review in any way, but some achievements would be great for a game that claims to be super hard because it gives you something to show off your hard work for. This game isn't BAD. For .98 it's pretty great fun, but it does need a lot of polishing up. As of right now I can't recommend it though.

If you can stand rather outdated graphics (although well crafted, it's no Skyrim) and a sometimes clunky, always bare bones interface - I highly recommend this game.
Combat:
No game has a more satisfying feeling when you kill a man on horseback and watch his body slump off the horse.  While some games (Chivalry, War of the Roses, etc.) have captured some of its 1st/3rd person medieval combat feel - and some games (Total War is the only one which comes to my mind, but there are others) have some of the tactical grittiness - the combat in Mount and Blade is its own class.
You can lead a small warband of soldiers around - paying for their keep, managing food supplies, training them through combat to become an elite fighting force - and make tactical decisions in LARGE army to army combats.  The interface, as noted before, is really clunky for this - however, the AI is reasonable in most cases, and you don't need to micromanage everything.  In the meantime, you can ride your way through the battle and utilize a huge variety of different fighting techniques.
Personal combat is intuitive, but varied.  It depends on aim, battlefield conditions, and momentum - making it feel less gamey than most games.  Each fighting technique feels balanced and unique - archery, thrown weapons, and crossbows are all very different ways of engaging in ranged combat.  Mounted combat feels very different than running around as infantry (and if my horse gets shot down, I'm immediately disoriented by the feeling of smallness and lack of speed - while others no doubt would be similarly confused if they had to get on a horse halfway through a battle) - and different types of weapons give different strategies.
Roleplay/Open World Stuff:
While the quests are very mechanical and bare bones (the dialogue is not poorly written, but it always makes it clear what is going on "behind the scenes"), the world changes based on your decisions and the strategies of dozens of other rulers/bandits/farmers and their bands.
You have a lot of different options to take.  You can pick up companions (who will fight alongside you and are fairly customizable, as well as having interesting stories and personal interactions - many will dislike certain strategies or other companions, so you have to pick and choose your style of play and the companions you keep), settle down and become a ruler (if a king lets you join up and get land... or if you take it for yourself), and help one of several factions conquer land and change the map of Calradia (a very simplistic, but evocative, world).
Even if you're a great ruler, you can face defeat - and your fates can change dramatically (you can get captured and lose all your armies - end up running in the hills, frightened by every bandit... or you might capture a powerful lord and ransom him for a fortune, doubling or tripling your tiny warbands size).
The game is good, is a bit old but still being good.

It's a bit of a departure from the first game, but still very good. The levels are more varied, some requiring drastically different play styles, which takes a bit to get used to. Most levels don't let you play with different masks, rather they are designed around a specific character's mechanic. I guess you could view that as a bad thing, but the tradeoff is that levels are more distinct and uniquely challenging. Also the bosses are generally better than the first game.
The story is a bit hard to follow since it's all told out of order, but it's pretty good if you can piece it together. And the music is great of course.

First off, as other reviewers have said, Hotline Miami 2 is harder than the first game. This increased difficulty feels more artificial than rewarding because of the larger maps, and the inclusion of more windows. This leads to a lot of deaths that feel cheap, as they force you to memorize the enemy layout, rather than moving through the level intuitively. All of that said, the inclusion of the ability to lock on to opponents is huge, and allows for a bit more precision.
The masks are more varied this time around, often drastically changing the way that you play. In addition to this, the different characters with their various fighting styles keep the game from getting stale. This is however, a much less adrenaline-fueled romp than the first game. The music is not as upbeat and exciting except for certain specific levels. This likely has to do with the tone of the plot, but for me it felt less fun than what I had expected.
The story is told through a lot more exposition than the first game, which I personally feel detracts from the visual story-tellng that game pulled off so well.
While this review sounds very negative, I would still very much recommend this game. I didn't enjoy it as much as the first, but I'm glad I got to experience it, and I enjoyed the game thoroughly.

I don't mind complexity in my games but it has to serve a purpose. In a first person shooter you wouldn't want to load a magazine bullet by bullet and release the slide every time you reload your pistol, but it works in Receiver because the whole game is built around the detailed functions of your firearm. Plenty of city-builders have complex systems like detailed citizen needs or production chains, but most pull back from having too many at once. Cultures does no such thing, piling on every possible system and consideration until you are running every facet of every resident's life. And if that somehow sounds like fun to you, well, read on.
Cultures - Northland puts you in charge of a band of plucky settlers in a cartoonish approximation of Middle Ages Europe. Each scenario in the lengthy campaign is heavily story-driven but at the heart of each you'll need to establish a thriving village and a standing army. You do this by gathering natural resources like wood and stone, using them to build workshops to refine them into more complex materials, and work your way up the enormous chain of upgrades and structures. Your settlements will sprawl like few others, with dozens of workshops ringed by a sea of dwellings and fortifications. It's quite a pleasure to watch your little folks putter along in their daily lives once you're established, moving goods and chatting with each other.
Getting established is the hard part, and it's mainly because of the depth afforded to your citizens. Every single inhabitant of your settlement is like a tiny RPG character, with meters for needs like hunger, sleep, and even socializing. They'll duck away from their duties to resolve these needs, so you'll need to keep their homes and food sources nearby. They also gain experience in the dozen plus different professions as they work, which is key to progressing because you can't staff the higher-level buildings until your workers in that profession level up as well. And if that wasn't enough, they also have equipment and inventories, along with special settings specific to their job like what kind of goods to make or which trading posts to visit.
Pressing spacebar with a citizen selected opens a menu with over a dozen different commands to issue them. Some of these aren't even necessary as the game uses context-sensitive right clicks (and in fact only issues orders with right-click, which threw me off when trying to build), while others are essential. You move your people around as you would in a proper real-time strategy game, except the pathfinding is atrocious, sending them on longcuts through dense forests instead of along the straight roads. This might be purposeful because your scouts can build signposts to mark paths, but this option is hidden among a dozen others in that tiny, cluttered spacebar menu.
The simple fact is that it will take you an inordinate amount of time and effort to do anything in Cultures, and you'll be required to do all that and more in each scenario. I haven't even touched on combat, or trading, or vehicles, or the religion system, after all. A game this deep and complex needs solid tutorials, but I could only get about half of them to even work. I did manage to extract the basics of orders, building, and combat so armed with that knowledge I started the campaign. The very first scenario has you defending a village under attack, using hero units that will earn you a game over if they die.
I don't think Cultures - Northland is a bad game necessarily, but it's not one I could ever recommend to anyone. The bewildering level of complexity formed from the crossing of so many disparate systems makes the audience for this game too tiny to even identify. It feels like a game from a completely different time, the kind you had to be there for at release and willing to devote weeks and months to playing. Well, times have changed and when I sit down to build a city or raise an army, I don't want to have to equip my people or put them down for naps. I mean, I already have two kids of my own.

After giving this game a pretty serious bit of time over the last month I have to sadly give it a thumbs down as a PC game. Now as for on mobile devices Id say its standard play with a solid art style. But for those of us on PCs here on steam  as maybe a pure ftp game its an ok casual time waster.
However the game is thick with micro transactions. It costs to skip many hour long( sometimes day long) crafting times.It costs for many cosmetic rewards you still have to first earn the right to use via game play.
Now the company wanting money is not some sin. But consider this. for the ultimate guardian pack they want 50 bucks. You get a few unique cosmetics, some extra storage a butt load of their dragon crystal points that still wont get you more then a few of the pricier point only in game items.
Now consider a classic but high quality pay once play forever fully finished MMO like Guild Wars. for 30 bucks you get the classic campaign trilolgy and for another 20 the eye of the north expansion. While old GW is far from dated. the graphics are still eye catchingly lovely, and easily destroy the cartoon style of this game. Game play wise, sure GW does especially during its lowbie levels use  common collect and fetch quest systems, but also has rich virbant stories, and many quests that demand the use of ones brain or at least reading the comprehensive wiki to develop winning strategies.
While I can see dabbling in this game from time to time, and using it as a chat room game, the moment I start thinking of spending a cent it loses out to many other games. Many of which I can get many hours of play in for a much more modest price.
Sadly this company seems more about drawing in a fan base that they can sell silly RL merchendise like shirts, novelty hats, and primitive physical calenders all with in game cosmetic items as part of the deal, to make their money. It feels like they are wasting alot of their development energy on limited time events, exclusive cosmetics that require buying some item that will act as free advertisment for them, and very little really spent on content or QoL improvments.
So while if I could Id rate it as an ok entry into mobile games, for steam pc gamers we just have too many better options to waste time or risk money on an EAG that shows little real potential to rival even old pc MMO like classic Guild Wars.

Some events take place prior to the first game while others come after. It can get a  bit confusing in my opinion, with it going back and forth in time.
I should also mention how gorgeous the game looks. A lot of indie/games tend to use retro style, and this is one of them. Except, this game makes it work like its a polished full 3d game. The animations are really awesome and fluid, and the designs for the levels is also really nice.
But all that aside, this game was really frustrating. Like, really really REALLY frustrating. It starts out fun but after a few deaths and stupid window ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t you just want to quit. The soundtrack really does keep you going though, and helped me get through some of the levels.
Anyway, I do recommend this game to others, but be warned, it is not friendly to newcomers at all.

It's a bit of a departure from the first game, but still very good. The levels are more varied, some requiring drastically different play styles, which takes a bit to get used to. Most levels don't let you play with different masks, rather they are designed around a specific character's mechanic. I guess you could view that as a bad thing, but the tradeoff is that levels are more distinct and uniquely challenging. Also the bosses are generally better than the first game.
The story is a bit hard to follow since it's all told out of order, but it's pretty good if you can piece it together. And the music is great of course.

First off, as other reviewers have said, Hotline Miami 2 is harder than the first game. This increased difficulty feels more artificial than rewarding because of the larger maps, and the inclusion of more windows. This leads to a lot of deaths that feel cheap, as they force you to memorize the enemy layout, rather than moving through the level intuitively. All of that said, the inclusion of the ability to lock on to opponents is huge, and allows for a bit more precision.
The masks are more varied this time around, often drastically changing the way that you play. In addition to this, the different characters with their various fighting styles keep the game from getting stale. This is however, a much less adrenaline-fueled romp than the first game. The music is not as upbeat and exciting except for certain specific levels. This likely has to do with the tone of the plot, but for me it felt less fun than what I had expected.
The story is told through a lot more exposition than the first game, which I personally feel detracts from the visual story-tellng that game pulled off so well.
While this review sounds very negative, I would still very much recommend this game. I didn't enjoy it as much as the first, but I'm glad I got to experience it, and I enjoyed the game thoroughly.

Quick review of this underrated game.
This game presents itself to you as a dark Alternate Reality Earth. It does it well with the whole mutants running about, Hayden becoming a super human freak of nature, and the russian backround.
Simple, Hayden the main protagonist is a merc that goes to russia to get a job done, he gets it done, shoots down a helicopter, runs into a mad scientist, gets shanked by a walking scrap of metal, gets infected, he tries to avoid transforming because it turns other people into horrible mutants, but eventually our protagonist: Hayden, instead of avoiding the transformation, he willing accepts it because the powers he slowly gains through out the game makes him very powerful, we are talking x-men levels here only much more violent.
Third Person "Action" shooter more like, it has a resident evil thing going on but it has a lot more focus on action combat gameplay compared to other third person shooter games. His main weapon isn't a gun which is why it is hard to classify this game as a third person shooter. His main weapon of choice is the Glaive, a very unique weapon type that i've only ever seen one action/hack n' slash character use, and that would be Van Helsing.
To make this quick, it is fun plain and simple. You can throw the Glaive as a projectile type weapon like a very violent boomrang, or get up close and personal by slashing people up. The finisher moves in this game are also awesome, It is a bit violent for my taste but cant deny it is very stylish looking well animated finisher moves.
Nice for a budget game. Which I assume this game is.
Nice sound effects for the Glaive, it sounds very blade-ish, the SFX used sounds extremely brutal when hack 'n and slashin away at legions of mutant freaks and generic soldiers.
The music gets pretty frigg'n scary though, the music is scarier than the actual game itself.
Haydens voice acting is great, budget game or not whoever his voice actor is did a great job. Everyone else is pretty junk though.
Badass (albeit normal human) merc for a Main Protagonist: Hayden, turns into a super human freak of nature, gains super powers such as creating shields made of pure energy to reflect projectiles, slowly gains metalic like armor, can absorb three elemental powers with his Glaive and use them against his foes ~ Lightning, Fire and Ice.
I also like his character design, it isn't often modern game designers that aren't japanese, chinese or south korean that make male characters actually look cool looking with a modest slim build and a cool hair cut, the hulking tall grunts from games like gears of war or god of war are very common and I don't like those types of designs for male characters.
Game is entertaining overall. It is a welcome twist on the third person shooter genre, throwing in super powers, a likable male protagonist with a cool character design, good voice acting, fun gameplay. Yeah, pretty gewd stuff.
Fair, only because to play with the Glaive weapon. Not many games have a Glaive class for fighting styles, it is a unique style of gameplay, too bad this version is extremely violent for the most part. Still fun though.
Fun game, if the price is below $5 on steam sale or if you can find a retail steam code cheaper, go for it, it is worth it just for the unique gameplay when you are tired of shooting crap all day, get up close and start slashing away.
*Likable main male protagonist, Hayden is a badass.
*Glaive is a badass unique weapon, a fighting style not used often.
*Decent graphics for a budget game, character models are good.
*Decent Storyline, better than most budget games.
*Finshing moves look very stylish and flashy, well animated and violent.
*No option to turn off blood and gore. (I don't like blood or gore in games, i prefer style and fantasy.)
*Buggy cover system
*Linear gameplay, no exploration or any extra discovery.
7.5/10 ~ recommended | Note: Only if you can purchase the game under $5, if not don't bother.

Let me preface this review first by saying that if I could get my money back on this game, I would. The Evil Within is another game that is trying to hop on the "survival horror" Zeitgiest that has been happening lately- and it falls flat on its face trying to do so. The many different play styles that this game tries to iencompass feels blocky and out of place. This is first experienced within the introduction level of the game, which in my opinion feels almost exactly like an Outlast clone, locker hiding included! During this short first level, you are chased by an angry juggernaught that you have no defenses against- oh, and you're limping as well. Not only is this extremely unforgiving and repetitive (you will die and repeat, trust me.) gameplay, it is totally misleading as to what the rest of the game intales. During the level transition cut scene, the game pushes into a Silent Hill-esque world with morphing, hostile, geography; But instead of instilling feelings of mystery and fear of the unknown and changing world like silent hill did, it leaves the player confused and a little annoyed by the abrupt shoe-in of this feature.
The second level is quite a difference experience. You're given your first weapon and are basically sent out into the woods without much direction or goal (think resident evil 4 sans clarity and fun). Once again overcruelty to the player entails with near invincible enemies and almost invisible traps. Your weapon becomes basically pointless as you are given very little ammunition to work with and are drowned in bullet-sponge enemies that can revive; that is unless you burn them with matches- which are also extremely finite within the world. Your only option at this point is to sneak around enemies, but due to thier sixth-sense detection systems and sheer multitude of them, this slows the game to a crawling speed that makes the game tedious and repetitive.
In conclusion, this game tries to blend Resident Evil 4 with Outlast and Silent HIll in the hopes of making a truly terrifying experience, but the only thing terrifying about the game is how badly put together it is, that and the hilarious amount of edgieness that they tried to cram into every nook and cranny. Do not buy this game.

For every moment of genius in The Evil Within, there's always a moment
of frustration around the corner. With one-hit-kill traps placed
haphazardly around each environment, ruthless enemy bullet-sponges,
and incredibly rare ammo drops, you'd be forgiven for assuming that
The Evil Within caters purely to masochists.
Make no mistake, The Evil Within is VERY difficult. It's the type of
game that will make you curse like a sailor, throw your controller
against the wall, and cry yourself to sleep. Even the game's hub area
(which you'd expect to function like a typical "safe zone" in this
type of game), is full of nasty surprises, waiting to pop out when you
least expect them.
It's plain to see that a lot of enthusiasm and creativity was poured
into this game, and I wouldn't expect anything less from Shinji
Mikami, the man behind the original Resident Evil series.
Each and every chapter is lovingly-crafted from start to finish, and
the pacing is excellent...as long as you know what you're doing.
I will freely admit that I died a lot during this game. A LOT. So much
so, that the pacing was terrible for me. I would spend an hour on one
chapter, and 3 hours on the next, struggling with a boss fight or
section that I just could not, for the life of me, figure out how to
deal with. It was tempting to turn the difficulty down to the "casual"
setting, but my stubborn ego wouldn't allow it.
So I dealt with the agonizing length between checkpoints, the enemies
who were immune to stealth attacks despite being in the
stealth-oriented sections of the game, the motion-sensing bomb traps
that were always placed just out of view, entire sections of the game
where ammo was so scarce that I had to either run or die, and boss
fights that seemed to last for eternities.
I guess the question I'd ask at this point is:
Does this sound fun to you?
It wasn't for me. By the end of the game, I wanted to rip my hair out
due to all the stress I'd endured. The only reasons I kept going were
to see the incredibly varied and distinct locations (seriously, every
chapter has its own unique identity. The devs did a fantastic job of
keeping things fresh and new throughout the game), and to experience
the intriguing, albeit non-sensical and hard-to-keep-track-of story.
I have difficulty recommending this game, but I'd say that's less of a
statement about the game itself, and more of a statement about me.
There's a certain type of person out there who will embrace this type
of unforgiving gameplay, and feel a great sense of reward in
conquering the seemingly insurmountable odds. If you've ever played
any of the original Resident Evil games, and you're looking for a
challenge, The Evil Within might be just the game you're looking for.

Never in my life have I seen a game that gave you a feeling of "Great game, but needs more work and polish to be great" that would last for 5 years.
The game is really fun, but it perpetually needs a bit more polish:
PvP works for 6 VS 6, but the balancing needs some work (it's tricky to balance 17 unique classes and develop new ones at the same time as making new content).
The dungeons are fun, but need more polish (dungeon mechanics are often completely unexplained).
NAtions all have different themes and are fun to explore, but need some more work (the government is completely useless, kinda like in IRL and the nations themselves are finally getting revamped in a few months)
Classes are fun to play, but need more work (some classes have aged better than others and prepare for people to telling you you suck if you don't use the optimal build)
The leveling and stuff is fun, especially when you are doing interesting quests (but there are still level gaps between questlines, occasionally leaving you to have to grind for 10 levels untill the next questline), but still better than a lot of other games.
The gameplay is fluid and fun, except whan it's not (expect some occasional lag when loading areas, the artstyle is beautifull, but it takes it's toll on toaster computers)
The comunity is great, really loyal and always ready to help other players (whenever they are not complaining about bugs and how slow the updates are, even thought they release them each month)
At the end of the day the game is fun to play casually, as long as you keep in mind it is being developed my one french studion that just doesn't have the same level of quality as the big companies out there. The game definitly has the same cute artstyle, tounge in cheek humor and heavy handed puns as the other games from Ankama, but this is par of the reason why I love this game and have been playing it for the last 5 years.
It's probably not a game for everyone, but I think everyone should give it a go.

At first impression you would be forgiven for thinking Layers of Fear is just another straightforward 'look around and spooky things happen' style of horror game. However, as you get further into the [sadly quite short, at the moment] game it becomes easier and easier to appreciate not just the impressive environmental design, but also the technical applications therein. The way the two mingle together makes for one of the most unique experiences you'll find, particularly in the indie horror market.
At the beginning of the game you're thrown immediately into your character's house with no direction. Initially it seems a bit directionless, but within a few minutes of exploring the house you'll find that you're put onto what seems to be a linear path with a few forks here and there. As you explore, you'll trigger numerous scares, ranging from your run of the mill objects flying off shelves, up to... Well, I'll leave that for you to discover yourselves.
I was continually impressed with how the game builds up tension, and then a false sense of security to get under your skin before dropping one of those many unique scares. You'll never see a scare tactic repeated, with the game constantly changing what you're finding. Sure, elements are borrowed between some scares - rooms repeating, or doors disappearing. But the ultimate result is always entirely different.
Even if the game did not expand on the content present, I feel I could still recommend buying it. However, I am excited greatly by the idea of the game being expanded on further. I believe that I have only just started scratching on the surface of the plot, which already has me hooked with only a few hints of who your character is, and their further... Issues, shall we say.
Long story short; This is an artistically and technically impressive title that any horror fan would be a fool to go without trying.

After playing few hours for free during weekend's free access.
If you have a group of friends to play with and you like Warhammer universe, by all means buy it and have fun.
However if you want to play it solo or with just one other person, then avoid it to save yourself a lot of frustration.
What is good about this game:
+ Interesting first person melee combat, with stagger effect when you are hit
+ Nice graphics of this fantasy universe
+ Few distinct heros to choose from
What is not so good (mostly when playing solo or with just 1 friend and 2 BOTs)
- Slow progression - only when mission is completed (and a single mission can take 30-60 min) you gain a piece of equipment to your collection, even then good loot is not guaranteed or a loot to class you played (you can get loot for a class you don't like), so if you fail mission after 50min you get nothing. Even when you get some loot it will be nothing fancy, to get fancy loot you need to play on higher difficulties and to play on higher difficulties you need real people not BOTs (see below)
- Weak BOT AI - bots don't use equipment like buff potions or explosives, they do not pick up and carry quest items, they do not use special attacks (at least I have never seen Bright Wizard to fire his AOE attack from his staff)
Conclusion:
It is a fun game to play with a group of 3 friends, otherwise look for some other titles to play solo.

So, as many people said the game can be a little boring if you don't have at least one friend to play it with. There were a lot of players who were clearly just grinding for loot, they would join midway through the game and leave at the end. Clearly they were hoping to join near the end so they could grind more efficiently but I have no idea when that gets fun. I spent the entire free weekend as the bright wizard which meant that I never needed ammo but if I used my magic too frequently I would literally explode and die. I could avoid this by waiting for my excess magic to drain out or by venting it out quickly at the cost of health. As someone who always plays the mage in a fantasy game I loved the feeling that I had unlimited magical power but with serious consequences for using too much. In a game where you have magic points or spells per session, I have often felt that my magic was limited. In Vermintide, my magic has no limits, it is ME that is limited.
The character interactions were interesting but honestly, I just wish there were more of them. The witch hunter seemed to interact the most, often just to tell the bright wizard and the elven way watcher how much he didn't trust them but hey, I guess that's his thing. The characters talked often enough but I really found myself wishing for the moments from Left 4 Dead when the characters would just have a conversation. I got a strong feeling for the personalities of these characters but had little to no idea of their larger motivations. So, for story telling I found that Vermintide fell a little short.
My biggest complaint for enemies was the rat ogre (the tank equivalent). It had far too much health and while I get that was the point I just couldn't avoid the feeling whenever it showed up that I wasn't doing any damage to it. It took two or three minutes to deal with it every time while most tanks from L4D were done in a minute and a half at most.
There were bugs and they need to be fixed but they never broke the game for me. Whenever we failed I usually felt that it was because we didn't work together well enough, not because there was something wrong with the game.
Hopefully the free weekend will revive the player base and bring some new life into the game. I finished all of the missions in the base game in about 9 hours on easy, but there is definitely more to do. I am going to purchase, but I have two other friends to play with. If I was alone, I would not get it.

Too put it blanky Vermintide is a reskinned L4D with inventory. And while it has some issues, I would recommend you get it during sale.
Pros:
- While it is clearly modeled after L4D, it does give it a fresh new set of paint, and doesn't seem all that similar.
- The characters are well designed, voice acting is great and enemies' overall design looks pretty stellar
- The hack and slash first person nature complements the setting very well.
- Very atmospheric, levels are quite long and thought out.
- Has an interactive customization of loadouts and forging system, which help give the player an identity.
- Difficulty setting which restricts players from playing above hard, forcing them to prove their skill to play.
- Has bots capability and host migration now, replacing the annoying Peer-to-peer system where all players are kicked if the host leaves.
- Has a captivating story instead of L4D's generic "zombie invasion" plot.
- Requires Co-operative gameplay to work, punishing stragglers and loners.
Cons
- Enemies are hard to destinguish from players due to the lack of borders around them constantly, also the general dingyness of it makes it difficult too
- Ranged weapons are underpowered and have limited ammunition, making the Mage much easier to play as, since her ammo is unlimited and splash damage fire is generally more reliable.
- Optimization issues.
- Crafting system is quite haphazard and awkward to work with.
- Inventory items are only collected after beating a mission, making grinding inevitable.
- As with many games, connectivity issues are amok and you'll lag like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ if your ping sucks.
- No workshop or mods.
- Bots are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
- Some of the objectives are dauntingly repetitive, and hauling slow objects while you're defensless, relying on your teammates to help you really sucks if you're playing with non-cooperative teammates.
- Incredibily slidy movement, combat can sometimes be clunky.
- No voice radial option, making communication purely text based.
- Not much indication in terms of audio or visual cues as to when your teammates are in peril or an enemy is close.
- The game doesn't seem to aid you at all in terms of finding weapons. You'll constantly find medical equipment during the start while your health is optimum, but there's a 50/50 chance it'll stop all together during the finale of the chapter.
Once again, good idea to get this while it's on sale. It needs work but I'd suggest you buy it. 6.5/10

Hotline Miami 2 is a very...
Well, it's a very interesting game.
Staying true to the original and not introducing many game mechanics may feel stale, but then again the first was so solid that you don't need to change much. However, the combat focus has drastically shifted from melee up close bashing to hallway and open room gunfights. It's an interesting change, and is sometimes fun especially when you tear through a level simply putting a bullet in every enemy's head, but the game is now far more difficult. The massive levels, while fun to rampage through, allow enemies to see you from offscreen and they are no stormtroopers. One careless step into the open and you may eventually need a new R key.
However, the game is incredibly fun still. The music is more intense and action feeling that the first game, with Carpenter Brut and Magic Sword adding their skills to the crew along with several others. The story, while definetly clearer than the original, is still weird as F**K, and takes either replays or research to fully understand. When you piece it together though, the end result is a wild intercontinental bloodbath of epic proportions.  New characters manage to spice up the gameplay just enough that you feel like it's not just a reskinned version of the first game, but stay familiar enough so you know what you're doing. It is a very good game, just very different than the first, and that isn't a bad thing.

Great Odin's beard; it's Cultures!
NOTE: I have not played much on Steam, but I played the Cultures games a LOT back in the day.
The Cultures series of strategy/city-builder or "society simulator" games were made by three of the guys from Blue Byte who were part of the design and creation of The Settlers/Die Siedler II: Veni, Vidi, Vici. Enough said! Regarded by many city-builder fans as the spiritual successor to the original Setters series; while I did enjoy Settlers 3 and 4 I feel that these were much better games. It's very similar to those however, albeit with a much more personal touch. From the micromanagement of the workers and people (e.g. you have to breed them and provide living spaces close to workplaces) and the RPG-ish elements (workers skill-up and professions/technologies are branching) along with a story-driven campaign, this under-rated classic is an absolute must-have for any fan of the city-builder style of strategy games.
Pros:
- Vikings!
- Excellent micromanagement
- Decent 2D/sprite graphics that still look great today (despite being over ten years old you can still use 1080p resolution and the UI scales well)
- Random banter and social dynamics of your little virtual Vikings; you actually care about each and every one
- Detailed progression of technology/professions
- Decent-enough story line to keep you engaged
- Roads (not required for transport but beneficial), singposts, trade routes and remote settlements on large maps
- Ships!
- Can suck you in for hours at a time...
Cons:
- ...can suck you in for hours at a time ;)
- Can get a little repetitive if you don't care about storylines
- Warfare can be a bit tedious and difficult (especially because it really hurts when just one of your soldiers are killed in battle *sob*)

I've been told some people are having trouble with grahpical glitches, I have a fix at the bottom of this review.
I loved this game as a kid and can happily say this release works perfectly. It supports modern HD resolutions (up to 1080) and I had no problem running the game. Even the multiplayer still seems to work. The fps is still low which is understandable for a 2D game but it means window scrolling is a little janky.
The game itself is a commodity based city builder that focuses on population and resource management over combat. It's unique from other games I've played like that because you control the lives of individual people, tell someone to become a farmer and they will, then promote them to a miller, then to baker, or send them to school so they can learn to be a tailor or a brewer. This is central to the games mechanics. It's The Sims crossed with Anno or Age of Empires and although it's not quite as strategic as AeO I can remember sinking 60+ hours into single levels just because it's so fun bulding and running your colony. It could have some more depth but I enjoy it a lot.
------BUG FIX------
If you're getting bugs while trying to play the game you can download a program called DXWnd found here:
As I said in my review, I haven't had any troubles so haven't done this personally but people who have told me this worked for them. I have used this method on other games so I trust it.
- After extracting the file run the 'dxwnd' .exe
- A little blank window will open, select the 'edit' menu and click 'add'
- A window with a bunch of options and tabs will open, fill them out as follows:
- "NAME:" = Northland (can be anything you like)
- "PATH:" = C:\Program Files\Steam\SteamApps\common\Cultures Northland\Game.exe
Note: you may have the game installed at a different location eg. "Program Files (x86)"
That's it, Hit OK and you should see 'Northland' appear as an option from the window that was blank before.
- Select it and go >edit>run and the game will run smoothly
You will have to launch the game using this program or have DXWnd open when launching it from steam every time.
DXWnd is a hook program that you can use to get a lot of old games running smoothly on new systems. I didn't create DXWnd.
is a trustworthy site for developers and you can get more support from the guy who made the program there if you need it.
As I said, I haven't had to use this fix myself so if you find any settings in dxwnd that improve performance even more let me know in a comment below and I'll add it.

Replica really is a hidden gem. I only find one flaw in the game, so I'll just say that first: the overall concept and implementation of it really excels, but writing may be too-comical or unrealistic/heavy-handed for some people, which may break the game for you, if you have very high expectations of it and also you think this topic shouldn't be tackled in a funny way.
Other than that, this game really comes together so well -- from the idea of censorship and government survillience, to the actual plot, to using the "phone" as the interface of the game, to how puzzles are implemented and solved using said phone, and all its visual and audio design -- almost everything comes together and compliment each other.
There are also many hidden endings (though some of them don't actually feel like an actual proper ending), so although the game is short for 1 play session (like 30 minutes, or if you are really bad at it maybe 1 hour), it actually mounts up to several hours of figuring out hidden messages if you don't resort to walkthroughs and try to hunt the achievements and endings yourself.
