A charming (warhammer grimdark) team-based horde-fighting experience that has differentiated gameplay through its 4 classes and risk-based loot system. Mood of the game crafted through fitting environments and lighting and an atmosphere-driving sound design. From the tell-tale sounds of unique skaven presence to the get-hyped percussive insistence of a rat ogre fight, I felt immersed and invested in the state of hte characters. So much so that straying from the main path to obtain a tome or two gave me pause.
It might not be good that the mechanics of this game draw heavily from the acclaimed L4D series, but it definitely is not a bad thing. The whole pitchforking re: it's a X clone, shouldn't dissuade you from trying the game out. I believe with sincere development, making a game after a "formula" will still yield unique experiences. The combat feels satisfying and the unique skavens, while reminiscent of special infected, feel and adds positively to the gameplay. Thematically it definitely earns a place in my heart!
Full disclosure though; While not having owned any warhammer tabletop sets, the fantasy (and its 40k cousin) universe has always enthralled me, so I definitely enjoyed another venture into this setting. I am also curious about 3rd party game engines and the fact that Vermintide was built on Autodesk's Stingray definitely piqued my interest.
Probably the biggest downer is the demanding toll it puts on my laptop (middling i7 with a GTX970). Granted it is not a custom-built powerhouse but I think there can be some safeguards in place that prevents the repeated overheating and crash-to-shutdown occurrences. I did come across suggestions to circumvent the abovementioned on reddit but having to trawl the web for compromises should not be the case. Optimization is a ongoing battle waged by the devs and I do wish them luck on that front as it will heavily affect playerbase growth that is critical for a co-operative game such as this.

What attracted me to this game was the SNES art style. It was also free. Anyway, Silver Creek Falls is a mystery/adventure game that puts you in the shoes of two detectives who are sent to the small town of Silver Creek Falls to investigate three bizarre crime scenes. It is a peaceful town so the sudden crimes that have been taking place are a little odd and considered to be related. That's up for you to decide. The story, which in this case is a third of the full game, is intriguing enough so far. Some of the writing is a little simplistic and cringe-worthy at times, but it does the job. The characters are fine, but it's still too early to draw any conclusions. One of the detectives is a big Boston sports fan while the other is recruited from the Scotland Yard.
The gameplay is fine, but it hasn't been too interactive yet. Most of the gameplay has been clicking through dialog and investigating crime scenes. At the crime scenes, you essentially walk around and click on blood splatters to collect blood samples. You also pick up evidence that might deem useful later on. Perhaps it's too early in the game, but right now none of the found evidence has come into play. I'm hoping that, like Ace Attorney, you are able to draw conclusions and make assumptions based on the evidence that you find. Maybe that comes later in the game...but right now none of that stuff has come into play.
Finally, the art style might have been my favorite aspect of the game. Characters are sprites and you roam around the little town and crime scenes which are also sprite-based. There hasn't been much to explore in the first chapter, but all the areas looked pretty nice. It would have been nice if the letters you find, as well as the map that you can reference, were consistent with the art style. They are regular images that just seem off-putting next to the rest of the game's assets. Anyway, not really sure if I'm going to continue with the three-part series. The story is fine, but the gameplay needs some improvement if it's going to capture my attention any further.

The first chapter for the completed Silver Creek Falls series, it is a detective RPGMaker story that has you investigating a strange series of murders in a quiet town.
The story is compelling enough, and heading into the crime scenes was enjoyable, with you gathering evidence and trying to piece the mystery. However, I had a few gripes with this game overall:
- There seemed to be no way to mess up your investigation, as leaving the crime scene without an important piece of evidence will trigger your partner to keep looking for clues, until he conveniently forgets to mention this once you've actually scoured the entire place. This avoids backtracking sure, but also tells me straight off the bat that it'll be a linear game too. Give me options if I collect everything, because I have that evidence, give me different routes, that sort of thing.
- Again with the linearity, once you'd leave the crime scene, you had to go straight to the second one, no freedom allowed. I criticize this because close to the ending of Chapter 1, you're forced to walk and thus given some modicum of freedom. However, this "freedom" didn't really mean anything as you could only go to one place. If you're giving me freedom to wander around the town, again, give me options.
I'm still recommending this because the cliffhanger ending got me intrigued to see what the rest of the story holds, and also since it's free, so I can forgive its small flaws.

Delicious bit-size "ambient platformer" that's more concerned with mood (primarily a the solitude that comes with sauntering through a deserted park) and sensory experience (lighting effects as they relate to revealing your environment) over gameplay. The subterranean world is gorgeous, and given the short play time, there's a feeling of there being "more" of the overall environment than the developers will let you see--whether that's red herring exits and rooms, or the simple promise of the outdoors.
Overall, a delightful and easily recommended mix of Night Sky, Mechanarium, Aquaria, and the current crop of free-roaming 2/2.5D platformers. Here's to a sequel that maintains the ease of entry and lack of handholding while working in some of the wickedly clever intralevel design of 1000 Amps.

This game has the distinction of being the first and only game that has made me motion sick through sound instead of graphics. The main character's primary sound effect is constantly playing in the background, but it's always biased completely to the left channel. After several straight hours of this, the next time I stood up, my inner ear was apparently completely scrambled...
In any case, it's a pretty charming puzzler where objects have a very distinct heft and feeling of weight to them. The game makes heavy use of physics, and many of the puzzles involve things like momentum, weight, reflection, etc. Built-in hint system ensures that you won't get stuck, at a loss on how to proceed, for long. The puzzles themselves are fairly varied (none are particularly taxing), and there's a distinct feeling of engagement and connectedness in the way you manipulate your character's actions and the way he interacts with the world. It's a feeling similar to touch controls, but more naturally suited to an analog stick.
Estimated time to complete: 3-4 hours (can be speedrun in about an hour)

It's so short, it's not really a waste of time, and it's good for a quick conceptualization of what a larger scale version would be like.

WAKFU is an interesting type of mmo, a grid based stratagy rpg. It's easily one of the top games of its genre and should be looked at. Just making a North America/ Canada server, from just the French server, the game its opening up.  Using the manga/anime tv series WAKFU, you embark on the story line journey of the World of 12 to climb and defeat Ogrest (an ogre) who pretty much messed up the world and is on this Mount Zinit. Now like most RPG games you choose a class. Here there are 15 (?) very diffrent style, culture, playing styles for the game. Foggernaut, Cra, Scram, Xelor, Huppermage, Elcaflip, Eniripsa, Sacrier, Elitrope, Rogue, Feca, Enutruf, Pandawa, Masqueraider, Sadida, Iop and Osamodas. Now the names are crazy, but everyone brings something new and diffrent to the table. Each class has specific elemental abilities witch is the base of the game. ELEMENTS. Bad guys have strength and weaknesses to the elements and so do you. Each area and boss and creatures all changes by the elements and what is happening in the game....So keep on ur toes. You and can change the elemental happenings by doing certain things in the ecosystem to help, or take advantage of, or find that the one boss will eat you cause fire does nothing to him at this moment. You can even change baddies to extinct or help them out along with your gathering items. Controlling the ecosystem and elements. Thats alot of power... Along with a class you take on a nation to help you politic, merchant, protect and help along against the Ogrest bad guy. Brakmar, Sufokia, Bonta and Amakna. Politics is very real with the economy and both are in according to your nation. Perks for your nation add to your crafting skills. Crafting in this game you can take them all. No choosing. Take on gathering skills to obtain items to craft, to up craftingskills . Its the usual RPG gameplay here, but its ALL available to you. There is mining, lumberjack, farming, tamming for cooking, armorsmith, close and distance weaponary, handyman, and just all sorts to do. Use these gathering skills and crafting to make your character better while you follow the story line through the World of 12. NOW, the aspect of the game is that it is grid, turn based, stratagy combat. No mobs or running to and frow baddies. You click, challange a group and go into tactical combat. You lose- you go back to a Pheonix save point. ( its not that bad)  Win and gain loot equipment and exp. ALL THE RPG GOODNESS. Equipment, level elemental spells and characteristics to be the best. The usual. Combat can be casual to slow to OMFG, I made a wrong move and the boss destroys you and your group. Remember it is turn based and planning and thinking is required...It's not a faceroll keyboard or click shoot till you hit the baddies.YES ! groups are made and incrouraged in this game like most MMO's. You also can have a sidekick to help you out. Sidekicks are leveld and geard by you and are earned through quests, missions, acheivments and such. Everyone starts off with the Astrub Knight. Hes a neat soldier, with a lance and melee, chopchops for you. Pets and mounts are also in game for fun and helping.  Custamize and collect pets, mounts and sidekicks to your liking or play style.So what class will you make? will you get to the top of Mount Zinit? and master your characters abilities for grid based stratagy combat!. It does have humor, the story line is pleasing with good music and voice acting. Its more fun then chess and checkers and its casual . The graphics and baddies can be a bit on the kid side, due to it being a kids ''cartoon''. The first dugeon bosses are a Cat, Larva, Chicken and Sheep. So yeah no ghoulies or anything to make your kids wimper. Also there is a problem that steam acheivments have not and seem not to be fixed yet for the game and the game of as now, is kinda low in number and population. BUMMER.

I was skeptical of the game, but it turned out to be quite enjoyable. If you're looking for a scary horror experience, you will be disappointed. A few "oh crap!" moments stand out, with some very tense fights, but besides that the horror elements and story can be ignored.
What it does stand as is a fun, enjoyable third person shooter, with a good variety of weapons, a nice upgrade system, and interesting, distinctive levels. The gameplay is fun and nice, but not necessarily easy, presenting a nice challenge on Survival difficulty. The controls are good as well, the usual fare pretty much.
The visuals are magnificent, and this may be the best looking horror game to date (right up there with Dead Space 2), they really put effort in to the area design. However, it comes at a steep disproportionate price. The game is very poorly optimized, framerates dropping very low at some points (below 30) on high end hardware without there really being what would seem like many polygons on the screen. Additionally, quality settings are oversimplified and lacking. While the the framerate lock and bars at the top and bottom of the screen are easily removable by a setting, good luck actually maintaining greater than 30 FPS.
It's not a masterpiece, but definitely worth a play through when it's on sale around $25 (if you have the hardware to support it).

The game is all around fun and frustrating at the same time as it's meant to be. I went into this game expecting very little horror elements and that's exactly what I got. It's not terrifying. I mean, c'mon, it's a third-person view! That alone was a dead give away! You can just expect to get startled by popping sounds, that's it. Now if this was a FPS game and things jumped in your face then we'd be talking about "scary".
I can agree on one thing, though: this game pretty much has no story. Not a weak story. Not a confusing story. Just....NO story. It felt like the creator wrote half the script, left the team, and a random newcomer filled in on the 2nd half of the script without reviewing the first half. It started off great, then in the later half it just got nowhere. The collectibles (newspapers, Sebastian's journal entries, missing posters, etc.) felt like they were irrelevant to the story of the game. Ruvik has no true motivation for being the caniving evil-doer that he is.  There's absolutely no connection for why Seb felt the need to "bring down this evil menace". Kidman is just a lost cause on a secret mission. Everything is all over the place.
I don't know. Maybe the devs intend to further elaborate the story through some DLCs. But again, that is a cash-grabbing strategy that one day might turn Bethesda into a EA brethren. You don't shred a game into pieces and force MORE money from gamers to fill in a story. No. DLCs are suppose to EXPAND upon a story, not explain it more. Way to blow your cover on that one, Bethesda.
But regazrdless, video games aren't about stories. Story-driven media is what you will get in movies and TV shows. Video games are about player engagement and having fun, and that's where the game delivered. Yes, there are some parts in this game that are mind-bogglingly annoying but things can be worked around and be counted as additional challenges. The game, for the most part, doesn't stick to its repetitive nature like alot of games these days do. It changes pace here and there and keeps things fresh. The transitioning between different environments and settings adds to the touch as well. And although people might complain about the traps in this game, I had a blast trying to disarm every single one I came across for the sake of collecting gears. By the time I finished the game, I still had over 100 gears left over that I could've used to produce agony bolts. Who's complaining about lack of ammo or resources?

Half of the game is Battlefield 1942 with updated graphics (I'll call this half the action game from now on)
The other half is a top-down view of Europe where you move assault teams of troops across the map (i'll call this the strategy game from now on)
Now these halves of the game can be played comepletely independantly, you never have to touch the action game if you dont want to (though you will have to pay for the fast-track to general) and you never have to touch the strategy game side if you choose.
3 factions in the game, US, German & Soviet. And these three factions battle each other for territory until one faction holds enough cities to be declared the winner.. then it all starts again. Some wars can be a few days.. some can be a month.
The strategy game makes the action game possible though. When a strategy game players assault team makes contact with an enemy strategy players assault team.. an action game match is made. The action players join, the game continues until there is a winner.. then that result goes back to the strategy game.
Did you hold the town in the action game? Then in the strategy game, the enemy retreats and the town remains being held by your faction.
Did you assault the airfield from the East and South and capture all the objectives? Then in the strategy game the airfield becomes your factions territory and can now be used to extend the range of your paratroopers and aircraft.
The depth of this game is what has kept me playing, and the development of it has a very long life span potentially. The developers hold a weekly devstream and after watching them over the months, i feel confident to say they are a great bunch. Handful of young talent and one of expierenced game industry peeps.
I simply cannot list all the features that make the action game as dynamic, and as full-filling as it is. I'd need to make a series of videos to fully prepare a new player to know what to expect.
Lastly though, the reason i've written this is because this game is worth giving a go, i gave it a go over a year ago and its now my main game. Is the game the same as it was then? Nope.. and again every few months the devs add a content update with X, Y & Z new features, weapons.. vehicles etc and the game will change a little again. You'll equip your soliders a little differently, change up your playstyle a little and hit the field for another war.
A lot of the negative reviews for this game and 90% of the forum posts are "meta complaints" essentially, or the devs made a drastic change to gather data or just see how something goes and the more vocal side of the community raised their concerns.
But the long and short of it is that this game is going to be changing for years.. the engine is there, the development team are cool and its free. People can argue theres some pay to win, but you gather that currency for free as you play and my main gun on the majority of my soliders is the default standard rifle without modifications.

Before i begin, let me say that the game as it is right now has several issues, including a bug with vsync that makes the game unplayable with broken mouse controls and recoil. If you have seen TotalBiscuit's WTF is... video you'd know what i'm talking about (note that TB didn't notice that this is caused from vsync). The workaround is to enable vsync, but this introduces input lag. The developers should fix this ASAP. But in hopes that they do, i'm going to ignore that for now.
Now about the game. AFAIK story-wise this is supposed to be the sequel of a book (Icarus Effect), which itself was a prequel to the story of Deus Ex: Human Revolution. Sadly the game doesn't seem to make much of a introduction to this and for the first hour or so you will feel disconnected from the characters since it starts assuming that you already know them. Personally i had never read the book (i actually didn't knew about it, but now i will try and get it) so it took me a while to get any attachment with the characters. As the game began i didn't knew why i should care about the main character, especially considering his background. The fact that the game seems to ignore some parts of the book didn't help either (at least according to people who have read it). Fortunately after a while, once you start figuring out what the actual story of the game is all about (which happens about when you meet the crook doctor, a few moments after TB decided to stop playing the game, if you watched that video) both the characters and story start to pick up and become interesting.
The game's visuals are ok, they remind me of some early 2000s games. The environments are good to look at, although if you have a large monitor you'll certainly notice the low texture resolution and the bad tiling in a few of them doesn't help either. Still, as far as environments go, they are nice to look at and remind of lower fidelity version of HR's environments. The worse parts IMO are the character models: they look attrocious, especially the heads of the woman junkies which are all over the place. The lighting on them equeally bad, as if someone didn't knew about smoothing groups in 3ds max or whatever modelling program they used and there doesn't seem to be enough animations for all the character actions (f.e. at several points the enemies will try to strafe left and right but there isn't any animation for that so they just slide with their feet motionless). The only good model is the one of the pilot you'll meet near the end, but even that looks like a bad copy of Faridah Malik (and apparently in the Deus Ex:HR universe all pilots must have a mole :-P). But if you can ignore the bad character modelling, the game looks fine. Technically it is quite simple, but as a theme the visuals work fine.
The best part IMO is the sound - the guns sound good and the music is really good. At a couple of places i just stopped playing for a while to listen to the background music. Most of it sounds like a remixed version of HR's music (which i suppose it is) but i think there are a couple of original scores as well.
Sadly, following the bad modelling the game also has bad voice acting with hilariously awful accents. The only good audio come from the TV broadcaster Eliza, which i assume uses the same voice actor as HR. The writing doesn't help either since in many cases you'll be left wondering why the writers thought that a specific line was a good idea.
The gameplay is basically a simplified version of HR's gameplay. You still have the hacking, shooting, sneaking, etc as HR and the original game, but the RPG elements are mostly removed beyond a very simplistic upgrade system (which most of the time isn't needed, except in a couple of areas where you have to use a specific augmentation). Also you can upgrade guns, but i didn't notice that, never needed it and finally decided to try it out almost at the end of the game but even after upgrading a gun to the maximum settings it didn't made much of a difference. Also there is an in-game shop where you get to buy stuff with in-game currency that you gain by doing stuff. I suspect that on iOS this was tied to IAP because the shop is available at any point (not just to some vendor or whatever like in HR) and contains almost everything you may want, including even a kit that brings you back to life when you die. This makes the game much easier, although the most interesting items are expensive enough so that you don't get them instantly. Still, it removes the tension from small things like running out of bullets (since the price of the bullets is very low).
The level design is ok, but for the first few levels it is quite linear. The interesting levels begin at the slums, where you start getting alternative routes and more areas to explore (incintentally this is where TB stopped playing). Up to that point it was mostly linear and played more like a tutorial than the real game. I think the devs thought nobody would have played HR so they wanted to reintroduce the gameplay - and did it in the worst way possible, by destroying most first impressions and filling the first few moments with awful tutorial panels with one of the most obnoxious voices you'll hear in a tutorial. The game however becomes even more interesting in the later stages like in the hotel.
Wrapping it up (and because i got bored typing this :-P), i think that there is a good game in there that tries to come out and the story is interesting, but the way it is told and the presentation (as far as animation and character models  go at least) isn't up to the task. I don't recommend it for the full price, especially considering the bugs that the game has, but i would recommend it if the bugs were fixed and the price was halved. It does have some interesting moments and does provide some story to the Deus Ex universe that seems to fit in, so it has that going for it. Also the gameplay, even if simplistic, can be enjoyable - if you can overlook the first hour or so.
I'm not generally recommending this game unless you are a fan of Deus Ex that is curious to see what this has to offer (and again, i'd recommend to wait for a price drop). If the bugs are  fixed and the price is dropped, i may change my recommendation to Yes, but even then be cautious about the other issues that the game has and mentioned above.

A charming (warhammer grimdark) team-based horde-fighting experience that has differentiated gameplay through its 4 classes and risk-based loot system. Mood of the game crafted through fitting environments and lighting and an atmosphere-driving sound design. From the tell-tale sounds of unique skaven presence to the get-hyped percussive insistence of a rat ogre fight, I felt immersed and invested in the state of hte characters. So much so that straying from the main path to obtain a tome or two gave me pause.
It might not be good that the mechanics of this game draw heavily from the acclaimed L4D series, but it definitely is not a bad thing. The whole pitchforking re: it's a X clone, shouldn't dissuade you from trying the game out. I believe with sincere development, making a game after a "formula" will still yield unique experiences. The combat feels satisfying and the unique skavens, while reminiscent of special infected, feel and adds positively to the gameplay. Thematically it definitely earns a place in my heart!
Full disclosure though; While not having owned any warhammer tabletop sets, the fantasy (and its 40k cousin) universe has always enthralled me, so I definitely enjoyed another venture into this setting. I am also curious about 3rd party game engines and the fact that Vermintide was built on Autodesk's Stingray definitely piqued my interest.
Probably the biggest downer is the demanding toll it puts on my laptop (middling i7 with a GTX970). Granted it is not a custom-built powerhouse but I think there can be some safeguards in place that prevents the repeated overheating and crash-to-shutdown occurrences. I did come across suggestions to circumvent the abovementioned on reddit but having to trawl the web for compromises should not be the case. Optimization is a ongoing battle waged by the devs and I do wish them luck on that front as it will heavily affect playerbase growth that is critical for a co-operative game such as this.

A beautiful atmospheric puzzle game that, without much back-story, throws you head first into the weird underground world you must escape from. The puzzle design borders on overly-simplistic (I dont even understand why there's an in-game hint system you can activate) logic puzzles hidden among the lush scenery that changes the deeper into the world you go. Game mechanics are simple and straight forward: you fly around and pick stuff up. The puzzle aspect uses these mechanics very well and to their full force. The story is left open to interpretation (just like all good art) and by the time you finish the game, you emerge with a sense of satisfaction at having completed your quest for freedom (or not, if you chose "the other path".)  Graphics are beautiful, charming and original (where else will you encounter a giant beating heart with a pace-maker underground?). Gameplay, while short (only took me about 3 hours from beginning to end), feels perfect for an adventure puzzler. All in all, a great puzzle game that's lacking slightly in replay value but stands out in visuals and atmosphere.

So I used to play Adventure Quest, Dragon Quest, Adventure Quest worlds all the time when I was just a lil kid at about 5 and stopped playing at around 12 due to a horrible balancing update. I remember there was a 3D game out and decided why not.
I can definitely say this is the same game I played growing up and loved, but it's also in a horribly unfinished state. Within my 1.6 hours of play time I've experienced bugs and glitches like crazy, clipping through the floor and dying and not being able to escape unless I teleport on time between the time I start falling and hitting the ground, absense of ambience sound/music, being transported to a different server than my friend when simply just walking to different areas, not being able to travel to my friend at all and among other issues.
Is the game bad though? No. In it's current state it's just unfinished, so unfinished it's funny sometimes just finding these bugs with my friend it was a good time.
If you played this game series before and you know it like I did, sinking 4 years of my life into Adventure Quest worlds weekly updates, I say play this game with a friend for the hell of it, or wait for it to be finished. It has potential to be the step up I was waiting for for the past 5 years.
I'm 18 now and it's still fun to me, even when the game doesn't even function properly half the time, but it's free how could I complain?

Pros:
o Basically what the title implies, it's a 3D version of the original Adventure Quest games, more so a continuation of
Adventure Quest Worlds.
o Updated frequently.
o Can play on phone
o Small, but not necessarily dead community.
o Can play on any PC (Low requirements to run)
o Less lag, and better servers than AQW
Cons:
o Repetitive quest (Currently being fixed as of Greenguard update)
o Not much content as of yet
o Player base is small: People usually only play when the game gets updated, because of easy late game access.
o Graphics/Basic gameplay might be a throw off.
o Not much reason to play this unless you have supported Artix in the past, or you for some reason like these type of
MMO styled games.
I like this game, but I'm not gonna act like it's a good game. Without the Artix title to go along with it, it's just another throwaway MMORPG. Despite this, I do like the simplicity, and sense of achievement (I used to play Adventure Quest, AQW, Runescape etc. So I'm used to these type of games), and I can see others vibing with this game the same way. Most likely if you don't like the game from the first hour of gameplay, you won't like the rest of the game.
The main thing going for this game, is the phone accessability, which goes hand and hand with the simplicity of controls, and makes the graphics less jarring (Phone games are expected to have bad graphics). Playing this on phone, vs playing this on pc, makes a lot more sense, but because there is pc access, I would prefer using pc, just for the added benefit of being able to rush through quest much easier.
Overall, I am 50/50 on this game, but I will recommend it just for the fact that I do enjoy it, despite the fact that most people won't.

Unmechanical is a lovingly crafted 2.5D puzzle sidescroller with tricky physics-based puzzles, lots of exploration, great visuals and is the first release of swedish developer Talawa Games.
The game is based on the Unreal Engine, which seems to have been the perfect choice of an engine for this game. The level design, the puzzles, the lighting, the controls - everything feels perfectly right here.
Talawa Games seemed to aim at a casual yet challenging puzzle experience. There is no health bar and no enemies in the game, so you can entirely focus on exploring the world of Unmechanical and solving the puzzles, which sometimes are challenging but never get frustrating.
It's an easy-to-pick-up game and doesn't require reading the manual to get used to the controls - you just need 5 keys throughout the whole game. You steer the cute little robot with WASD/left thumb stick and activate your tractor beam with Space or X/LT/RT on your controller.
Unfortunately, the playtime is only about 2-4 hours depending on your puzzling skills and getting some of the achievements is actually a bigger challenge than solving most of the puzzles in the game. Even though it would be great to see more of this game with new levels and puzzles, I feel that the length of the game worked out perfectly. Other games tend to repeat puzzles over and over to artificially stretch the playtime - fortunately, Talawa Games didn't do this with Unmechanical.
Unmechanical is a casual and extremely relaxing game and the ambient music adds a lot to this, so it's the perfect game to grab a controller, sit back and enjoy some puzzling.

This is an amazing game, one of the best co-op experiences if I've had in a long time.
It fixed a lot of what I didn't like in similar games, such as enemies that instantly knock you down and require help. There's a backstabber enemy you can dodge and push, a grabby enemy you can both dodge and hit before it hurts you. Its overall extremely satisfying to take these out on your own, but if you do get caught, there's a lot of ways allies can help.
You completely can fight every enemy alone, on your own skill, you just won't, because it's better to work as a party.
They didn't have to hardcode impossible situations to force teamwork, the game is naturally challenging, and you'll want to work together.
The characters are interesting, with tons of dialogue and banter for different levels.
There's tons of weapon variety, which have perks which you can upgrade and change however you want to make what suits you.
I didn't think this game was going to be half as good as it was, it really is amazing.

It's tough to recommend this. It seems to serve as bait to get people to buy the other 2 chapters. They could've just as easy made it one complete game. I've seen massive RPGMaker games going for less than $5. To get the other 2 chapters of this story, it would cost $9.98. That's a bit much.
Unlike many of the other RPGMaker games, this one strays from the typical [J|A|C]RPG storylines and goes with a crime/investigation mystery story. It's fairly predictible most of the time, but that's okay. The genre tends to be that way for the most part unless the writer happens to be really good with setting up mysteries.
I haven't played the other 2, so I can't speak for the series as a whole, but this chapter is extremely linear. The map is very small, and each scene is limited. The only actions available are collecting things, examining prop items, talking to NPCs when required to continue, and entering/exiting a scene. They all must be followed in a given order. The characters aren't all that special, either.
The only reason it would take more than 15-30 minutes to complete is because of the extra fluff dialog, such as the history of the park. Or, in my case, you miss some things needed for the Dracula achievement, so the first scenes would need to be played again.
With all of this, I'm still recommending it.
So, for it being free and short, you may as well give it a go if you have any interest in light mystery stories.

I spent with first game 100 hours and I am about to beat this time with the second game. I don't remember other game which I would play so long after my school years passed. Why? What do I like?
Matches are fast to play. No long waiting for actions of another player.
Automatic gameplay creates specific environment and rules. It is fun to watch.
The strategy is the key to win. Only 7 cards in the deck but billions of combinations. You can make offensive or defensive decks or balance both sides.
Low rarity cards are powerful. You can make strong combos by regular play.
Every deck has a weakness. Learn some tactics in the campaign.
I usually don't mind my position on ladder much. Be ready to fight my crazy combinations.
The best feeling when I see my invention/combination used by other players. (Maybe it is just coincidence.)
There are 4 types of card battles. Here is my view:
Classic mode - playground to test your deck. If you have some strategy then there is high chance that you win more than 50% matches. You can assign the first target to creatures but I prefer to ignore this option as preparation for Ladder matches (Pro and Hardcore) where you don't have such option.
Pro mode - it is possible to adjust deck - choose 3 cards and see 3 cards of the opponent (only creatures), then other 2 cards and other 2 cards. The target is to hide your strategy or mislead your opponent and at the same time, discover opponents strategy and adjust deck. The position of every card matters.
Hardcore mode - Gameplay of 3 decks is chained. You choose whole decks and you can react to opponent's selection. 1 deck can beat even all 3 decks but it is not common. The extra strategy is brought by effect transfer. Decks transfer all positive and negative effects to fight the next deck.
Arena mode - Sanctuary for Pay2Win screamers to prove that their losses are caused by money. Same cards available for you and opponents. It is just about skills.
If you like the strategy planning over the push for the next move then this card game is worth your try. The game is still fresh. The community is rather small and nice. You can make a big progress and reach top positions without spending a cent. I am using 1 - 3 stars cards and I am able to reach TOP30 (I am just not so time commited to stay there).
One tip for playing in the window mode. How to make it work:
1 Decrease display resolution to desired window size for game
2 Run Game
3 Alt+Enter
4 Close Game
5 Increase display resolution
6 Run Game (it will start automatically in the window mode)

Hands down, one of the best TCG games I've played (and trust me, I've played THEM ALL)
First of all, let's talk about the beautiful art style. No other game on the market is as gorgeous and creative as ECB2:DR. Every time I purchased a card I was in awe. From wonderfully rendered knights to terrifyingly real dragons, every piece of artwork drew me in deeper in to the world of the game.
The UI is very beautiful too! Most TCG games are hard to navigate and difficult to understand. It's sometimes a chore just to even get in a game. This game had me up and running ASAP. The tutorial was very helpful and I felt like a pro in no time.
Enough about how it looks. You want to know: Does this game deliver? Buddy... I'm here to tell you, the game delivers BIG TIME. I hesitate to use the word "addicting" because drug and alcohol abuse are serious issues, but man I couldn't stop playing ECB2:DR all night! It's simple enough to be good quick, but challenging enough to drive you to hone your skills and become great.
It's hard to even compare it to other TCG games. Hearthstone and Legends? No thank you. Those games look like they were made for little kids! Hey, don't get me wrong, little kids need games to play too. That's totally fine! But if you're looking for a more intense, more challenging, and more fun experience - look no further.
Bonus: The music is GREAT! Normally with games like this, I'll just turn down the music and listen to something else, but I found myself totally jamming out to this! Does anyone know where I can purchase the soundtrack?

Actually really enjoyed this. Being a mobile port it's not as good as Human Revolution: It's reduced and simplified in a lot of areas. Inventory management is gone and replaced with a strange in-game shop-inventory hybrid and many gameplay mechanics have been altered to try and remove elements of physics from them: Dead bodies disappear instead of the player having to hide them; objects like crates can not be picked up, instead they slide out of the way when interacted with, behaving like doors (special doors that require the heavy lifting); jumping has been removed and replaced with a vaulting-over-cover-system (which in my experience was the most buggy feature of the game).
The interface and controls bear the mark of the mobile platform in many places but it has largely been converted to work fluidly with a keyboard and mouse. The F1-F4 keys still activate augmentations, the number keys can still be assigned to hotkey inventory items (and augs as well actually), G still quickthrows grenades, etc. All that is obviously missing is (as said already) the jump button and the ability to aim down the sites (which makes the process of firing a scoped weapon a strange one and stands out as the one big issue of the controls for me). Menus are easily navigated with the mouse and all "click and drag" elements from the mobile UI are easily navigated with the mousewheel. Even things like the ability to use keypads with the numpad and backspace key are intact in this game. The controls are unfortunately not rebindable though, which is a shame, though I don't think I would have changed any of them if I had the option.
Controls are not as fluid as Human Revolution though after half an hour I can safely say I stopped really noticing any initial clunkiness and found the game quite mechanically enjoyable. I played mostly stealth but the few firefights I engaged in were quite fun even if, again, a bit clumsier than Human Revolution in both player control and enemy AI.
As for the story: It provides more conspiracies and betrayals as you would expect from a Deus Ex game. It's fairly typical of the series though with some rather over-exposition-y dialogue in many parts. This is also intended to be an episodic title and so this is only part of a storyline (a storyline that actually started in the Icarus Effect novel) so don't expect a conclusion here. Quite the opposite: it ends on a cliffhanger.
In almost all instances this game is basically Human Revolution in miniature with reduced functionality. It's quite sort too: It basically has the content of one hub area from Human Revolution and a similar length. How long it takes you to get through it will depend hugely on your playstyle but if you go straight from objective to objective shooting your way through you could easily finish it in one sitting. It's intended to be an episode game so hopefully more levels will be forthcoming.

It's rough around the edges, but the core gameplay is too good to ignore.
The Evil Within is the latest creation from Shinji Mikami (Resident Evil, Resident Evil 4), and it shows.  Tilt your head and squint and you could almost mistake this for Resident Evil 4.  While TEW certainly carries over some of Mikami's horror staples, it has a stronger emphasis on horror that distinguishes it from his previous works.  Enemies are incredibly dangerous, resources are scarce, and the gore has been turned up 11.
At its core, The Evil Within is a tense action game with some minor stealth elements that grants the player a staggering number of tricks and techniques for overcoming its brutally tough enemies.  Protagonist Sebastion Castellanos quickly arms himself with the standard Pistol, Shotgun, Sniper Rifle, Grenades setup, but augments it with a devastating and fun weapon called the agony crossbow.  By disarming traps hidden throughout the levels, Sebastion can create a variety of special crossbow bolts, including ones that explode, shock, freeze, burn, blind or poison foes.  This is only the beginning of the game's amazing combat system.  The player can use all these, along with stealth kills, environmental hazards, and the occasional torch or hand axe to tear through the game's creepy, zombie-like foes (and other assorted monstrosities).
It's no cakewalk however, even basic enemies can take a ton of punishment, but the game never feels like you're facing bullet sponges.  The enemies are tough to kill if you just pour hot lead into them, but by destroying their skulls with headshots, stabbing their brains with your knife, or burning them, you can put them down for good.  This leads to the fairly interesting match mechanic.  Once an enemy is downed, Sebastion can use a match to set their body (and possibly other adjacent bodies) ablaze.  Matches are one of the few resources that feel plentiful, so resourceful players can do fun tricks, like shotgunning a group of enemies down then setting the whole group alight with a single match.  Resource conservation is rarely ever this satisfying or fun.
The game is also incredibly varied, with different mechanics often showing up for only a chapter or two before quietly exciting the game.  It works well, because it keeps each chapter interesting and fun, but the more obnoxious foes you meet won't get a chance to really grate on you, since they'll be gone almost as soon as they've appeared.  With 15 chapters full of unique and interesting scenarios, The Evil Within definitely never becomes boring.
In fact, the game will remain interesting even into extra playthroughs.  Thanks to a variety of difficulty settings (including the horribly unfair 1-hit-killathon, Akumu mode) and New Game+ goodies, there's a lot of stuff to do in The Evil Within.  The systems are complex enough that your first playthrough almost feels like a tutorial, and future playthroughs are incredibly fun as you take on old encounters with far more skill and knowledge of the game's systems.
It's not all roses however, as The Evil Within has some serious shortfalls outside of its gameplay.  The story is unclear and ends on a very unsatisfying note (though the DLC promises more).  The game also suffers from a slew of technical issues, including a bizarre tendency to hover around 30 FPS, even on a very strong graphics card.  Some poor animations and minor bugs are certainly present as well, and it really makes me wish Bethesda was more willing to release games when they're ready rather than rushing them out the door.
The Evil Within's core combat systems are so detailed, fun, and varied that it's easy to overlook its few problems.  I highly recommend this to any fans of survival horror, or anyone who wants a challenging action game with great combat.

Before I begin I'd like to say this is a great game if you have a child between the age 8 - 12(Which I believe is the target audience for this game) and they want to get into MMO's.
I play this with my Son, he seems to love it even though all he does is follow me around and attack the things I attack.
I can't imagine any adults playing this without their child being the soul reason. About 30 minutes in I wanted to drink all the bleach in my house. Each zone that I've been to has consisted of 2-3 Monster types with 1-2 Bosses with quest that make you kill each of those monsters over and over and over, I started to actually feel sorry for the monsters. The quest will get you to the level required to adventure into the next zone.
Grinding is a snore fest, the same abilities you have at level 1 you'll have at level 12 (My level atm) If you get new abilities later towards endgame (If there actually is Endgame) I'd be surprised. Monsters are either incredibly tough or not even a challenge. With at least two people attacking anything (So far) there is no challenge.
Crafting is mindlessly grinding the mobs in the zone you're in until you have enough materials to make the gear plus buying some of the materials from the vendor who is also the crafter. After that you pay the gold or the ingame currency and wait the time for the NPC to make the gear. From what I've seen if you get the gear from each zone your character will be strong enough to do most things alone.
Dungeons, so, they're not that great. My Son and I farmed the gear from the first dungeon and replaced it as soon as we got to the next zone with much better gear. I suggest doing the quest for dungeons and moving on. I could be wrong about this later on but right now Its just not worth it.
The Community so far has been nothing but helpful. I've not spoken to a person who hasn't offered to help kill a group monster or offering help with how to do something, where to find something etc. Its refreshing to know that not all MMO's have a terrible playerbase.
I know the game is in Early Access so I'm not going to pick everything apart because the game runs well and I can't imagine you'll need a high end pc to run it. I haven't experienced anything that would keep adult players interested its a game you can play with one hand while watching TV or eating dinner but if you do have a child that wants to play MMO's this would make a perfect starter for the.

Its still in beta but sofar its worth it all. The premium ingame currency is useless so it pretty much forces everyone to grind and play fairly. although you can use it to buy cosmetics.
I strongly suggest that you buy one of the guardian packs if you plan on buying premium currnecy

I'd first off like to start by saying this game BARELY made it into my recommended side of things, but anyway onto the review.
Deus Ex the Fall was a phone game that DX fans whined and clamored to be on PC, and Square Enix granted their wish. The Fall is very ambitious for a phone game, boasting voice acting, decently sized areas and ok graphics on a phone. When ported the graphics didn't get upgraded much at all but to me this is fine as I've never been one to be a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥ and even consider most modern graphics more than we need these days in leu of putting the funding more towards gameplay and features. The area will of course feel small for a PC gamer but this reminds me a lot of Metal Gear Solid Peace Walker when it got ported from PSP to consoles, the areas are about equal in size. Voice acting at times gets very cheesy.
As far as gameplay goes, its very solid Deus Ex HR gameplay which is a good 95% what saves this game. All Human Revolution features are there and it has a solid system that lets one play stealth or action. Hacking apparently got on some peoples nerves in HR because they added a new item called an auto hacker, also present in HR Director's Cut, this will automatically succeed on any hack you perform though you still need a high enough hack level to initiate the hack on any given terminal. While I didn't use them myself its nice to see more options for people who really didn't care hacking to still be allowed to have fun. Take downs still feel good in this game but now the bodies just disintegrate instead of being require to stash them, which for stealth fans like me is a little lame but not enough to really be up in arms about. Even in a tiny mobile title like this they attempted to have several nooks and crannies for one to explore giving that feeling of exploration that any DX game needs to be successful.
Now onto some of the major problems which pretty much all come down to "porting woes". Many people have reported problems with the game most I have not personally experienced but I did run into one or two.  The Hacking UI scrolling and mouse sensitivity do not work unless one enables vsync, which for many doing so makes the game run very sluggish, I was one of the few that didn't have the entire game crap out on me doing this but even I noticed a performance hit once it was on and it would get worse over extended playing periods. I also had extended playing periods due to the fact I didn't want to have a currently existing save bug that occurs near the end of the game where it'll load you up into a non-interactible world every single time, and due to the game having a single save file (another flaw with the game) will force one to format and start the game over. My last complaint but one I should have foreseen was the fact the game ends on a "To be continued" making it episodic, I've always had things against episodic games, its splitting a game up needlessly in an attempt to make more money. Now The fall offers more gameplay at $9 than Missing Link did at its launch price of $15, most didn't get Missing until it went on sale, and that is exactly what I recommend with The Fall, its a fun game by all rights, but its problems do not warrant a full price purchase.

It does a wonderful job in painting a picture (so to speak) of the decay of the human psyche after prolonged exposure to certain traumatic events that may happen in ones life. I highly recommend this title, it's atmosphereic horror at it's best and yes it includes some jumpscares but they actually make sense and aren't thrown in the player's face too much.
I would only have one minor complaint and that is on occasion the framerate drops. It seems to occur prior to imminent game event triggers but apart from that it's a depressing, house-shape shifting, hallucinogenic, creepy in-depth journey into madness.
So far the experience is around 2 hours of gameplay and I'll be looking forward to more!

It's like warcraft 3, but the hero mechanics is taken to amazing depths.
You can have summoners, "leaders" (provide morale/eco boosts), fighters, mages, and any mixture of the four that will and do change the battlefield in your favor - granted you grind the campaign (or skirmish) long enough.
Said heroes are entirely customizable and can be moved from campaign to skirmish to multiplayer matches with relative ease, the concept is wonderful and hasn't been reproduced in any other RTS that I know of.
There are around ten or so different races, with different art and tech trees, but they're hardly impactful. The spotlight is on the heroes (and for good reasons).
I really recommend this without the forced mod that gives a timer to summoned units though, takes the fun out of playing demons (or any summoner type).

Talawa Games; A team of students from 'Future Games' a Swedish games education project puts the heavily (over) used Unreal 3 Engine to use crafting a satisfying experience that only falls short for those wanting a well told story. Controls are devilishly simple yet never serve too tarnish or cheapen gameplay. You control an unnamed robot with an unflinching disposition that excels in 4 tasks with unmatched execution: Flight, Transporting Small Objects, Slamming into EVERYTHING, and of course, look like a precious metal child with a propeller cap. The visuals evolve as you progress, following the style of the puzzles. Locals include watery caves that evolve seamlessly into a bizarre fusion of metal and flesh. Musical queues provide confirmation when progress is made, giving a well deserved feeling of relief and fits in just right with the space around you. For 10$ Unmechanical provides enough content to satisfy without overstaying its welcome.

Mount and Blade Warband is a very unassuming game; it was initially released in 2010 and didn’t have a large marketing budget, at least not one that would make the average gamer think I totally want to play this game. Mount & Blade takes place in the fictional, medieval land of Calradia where there are six kingdoms (each vaguely resembling an actual historical culture) vying to rule over all the others. That’s about it as far as plot goes; everything from the moment you boot up the game is a story that’s unique to you. The player’s own story is chosen at character creation, where the player can be, for example, a child of an impoverished noble or a street urchin. Choices that you make during the game stack on one another which have an impact on dialogue. If you spend a good portion of your time looting villages and raiding caravans, lords may begin to regard you as a criminal. On the flip side, if you choose to help out specific kingdoms you may be awarded lucrative mercenary contracts (these have their drawbacks as well). There are of course various things that remain constant throughout anyone’s playthrough – things like towns, kings, types of food, weapons, etc. That said, there is no overarching storyline – you are entirely left up to your own devices. I have been playing this game on and off since before it even came to steam, so my steam record is NOWHERE near what it should be if we count it all up. So, it is safe to say that I am a veteran player to this little tactical rpg.
Pros
Cute, fun graphics
Player controlled market
Player controlled environment
Decent Music
Large amount of content
Decent crafting
Individual houses
Cons
ANKAMA support has a reputation for being bad
NA servers are given no love ever
Player base only peaks on weekends
Leveling solo is a SEVERELY painful experience
Constant revamps of classes and HUD
Cash shop
Arguably, the market being player controlled and the environment being player controlled can be considered as both cons and pros, because there are just simply more people that will hack down trees/flowers/crops/mobs and not care to replant as opposed to those that attempt to regulate the environment. The market was fudged over by a duplication bug some time ago and well, you can add that to a list of bugs the developers haven't fixed since it happened.
Most of the content updates over the last few YEARS has always been LATE GAME. So if you aren't at least level 140, don't bother looking it over, because you still have literal MONTHS of grind ahead of you if you just started. In fact, ANKAMA has made it to where the leveling system can cause even veterans of the game to simply quit because of how unfair it is. The game still has bugs in it from after they went from sub only to free to play, but you know, that content update is more important.
With the recent changes to Astrub, it should be a lot friendlier to those just starting out, but it is more like it is preparing you for the other nations and the festival of non-stop grinding. Also, I have seen several times where the areas are completely erased of their resources and had my chat spammed by their "helpful" guide npcs screaming for someone to replant.
I have watched this game revamp and revamp and revamp again, changing areas, leveling, classes, crafting, hell, they even changed out armor elemental stats to some form of praying to RNG Jesus that you get what you need and don't have to either grind out the resources to craft something to play the RNG on it again, or go look at the over priced market and hope someone is nice enough to list it reasonably.
I could go into depth and detail of how FUN and EXCITING this game used to be, before it went free to play. Back when developers LISTENED and HELPED us actually get better at their game. When political wars MEANT something, and crafting was pretty damn USEFUL. When our classes weren't so CONFUSING and NERFED to the point of only three or four being actually viable to unkillable. PVP is so unbalanced that I would rather beat my head into a fence post than actually do it, as are most of the late game boss battles. They DESTROYED what used to be a new and exciting tactical rpg, and instead replaced it with whatever scraps they could patchwork together from their constant taking away and altering.
This rant doesn't even begin to cover how broken you can become through the pay to win system. No, you can't buy armor sets or weapons from the shop, but you can get sidekicks or a hero system to bring in your other character's, so you wont have to bother with other people for leveling. You can buy special mounts and pets that will boost your stats to apoint where it might not matter what class you are playing. And if you don't like your class? Well, they have a solution for that to. Don't want to wait for that free reset after hitting a certain level, or grinding out the reset quest? Yep, they even have a fix for that. Want to level faster and get better loot while doing it? Also in the cash shop. Feel free to break your bank on the game, but oh don't forget, you can only do it through steam because the site's exchange GIVES OUT BETTER BUT IT HAS BEEN BROKEN FOR YEARS.
TL;DR
This game could have been great. Instead it is a broken system split 90% grind, 5% accepting Ankama's bull*hit, 3% sitting in front of Pappy Pal's with the other veterans, 1.9% either fixing or breaking the ecosystem, 0.1% hoping it might one day get better because you haven't yet realized it never will.
If you want to try it, go for it.
I just can't recommend it in this state when I have played what could have been.

Noodling around Deus Ex land one more time was fun.  Sneaking, evading guards, the Human Revolution hacking mini-game - at times Deus Ex: The Fall felt like the real thing - but honestly, as a PC title it's a joke.  The gameplay is Junior's first Deus Ex adventure, and user interface, textures, tiny maps, single save game slot, disappearing bodies, non-rebindable keys all remind you: this is not a port of a mobile game,
.
And the bugs...  Configure your speakers in Windows to Stereo or voices won't play, with subtitles only appearing for a fraction of a second.  And there were severe mouse issues - sometimes I would try to open a door, but had to click the "hack" button several times before the game noticed.  Also choosing the correct NPC for dialogue was a mini-game itself - how do I position myself to speak with
one? - with the bonus hazard of a container or door sometimes conspiring to steal my selection.
Wouldn't be fair to comment on the shooty bits, since I always sneak around pacifist style in these games.  Maybe it's great, maybe it's garbage, but for Deus Ex, who cares?  If you are looking for FPS action, headshots, running around the map like Rambo, you bought the wrong game. :)
So I've scoured the map for side quests, rummaged through every bin, spoken to every NPC I could find.  Guess it's safe to move to the next hub.  So I get to the choppa, a cutscene plays, "TO BE CONTINUED" appears and I discover I've completed the entire game.  Oh, right, $10.
If you're a huge Deus Ex fan, and/or you have a good imagination maybe it's worth that price.  Otherwise I would call this a classic "wait for a 75% discount" situation.
p.s. For one fanboy mini-letdown I couldn't find the original Deus Ex main title playing anywhere. :(

I had fun with parts of The Fall; wouldn't have finished the game if I didn't enjoy
of it.  But I enjoyed the feeling of being in the Deus Ex world more than the actual game I was playing - if that makes any sense.
If you loved the previous Deus Ex games and want more of that world, this is as close as you're going to get.  Stealthy gameplay in a science fiction near-future, shadowy government/corporate conspiracies, sounds great!  But none of that happens in Deus Ex: The Fall - it's just your imagination filling in the gaps in the barren in-game world.
Deus Ex: The Fall feels like an outline, or a rough draft, the bare skeleton of a Deus Ex game.  You can crouch, sneak, read notes, crawl through the vents, knock out the guards.  But it's all so
.  There's no depth, no moral ambiguity, no double-cross, no surprise.  No huge map where you explore, scout out the opposition, make plans, maybe fail and try again from a different direction.  You see a guard, you see a vent, you crawl behind the guard, you knock him out.  Then his body disappears.  Repeat until you run out of guards.
If you've never played the original year-2000 Deus Ex, I recommend playing that game instead.  It's ancient by video game standards, and looks it, but it puts Deus Ex: The Fall to shame.  The last time I played was with a mod called "New Vision" which greatly improves the graphics but leaves the underlying game alone.  There may be other mods available by now, I haven't kept track so you will have to research that yourself. :)
It's good for what it is, and what it is is an iPad game.

I was a massive fan of Deus Ex: Human Revolution, and I was expecting a lot from this prequel. However, if the lack of the ability to jump says anything about this, it seems like a MASSIVE technological step backwards from DE:HR. Using a controller, the hacking system is unusuable, due to the sensitivity for the controller jumping many magnitudes as soon as you enter into the hacking mode. On top of that, the combat system is messed up, and the stealth system makes very little sense. Some enemies can hear you from across the map, while others are nearly entirely deaf. Enemy bodies disappear, making the entire body-hiding mechanic null and void. Also, it's nearly, if not wholly, impossible to get a headshot in the game, which instantly makes it impossible to kill someone from a distance and not alert every enemy around, once again destroying the stealth mechanic. The cover is ridiculous as well, my head bobbing clearly above the edges of the cover, with oblivious enemies glaring intently at me without seeing a thing. It's really a twisted combination of irritating, confusing, and hilarious.
Overall, I feel like this game was a waste of money. Perhaps some serious patching could fix the gameplay, but either way, the game is depressingly short, and the saving system is also pretty jacked, since there can only be one save at a time, and the game doesn't even save after completing a mission, only on a level change.
This was a sad waste of money in its current state, and has hurt my faith in Square Enix as a company.

This is a weird game. It is a really unlique take on space strategy, with many new ideas and other genres mixed in, but that still works.
It is really cool how you don't directly control any faction, but manipulate them by helping here, pushing here, pitching one against the other. So instead of building structures and training units like most strategy games, you have a somewhat complex simulation of each planet and its faction and you interfere through diplomacy, subterfuge or just by investing time/resources. You have a combat system that is a kind of turn-based bullet hell - you move your ship in complex paths and dodge projectiles and attack stuff. It isn't my favorite part of the game, but even if you don't particularly love the style it isn't obnoxious and doesn't get too much in the way. Very innovative, and I've seen plenty of worse tactical combat in strategy games.
I definitely recommend this for strategy games fans that want something new, there isn't anything quite like it. It is however a bit hard to learn, and not what I'd recommend for beginners in the genre.

The Last Federation is a interesting and different take on the 4X genre. Rather than plan as an empire, you plan as a lone figure, with the aim of getting all of the different races into one galactic federation.
Because you have little direct control, you need to work out how to nudge things to get the result you want, especially if playing with the aim of ensuring that all the different races are in the final federation. A lot of your time will be spent on 'dispatch' missions, while you watch galatic events around you, building up money and favour with particular races.
The diplomacy of the game is the really interesting part, much more so that the combat. Different alliances can form depending on circumstances, not just the Federation the player wants, and as the interact with other races, races can become bitter enemies or firm friends. Overall, it's not a game for everybody, but if you are looking for a really different variant on the 4-X genre, I highly recommend it.
Arcen is also amazing at keeping the game updated and doing bug fixes and balance changes as well, which I think really help the game. The DLCs are good, and are worth looking at if you want to get more from the game, but I can't quite give them the same enthusistic recommendation as the base.

The concept of this game isn't bad. The graphics aren't bad. The sound track isn't bad. Where this game fails is a LACK OF PLAYER CHOICE, and issues with the combat mechanics.
What I mean by a lack of player choice is while many options are always presented in a sandbox-type open environment, the simulation mostly plays itself and the effects of you actions are unclear.
To win my first game after experimenting with various actions trying to see what I could do I figured out that the most important aspect toward forming the federation was getting the races to like each other. However, most of your actions don't impact this. You have an option to directly promote relations between two races but all that is displayed is a ticker of the influence gained each month. Click button and wait is not a game.
Slightly more interesting is you can suggest a race build certain buildings that have positive and negative influence gains, but there is no net gain under the current version. You sacrifice relations with one for gains with others.
For my first game I simply built hideaways on four of the races and set myself to help build armada for the federation. then 2x speed to the end and Yay! Victory with a federation of 4. Kind-of lame though to just 2x speed to the end.
The issue I have with the combat is some of the ships are too hard to hit. The just zip about and you don't seem to have a reasonable counter to this behavior because your targeting doesn't work well against this. Also, as the timeline progresses it appears the races ships invariably become ridiculously strong compared to your ship so the point of any tactical combat is suicide. That's a shame because the tactical combat was my favorite part of the game.

Clown House. It's a first person game where you search for a randomly generated key inside of a "house" with randomly generated evil clowns. I say that because there's always 3 clowns, but one of them randomly tries to kill you. (For some reason, it's ALWAYS the one near the bed for me.)
Aaah....This game...Stay away.
Right now as it is, I wouldn't recommend it. At all.
The music is plain, not much to say. The graphics are somewhat standard for a Unity engine game, which isn't that bad, I guess. That's where the "neutral" points end.
Let's look at the negative points.
- Whenever you walk, or look around, there is some kind of delay that gets disorienting most of the time. It's like, if you were a truck. You try to walk, and it takes a second or so before you reach top speed...Or stop completely. Also, that happens when you look around. It's annoying.
- The "House" itself. Bloody hell. It's MINUSCULE. 3 rooms, one corridor, and the bathroom. That's about it. Not even a second floor, nothing. Finding the key is pretty easy....
-...And because there are few locations where the key can spawn, you can finish the game in less than 30 seconds most of the time. Seriously, in 10 minutes, I finished the game 17 times, trying to see if something else happens, but nope, ain't having that.
- The clown behavior, even when they try to kill you. Most of the time, it's the same clown for me. And it's not even scary at all. You hear a scare chord, before he sloooowly walks behind you. You aim, shoot, he's dead.
- The game is pretty buggy, still. If you step on the body of a clown, the fragile integrity of the game universe might collapse. Like, for example, I step on the body of a clown, and I flew through the ceiling for a second or two, into a dark gray void. But most of the time, I step on the body of a clown, and the game flips me around completely, which is ♥♥♥♥ing annoying.
- Shooting clowns. It's not even that satisfying. You click, a weak BANG sound plays, and he falls, dead. That's it, folks.
Stay away from this game, at least in it's current state. It needs lots of fixing, and perhaps more content. It's a game so bad, that's not even funny in it's state. It will fail to entertain you more than 10 minutes. And you'll see the end of the game ("You escaped the house, blah blah blah" screen) in less than 20 seconds if you are lucky. There is NOTHING to it. It's rather boring.

To make on thing clear before I start. This game is a very enjoyable experince and I would reccomend it to any one interested in the Sonic series or intruiged by fast paced action. But these words come from the mouth of an avid Sonic fan, whos has been playing this game for a large portion of thier life. I will not be blinded by nostaliga, but it most certainly will be a factor in my opinion. For the large experience I have for the Sonic franchise as a whole you think I would have a more conclusive opinion on this game, but for the many hours I've spent playing this game I've come to see it as a game that, while fun in most areas, has several flaws that start to build up into something underwhelming. My problems do not stem from the story, despite It's incrediblely strong feeling of 90's attitude, nor from the visuals, which are mostly appealing and aren't jarring to the eyes. I, like most people, find flaw in the gameplay itself. For a bit of backround I spent a large amount of my formative years playing the Sonic Advance games and the first Sonic Adventure. I hadn't played much of the classics but when I did I sucked balls at them. So when I originally got this game on my Gamecube I was too young to notice many of it's flaws but too inexperienced to compare it to many other games, Sonic or otherwise. I enjoyed most of the game, but avoided the Chao Garden like the plague. Coming back to it after 10 years or so lets me make those comparisons and analyse it further, and even though I can find enjoyment in all of the playstyles I will not deny that the treasure hunting and shooting stages are inferior in multiple ways to thier SA1 counterparts. Not only that but the shooting stages control so weirdly, particulary in terms of turning, that they can prove to be unenjoyable slogs much of the time. But almost all of this goes out the window in the Sonic and Shadow levels. High-speed action, invigourating music and impressive spectacle, all wrapped up in a very fun set of stages. Not only are these much more fun than the ones in SA1 they are some of the best stages in the series history, before and after the games release.

There is no real "Trader" in this game.
It should be "16bit load save again".

16bit Trader is a management game, where you try to become the richest merchant in the entire land.
Story:

In 16bit Trader you are a merchant, whose father is murdered by the richest merchant in the entire land. You decided to take action and to become the richest merchant in the land by getting one million gold coins, cause that's how most people take up revenge right ?
Graphics:
The art style of the game is all just static images that don't have any animations what so ever. The only animation in the entire game is the head of a merchant moving up and down. All the cities in the game look exactly the same, so get ready for the tedium cause the worst has just begun.
Audio:
There's only one song in the entire game and it loops forever. It gets so tedious that after 30 minutes, I had to mute the game, because the song was driving me insane. Also the game has sound effects like swords clashing which are so loud that you will go deaf.
Gameplay:
Now this is where, the game shows it's true colors. When you begin, the game teaches you about reselling items at a higher price in cities. So what you have to do is go to a store, buy something and sell it somewhere where you can get a profit. The game tells you to learn the prices so you can use it to your advantage, but that doesn't matter at all. Once you actually begin trading you notice that when you leave a city and come back the store prices change at random which makes learning the prices and using them to your advantage impossible.
There are also travel costs. Each city is a fair distance away and you have to pay to get there. Sometimes there are random events like in Oregon Trail where you get stuck in a certain location for a couple of extra days and the most annoying thing in the entire game thieves and the Kraken. When you encounter thieves or the Kraken they delay you by a couple of days and steal a random amount of your gold. It's always random and in one of my attempts to finish the game they stole almost 85% of my gold which made, it impossible for me to travel. The game let's you hire mercenaries, so when you travel they reduce the risk of the chance of the thieves attacking, but let me tell you, it doesn't matter if you have 3000 men with you, those two measly thieves will still steal anything you have on you.
The game also has side quests, which you can do to get cash. Most big cities have bars and shops which contain side quests. All of the side quests are basically travel to one location and then to the next one and then to the next until you finish. After you finish you get some gold, but the problem is you spend way more gold traveling around those locations and your trips don't pay off in the end. This makes side quests a time and money waste.
So the game cheats any chance it gets and you might be asking is there any chance of actually completing it ? Well after a while you start to give up hope but there is one way to complete the game and that's diamond farming. The game contains mines which have diamonds, which you can sell to get insane amounts of gold. Go to the bar, buy a drink for someone and get a map. Then hire mercenaries and mine to get diamonds until you reach the million. This the only exploit you can use to finish the game as trading is all luck and no pay, while the diamond farming glitch helps and even then it sometimes screws you over with the fact that you find nothing in the mine.
Verdict:
16bit Trader is in every sense a terrible game. It has a steep learning curve, the main gameplay mechanic doesn't even work and to finish you have to cheat just as much as the game which should never be the case. In total, I had 5 attempts to finish the game and with that farming technique I finished the game in 3 hours. The game is just a waste of time and not worth your cash.
Final Rating:
1/10

Cons:
- Main gameplay mechanic is broken
- Glitchy
- Story makes no sense
- Audio and Graphics suck
