Playing as a pair of detectives on their first assignment after being freshly paired together, you must investigate the grisly murders that have befallen a small, sleepy town in the Southern States whilst also searching for the whereabouts of a missing person connected to the case. Investigation here basically involves examining and collecting blood at three different crime scenes as well as picking up any items littered throughout. It's all very minimal and arguably more focused on story over gameplay. Between that and its old school, top down, RPG aesthetics, it reminds me a lot of To the Moon, though without that particular masterpiece's nuance for a well-crafted and touching story.
I'd review this game positively, not because I'd necessarily recommend it exactly, but more because, while I personally found it largely forgettable and mostly a non-event, it feels pretty clear that it was made with sincere intent that means well and wants to pay respect and homage to the inspirations that informed it. That and because, being free, there's nothing to lose by anyone interested in it who has an hour to kill. Though I would warn that there are some aspects that may potentially bother, like the fact it can only be played in a very small window with no options to adjust anything, and the only controls of any meaningful use are the arrows keys to move and the Enter key to examine or use items.
Given that it has "Chapter 1" in its title it should come as no surprise that a follow-up is also available, and by the end of the game I very much felt like this is serving as a teaser to try and entice people in to purchase the second part more than anything else. To be honest, nothing about it grabbed me that much though, so unless it was on sale at a large discount I wouldn't be too concerned with making that purchase myself and finding out what happens next. But, you know... good luck to 'em an' everything!

The graphics were nice and voice acting was still a new concept to the gaming world. Above all else though, the reason to play this game is THE CHAO GARDEN!!! The Chao garden is essentially a tomogatchi like minigame that steals the show. Chao Garden was ahead of it's time and it still holds up today.

I played my way through it, the night of release into Early Access, going into it without any knowledge of the game other than the trailer videos and people's reviews saying it was amazing. I pretty much loved it, minus a few minor things here and there that really aren't big enough to mention. For an Early Access title, this is unbelievably polished. I mean, I didn't notice any significant bugs whatsoever. Controls were a little different from what one might expect, but they were smooth and mostly easy to use. Most of the voice acting was very good - not stellar/amazing/whateverotherhighendadjective, very good. Certain points it was a little meh - but that may have been intentional, depending on how the rest of the story goes that hasn't been included yet.
Given my overall desensitization to most horror, there was really only one scare that got me, when I was *not* paying attention to or thinking about what was going on in front of me. What should have been an obvious distraction went unnoticed, and then the scare got me... pretty decently at that. I will give them kudos for that.
Overall - great game. REALLY great game. If you love horror, you should play it. There's a chance it might not be your style, but for the vast majority of people who love horror... it's a doozy. Now, as far as Early Access, you might want to wait until it's finished, because when they do get around to finishing it you may not feel like playing through the whole thing again. That would be kind of terrible to never want to get around to seeing how good it really gets, so if you think you might lose interest in playing again, by all means wait until final release.
Now, some suggestions to the developers:
-A bit more interactivity for progression might be good. I think it would be a little more fulfilling to perform some kind of tasks in the process of moving through the game. What you did with the combination lock or the  gramaphone (despite the music being kind of grating) was a good start. More puzzle-y things, please!
-There should be more moments building up tension. For people like me, jump scares rarely ever do the trick. You got me once, so again - kudos, but I need something more to make me slowly expect that a terrible thing awaits me. I might go with more glimpses of the ghost, where you notice, but don't know if the ghost is still waiting for you there...
-Give the wife a voice. We hear the main character speak quite a few times, but it would be nice to have the same sort of connection to another character. The wife being so important, in the notes, it seems like she should have that.
-I'm hoping you build up the rats a bit more... there's the one scene with the rats and the paintings that kind of runs with it, but I think they could play a little bigger role in the madness the character experiences in the game.

For under $10 this game is a great horror even for early access. Strong influence from PT which is a good thing. Get it if you're looking for alot of jump scares and walking through the biggest house in the world.

AdventureQuest 3D. Artix Entertainment's upcoming game that will hopefully save the company from bankruptcy. Unfortunately, that hope is soul-crushingly misplaced. The fact of the matter is that AdventureQuest 3D is a terrible game. It suffers from the same problem that plagues all of Artix Entertainment's games. It's boring and repetitive. Plus, the choice to make a multi-platform game ultimately cripples the final product. The game is an unfocused mess filled to the brim with forced grinding and repetition.
I downloaded this game in March of 2016. That was a year and a half ago from the current time I'm writing this and is also the reason why I have a grotesque amount of playtime on this game. The game itself hasn't improved in the slightest during that period of time. Regardless, the idea that my personal playtime would somehow take away from the points made in this review is absolutely absurd.
Let's start with the graphics. This game was made with the mindset of creating a multiplatform game. A game for computers and smartphones. Due to this, the game had to downscale its graphics intensely. This game looks like it would belong on the DS. Because of this decision to make the game accessible to mobile gamers as well as PC gamers, you're basically playing a mobile game that was ported to your computer. The render distance is atrocious and no settings exist to modify it, which leads to spectacular moments where chunks of terrain disappear and the people standing on top of said terrain just float there. The amount of content expected for a mobile game is FAR less than that expected of a PC game. Mobile gaming is a fad that lasted for little more than a year. If the game continues down its current path, then it won't be rated anything better than mediocre.
"Combat" consists of rapidly pressing the skills that aren't on cooldown until you win or lose. When there are only 4 buttons to press, each battle becomes an exact copy of the first one. Enemies are just hitboxes with different health and stats. There isn't a fundamental difference between enemies. You would fight a massive dragon the same way you would fight a dumb goblin. The bosses have the occasional skill here or there, but these are usually limited to doing more damage. To win a fight, you just need higher numbers or more people. Not once does the game require you to do anything remotely resembling brainwork. Press the buttons until you win. Repeat until inevitable boredom. The multitude of classes doesn't help. All it changes is some visuals and the order you press the buttons in. The decision to also adapt the game to mobile hinders creative progress, as 4 skills per class isn't nearly enough to have a fun and balanced class system. No matter how many classes they implement, it won't fix the combat itself. Adding more classes just adds more ways to do the same mundane task.
The Controls are pointless and don't add anything to the game. Why is there a jump button? Oh, for platforming. Why is there platforming in an MMO? Jumping adds nothing to the game aside from bugs and terrible map design. When you do a dungeon, there are often points where you have to jump. This would be fine if it was implemented well. But instead, you can stand on any slanted surface. On one map, you can climb the invisible boundary wall until you go out of bounds and fall into the void. There are no situations where having a jump button adds to the game in any way. There are travel forms to move around faster. Except the vast majority of them are only accessible to players who pay real money, which makes the game pay-to-win. In this case, it's more of a pay-to-get-this-crap-over-with-faster.
The quests are absolutely terrible. Every quest is either "Kill X monster X amount of times", or "Click X object on the map". The quests never deviate from each other, and only add to the boredom. The game mistakes "difficulty" for "taking a long time to finish", rather than "requiring skill at the game". Quests for equipment isn't much better. Most of it boils down to "Kill X monster for X reagent and then wait a few hours". None of this is difficult. It just takes time. Getting items is an inevitability. Just keep pressing buttons until you get the items. Rinse and Repeat. The story itself isn't much either. You load into the game and you're thrown into a battlefield. What's going on in this battlefield? Some skeletons and knights are beating each other to death. Why does this concern your character? Why would the player be invested in a random battle? The dialogue is bland and sounds like it was made up in about 15 minutes. The cardboard cutouts the game tries to pass off as characters are forgotten immediately after they're introduced; by the player and the game. The game is a massive grindfest with no variation except for the colors and the names of the monsters.
Overall, there isn't much else to say about AdventureQuest 3D except: "It's boring". It's a faulty product.  The game certainly has potential, but it needs a massive rework before I'd recommend it to anyone. Make the quests less repetitive, make the map design make sense, but most importantly make the game fun. Currently, there's no reason for anyone to come back and revisit the game. It's bland, repetitive, and lacks any engaging substance that would make players come back to it. I'll give this game a generous score of 3/10.

Alright... I've been playing AQ3D/AdventureQuest 3D, from it’s very start on Tech Demo, to this day. Although the game has gotten good amount of updates and has tried to improve it's graphics, the game is still slacking with the content. Render distance is terrible and not adjustable at the moment of writing this, if you go too far off, some graphics can pop in and out on the distance. I don’t want to nail too hard on the graphics, but they are absolutely horrible, the game wasn’t meant for PC, it was meant for Phone. They should have pushed more development to create the game better on for PC, since the Mobile gaming is dying. Now, let’s get onto the next concern… Content, and affordability. AQ3D is mostly about of grind, which can be fun for some people, but it lacks with other type of content. There is no “Fun” ways to spend your time with in the game, you either run through the map killing monsters, do quests, or grind for mergeable items. The game is free, and a lot of it’s content is free, so that’s very nice + sign for the players, but how is it for the company if they aren’t making enough dough. I’m concerned about of this, because a lot of the artists and developers are doing long hr’s and players aren’t putting that much money on the game. Not to mention the seriously low player-count number. I rarely see over 1k people online counting from both servers at the same time. The average player number from counting both servers is usually around 700-800. I understand that new content brings in more players, but the numbers for game like this are honestly extremely low and very scary, and make me wonder how long can AE sustain efficient updates for the game with this rate.
But let’s get back to criticizing the game itself. Overall, the game isn’t too bad. It serves it’s purpose, and the gave is been updated as i’ve said. I hardly play the game anymore, but as you can see by my “Hr’s played count”, it’s around 500 Hr's almost, not including the Hr’s that i put in then AQ3D was still a Browser game. But i will say this… Artix Entertainment has to stop looking at the Mobile gaming market. If they are capable of taking down the Mobile version of AQ3D, and focusing on it on only for PC, i’m 100% sure that the game would be build more properly and would be more sturdy. The game isn’t perfect, but it is satisfying for little while. If you like games with lots of grinding, and where some of the games items go Rare every now and then, i do recommend it if you are show off person. Other then that, the game is very time consuming. I wish they could bring a better communication system also to the game, because a lot of the people love talking with each others. Will see what the time will bring with it to the game, but right no… Looking at the game and it’s progress, they are claiming that the game is ready to go for a lunch, because they have stated that AQ3D is almost ready for it’s full release. If i were them, i would seriously reconsider this at least for a little bit, since to me, the game is nowhere near to be call’d ready. There are still loads of bugs.
Wish the best for AE and AQ3D, but i’m going to stick with AQW. Total review score 6.5/10.

Heres the issue i see... People are too critical to just enjoy a lot of games these days.  Especially survival horror.   Accusing new titles of being unoriginal or copying mechanics from previous titles.  Ok well developers are attemting to give you what you loved most in games that helped make this genre as successful as it was,  things that gamers themselves post about in forums.  the bottom line is that its very very unlikely we will see a new release that is 100% unique.  Its about building on the best parts of previous success and improving or trying to create ways to make it new and interesting.
People get so worked up over the media hype of a game, expecting the same shock value they once felt when this was all new and fresh.  Great games of today are on par with novels or movies with the ability to tell a story that is interesting and interactive. The success of RE1 wasnt because of its 60fps or amazing non-chunky playstyle even the acting was sub par.  Its success came from the ability to provide gamers with shock value,  cheap thrills based on a culture that wasnt already numb to the visual horrors it had to offer.  Today there is little out there to offer those same feelings within us, so can we blame the game?  I think not.
I truly believe that if a developer allowed all the self proclaimed critics to solely influence a next gen SH game right down to the mechanics,  it would be a disaster.  Its possible that all these harsh reviews from gamers influence the genre in a negative way.  Making developers a little more reserved when attempting something new and radical.  creating the mentality of "dont fix what isnt broken".
We are the spoiled child ,  who can really never be pleased.  Our own attitudes for the most part prevent us from just

The Evil Within is better than most people are giving it credit for.
If you like survival horror at all, you should at least give this game a chance.  I found the entire experience to be enjoyable and there are moments of total brilliance tucked away in this game.
The two major complaints that have been posted about the game include:
As for my experience, the letterboxes were a bit disappointing at first but after playing the game for about 10-15 minutes I began to realize that the letterboxes weren't really bothering me and that they weren't really getting in the way of enjoying the game.
I didn't run into framerate issues either with the exception of one very small house where the framerate dipped into the 15-25 fps range.  That was it though.  The rest of the game was very playable and the area with the framerate issue was literally an extremely small house in one small part of one chapter.  It really wasn't a big deal considering how much detail the environments have in them.
Now that I've touched on the main complaints of the general public, on to the game.
Ultimately I really enjoyed playing the game and ended up replaying the additional new game+ mode that is unlocked after completion.
The game leans more towards being a "Psychological Horror" and while it may not be subjectively "pee-your-pants" scary it does a great job at building tension.
players will notice all kinds of subtle things that will try to mess with your head throughout the game
Even though it's a PC Game, I recommend using a controller for this one as it was very comfortable.

7/10 - A BLOODY AND ATMOSPHERIC DELIGHT
Just finished my first playthrough of this game and i thouroughly enjoyed it, but it certainly has its flaws, however i would say it is a must buy for anyone who likes horror games.
PROS:
-The atmosphere and visuals are both incredible. I could say this is the most atmospheric game i've played. I felt incredibly abosorbed into the world. The game does a very good job at pulling you out of your comfot zone. Just as you're becoming familiar with an area and enemies you will all of a sudden be pulled into a completely different, unrecognisable area with no idea what new threats you're about to face. It does this A LOT.
-The story has taken a lot of flak due to it being loosely explained. It's a tough thing to comment on, while i found it mildly frustrating i also appreciate what it did. It didn't want you to know any more than the main character. You had to do your detective work and piece the puzzle together to get a grip on the situation you're in, where you are, what it all means. It's just very difficult to do. Overall my lack of understanding in a way enhanced the gameplay as the feeling of uncertainty and confusion absorbed me into the main characters situation and own feelings more.
- The gameplay is solid and not as straight forward as say RE4. There are usually numerous ways you can go about situations. The new stealth mechanic is a welcome addition and i found myself using it a lot. I would always try to see what was ahead and plan how to use the least ammo possible through the use of stealth kills, environmental hazards or avoiding enemies altogether.
CONS:
- The characters are completely emotionless. They just aren't reacting naturally to the situation surrounding them and it pulls you right out of the experience. One of the reasons i didn't feel scared is because my character didn't show any fear.
-There are noticeable similarities to RE4, both in the gameplay and the enemies, and to me that's where it faltered. I wanted it to be it's own thing, not something that had been done before. Even in the later levels the zombies start packing machine guns (like the island in RE4) and all the tension just drops.
- It's a bit too heavy on gun use to remain scary. I never really found myself running out of ammo. I was playing as stealthy as possible so i was probably conserving it very well, but i wanted to feel more like i was struggling for it and i had to rely on stealth. I always felt i had enough stocked up to keep me alive when the stealth failed. I wanted to feel more like i was trying to survive against unspeakable odds, and i just didn't. There are harder difficulties though.
- It wasn't scary. It was very tense, constantly, but there were no situations where i felt genuine fear except for one boss. As i said above the fear is dampened by the weaponry. This isn't your Amnesia or Penumbra experience, it is much closer to RE4 but with the action being optional most of the time.
- The end boss was a joke. It's so infuriating when a great game has a♥♥♥♥♥♥send off. Story wise (after watching a theory video on Youtube) it's actually kinda cool, but gameplay wise it's the easiest "fight" in the game. A sequence of "reaction events" and it's over. It's not like QTE's where you press a button though, you do have full control of your character. I expected far better though.

The perfect example of why more =/= better in video games.
Where the first game was a tightly designed masterpiece this game is bloated and full of hundreds of little annoyances that really ruin an experience so reliant on repeatedly doing the same thing to win. Poor level design (♥♥♥♥ing windows), enemies shooting from off your screen, inconsistent AI reactions and patrols (normally a great feature in games but not here), randomised AI weapons and occasional glitches really ♥♥♥♥ing annoy you when they get you killed cheaply during an otherwise fine run. It's also much more likely to limit your options if you take the wrong weapon (i.e. not a gun) with you through to the next level's start and in general the game is a lot more limiting in terms of playstyles than the first.
Having larger levels hurts in general since you'll be losing more if you die and really just results in boredom. It also makes hunting down that one remaining enemy before your combo dies a common experience contributing to the 'only one right way to do a level' issue
the general slow feeling of the game. Indeed the first game's addictive and fast, brutal combat is now just a slow trial and error memorisation game where 1/10 tries will be ended by something largely outside of your control like the ai acting incorrectly. I'm all for difficult games but they need to be challenging, not frustrating.
Jumping between characters out of order might have made for unique storytelling but in terms of gameplay it's ♥♥♥♥ing annoying to swap from one set of abilities to another and back again repeatedly. Frankly the game also feels a little long in a bad way with lots of the earlier levels being quite samey. This isn't a huge issue, I suppose, and is probably better than it being too short but the game is still introducing new enemy types and characters with new gameplay styles (13 in total, not counting masks) in the 20th ♥♥♥♥ing level. Hard mode helps a little but isn't an option for your first time and makes the game even more frustrating by ♥♥♥♥ing with the level design and weapons.
On the subject of the story specifically it wasn't terrible by any means (other than the ending...) but it wasn't worth the effort of piecing together the timeline of the various levels. I personally preferred the original game's approach of limited exposition and showing over telling also. Here we just have a ♥♥♥♥ton of characters dumped into the game who are introduced and eventually dropped with no real purpose or overall plot. If we're going to have a story that so often gets in the way of gameplay and pacing it should at least be a ♥♥♥♥ing good one.
In theory there's more replayability here as not only can you try for top scores on each level but also play the game through again on hard mode and have a ♥♥♥♥ton of different playstyles available. In practice I doubt I'll bother playing it through more than once on each mode while I still play the original game through now and again after 100%ing it. Part of this stems from the problems with hard mode. While it's good that the developers didn't just throw more enemies in and call it a day there are cases where levels are nearly uncompleteable with the wrong weapon (and god help you if the RNG gives guards the wrong weapons too).
I'd probably still recommend picking it up cheaply and playing it through at least once and it certainly isn't all bad. There are few games of this style and fewer yet worth playing at all and had this game come before the first one I'd probably be a lot more impressed. The soundtrack is good and the art style is fine though one level at least is annoyingly dark to the degree of hurting gameplay (maybe an intentional choice but difficulty for the sake of difficulty is again a poor decision). The game just needed to be more focussed to be truly classic like the first.

There are many little changes that destroys the Battlecry feeling for me, mostly about the hero development.
In WB2, you gained XP from a battle (in WB3, the ironman mode, the only mode besides standard, deletes your character after every battle, victorious or not) and you could choose your caste at level 2. But not every race could become everything, they had their specialities and restictions, but interesting cross-developments possibility due to special race boni.
At level 3 you could choose from different specialities. Then, with every new level, you could increase your stats, skills, perks or spells.
Now, in WB3, you can choose with every race every class right from the beginning. No race-specialities or restrictions. By level up you simply do a 'two click' improvement. Choose 1 stat point, then 1 skill point. Nothing more. No perks, no spelltree.
The campaign mode is refreshing, now you can deal with items and get very fast very rich. Buy troops, in every battle up to 20 additional units right from the beginning, next to the troops you can choose commonly for the fight and those you can summon.
There are some new races too (these new units are kinda Jurassic Park & Scorpion King remakes), but I need some more time to check them out completely (if I do that at all, I loved my mortal but strong hero back in WB2 in ironmode. Now, with no working ironman mode, it doesn't matter if you win, survive, die or whatever. You can gain 2 levels even by completely failing). Besides that, it is ridiculous easy now. Even 'very hard' battles are like a walk in the park.

I'm recommending this game with a warning: it's fan-modded, and it sometimes crashes to the desktop in the middle of your game, which can be maddening.  I've experienced other odd, one-off bugs from time to time, like being declared victorious when the enemy kills my hero instead of other way 'round, and unusual unit behavior occasionally.  But I was such a huge, drooling fanboy of WBII, which sadly is not offered on Steam, that I had to pick up WBIII for 10 bucks.  It's not all that different from WBII and still contains all the elements that made the original great: persistent heroes, different races to lead (with genuine differences in gameplay), towers that you can occupy to make them stronger (wish AOE had that), and no-fuss resource gathering which again you can strengthen permanently by adding workers (though "permanent" assumes the enemy won't convert your resource).  There is also some really good assignable AI for your units, with an unusually large number of choices, from RAMPANT (stomp around the map attacking everything) to GUARD to FALLBACK 25% HEALTH and PATROL and so many more.  The only time the game really gets fidgety is when the enemy and you keep converting the same set of resources over and over and over, at which point you really have to just break the cycle and start making advanced units to go wipe him out.
TL;DR?
A really good RTS in its day, with some unique features that make it still a blast to play.  This version is fan-modded and sometimes quirky, sometimes buggy.  For $10 it was a no-brainer for me, but modern gamers with no history wth the game may find it quaint and dated.

While the game itself never delivers on the Lynchian promises made by the trailer and fails to touch upon moments of genuine tension, Silver Creek Falls remains an enjoyable experience for forgiving players.
The core mystery works as an excellent hook and I quickly found myself wondering how it could all possibly fit together and the soundtrack, while not excellent, does a fair job.
What detracts from the experience is lazy design. While I fully understand the limitations of the RPG Maker engine (such as the graphical quality and the cookie-cutter feel), there are issues within the game that arises not from these limitations but rather from a failure to properly beta-test. In dialogues the text will on occasion go beyond the borders of the box. Punctuation's seem to be a frequent victim of this. The game works fine when you do exactly as expected, but deviate just a little and the cracks begin to show.  Characters will gladly repeat the same dialogue over and over with no awareness of the player already talking to them five times prior. This is lazy design, especially considering that the game is extremely short.
The English used is for the most part decent with a few oddities pulling you out of the experience. A brief stint with actual voice acting is both hilariously flawed and adorably earnest but also terribly overwritten. In general, the game is a linear hallway leading you by the hand from point to point and I can't help but feel the experience would be more immersive had the player been given the option of navigating the town and encountering more people. Allowing a more natural progression of events to take place. As it is, the game occasionally grinds to halt to deliver clumsy exposition. Parts of the plot come across as very forced, and the inexperience of the writer (and the crew in general) shines through in these moments. Characters never feel either quite human or have that subtext of being just a little off that is so often a staple of these detective stories.
In conclusion I will say that Silver Creek Falls: Chapter 1 is a great "first game". Beneath the clumsy and lazy design there is a compelling mystery to be solved. The big picture works, but it's all the little things that detract from the experience. The whole is better than the pieces that form it.
This is a game that could have been thrown together in a week, but I still enjoyed it for what it was. Both as a game and as a study in what can be done with the RPG Maker Engine.
Should you get this game? Yes.
Will I play the next chapters? Maybe.
Will I pay money for this game? No. And neither should you.
In short: A good first from a creative team that does show some potential. Play it.

Very unique game, quite one of a kind. You play as a Hydral - lone survivor of your race, now responsible for managing lesser, younger races. Depending on game type, your goal may be either unifying them against common foe from outer space (invasion), creating a federation to ensure your own survival as a god-master of this federation (classic) , or betraying already existing federation (betrayal).
The spice is , that you can't directly manage other races, and you are no god. All you have is a stolen prototype ship, a bit of technologic leftovers from your departed race, and abysmal reputation of repugnant, tyrant species.
To achieve you goal you have to use more subtly approach - fraud, steal, lie, frame races in front of each other and help them negotiate deals with each other. Be a real diplomat. Or simply provoke them to bomb each other into nonexistence - the choice if yours, but keep in mind - unlike classic strategy games, the most "direct" approach is actually the longest way to victory in this game.
Well, i guess thats enough info for the start. Game provides excellent tutorial - everything will be told to you in a very convenient pace, just make sure you don't skip it.
Good luck managing your little pets, Hydral.

I try my best to be an informed gamer, but this came as a surprise to me. When I saw that DX:HR had some new DLC, I got really excited and pre-purchased The Fall. What I didn't know was that The Fall is not DLC, it's actually a PC port of a spin-off mobile device game (tablets, phones, etc.) which translates poorly to PC.
Clunky mechanics, unresponsive controls (with no ability to re-task buttons), sub-par voice acting, and less than exemplary graphics for such a new game makes for a bad excuse for a PC game.
It looks to me like this games would be perfect for tablets and the such, its original market,  but it does not seem to me that The Fall can stand on its own as a PC game. I recommend this game to anyone who holds story above gameplay (The Fall chronicles the missions of the aug spec-op team that captured Dr. Reed and attacked Sarif Ind. before DX:HR) but not to anyone who prefers an immersive gameplay experience parallel to the story.

At first glance, this game looks like it has potential; the graphics look beautiful, the reviews seem mostly positive, and the promise of a well constructed underwater adventure game... well, my hopes were high coming in. Sadly though, it has long been proven that appearances can be deceiving, and Song of the Deep pulls the wool over your eyes the moment you start.
Let's start with the basics: the initial background looks gorgeous. There's multiple layers to each area, each animated differently, and generally stacking atop each other to create a visually pleasing experience. With that said, they tend to be wildly inconsistent in execution; many of the seabed levels have problems with props in the foreground blocking your sub, which near the endgame can be incredibly aggravating, as a couple moments of confusion can cause you to take a jellyfish EMP to the face and get instagibbed. Other areas are bare, lifeless, and seem like a waste of potential. Do take in mind too, that this is all happening while the framerate maddening jumps from 25 to 10-15 FPS, depending on action & particular backgrounds. For reference, this is all on the lowest resolution (which is the only option, as specific graphic settings do not exist), on a computer that can quite comfortably handle a heavily modded Skyrim on High settings.
This game can't seem to make up it's mind as to what it wants to be; it tries to be part adventure game, part action game, part storytelling game, and part puzzle game. Instead of choosing maybe one or two aspects, and polishing them to a shine, it tries to be everything at once, and consequently fails at everything.
The story left me completely uninvested, the characters failed to make my sympathize or care at all about them, and the overall plot just felt weak. I found the narrator to be annoying, as she yammered on every time I collected an upgrade, reloaded a save point too many times, or narrated a cutscene that I could have easily guessed the plot to. The end also have very, very little payoff for the pain leading up to it.
The puzzles only become more obnoxious as time goes on. Most revolve around instant-kill traps, heavily repeated trial-and-error setups, or mechanics that are never fully explained. As an example, in the middle sections of the story, the game adds light-reflection puzzles into the mix. However, in the span of just two areas, it goes from introducing the mechanic, to figuring out what light goes where, in a room with easily a dozen and a half beams going in opposite directions, and controls that blend in too easily to the background. And they don't get any easier, either. Near the end, I kept dying to this maze bit, where you have to outrun a group of enemies while navigating hazards and obstacles. Most of the time I'd make it 90% of the way through, but where I died the most was at a set of timed obstructions, which would always be closed as an enemy spawned on top of me, entirely out of my control.
Exploration is supposed to be an integral part of unveiling the world around you, and subsequently getting enough currency to buy the very much needed upgrades you'll need to survive. This, however, is also very poorly executed. You'll very quickly find items & areas locked behind impassible barriers, such as a wall of lava, or a thick sheet of glass. Now hiding items in starter areas isn't a new concept, but this game again fails heavily in it's execution. If these items were unlocked in the next area, like if the locked items in level 1 could be entirely unlocked after beating level 2, than I'd say it'd be a good mechanic. But this is very much not the case, as most will be locked until you're 3, 4, sometimes 5 story chapters past that section, and at that point there's usually too much area to cover to be interested in exploring a low-level area again. This is also haptered severely by the lack of autosave points; saves are only allowed at very specific, very inconveniently placed checkpoints, and may a time I'd die after exploring 2-3 loot areas, and have to start all over again.
Combat is borderline offensive in this game, hence the previous comment about lack of focus. Your sub is ridiculously immobile, while enemies are either ridiculously mobile, or have vastly superior ranged attacks than you. Add on a limited "special" pool, and a very limited health pool, and then a level progression system, where enemies get meaningfully more powerful as the storyline progresses, while your health & energy don't grow in any meaningful way, and the final piece clicks into place.
From a story perspective, I can see why your sub would be limited in such a way, as it's basically a collection of flattened sheets of tin cans, held together by previously used duct tape and spit. But from a gameplay perspective, it's genuinely an awful setup. You'll very quickly realize how immobile your sub is, even with all the propeller upgrades. Same goes for your special energy, and your very minuscule health pool.
Couple these points with enemies that were specifically designed to be obnoxious, and only keep becoming more obnoxious as the storyline progresses. Jellyfish can break the underwater equivalent of the sound barrier, chase you relentlessly across the map, and fire off EMPs without even being directly in your face. Later on, they gain the ability to tank multiple special hits, split upon death, and instagib your sub in a huge kamikaze-like explosion. Lantern fish tend to fire projectiles offscreen, or through terrain that you can neither shoot nor pass through. Both species of crustaceans tend to position themselves where their weakpoints are otherwise impractical to hit. And anything that fires torpedoes, and/or is a stationary defense structure, is generally rage-inducing.
Every encounter is specifically created to be annoying. Moving from save point to save point usually involves fighting your way through 3 or so waves of respawning enemies, some of which you can't reasonably skip. Open areas tend to be safe, but anything with a constricted space is almost certainly trapped. Certain story areas will typically revolve around fighting waves of enemies around stationary defenses, again capitalizing on your severe lack of mobility and offensive tools. Again, pair this with obnoxiously spread apart save points, and you'll begin to understand how every encounter was made to be unfair and stress inducing.
Finally, the upgrade system. In short, everything useful is generally very expensive, and hidden behind several layers of bad upgrades that you have to purchase first. For example, upgrading the torpedo launcher (which I found to be your best defensive/offensive tool) requires you to purchase the very specific to use upgrade that turns it into a very ineffective, rotating "shield", that seemed too situational for proper use. The only damage upgrade is hidden at the very end, too expensive to reach by the time you got around to it. Similarly, things like health & energy regeneration, which are both very important to your survival, are equally obnoxious to get, due to their stupidly high cost. Consequentially too, direct health and energy upgrades cannot be purchased, they are instead only obtained through exploration, which as previously mentioned was made to be as frustrating and unrewarding as possible.
In conclusion, my experience with Song of the Deep was a very brief moment of hope, followed by a very rapid decline into frustration, anxiety, and general loathing for the game developers, and their very obvious lack of balancing skills. At no point in this game did I ever have fun, and at the worst of times, I kept just wanting it to end swiftly.
By far one of the most poorly executed games I've ever played, which is a shame, as it showed a lot of initial promise. Therefore I cannot recommend it to anyone, even if it were to go on sale.

The BEST worst (or worst BEST) purchases I've ever made.
PROLOGUE OF THE REVIEW:
After reading a ton of reviews, seeing some gameplay vids, I've concluded those people are just shills trying to make an "avant garde" game sound like something it totally isn't.
Why would they do that?
Because no one would buy this FRIGGIN' type of game as-is, at-all, ever--if they truly knew what genre it is. UNLESS, they've been duped into buying it cuz others have misrepresented its genre. OR, they're familar with this genre, or want something entirely fresh, or are cult-like followers of the developer (we've seen them folks around before, haven't we people?).
So this devolves into semantics, which is not good start for this game.
It appears to me: fans seem to go out of their way to paint it incorrectly.
Despite that, IS THIS a GOOD game?
GENRE IDENTITY CRISIS:
First, let's clarify the game's genre.
It's unique. That sums it up.
In my opinion, it's a TURN-BASED PUZZLE GAME in a SCI-FI STRATEGY SETTING, with some ARCADE-LIKE ACTION SEQUENCES.
GAMEPLAY:
You START out at the menu with a plethora of gameplay options.
Honestly, these don't mean diddley squat because the game is like NOTHING you've ever played, it makes no sense to tinker around with any of this. Seriously. Instead, just try to pick what seems like the "default" gameplay, and start. This way, you'll get an idea of how it is. If you want, you can adjust things to make it "easier" for noobs, err, newbs. Which is hilarious because...
...after you click through the pages of still images reading all the text telling the story, you'll be dumped into the game and have ABSOLUTELY NO BLOODY IDEA WHAT THE HECK IS GOING ON.
There is a MAP of "space". Fans call it "map of the galaxy".
What a joke.
It's roughly around 10 planets/locations.
SO, you play this monsterous alien hydra titan that looks like it could devour Cthulhu.
Your the last of a race whose world/people are wiped out, and you can work to unite the races or destroy 'em or whatever. You don't control "your own empire". You're more of guy "behind the scenes" spending the entire game manipulating the other races.
Other races have 1 Planet.
NOT some "empire".
So how do you PLAY THIS?
You basically spend almost the whole game clicking on menus.
You can click on the other worlds/places and you immediately "zip" across to there.
Then, you get to access THEIR menus, to see the things you can click on to do.
Like: hire some guys, hire some researchers, help them develop something, sell them some tech, help with something else.  Very detailed menus (and everything is detailed UP THE WAZOO with descriptions), explain the PROS and CONS of each option.
Approx. 80% or more of anything you find on any of the menus you are told YOU CAN'T DO, because you need to raise rep, or do something else, or get special points in something, and there's a huge plethora of INFO about each of those things to figure out what the hamhock-heck they are.
If you CAN ACTUALLY find something it WILL let you do...SHOULD you do it?
AND THAT'S where the genius of the strategy/puzzle aspect encompassing this game is at!
Doing an act, might lower relations with another race, for example. You might upset "the balance" or whatever.
If you decide to do the act, you...CLICK to do it.
Then, just spam END-TURN until a text pops-up and says something like "OK, THAT'S DONE".
Actually, it's way more "wordy" than that. But..."SAME DIFFERENCE!".
So you see if you got credits or points in something, it goes from 500 to 625 or whatever.
Big accomplishment! Rep with these guys goes 100 to 105 and THOSE guys, moves 95 to 85. Or whatever.
That's it.
At some point, you get to do other things. You just have to do all this kind of stuff alot.
AND I MEAN, ALOT.
Making it easier, is you can set the "End Turn" thing on a sort of "AUTO-PILOT" so you don't have to tire your fingers spamming. Rather, the game will end the turn for you, sparing you the tediuous monotony.
Some "things" you get to do, will take you to an "ARCADE GAME" where you have to dodge spinning balls, and stuff.
Reminds me of the simplicity of Space Rangers 2's "Arcade Sequences", but in SPACE, like above a planet, with way better graphics. The Arcade Sequence, like most Arcade Games, plays out in "real time". Get hit too much by the bullet/object spam orgy things, you die.
So, don't let that happen!
After that's over, it's back to the "space map", clicking on menus to see what else teh game will "let you do".
The SPACE-TECHNO soundtrack, makes this all feel REALLY important.
What makes this game so cerebral, is that YOUR decisions AFFECT the huge galaxy...of like around 7 measily planets. Maybe one races destroys another, ALL OF THE SUDDEN! Or destroys the one that are your puppets...it feels like a historical gaming industry moment!
Incredibly thought-provoking, worthy of thousands of pages of forum drooling!
So deep and provocative, and IN NO way randomly generated. It makes the game feel comparable to the Encyclopedia Britannica, reading Aristotle, or Homer.
No, literally on that first one. Just one page about anything in the game, is loaded with so much detail, it's like a novel. You should get a Steam Achievement if you actually read just one of the pages (in its entirety).
And some fans claimed this was a 4X game, where you build fleets and conquer them like in Master of Orion, GalCiv, and other well-known 4X games. Others, compared it to being "just like Drox Operative" (which is an open-world ARPG arcadish space-ship game).
It ain't. Not even close!
Others know FULL WELL, the type of game it is...like an overwhelming aroma that splashes into the mind, then swirls, and swirls around.
**OVERALL RATING** : E=mc^2 out of 10.
PROS: So many menus you get to click on, surrounded by really good static backgrounds with great artwork, some animations. Visually, it's very colorful. It's like reading a 1000 page Isaac Asimov dribble with rainbow rave-party club lights dancing on the pages. Sometimes GREEN txt, sometimes another color. The artwork is top-notch, the story setting itself is very good, and I enjoy the idea of playing some mastermind behind the scenes. The game offers differing gameplay types. Given how enriching the moving dots & triangles on the "space map" are, the entertaining evade and/or blow-up everything Arcade sequences are, I decided the route of wiping out everyone. (Any surprise?).
CONS: I can't think of cons with the game, but rather, with the rabid fans that misrepresent what type of game this is. THEY ARE THE REAL CONS. So are some reviewers with their videos, only showing the (few) "mass-appeal" aspects of the game [example: skipping CORE GAMEPLAY, and showing only the "arcade" sequences. Many "REVIEWERS (and THE DEVELOPERS EVEN), do this]. That's really LOUSY. Many "reviewers" give-up early (and maybe the DEVELOPERS TOO?) and say "HEY, BUT IM SURE IT'S COOL AND YOU CAN DO ALL THOSE THINGS LIKE SOMEONE ELSE SAID." and then END their video.
In truth, they don't want to waste another minute to play it more.
That sucks of them. Right?
SO BEWARE all the false reviews. Take the time to watch an ACTUAL gameplay vid that's like AN HOUR LONG (at least), that DOESN'T EDIT OUT THE CORE GAMEPLAY (all the menu-clicking action).
CONCLUSION: This is a PUZZLE game at its heart, involving lots of menus, clicking and waiting for something to happen. You're more likely to have to take a dump before anything does.
There's nothing wrong with that.
You need patience.
If you're a NORMAL gamer who prefers DooM or CoD, you probably won't enjoy it.
If you're a gamer with SPECIAL NEEDS in gaming, with matured, refined tastes, you'll appreciate a slow, "cerebral" challenge.
And if you love reading, like a vampire loves blood, this game (and this review...) WILL leave you sated and quenched.

You start with three weapons on your ship. Along the way you discover or buy new weapons. But there is no way to know whether these are better or worse based on the descriptions. Other than these eccentricities, and there are many, the game is actually fun. You try to keep things balanced or unbalanced based on the situation. There are a lot of options to achieve goals. This is probably the most regretful review I have to make since I'm a huge fan of the first Hotline Miami game and was really looking forward to playing this one. Unfortunately, while I blew through the first one and loved every minute, this sequel was disappointing and hard to fight through.
Firstly, the controls were sticky: I'd latch on to walls and get slaughtered, unable to move around the corner or turn enough to attack. Often the bullets would even pass through the enemy or the doors wouldn't register connecting with the enemy. In both cases, I was quickly killed and made to start over.
Second, the story was too jumbled. It was an absolute mess. I understand the idea of running multiple storylines and that storylines needn't always line up perfectly, but this wasn't a good way to do it. The stories would switch almost chapter after chapter and, while they might sync up, most times they clashed harshly. Further, the stories weren't that interesting. There was two that I enjoyed, but the others just seemed boring or pointless. In trying to use so many perspectives, the developers ended up muddying the story.
Finally, the level design is far poorer than the first game's. They gave big, open rooms and gave most enemies guns. Coupled with sticking to the walls, I was often the victim of ten simultaneous shotgun blasts painting the walls with my brain. This could just be my own poor skills, but it often turned the game away from the quick-paced gorefest of its predecessor and toward a strategy game where I waited behind walls for ambushes and lured enemies into choke points. I may love strategy games, but I don't play Hotline Miami to get my fix.
As a successor to the wonderful Hotline Miami, this is a poor one. It has much of the aesthetic feel of the original, which I adored, and the themes are both an expansion and faithful redesign of the orignal game's. However, the problems I stated previously ruin the otherwise good experience. If there is another sequel, I will still purhase it and play it through. However, after this, I might wait for the sale. Preferably, a big one.

Ah, Deus Ex: Human Revolution! That was and still is an amazing game! Later, Eidos Montreal revealed that they were working on another DE title. How excited I was! More Deus Ex! Bummer, Mobile platform only...
On Mobile, the game seemed to perform well and was decently rated, for a mobile game! Now that Eidos Montreal said they were going to bring this DE: The Fall to PC, that was good news! Or is it?
In this game, you play as Ben Saxon, a Merc that used to work for Belltower Mercenaries. After some incident, you're recruited by Namir, the antagonist of Human Revolution, and sent somewhere for assassination. Now, your guy, Ben, develops a conscience and decides to quit Namir's friends and pals, the Tyrants. And that's where I am at, in the game now. I'll update this review once I finish this digital-only game but still, here's a rundown of PROS and CONS that I'm experiencing currently.
PROS:
+Interested in more DE backstory? The Fall shall fill that craving! Many PDA to read infos, so you get to know some more.
+Hacking minigame is the same as Human Revolution.
+Music by same composer as HR. Really great... when it works!
+Voice acting is okay, more or less! It's not HR quality, but serviceable for a "Mobile" game.
+Deus Ex GOTY free with this purchase... well, at this point, if you still haven't got DE GOTY, you should get The Fall!
CONS:
-Straight Port from Mobile to PC. Nothing "extra" or noteworthy added in the PC version.
-No rebindable keys for Keyboard AND EVEN Xbox 360 Gamepad (totally unnacceptable and hopefully patched later on)
-Wonky controls. The sensitivity of the mouse feels way off. If you can't adjust your sensitivity "on-the-fly", you'll likely have issues with this game!
-Lots of sound clipping and worse, sound crash at times. Best advice, active subtiles if you want to "hear" a nearby enemy!
-Many annoying "help pop ups".
-Unintuitive menus.
-Poor AI.
-Visuals/Graphics/Animations are all really bad. Low res textures, wonky/stiff animations.
OVERALL:
Well, kinda disappointed really. Sure this isn't a AAA full game but I still expected something decently done for the porting, alas, it wasn't. It's like this port feels rushed, no special love added in the PC version. Granted it was designed as a mobile game so no one should have expected a killer treatment but at least, a working game would've been greatly appreciated!
RECOMMENDATION:
So, since I haven't finished the game yet, I'll finish it off in the coming days, unsure when as I'm flooded with PlayStation 4 titles all of the sudden!
So do I recommend? Not really. Not at full price! And at least not right now... better wait until this game get's properly patched, especially for the audio issues and wonky controls! By that time, it may be in a Steam sale!
RATING:
5.0 / 10

This is an HONEST, no nitpicking, everything covered review.  Graphics are what you would expect from a mobile phone app turned PC port. If you go into the game expecting mind-numbingly good graphics, you'll be disappointed within the first few minutes of gameplay.  Combat is fine using mouse and keyboard, I had no issues whatsoever, aside from the occasional headshot not taking out an enemy.  About the bugs people have been experiencing...I didn't encounter any at all, so I can't really comment on them, though I almost wonder how many of those people who claimed to have extraordinairily bad bugs actually bought the game, or bought the game but used a NO CD exe so they can play without Steam.  Legitimately playing the game on your chosen platform usually will make your game play like mine did.  Smoothly with no bugs to speak of.
Music was fine for what it was, as well as the sound effects.  I rather thought that they re used some of the sound effects from DXHR, as I swear I could recognize a lot of the sounds from it.
Comparing this to DXHR and basing your opinion solely on that is dishonest and in my opinion, just plain wrong.  It is clear from most of the reviews that I read, that 90% of the reviews, compare the game to it's predecessor, most of their complaints centered around the graphical content, which in my opinion as stated above, are nice for what they are, not the best but still fine.
The ONLY gripe I had with the game as it is, was the fact that when in "invisible" mode, you could literally stand in front of an enemy and they would never know you were there.  Perhaps I am being a bit overexxagerated on this, but to be invisible and the enemy not hearing you breathing after running 50 yards in 3 seconds is just....meh.  Again, not really a complaint, I suppose it's by design that invisibility also masks your breathing *shrugs*
Overall gameplay was decent, was rather surprised that the game is episodic based, and more episodes will be released in the future.  I personally thought that was a nice touch, as it keeps us wanting more and more, and wanting to know more about the characters themselves, what caused them to get in the situation they are in, etc.  I think more games should do this, release in episodes, with huge cliffhangers.  In my opinion that is where game designers can really flourish and make the story truly unique because you'll never know what happens next, until the next episode.  Also, the choices you make in game can affect end game scenarios as well.  All in all I say well done.  Looking forward to the next chapter!

This game has been beta/early access for nearly a year now, and I have to say its been a great 15 hours of gameplay so far. When you first start off you will experience a little funky problem with how to use the camera perspective, but after an 1 hour it will feel normal and you will get used to it. The graphics arent amazing but its tolerable to the human eye, if you cant handle these graphics you obviously havent played the old school AE games, so if you have not I highly encourage you play those aswell (Adventure Quest, Adventure Quest Worlds, DragonFable). This game has a fun storyline, with sidequests usually being dungeons, the dungeons are filled with mobs that give you different materials that you use to craft different equipment, all with unique stats and designs.
The story currently takes approx 12-ish hours to complete(thats how long it took me to reach the current end of the story). (STORY ISNT FINISHED YET). I also want to talk about the whole crafting aspect. The crafting aspect can be a bit of a nuisance at times, but the stats are much better than items you can straight up buy from certain npc's. You will start realizing you need to start using crafting if you want to be able to solo certain mobs at around level 10 and the crafting ranges from 1 hour to 2 hours in the level 10 area, then goes up to 2 hours to 4 hours in the capped level area(level 17 currently).
If you do happen to be done the current story, there is a cool variety of side quests, quests that give you cool cosmetics and other quests that get more into the story of different characters. If you have noticed that some updates are a bit small its because AE is STILL updating their old games aswell, that shows how commited they are to a game no matter how old, and guess what, those games still have people playing it, and those games are like 13 damn years old! GJ Devs!
Time for the paid stuff...There is a Guardian class that costs $20 to buy (Not sure if its USD or CAD), then theres a the whole Dragon Guardian Pack that costs $50 to buy, but this is suppose to be the best class in the game, but its not like its gonna be completely Over Powered, its a bit better in stats, but its mostly for the cosmetics anyways. Then theres also another currency in game called Dragon Crystals, that cost $1.99 for 200, $4.99 for 900, $9.99 for 2000,  $19.99 for 5000 and $49.99 for 15000. The only real purpose of these Crystals is to buy morphs/cosmetics but its not a big deal since your armour changes usually all the time when you get new equipment. Though...these crystals are also used for buying craftable equipment instantly without having to get the resources nor the gold. They are also used to increase your amount of bank slots in the storage/bank.
What can I say, every free to play game has its paid stuff too, its not like any of the paid stuff is a must buy. But they do make your life a bit easier and cool looking.

Oh, the nostagia that hit me when I saw this in the steam store on that cold day October 15th, 2016. Oh the memories that fled in from the days of my corroded childhood and the copious amount of hours I spent of this game. And OH the disappointment, hate and anger that filled my head when I played this game. You would think that hundreds of people or a major and legendary gamedev like Artix Entertainment would somehow make this legendary aspect of making a game like Adventure Quest into a 3D MMORPG and re-capture that nostagia into an acurate portrayal of a game would be feasable right? No. No amount of disapointment and shame could soften the impact that this game made to my mental state. As a child, I loved this game! I made more than 50 characters on all the servers and other franchises that Artix made, beat all the bosses, had tons of friends that made me smile and laugh genuinely, and most importantly, was fun! I remember playing with my little brother and older sister, wired up on our old Intel Dell machines, and we enjoyed ourselves! I even bought the yearly subscription to be a guardian ONCE. Ah, the things that we all did in this legend of a game, forgotten by time and covered by other major titles. But when I heard that AQ was going 3D and MMO, my nostagia boner went up and I quietly observed the development. Didnt look nice, from what I originaly saw, but it looked fun! I could not wait to call my brother so we could play once again to this sequel, expecting that level of grandeur and caliber that we had as children.
However, like everything I love and hold dear, Artix ♥♥♥♥ed this up for me. Big time.
I don't want to go into detail as of why they did so, but I will say this:
What they've essentialy did is combine a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ engine with even ♥♥♥♥♥ier assets. The combat is unsatisfying, the quests are bland and overwritten, the mechanics and features are just..... no, and even worse? That nostagia is gone. That magic that AQ had (even in 3D) just killed itself. Artix messed up and now we had to pay the price of our childhoods (and the ridiculous microtransactions). For new peple coming in, stick around and maybe find a new purpose and value in this franchise. But for vets; If you value your precious childhood memories and your sanity, STAY AWAY.
Overall, I give this a salty, SALTY 3/10. Perhaps the actual version of the game will be better than whatever.... THIS is.

This.Freakin'.Game,man. This.Freakin'. Game. I'm not usually one for anything horror-orientated( I bought Amnesia on sale a while ago and still haven't worked up the nerve to properly play it), but I'm so glad I went for this game. Considering the 'early access' status I was expecting something half-finished, but this game really delivered. This is a really clever horror game, which perfectly creates an ambience of unease and creepiness throughout each room. There are one or two jump scares, but it's mostly the atmosphere that's chilling. You play as a washed-up, mentally unstable artist, finding out more of his story as you make your way through the rooms of his house picking up items that trigger memories. It's kinda level-based in that a lot of the time some doors will be locked until you find a specific item to make your way further into the house. As well as this, the surroundings will move and shift around you as you explore, sometimes sending you in circles. This - I imagine - is to reflect the man's damaged psyche. This is used to great effect and as I said above, it's not so much about jump-scares, but more about being chilled-to your-core-by-something-just around-the-corner-which-you-swear-is-there-but-you-can't-really-see.
This game is a very intelligent horror that does an excellent job of putting you ill-at-ease. The visuals are beautiful, and considering it's this good at 'early access', I can't wait to play the full thing. There are one or two minor things that need to be ironed out, minor being the operative word; like advanced graphics options as well as maybe controller config.( the look sensitivity kinda bugged me), but nevertheless this is well, well worth the money.
8/10

Great game that finds some middleground between games like Resident evil 4 and Outlast.
The thing about it is that you're not by far as helpless as you should be.  But nonetheless the game offers a great survival experience. The first half of the game is incredibly tense and the game peaks in chapter 9 for suspense. After that it kinda becomes a rollercoaster of action scenes but still enjoyable to me. The biggest problem with the game however is the story or rather the lack of it that is. The first few chapters you're pretty much clueless which is fine and adds to the atmosphere, halfway through the story seemed to become pretty interresting but it just stopped explaining whatever was going on.
The game just kept adding more question without answering any of them. I kinda hope they will fix that with the DLC but that shouldn't have been needed at all.
The gameplay itself, the unique bossfights are awesome I enjoyed every second playing through the areas.
The game only uses a few weapons, which basicly comes down to a revolver, shotgun, sniper, magnum(strong revolver), which I think is a good thing yet the crossbow does not make a whole lot of sense. It has several functions like impale (duh), flash (huh?), explode(ok I guess), freeze (say what?), electrify(oh common), fire(ok that actually is useful considering you want to burn corpses, but what?!?) Anyway it adds some strategy into the fighting without the need of several types of equipment so let's just roll with it.
The upgrade system is fairly simpel and lets you chose how you wanna play the game, so thats a plus most definitly.
All in all I really enjoyed playing the game even though I was expecting a cool twisted story.

Shinji Mikami's The Evil Within is a fun, but somewhat flawed game. I got hyped up cause of the pre-game trailers, and received word that he would be doing this game. That bought me in fast, and I somewhat regret grabbing this game at full price. I wanted a reinventation of the genre, and instead I got Resident Evil 4: The Add-on, or 2.5. This review will be spoiler-free.
The Haunted, which are the main enemies, can prove to be a challenge, and can swarm you fast. It makes me wish the Bosses were the same. Some of them are interesting, but some of the other ones can be cheap and frustrating. For the gameplay you mainly use your revolver, and kill enemies. For the ones who fall easily, be careful cause they can get back up. You can use matches to burn them, but try to decide wisely on which ones to burn. Some are dead, and some are not. You get limited matches at the start. It's not an orginal idea, but it works alright.
Other aspects of gameplay include using the Agony Crossbow, and It rocks. You use many different ammo types like freezing, blinding, fire, poison, and etc to wreck your enemies, and it's fun. Just save up a lot of ammo. You do this by disarming bombs, and searching around the enviornment, and enemies. I love the weapon, and at least you get it in the early half of the game. Unfortunately I wish I could say better things about the details, or graphics of the game.
The graphics are a mixed bag. With the new update it looks better, but the only drawback is the black bars on the sides are still there. I could've messed with the console, but I don't know or feel like why that's a good thing. It should've been fixed in development.
The one bright side of the game is that the villain (Ruvik) is voiced by Jackie Earle Haley. He does a great job voicing him. He feels threatening, and scares you well, and does try to kill you at points. I want more of this kind of boss.
The Bottom Line: Wait for this to go on sale and then try it for yourself. I have very mixed views on this game. It feels rushed, and has some great potential, but kinda squanders it, and I just hope they learn to make an even better title.

A pixelated rainbow of blood, violence, and drugs. Hotline Miami 2 is something I put off on playing for the longest time and coming back to it now, I realize how much of a mistake this was. Assuming you played the first one, it's more of the same and true to what made the first one such a hit.
Game is still the same winning mechanic of the first one, constant kill and constantly being killed, the game has moments where you will get frustrated but the main thing that always must be remembered with Hotline Miami is if at first you don't succeed, die, die, die, die, die and die again until you pull it off. Your death count will contribute to the satisfaction and as you get better only makes the game more intense and you'll want to try different and more risky tactics and perks.
Music is great overall in its sound, feel, and fitting to each scene in the game and really helps with the feeling of rushing around in an ultra fast pace murder-spree in each level. Hotline Miami is well known for the quality of its soundtrack and will have you looking up the tracks and playing them over and over.
Hotline Miami mainly is about the violence but the story has some continuitiy from the first one and is given to the player in small opening and intermission snippets that always make you want to know what happens next, with the amount of violence always going on the game pulls off several twists and cliffhangers using several different characters (In contrast to the one or two you could only use in the first one) and actually had me trying to push myself to get more levels done to find out what was going on. While the game excels most in it's gameplay, Hotline Miami will keep your attention snared and guessing as you play your way to the finale.
Given how fast and how quick everything happens, Hotline Miami 2 will have quite a bit of replay time after you beat it. Levels give you a grade based on how fast and how bold you are in completing them to disincentize cautious and calculating gameplay. Hidden content is available however it is not as abundant as compared to the hidden puzzle and masks to be found in the previous one. There is also a level creator available which I have yet to mess around with extensively, but there are many custom campaigns available for download off of youtube to extend the life of the game if you do get tired of the base campaign.
The one main irk that I had with the game was with the masks.
In the previous game, you played as Jacket and had at your selection a large number of masks to customize your gameplay, in the second one you have a bigger variety of characters that while this makes it seem like different options are always available, the game feels like the number of perks isn't as abundant even if some from the first are a bit low on how useful they actually are. One of the things I liked about Hotline Miami and one of the things that was so signature about it was the animal masks, and in the second one there is far less appearence of them over featuring different characters and allowing more story to be going on. Still, while this is not a large annoyance, the first thing I think of with the game title is the animal masks paired with a bloody weapon, which Hotline Miami 2 has thinned out the former.
That issue aside, I really enjoyed the game and would definately recomend it to anyone looking for a fast paced arcade action game or anyone like me who held off on purchasing it when it was initially released.

To express my mixed impressions of the gameplay and Steam's overly simplistic rating system, I'll leave a positive rating but also explain why the game fails at its intended concept. You see, for a game where you supposedly work from the shadows to shape the world order you want, your most effective actions by far are the most direct ones. Unless you play as a pacifist, it's incredibly easy to just buff the races you want with technology and massive fleets, and eliminate the troublesome races. You can tell a race to produce fleets twice as fast, and then sit at their planet while adding literally a 20x modifier on top of that. Then when they go to invade the race you tell them to, you singlehandedly wreck the opposing armadas and then commit genocide by nuking the planet from orbit. It's beyond ridiculously overpowered, it's broken. Maybe the Invasion mode from the first DLC works better due to being combat-focused, but most ways to play the standard Federation mode are rendered incredibly easy if you use the direct methods. Serious rebalancing is needed to make it into the shadowy cabal-simulator it's made out to be, but in lieu of that, just removing the armada construction option and the orbital bombardment would go a long way towards making the game more challenging.

Getting into DE:TF is a real chore. This game is a poor iOS port that is littered with bugs, so be warned before you go out and buy it!
DE:TF is a prequel to Human Revolution and follows the augmented soldier Ben Saxon who is on the run from the Tyrants (the very same ops unit that Adam Jensen faces throughout Human Revolution). The game has a suitable plot for its length, but the game is heavily padded by 5 side-missions which actually make up the bulk of content in DE:TF. Almost the entire game takes place in Panama city and the surrounding buildings, and will have you backtrack across previously cleared areas a few times when doing missions. The game also has a "New-Game Plus" feature (NG+) where you start the story again with all your previous augmentations & weapons. This sounds like a good idea, but honestly NG+ is far far far too easy and you can breeze through the second playthrough in just over an hour (I would know, I did it).
The game itself plays fairly similarly to Human Revolution, except that everything is more sluggish and awkward. As of the time of writing. the keys cannot be rebound which made gameplay irritating in places. I personally really dislike C to toggle crouch instead of L-Ctrl and rebind this in every game I play. The cover system can also be a glitchy (I fell through the map to my doom twice while trying to get into cover), but for the most part it is at least functional. While the gunplay is downright awful, playing the game as a non-lethal melee character is surprisingly rewarding and quite loyal to the same playstyle in Human Revolution. There are a few hidden paths scattered around that allow you to approach (or avoid) your enemies from various angles.
The graphics & audio of DE:TF are almost criminally bad. Even while staying loyal to the overall aesthetic of Human Revolution with the art-style, this game still manages to look terrible. There has not really been much of an attempt to make them suitable for a PC release, with the textures and character models in particular looking incredibly bland.
The audio is the real crime though. The sound effects and OST ripped straight from Human Revolution are decent enough, but the sound frequently cuts out. It makes following the narrative very difficult as the voice-overs are skipped. What makes this even worse is that when the audio skips, the subtitles do too, which is absolutely INFURIATING as it prevents you from at least reading the audio you are missing. As well as ruining the story, the absent audio also destroys the atmosphere of the game and often leaves you running about in total silence.
I cannot recommend this until the audio is fixed. Until then, avoid DE:TF unless you are a die-hard fan of the franchise and really want to know a little back story behind Human Revolution

Sonic Adventure 2, despite the hate it sometimes gets, is my personal favorite out of the Sonic franchise.
The game has some heavy tones, like the death of Maria, or the impending doom of the Earth, but it manages to remain light-hearted and fun, which I find to be absolutely brilliant in the plot. I also don't mind the cheesy lines the characters tend to spew, it's a game about a bunch of animals in shoes, it'd be surprising if it wasn't cheesy.
As for gameplay, 2/3rds of the game are great, Sonic and Shadow stages being the very high points, and Kunckles/Rouge treasure hunting also being fun, despite the radar being worse than in SA1. Also, Security Hall can go choke on a bag of phalluses, what a terrible level... The only bad gameplay style is Tails/Eggman mech levels, and I can forgive those, just complete them and never go back to them.
And don't get me started on the music, the OST for this game is playing in my head 24/7
To sum up, this is imo the best Sonic, or at least the best 3D Sonic to date.
9.8/10 (the 0.2 is for mechs and Security Hall)
