This brings back memories.
I never got to play Warlords Battlecry 3, but I did play the first one extensively when I was a little kid. I enjoyed the combat mechanics to a degree and loved the idea of retaining troops and a hero after each map. This game brings more of the same and then some. That is to say, the same sprites that were used in the first and second games make an appearance here in the third game as well.
The leveling mechanic in Warlords Battlecry 3 is done right. Your hero gains experience as the match goes on and can even level during the match (something that could not be done in the first one). Tons of classes and races allow for moderate choices which can dramatically alter your game play.
The varying abilities that are available for warlords to take can alter everything. Abilities like Engineer make your building have more hp (think tower defense), while merchant lowers the price of all units universally (good for swarm tactics). Abilities like constitution make warrior warlords a pain, while specific classes such as pyromancy can make enemy warlords dangerous. A well built warlord can take down an army in the blink of an eye, as long you carefully watch the battle unfold.
If the Hero concept does not sell the game to you, then maybe the races will. There are 16 different races, each with unique troops and abilities to really add variety and replayability. Although some units are shared by races, you'll be impressed with the selection given here! To add to this, each race has a unique titan that can really change the tide of battle.
Titans are units that can only be built near end match when most upgrades have been researched. After it is available, it takes a while to build and if it dies, its gone for the match. However, Titans can mow down armies without flinching, provided they don't get overwhelmed! (If you don't like this concept there is an option to turn this off, but why would you?)
Finally, the campaign is truly something to behold. Loads of side missions and ambushes add for a significant amount of reputability. The mainline of the campaign is not all that exciting and ends quickly but the significant amount of side mission will more than make up for the weakness of the mainline in the campaign. The missions are also quite varied too. Tournament pitting you Warlord vs others as well as defense missions and elimination missions leave the campaign quite varied.
Although my overall view of this game is highly positive, I would be boldly lying if I did not say there were problems with the game as well. Bugs that were very annoying in the first game have made a return here. I experienced an average of "1 crash every hour", but most came from multiplayer. I am unsure if what was causing the issues but it was a problem for both Windows 8 and 10. Low max resolution can be a little annoying to some as well (although it didn't bother me at all).
The most important problem by far though is the AI in Warlords Battlecry series. Sometimes you will start a match and the AI will be vicious. They will quickly swarm you and be relentless for quite some time, even on easy difficulty. This can be fun at times but frustrating as well. Other times, The AI will suddenly refuse to continue on and just give up or make baffling mistakes. I watched the AI walk a Titan into a field of towers and let it die. Afterwards, maybe 10 minutes later, it brought an army that wiped the board in seconds without losing many casualties. The AI also makes VERY bad decisions with their Warlords which will handicap them (but to a lesser extent). Suffice it to say that the AI is definitely passable and a capable challenge, but could benefit from a little work.
The good
+ Warlords
+ Retinue of generals
+ Loads of varying Classes
+ Loads of different Races
+ Titans add a new level of combat
+ More fleshed out mechanics
+ Building art style is nice
+ Soundtrack is decent (and easily modifiable if you want to make a custom soundtrack)
The Bad
- Still filled with some annoying bugs
- Crashes are horribly common (I would go hours without having one, then have 3 in 10 minutes)
- Random AI can sometimes be REALLY hard or REALLY easy.
- At times, maps are not optimized for the AI to understand. (Some maps cause the AI to become brain dead)
- Max resolution is 1280x1024 (which you get used to quickly but still should have higher resolution available)
- The fan made patches for this game are forcefully implemented here. (It is obvious that Steam and GOG did not spend any time playing the game as one mod adds a silly profane comment when building conversion occurs.) This is not a deal breaker, especially with this game, but I hate when stuff like this happens. I want the option to mod me vanilla game, not be given a premoded version.
Overall, I give this game a 9/10 and recommend it for Warlords series fans. Its a good strategy game for anyone but its massive compilation of Warlords units (especially from Warlords 4) was awesome. This game is rough around the edges and some support would really help smooth out the problems. None of the problems I encountered were ever bad enough to make me upset with the game. If you're thinking about this, give it a go!

Shinji Mikami's The Evil Within is a fun, but somewhat flawed game. I got hyped up cause of the pre-game trailers, and received word that he would be doing this game. That bought me in fast, and I somewhat regret grabbing this game at full price. I wanted a reinventation of the genre, and instead I got Resident Evil 4: The Add-on, or 2.5. This review will be spoiler-free.
The Haunted, which are the main enemies, can prove to be a challenge, and can swarm you fast. It makes me wish the Bosses were the same. Some of them are interesting, but some of the other ones can be cheap and frustrating. For the gameplay you mainly use your revolver, and kill enemies. For the ones who fall easily, be careful cause they can get back up. You can use matches to burn them, but try to decide wisely on which ones to burn. Some are dead, and some are not. You get limited matches at the start. It's not an orginal idea, but it works alright.
Other aspects of gameplay include using the Agony Crossbow, and It rocks. You use many different ammo types like freezing, blinding, fire, poison, and etc to wreck your enemies, and it's fun. Just save up a lot of ammo. You do this by disarming bombs, and searching around the enviornment, and enemies. I love the weapon, and at least you get it in the early half of the game. Unfortunately I wish I could say better things about the details, or graphics of the game.
The graphics are a mixed bag. With the new update it looks better, but the only drawback is the black bars on the sides are still there. I could've messed with the console, but I don't know or feel like why that's a good thing. It should've been fixed in development.
The one bright side of the game is that the villain (Ruvik) is voiced by Jackie Earle Haley. He does a great job voicing him. He feels threatening, and scares you well, and does try to kill you at points. I want more of this kind of boss.
The Bottom Line: Wait for this to go on sale and then try it for yourself. I have very mixed views on this game. It feels rushed, and has some great potential, but kinda squanders it, and I just hope they learn to make an even better title.

I admit, I was a bit of a naysayer of this game early on. But in the end I'm a bit surprised with how much I liked it. The first chapter is terrible, starting with the typical later day Resident Evil action set piece (complete with someone that would be at home in the Matix), and followed up with an awkwardly scripted stealth sequence. Get past that though, and I think you'll  get into the game. It's clearly heavily leaning on Resident Evil 4, and that's not something I mind. It's not really scary but it does have some great atmosphere and creepy monster designs. It gets pretty action heavy, especially toward the end, so your taste for the game will probably depend on if you liked the RE4 era changes or only want the old Resident Evil flavor.
It does have some downsides, like the technical aspects that have been widely discussed. One of the weapons you get is a crossbow with like 7 different arrow types which makes switching between them kind of clunky. Lastly the story feels incomplete. I don't mean in the sense of it being dumb or making little sense (though it does have helpings of that) but it clearly feels like some of the major questions of the game are going to be answered in the upcoming DLC. While I'm all for DLC that feels substantial, this game feels like it's going to flat out require it by the end.

Just finished the game, and I must say it's dmn good! Gameplay brings old times of early RE and Silent Hill. I had no techincal issues at all, maybe few fps drops but  my PC isn't even close to "high end". This game have all pros and cons of old type survival horrors since they were made for the consoles in 1st place. So on one side we have crappy camera angle, awkward controls (Gamepad helps a lot, yet is completly playable on Keyboard+Mouse), save points (there are also auto-save checkpoints). Difficulty is ok, death count at the end of the game for me was 91 (sometimes you just die on purpose cause you wasted too many ammo on simple encounters or at least I did that), you can upgrade main character with currency found during the game, yet it's not obligatory, you can finish game without it, I'll take it as a good thing since you'll never hit a wall cause you didn't upgraded ammo capacity for example. Graphics are... very atmospheric, but textures on some objects are terrible (thanks to consoles), on the other hand enemy models are top notch. Sound and music are on the spot for building tension in right moments. This game is very underrated on metacritic due to same "console port" issues but really, rate the game itself instead of crying for 30fps cap (you can switch for 60fps now). I agree that characters aren't memorable, and story left too many unanswered questions but probably we will get them in DLCs. For me it's solid 8/10 or even 9/10.

A solid good game from Insomniac, which is sad to say, because Insomniac makes some of the best games.  Ratchet and Clank, and Sunset Overdrive had me looking forward to something extremely unique and superior to other games.
Song of the Deep isn't that game.  What you have is a rather tame but interesting underwater metroidvania game where you look for your father.
This game is similar to Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet in that the player must explore the entire world. trying to discover what happened to her father, and eventually gets pulled into a larger story, but the story doesn't really stick with me.  Yeah "I need to find my father" was interesting but ultimately after a while the story felt generic and just a reason to go from place to place.   It even attempts to use a sweet narrator voice, trying to evoke what I think was a Bastion style story, yet the narrator speaks rarely, so you almost forget about the narrator by the time she speaks again.
The gameplay however is solid, and enjoyable, and the exploration usually works.  There's an awful lot of backtracking though (And an an awful lot even for a metroidvania game) but each time you go through an area you have new powers, however I feel like those powers were back loaded, so you get some really cool weapons, but almost at the end of the game, at the same time you never feel very overpowered, and I enjoyed that.
On the other hand the game is a bit slow paced, you do get a "boost" from your ship engine, but you're not going to be zipping around which could have improved the game's flow a bit.
Yet I found the game a bit charming. Not great, but better then average.  I recommend the game, though I got it in a bundle, I'd probably put down 5-10 dollars on this game with out a problem, though I would put insanely twisted shadow planet above this as I just think that game was a little better on the gameplay side (though completely lacked a story), where as this game has solid gameplay, it often had a slightly frustrating puzzle to find an object, or required the player to drag objects around a bit too often.

I have mixed feelings about this game. The people who made it clearly put a lot of love into it, but it seems to have run out of budget somewhere along the way. Basically, it has great foundations, but is very rough around the edges.
I really liked the level design and environments. The regions were unique and memorable, with different structures and aesthetic behind them. The enviroments are very detailed and pretty, filled with little creatures, corals, rocks, and other things you expect to find at the bottom of a sea. You can tell they put a lot of effort into this department, and it's definitely this game's strength.
I also liked the story. Just about every other metroidvanias has a nonexistent or extremely bare-bones story, so I was pleasantly surprised by how decent Song of the Deep's story actually is. It's a heartwarming "children's betime story", and follows the theme very well. I also liked the addition of the narrator, which added a lot of flavor to the story. It's not great by any means, but it was surprisingly good.
In many other departments, however, you can feel the game's lack of budget or attention. The animations are terrible; many of them look like they were done with Unregistered Hypercam 2 and MS Paint. The enemy variety leaves much to be desired, and many of the late game enemies are basically the same early game enemies but recolored and upgraded.
Overall, if you really like the theme or aesthetic, you should definitely get this. Otherwise, there are better metroidvanias you could be playing: Hollow Knight, Ori and the Blind Forest, and if you can get your hands on them, 2D Metroid or Castlevania games.

Hotline Miami 2 is an improvement on the original Hotline Miami in a lot of ways. It's oriented around  more than just one psychopath now (which aside from being completely different people, can have subtle differences in-game combat wise or completely unique from the average psychjoe), gives guns a much bigger spotlight in comparison to the original, while also attempting to keep melee weapons in an equal ground. The thought of actually using any firearms in Hotline Miami was a turn-off; in Hotline Miami 2, however, you don't bat an eye on using one.
Just like the original Hotline Miami, there's no room for error. Universally shared is the fact that you can't survive a single swing from a melee weapon; however, some characters can survive more than one shot. Despite this strength, many weapons are still a powerhouse and shoot very fast, typically leaving the second-chance to situational moments.
Not much has changed in the way of enemies in Hotline Miami. There is, however, a new enemy which dodges projectiles (this involves firearms!) and can only be killed with melees, called the Dodger. There's also new enemy factions to fit in with the multiple characters. While they act exactly the same, sans some special enemies such as the previously mentioned Dodger, they help expand the story further.
The weapons in Hotline Miami were a small pool. While not improved much in Hotline Miami 2, there are
improvements. Some weapons are shared with multiple factions, like the typical pump shotgun or knife, but on the same note, some are faction exclusive, like the Uzi or the AK-47.
Most, if not all, of the games levels are heavily plagued with unfair deaths. Many times will you find yourself being killed from offscreen enemies and supremely poor level design; downright stupid level design at that.
Every level,
, has long corridors, thoughtless enemy placement, and
This is further exacerbated with Hard Mode! Not only does Hard Mode make it so throwing weapons reduces their total ammo (thanks to whoever thought that♥♥♥♥♥♥up while on some meth), but it also adds MORE enemies.The extra enemy placements are even worse, forcing you to play strategically.
Overall, the gameplay is great, but the levels included are a mess and really make you feel horrible when you're stuck on them. Replaying it a second time is great, however. If there's one thing that both fans and critics of the sequel to 2012's violent and neon colored indie hit Hotline Miami can agree on, it's that Hotline Miami 2 is anything but more of the same. With tons more characters, stories, and world building, HM2 is definitely a much farther reaching and ambitious game. There's a non linear and cryptic story which jumps to the future, present, and past of the first games events in no set order. It goes on to show us such things as Jackets past and motivations. What other agents of 50 Blessings were doing at the time and why. How 50 Blessings functions and what it's real goals are. And how the world itself has reacted to one mans vigilante murder spree and how it now tries to understand and make sense of it. You'll most likely have no idea as to what the story means or how the events of each protagonists story relates to one another after your first playthrough. It might take multiple playthroughs, and it might even take looking up forums or other websites to finally get the full picture. Once you do however, you'll gain a whole new understanding of not only HM2, but it's predecessor as well.
Now that I've talked at length about the story, let's talk about the gameplay. Like the story, the gameplay of HM2 is also quite different. Levels are now large and sprawling labyrinths filled with enemies that are well out of your field of view. Patience, stretching out your view with shift as far as possible, and baiting enemies you can't safely reach or attack are now the name of the game. Each character you will play as has their own styles of play as well. Some have different weapons, some have masks, some have multiple people, and some simply start with nothing. Because you never know who you'll be playing as next, becoming competent with each character is also important. None of these elements are outright bad or broken. Again, it's subjective and whether or not you enjoy it will come down to your own preferences.
In conclusion, Hotline Miami 2 is a game that does almost everything differently then it's predecessor, and your enjoyment of it will come down to how much you either hate, love, or just accept these changes. But hey, at least the series went out with a bang, am I right?

This game is not for everyone. It's a nonstandard 4X game with heavy emphasis on diplomacy, and is extremely niche in an already niche genre. If you don't think manipulating everything from behind the scenes is fun, then walk away from this game and never look back. However, if you do enjoy that, then this game might be for you.
The Last Federation is a well-designed strategy game with a surprising amount of depth. You play as a lone mercenary, and watch as the AI builds its empires. Your goal is to nudge the AI in a way that will ultimately create a Federation that spans the solar system. Your actions rarely have an immediate payoff, but over time you can decide which planets become wastelands and which ones become paradise. It's a thing of beauty, to subtly change a few numbers early on, and watch the butterfly effect go.
The combat system is a turn-based bullet hell, where you can manage power distribution, plot out movement, and use weapons/abilities. The tutorial places a lot of emphasis on combat, but managing RCI and influence is far more important. While you can hold off an overwhelming invasion force for a while or smash apart a stalemate, combat is only one tool out of many in your arsenal. It's up to the player to figure out when to get their hands dirty, and when to sit back and help build up armadas.
The game has an excellent soundtrack, shiny art, and a very coherent design. The story is solid, if a bit cliche. The game has a rather light-hearted tone, with blurbs of snark and sarcasm coming from your AI assistant as the solar system evolves. The screen does get cluttered later in the game, but the option to clean it up does exist. Critical information is very well presented and accessible, but may get overwhelming to new players despite the tutorial. The developers have given an incredible amount of attention to detail, to the point where I can still discover new interactions after 40 hours of playing the game. There are many mechanics and interactions that go unexplained, although there is a bit of appeal in discovering them for yourself.
It's impossible to do much on your own in The Last Federation. You just can't hope to make or break interplanetary empires with your single ship.  You will have to rely on the various AI races to do the dirty work for you. The DLCs add in new game modes, but the gameplay patterns stays the same: AI does the heavy lifting, and you guide it and stack the deck in your favor. With a randomly generated solar system, there's a healthy amount of replayability. The game does stagnate after you figure out the optimal strategy, but there's a lot of fun to be had as you learn it.
The Last Federation is a solid, niche strategy game. If you're looking for a standard 4X game, you will be disappointed. If you're interested in this game solely for its combat mechanics then I would advise against getting it, because it's only a small portion of the game itself. But if you're looking for a strategy game with heavy emphasis on diplomacy and manipulation, then I would strongly recommend it.

There are many reasons as to why Warlords Battlecry III failed to set the world on fire, but if you look hard enough, you'll find one of the most dedicated and passionate fan bases in computer gaming today; a community that, like myself, just can't seem to put this excellent game down.
Battlecry III is a cult favourite then, a title with an enduring legacy that fans have continued to support over the years with a wealth of quality mods, maps, and patches that either improve, enhance and otherwise expand this wonderful blend of heroic fantasy and real-time strategy.
As an RTS, Battlecry III is both original and familiar. Usually you'll start by exploring the map and guiding your hero unit to resource mines that he/she/it can convert to your side and choke points that need to be guarded against enemy scouts.
Meanwhile you'll have your worker units busily constructing a base and once those precious resources of gold, metal, ore and crystal start to pour in, it's time to produce new units and upgrades that will strengthen your chosen plan of attack.
Before you can take part in this skirmish however you need to create your own hero and here is where the fun really begins. Battlecry III makes one crucial change over its prequel; a change that improves the overall game significantly.
Unlike Battlecry II, where heroes developed down a more stringent path, Battlecry III streamlines every heroic class and allows you to experiment with each one right from the beginning.
Sure, it may not be the best idea to create a charisma-starved undead merchant, but the game isn't going to stop you from trying it! Maybe you like the idea of creating a noble knight who practices the dark arts of necromancy? Or a wood elf who summons demons? Perhaps a plaguelord alchemist? A dwarven healer? Or an orcish paladin?
The combinations are truly endless and with 16 different races, 29 heroic classes and even more skills, weapons and experience points to gather, you're bound to find something here that suits your preferred play style.
Battlecry III is made even more memorable by its charming sense of humour and rather old school isometric 3D graphics. Each battlefield unit has plenty of fun sound files and animations that makes for many a colourful confrontation loaded with more personality than a dozen similar titles I've played over the years.
The majority of this characterization comes from the contrast between the good, neutral and evil races; something that is amusingly highlighted when their respective units are clicked in-game. "The age of heroes has ended!" yells the dark rider, "buttercups and rainbows!" squeaks the diminutive fey sprite, and "when is dinner?" inquires the oafish orc giant.
The main campaign mode is made more interesting this time around too with a dedicated storyline accompanying your conquests across the land of Etheria and a developing narrative that explores your hero's effort to seal away Gorgon; the feared fifth horseman of ancient legend.
It's here though that you start to recognize the one thing that's really holding Battlecry III back; its budget. It's clear that the creators put a lot of love into this game, but as reviewers pointed out at the time, there are several aspects that feel a bit underdeveloped and old-hat; no doubt a symptom of time and budgetary constraints during its production.
There is a raft of missing content from Battlecry II for one, including unit sound effects, quests (in-game challenges that crop up from shrines) and certain scripts for hero builds and AI behaviour. Whilst graphically the game looks more detailed than Battlecry II, it's a shame that some of the second game's vibrant colour has been lost during the transition.
Also upsetting is the amount of bugs, balance concerns and the shoddy net code that is terribly unfit for purpose. Battlecry III is a great game to play with friends, no doubt about it, but good luck getting your session to sync up correctly first time.
Getting back to the point I made about the story; it's also a shame that the final campaign mission doesn't feature a final showdown with Gorgon himself, as you merely fight his minions in a gauntlet-style survival encounter whilst an anti-climatic timer ticks along in the corner.
At many of these points you get the feeling that the developer's time and money simply ran out, leaving the game in a disappointing state of 'almost there'.
Luckily the fan community for Battlecry III has gone well beyond the call of duty with several talented members continuing to improve the game with both Infinite Interactive's blessing and their assistance.
Armed with a portion of the game's source code, a dedicated cult of modders have gone on to create brand new patches that fix bugs, balance units and in some cases add completely new content such as a summoning timer and the awesome monk hero class.
Without these community patches Battlecry III would be a much harder sell and it really speaks volumes about the raw passion and energy that has gone into these fan-made enhancement projects.

Another reason I have continued to appreciate this title over the years is my belief in this truly being a game without boundaries.
When it comes to heroes for example, there's no level cap and therefore no limit to how absurdly powerful your favourite little avatar can become.
If you truly are dedicated enough to make it past level 100 then expect to see the game balance busted wide open as your epic hero reigns death upon your enemies with lightening fast attacks, devastating spells and a heavily discounted legion of augmented troops.
Once again, it may be a little crazy, but the game isn't going stop you from trying it, because if it's fun, what else really matters? Admiteddly, there is a lot standing in the way of Warlords Battlecry III being any good.
The art style looks dated, the netcode is barely there and it’s blessed with more than its fair share of bugs and balance concerns.
Nevertheless, this is a game that will suck you in for hours at a time and truly astonish you with its replayability, sense of humour and irresistible marriage of strategy and open-ended RPG elements.

The very first thing that you notice about Layers of Fear is its atmosphere, quickly followed by its horror aspect, accuratly called "Psychedelic Horror". What I really like about this game is that you can take the time to appreciate the enviorment, and that the game does not rely on creating a monster, or jamming some sort of ghost into your face in virtually every moment that it can. In this respect the game excels.
With that being said, however, the game does not really have the best interaction with its enviroment. The enviroment is exellent, but in my playthrough it was mostly there for show. so there could be improvements with the interaction and thinking. The storytelling is absolutely amazing, yet interaction and thinking is not quite there. The game could improve with some more puzzle mechanics, or at least some more interaction with the enviroment to make the player think and at the same time allow them to enjoy the atmosphere while playing the game. Another thing that could be improved is more erractic gameplay. By this I mean more unpredictable motions. I was reading a few other reviews, and something that I could agree on was some predictability (Picking up object = Door slamming shut). This is a difficult one for most games due to the player being on edge and prepared about 90-95% of the time throughout a horror game. The trick, however, is to manage to pin down that 10-5% where the player is not expecting something to appear. There are a few points in the game that really got me, but if you managed to add even a little more of the unexpected and erratic moments, than this could become an incredibly enjoyable game. However, if you do make these changes its crucial not to take away from the enviroment or storytelling. Those two factors alone make this game a real gem in my opinion.
Overall, I really did enjoy playing this game. The atmosphere, psychedelic factor and storytelling, as stated above, really makes this game stand out from the crowd. Yes, there are a few things that could be improved, but its honestly worth the 10$ (or 8$ from the sale) and more (once the game leaves early access).
for those who found this review to be TL:DR, than here:

Difficulty is ok, death count at the end of the game for me was 91 (sometimes you just die on purpose cause you wasted too many ammo on simple encounters or at least I did that), you can upgrade main character with currency found during the game, yet it's not obligatory, you can finish game without it, I'll take it as a good thing since you'll never hit a wall cause you didn't upgraded ammo capacity for example. Graphics are... very atmospheric, but textures on some objects are terrible (thanks to consoles), on the other hand enemy models are top notch. Sound and music are on the spot for building tension in right moments. This game is very underrated on metacritic due to same "console port" issues but really, rate the game itself instead of crying for 30fps cap (you can switch for 60fps now). I agree that characters aren't memorable, and story left too many unanswered questions but probably we will get them in DLCs. For me it's solid 8/10 or even 9/10.

So, to begin, I got this game as a gift, as a disclaimer.
Now, big question: should you get this game for the current list price, 60 USD? Thats a very difficult question, but I would have to say that it certainly is substantial enough to warrant a high-price purchase. My current hours on time of writing (23.7 hours, give or take a few hours for extended breaks and AFKs,) you are definitely getting your moneys worth in terms of content. Whether that content is substantial is what I hope to clear up.
I won't reiterate the basic premise of the story, but I was disappointed by how dull it was. The set pieces that make up the level had the potential to tell a story, but exploration is both expansive and restrictive at the same time. To clarify, the set pieces are often quite large, with multiple routes to move from one objective to the next, but exploration yields only upgrade materials and ammunition, and if you find a file or a lore piece, it most certainly will be in an obvious place. No interesting stories told by the scenery (though at times, it is quiet impressive,) and exploration only yields in-game pick ups. If you're looking for a substantial story with interesting collectibles that flesh out the world, this is not the game for you. Even the save sections, in which you are transported to an asylum via a mirror which acts as a hub for unlockables, upgrades, and saving, are rarely creepy (the nurse sounding more tired than creepy), and the lore pickups found in these sections are things that are revealed elsewhere, rendering them redundant.
However, despite the game's horror stemming from the comically over-gory environments falling flat, the actual survival part is where this game shines. Limited ammunition helps drive the point home that you have to be disciplined, resourceful, and smart in all your encounters. All your upgrades are either for ammo capacity upgrades or bonuses to your sprint, melee damage, or health, which will increase survivability in your environment.
The most interesting part of your arsenal is the agony crossbow, which uses different types of bolts to different effects. For example, a flash bolt allows for a stealth kill from any angle while the enemy is stunned, and a freeze bolt allows for a one hit kill from any ranged or melee attack. The inherent usefulness of the bolt determines its price in crafting (which is done with the single press of a button) assembled from spare parts found in pick-ups and environmental traps. This allows you to scrounge enough ammunition in case you run out of your primary ammunitions (and you will, often.) Though, your melee attacks do nothing but slow attackers down, making ammunition management that much more important.
In what feels like a tribute to resident evil, any body can be burned to convserve ammuntion, if its been downed, or directly above the body of what you are about to burn. Though this can save on ammuniton, at starting, you can only hold five matches until you run out, with upgrades allowing you to carry more in increments of five. This can help save on ammunition, but matches are as rare as bullets (and the prompt for lighting creatures on fire is often unwieldy and buggy at best, which makes a certain boss fight nearly unbearable). Thus another survival element is thrown on top.
Where this game doesn't excell is in stealth. The first few chapters do a good job of getting you into a stealth mindset reminiscient of outlast, but after around the 4th chapter, the stealth is almost completely phased out in favor of gunplay, and indeed, a few chapters are devoted to this. I feel this as a huge missed opportunity, as it highlights probably the games weakest points.
I can't say I was ever scared, horrified, or startled, but the game excells at one thing: stress, and often in a way that makes the experience feel authentic. Often, you'll have to fight a boss using only what you have at the moment and what you can scrounge up, every further encounter leaves you with a sense of dread and unpreparedness, and everything, til the very bitter end, feels like a struggle. Despite the game's weak ending, you will feel a sense of accomplishment after any chapter, knowing that it was your cunning, ingenuity, and sheer perserverence that brought you through to the end.
Despite my gripes about it, I saw myself snagging any chance to play this game in my free time, wanting to perservere through to the end. Though the ending sets the stage for DLC, I give this a reccomend, if only because you'll be getting your money's worth.
Be warned, this game has its fair share of problems, so this is a weak reccomend.

As of now (Feb2016) the game is early access and only a sandbox building / machine / vehicle builder. There is no "game" or goals, think of it as a box of Legos to play with by your self. I like the graphic style which is what you see in the steam screen shots. However i wish the devs would remove the pile of sticks coming out your characters back pack. Its really not needed and makes you wider then you need to be.
As others have said, unless you are the creative type you will not like this game. This game will not entertain you, it is for those who can entertain themselves.
The game still has a long way to go and hopefully many improvements are made to it. The game seems to be solid as far as no crashes or huge bugs. Only one clipping glitch that i saw was when falling aircraft hit the ground sometimes the landing gears clip into the ground and then become stuck there. No more movement. You can manually unstick it using the building platform / hoist. The UI is also a little simple and could use many improvements to improve the efficiency of building things.
The materials to build with are limited so far. They have two types, raw material like wood and metal which you can place as blocks (think minecraft) in any shape size or configuration. Thats pretty much the foundation (walls, etc) of what you build. Then there are objects you can attach, bearings, switches, engines, wires, plants, stairs, rails, I-beams, etc. However these objects are one size fits all. You can not adjust the size of them. Example, a step for making stairs is 1x6. You can not stretch it, make it smaller or cut it down. So your stairs are 6 wide, or 12 wide, or 18 wide. This limits the creativity a little when you have to build things that fit into the devs blue prints of what they offer you to work with.
There is a whole list of things i wish the devs would change or add to make the game more flexible. Such as being able to assign objects (like engines) to more then one switch or button at a time. Or assign buttons and switches to other buttons or switches. Example: wire a bank of buttons to a single button so when you push the one button the other buttons get activated.
BUT this is early access and still under development so i do not hold any of these issues against the game. The game has a lot of potential and i hope they really flush it out in the near future.

I could only bare to play this game for a handful of sessions. It was completely boring and derivative. Everything in it is ripped wholesale from Left 4 Dead right down to the animations that characters do while using their medpacks. The suspension of disbelief did not last long, at least, for me.
Even the special Skaven are exact duplicates of the special infected from L4D2 but make far less sense. When a smoker is literally strangling you with a tentacle it makes sense that you might not be able to free yourself without help. But why is my veteran, dwarf ranger just standing there flailing his arms like an idiot just because there's a hook resting on his shoulder? We're talking about a guy who survives the harshest wilderness climates alone and fights off massive, wild beasts on a daily basis but one Skaven with a hook weapon is too much, I guess.
These may seem like a petty complaints from the outside but the game is loaded with things like that and it just all piles up into a mess. The game tells you "Get to the watch tower!" but doesn't tell you where that is. There's a section where Skaven will endlessly spawn until you blow up a door with some barrels of gunpowder which, stops them for some reason. But again, the game tells you nothing so unless you just happen to see the gunpowder and then figure it out yourself, you'll be there for a long time just fighting and dying. On top of all this the gameplay is rather dull and extremely repetative. The only thing that spices it up is trying out the different characters, the loot system and, different maps of which there are few.
Just to end my rant I'll mention that Vermintide is also a $30 title with full priced DLC and no workshop or modding support. I absolutely loved Left 4 Dead and I'm a massive Warhammer fan but I had to force myself to play this game. That says pretty much everything you need to know about it.

Played this on free weekend, and had quite a bit of fun with it. I've seen quite a bit of mindless backlash to this from free weekenders I would like to address personally: (Yeah, this isn't so much of a positive review as a counter-negative)
-"It's a Left 4 Dead ripoff!" I don't like using the term ripoff myself. I think the idea Left 4 Dead should just have a monopoly on the 4-player co-op horde shooter genre absurd, but the reason why I don't consider the game a ripoff is because of its large focus on melee combat, the "Tomes" concept that allows you to sacrifice the ability to carry a healing item with you in exchange for better loot at the end of the mission, and the idea of every character acting differently and having a different weaponset changes it. Not to mention special enemies are altered from Left 4 Dead with the Ratling Gunner being a completely original and interesting idea (Basically a guy with a minigun who stays mostly stationary and targets 1 player at a time, leaving that player to find cover and the others to take the minigun guy out). However, obviously this game is very similar to Left 4 Dead.
-"Enemy AI is bad" It's a horde shooter. 'Nuff said. I do find, however, the fact that enemies are actually very inconfident outside of groups interesting. The weaker guys often stay away from you unless they have pals.
-"Melee combat is bad" Sort of. For the typical horde it's generally spamming leftclick, but the Stormvermin special enemy are brawlers who actually require practice and patience to kill due to their armor negating all but the heavier attacks in all places apart from the head. Melee combat could be better, could be worse. It is satisfying, for sure, but often brainless apart from the aforementioned Stormvermin who mandate you go for the head and dash away from their attacks.
-"Performance issues/crashes" I never noticed any, but I only speak for myself and my PC's not low-grade (It's not a god rig by any means, but it's fairly up to date).
-"Classes are very similar" I actually like this approach. There is no "Healer class" and "Sniper class" and "Tanky class" ecetera. The five heroes have strengths and weaknesses, and that's it. Nobody's saying your Witch Hunter can't go on the front lines, because while the Empire Soldier would be the ideal character for that, the Witch Hunter can still easily hold his own through his melee weapons.
-"All you do is mindlessly kill weak enemies" Kinda the point of horde shooters. The grunts go down easy, there's a lot of grunts, get used to it. It's when a special enemy comes in and challenges you when the actual fight begins, as it were. The grunts are just a distraction and occasionally get you from behind to eat away at your health.
That's not to say every criticism of Vermintide is in fact invalid. In fact, I'd trust the reviews from people who have played this game for 50+ hours more than this one. They've played longer and understand the game better than I do. However, from what I have experienced I think writing this off as a bad Left 4 Dead ripoff is an unwarranted dismissal of a game that's more than passable.
I would, however, certainly recommend this on sale as opposed to full price. I think this is worth the cash, but I think your money would be better spent somewhere else at full price. For what this game is, though, it's certainly enjoyable.

This is far and away one of the most entertaining mods out there. The learning curve is certainly a little steep and there are balance issues that manifest on certain maps (there are a massive number of custom maps), but all in all this is one of the most well-crafted little free mods out there. The developers update the game on a somewhat infrequent but regular basis, and their releases are pretty uniformly stable.
In terms of gameplay, there are few modes: point capture/hold, deathmatch, "trinket" (sort of like an inverse team hot-potato deathmatch mode), and bounty (capture the "flag" with a lot of "flags"). Each one rewards certain playstyles more than others.
This mod has been out for some time and has a fairly experienced cadre of regular players that are pretty good. This can be frustrating for new players at first, but provided that you're willing to die a few times to learn how to play, it won't take too terribly long to get up to speed. I played the first PVK--which was an HL1 mod--many years back, and the devs never "finished" it (in terms of classes and gameplay). It looks like they're making more steady strides toward completing this one. I haven't seen a CTD bug in years, and a good game gets a little better with every update.
Give this one a shot. I was drawn to the novelty that is a game where three teams from far-flung places and times smash into each other, and I stayed for the challenge, the fun, and humor. If nothing else, play once for the pleasure of sending your attack parrot to peck someone's eyes out. And then once more to be a viking lawnmower. And maybe one more time to fart someone to death.

Hotline Miami 2 is an improvement on the original Hotline Miami in a lot of ways. It's oriented around  more than just one psychopath now (which aside from being completely different people, can have subtle differences in-game combat wise or completely unique from the average psychjoe), gives guns a much bigger spotlight in comparison to the original, while also attempting to keep melee weapons in an equal ground. The thought of actually using any firearms in Hotline Miami was a turn-off; in Hotline Miami 2, however, you don't bat an eye on using one.
Just like the original Hotline Miami, there's no room for error. Universally shared is the fact that you can't survive a single swing from a melee weapon; however, some characters can survive more than one shot. Despite this strength, many weapons are still a powerhouse and shoot very fast, typically leaving the second-chance to situational moments.
Not much has changed in the way of enemies in Hotline Miami. There is, however, a new enemy which dodges projectiles (this involves firearms!) and can only be killed with melees, called the Dodger. There's also new enemy factions to fit in with the multiple characters. While they act exactly the same, sans some special enemies such as the previously mentioned Dodger, they help expand the story further.
The weapons in Hotline Miami were a small pool. While not improved much in Hotline Miami 2, there are
improvements. Some weapons are shared with multiple factions, like the typical pump shotgun or knife, but on the same note, some are faction exclusive, like the Uzi or the AK-47.
Most, if not all, of the games levels are heavily plagued with unfair deaths. Many times will you find yourself being killed from offscreen enemies and supremely poor level design; downright stupid level design at that.
Every level,
, has long corridors, thoughtless enemy placement, and
This is further exacerbated with Hard Mode! Not only does Hard Mode make it so throwing weapons reduces their total ammo (thanks to whoever thought that♥♥♥♥♥♥up while on some meth), but it also adds MORE enemies.The extra enemy placements are even worse, forcing you to play strategically.
Overall, the gameplay is great, but the levels included are a mess and really make you feel horrible when you're stuck on them. Replaying it a second time is great, however. Hard Mode is also a nice challenge once you know enough about the game, but take this with a grain of salt; it's only for those with thick skin.

Cool concept. Very poorly executed.
Really enjoyed the start of the game, and the combat, but nothing is well explained, and the tutorials are frankly pretty confusing. My main issue is that I'd spend a bunch of time building up relations between two empires, only to have them form an "anti-federation alliance" before I get a chance to form any kind of federation, despite the tutorial saying they'd only do that AFTER you formed a federation. Sounds like a glitch, but maybe I just missed something?
On a more meta level, the game doesn't seem to know if it wants to be a spreadsheet simulator, or a bullethell space game. The devs took the middle road of just using the worst features from both genres and making a sub-par game in both genres.
Bullet Hell:
The bullethell ship-battles are much too busy and convoluted, and none of the abilities seem to have much impact, even on ultra-easy mode. Having to switch between anti-shield and anti-ship is cool, but it's impossible to tell what are fighters and what are missiles, or what team any ship is on. Dodging attacks isn't really even an option with all the chaos going on in a large battle, so you just have to hope your shields are up to the task.
The 4x style management sim is even more bland and confusing. Every task you attempt takes months to have any meaningful impact, locking you in one place while you fast-forward through tons of war and politics and have to just cross your fingers that the galaxy hasn't imploded while you were collecting space debris. On top of this, every single empire seems to have a different method of interacting with the player, none of which are explained at all. Mechanics like the diplomat seem to serve no purpose at all except to make you click a spot in the menu every time you meet an empire, since there doesn't seem to be any downside to having them and they're essentially free to purchase. There are quests, but I was never able to figure out how to actually go do them, since visiting the relevant planet never made them turn up in menus.
I'd recommend not wasting your money on this lemon.

Very fun little game. The staggered tutorial does an excellent job of making it easy to understand the mechanics and how the different races act and interact, and there's still a lot of depth to play in. Fairly short compared to a lot of other strategy games (eight planets, with no breakdown of area beneath "planet"), but there's a high replayability factor from trying different approaches and having different races be "first landing". As others have noted, you're a lone diplomat in this one - all your efforts are through diplomacy, but that will sometimes be gunboat-flavoured.
The Betrayal gamemode DLC doesn't have a lot of replay to it (you're out to paint the map) but *is* rather cathartic after having to deal with bickering races doing stupid things and adds some fun planet-management mechanics. Certainly the closest to classic strategy games.
Invasion (the other DLC gamemode) is interesting, as whilst it's relatively easy to get the various races to agree to attack The Deadly Invaders™ the difficulty really lies in having them be strong enough to win, and agree to help protect each other. The resulting Federation, though, feels probably the most natural all-races one of them all.
Highly recommend playing, especially if you can pick it up on sale.

Longer video version of this review:
This game starts off with a bit of storytelling about a girl named Merryn and her father, who live near the ocean, where he would go fishing. Unfortunately, he doesn't return from his latest trip, so she decides to build herself her own little submarine to go looking for him.
This is a metroidvania game that takes place under the sea. You float around in the water, collecting coins and treasures to purchase upgrades for your submarine, which you get from a giant hermit crab. Funny, he doesn’t look that intelligent. What does he know about selling stuff?
This game has an annoying bug where in every new session I would play this game, the prices for items seems to disappear, and then reappear in the next session. I don’t know how to make this not happen, but it’s absolutely ridiculous.
You also fight off enemies too, because video game. You've got your close-up enemies, long-range enemies, and enemies with certain weak points. You can apparently throw things at the enemies by grabbing it, and letting go while you’re moving. Take notes: While you’re moving. Otherwise you just drop it down below you.
And of course, as with most games, you eventually come across a boss, which is a giant spider. I actually really enjoyed this fight. It changes the mechanics around in each phase. I did talk about the battle in my video review, but I won't here. After the battle, you release a baby creature from one of the food capsule things, and your character decides to name it Swish. Swish wants you to follow it somewhere. But honestly, what I would recommend after getting a new weapon or item is looking around for goodies you couldn’t get before. But be careful, because after fighting the giant spider, the enemies get stronger than before. And more so as the game goes on.
You get three different projectile weapons, electric-looking balls, lava balls, and ice balls. The electric and lava balls can be used to break certain stone walls that block you from other areas. But there are some walls these won’t work on. You have to use the ice balls to harden the lava walls so that you can break them and pass through. But besides that, these projectile weapons can be quite useful against enemies.
You get a sonar emitter from the Deep Light. You can actually use it to discover secret paths in the walls, as well as use it against the sonar defences to open some of the doors. If you see the treasure symbol on your map, but you see nothing there, you can also use it to reveal the invisible chests.
the puzzles with the spinning turbine things I could do without. I’ve gotten so angry at this part. You have to use one of those big explosive balls to blow up walls and stuff to get goodies. In order to do some of this, however, you have to use your ice projectiles to make them float up and magma to weigh them down. But the biggest problem has been entering the same space with the explosive so that I can push it out. But I always end up separated from it. It’s very frustrating, and I don’t think the frame rate helps any.
The aiming can be kind of off sometimes when I’m fighting enemies or trying to shoot at big blowy-uppy balls. I sometimes cannot see where the cursor is, and I can’t always get my sub to move the direction I want. You know that sense you have when you move your mouse and you know exactly what direction the cursor will move? That seems to be a bit of a missing element in this game. Or maybe that’s just me. I dunno.
I ended up rage-quitting on the way to the lair of the Rimorosa. There is a part with a bunch of lasers that you have to avoid, but with the way the frame rate is, I couldn’t turn my submarine in time to avoid the lasers. Honestly, I don’t think it’s a bad game. It was actually pretty good up until that point. So I will still recommend it.

While I do not work as an artist professionally, I have been creating digital art since the mid 1990s, and in doing so have used a wide range of 2D and 3D applications. My main focus are space and Science-Fiction.
If am working on a texture for a planet within a space scene for instance, that usually means painting from scratch with the occasional use of my own and public domain stock photos, as well as NASA resources. That is time consuming, and while fun, not always practical.
The software is very intuitive, and especially if you have prior experience with 2D/3D software packages such as Photoshop, Vue, Lightwave, Cinema 4D, 3D Studio, and Bryce - to name a few - this will not require much, if any, learning.
Is the asking price justified? A clear 'yes' from me, and I am including the PRO edition in that. One of the main reasons is that this software allows you to generate professional level 16k textures which usually hold up even in extreme close ups. Add to that the real time creation process, time saving, and ability to easily add and remove features, $80 is more than fair. It also doesn't feel clumsy and unfinished like most Early Access titles.
If you want to expand your horizons, and add a time saver to your workflow, then look no further.

This is a very iffy game.  Don't go into this game expecting it to be the next Resident Evil 4 and you should be alright.
Graphics
After a patch or two this game is playable on keyboard and mouse and I now wouldn't play it any other way.  The graphics are on par I would say but nothing spectacular other than a few scenes.  The graphics settings do about the bare minimum to satisfy anyone but them removing the 30 FPS lock was a big deal.
Story
At its bare bones you won't find anything signifigant in terms of story here.  It seems as if they left some of it out on purpose to make room for the season pass featuring a side character from the main story.  The story has some depth to it if you want to study Kantian constructivism but at base value it is mediocre at best.
Gameplay
Probably the best part about this game is the gameplay.  It plays like a much smoother RE4 and even like a Dead Space game.  There are lots of places to set traps in order to conserve ammo and play it how you want to.  The stealth sort of falls flat on its face but the other raw gameplay is quite enjoyable in my opinion.
Spook Factor
It has its few moments of absolute terror, such as one iconic boss fight which leaves you screaming, but other than that there is a lot to be desired in terms of spookiness
Overall
I would reccomend this game but on lots of precautions as it must fit the type of game you like (action third-person, survival) otherwise I dont see any jaw breaking thing about this game that could make you change preferred genre for it.

Played this on free weekend, and had quite a bit of fun with it. I've seen quite a bit of mindless backlash to this from free weekenders I would like to address personally: (Yeah, this isn't so much of a positive review as a counter-negative)
-"It's a Left 4 Dead ripoff!" I don't like using the term ripoff myself. I think the idea Left 4 Dead should just have a monopoly on the 4-player co-op horde shooter genre absurd, but the reason why I don't consider the game a ripoff is because of its large focus on melee combat, the "Tomes" concept that allows you to sacrifice the ability to carry a healing item with you in exchange for better loot at the end of the mission, and the idea of every character acting differently and having a different weaponset changes it. Not to mention special enemies are altered from Left 4 Dead with the Ratling Gunner being a completely original and interesting idea (Basically a guy with a minigun who stays mostly stationary and targets 1 player at a time, leaving that player to find cover and the others to take the minigun guy out). However, obviously this game is very similar to Left 4 Dead.
-"Enemy AI is bad" It's a horde shooter. 'Nuff said. I do find, however, the fact that enemies are actually very inconfident outside of groups interesting. The weaker guys often stay away from you unless they have pals.
-"Melee combat is bad" Sort of. For the typical horde it's generally spamming leftclick, but the Stormvermin special enemy are brawlers who actually require practice and patience to kill due to their armor negating all but the heavier attacks in all places apart from the head. Melee combat could be better, could be worse. It is satisfying, for sure, but often brainless apart from the aforementioned Stormvermin who mandate you go for the head and dash away from their attacks.
-"Performance issues/crashes" I never noticed any, but I only speak for myself and my PC's not low-grade (It's not a god rig by any means, but it's fairly up to date).
-"Classes are very similar" I actually like this approach. There is no "Healer class" and "Sniper class" and "Tanky class" ecetera. The five heroes have strengths and weaknesses, and that's it. Nobody's saying your Witch Hunter can't go on the front lines, because while the Empire Soldier would be the ideal character for that, the Witch Hunter can still easily hold his own through his melee weapons.
-"All you do is mindlessly kill weak enemies" Kinda the point of horde shooters. The grunts go down easy, there's a lot of grunts, get used to it. It's when a special enemy comes in and challenges you when the actual fight begins, as it were. The grunts are just a distraction and occasionally get you from behind to eat away at your health.
That's not to say every criticism of Vermintide is in fact invalid. In fact, I'd trust the reviews from people who have played this game for 50+ hours more than this one. They've played longer and understand the game better than I do. However, from what I have experienced I think writing this off as a bad Left 4 Dead ripoff is an unwarranted dismissal of a game that's more than passable.
I would, however, certainly recommend this on sale as opposed to full price. I think this is worth the cash, but I think your money would be better spent somewhere else at full price. For what this game is, though, it's certainly enjoyable.

5/10 didn't find it very fun at all despite my positive bias for the genre, but I'm sure it's fun for someone out there.
You may stand to have a good time if you've never played Mount and Blade or Chivalry. It does feel as though the game was made with love, but it's still an awkward, clumsy, and unpolished combat experience. I'm easily satisfied when it comes to melee combat but this game was actually hard to enjoy. Fights are just people running around each other swinging and swinging and swinging their awkward weapons until they die. They're long and unfulfilling.
If you're using one of the weapons worth using (as in, non-ranged and not one in which you hold down the attack button to repeat the little "chop-chop" animation), you look in a direction to choose which of your three attacks you're going to do, and there the weapon stays for as long as you hold that button. The idea is this "charges" your attacks, which is a welcome mechanic, but all it does is slow down your attacking. There is no flow, no comboing, no way to mix it up. You have three attacks that won't ever change and they're all made for a very small hitbox. You really can't drag it around either as you can in the aforementioned games, leaving you feel less like a warrior and more like a theme park robot. And in the event you raise up a fully charged attack, know that you aren't going to kill anyone. Everyone has what is effectively a dual health bar - one for health and the other for "armor" - and you'll be hacking at even an archer for quite a while before they die because of it. Seriously... You'll take your greataxe, walk up to an archer with a fully charged attack, bring it down on their head, and they'll just look at you like you were stupid to try it. Then they just walk away as you try to hit them the 3-4 more times it takes to kill them.
There exists a parry system like that of mount and blade, in that you must look a certain direction to ready the right parry. It's potentially nice if you have the presence of mind to use it, but in all likelihood, your opponent is going to miss that attack that you're prepared for, and most fights are just exchanges of swings. Parrying only seems worth it if you're incredibly practiced at it, and if you're using it in a duel, otherwise you just want to get out as much hitting as possible.
Everyone is appropriately mobile, at least. The base run speed is quite fast and perfect as such, and everyone has a nifty little roll they can execute, although I'm unsure of how applicable it really is in a fight. You can't roll and transition smoothly into an attack.
Are the teams balanced? I haven't played enough to say for sure, but it seems the pirates generally come out on top. In a game where hitting people to death is a tedious experience, the characters that can just shoot you as well as place powerful explosives are probably going to have an edge.
Pretty fun.

This is a tough one.  Not recommending this title despite wasting many, many hours playing it would seem dishonest...so I'll "not recommend" it with conditions.
I thought I loved what this game was trying to do but after playing it, I'm not sure even that much is true anymore.
The original Mount & Blade was ground-breaking;  Warband was like having having three scoops of ice-cream!  I didn't even know that was possible!  Viking Conquest is more like your brother's promise to return your stuff in the same condition.
Fortunately, they simply modded the best game ever so in the end, it comes out to a pretty great gaming experience anyway but kind of in a, laughing at a B-movie, sort of way.  The language and dialogue options are funny and sometimes infuriating, particularly in the early parts of the story.  The odd "SCRIPT-ERROR" warnings seem like something that should have been fixed long, long before it was ever released.
Just when I get really infuriated with the bugs and glitches, something redeeming will happen and make me love this game...just a little bit.  For example, while sailing my fleet along one afternoon, I noticed a lord and his ships stuck on some beach and decided to go have a chat.  "What are you and your men up to?" I asked, pretending it was asked in a rather threatening manner.  "I don't know" was his reply and I nearly spit coffee all over my monitor.  I thought to myself "Fair enough then" and continued on my journey with a smile on my face.
There are quite a few oddities in here but I'll try to touch on the ones that stand out in my mind right now.  Very few lords appear to have much interest in women.  Not only does this cramp the wanna-be defender of ladies' rights style but it also makes for a harsh world when wives are some of the few people who can give you good directions.  This rampant "bachelorism" is making it really, really hard to find people!  It also makes the feasts into veritable sausage-fests.
Then there is the racial "harmony" aspect.  Personally, I find this disconcerting on several levels - primarily, this was clearly a decision someone made because the original game certainly made an effort to be much more inclusive and representative of human populations.  Everyone in Viking Conquest is white!  Every sailor, wool merchant and mercenary.  This is simply ridiculous not only from a realistic viewpoint but from an historical and archaeological one as well.  Science, archaeology and the historical record itself all attest to the fact that human beings have met, mingled, traded, fought, bred and cried together since before we ever came down out of our trees.
Then there is the cloning program.  Whatever cloning technology the people of Skyrim used to make their children, these folks are using to make tavern hosts.  Speaking of women...I always thought Irish women were particualrly beautiful, I never had a clue that there were only about two of them and they both look like they could lift an ox with each hand...while planting a field of wheat and giving birth!  Lady Mor...she is strong like traktor.  Maybe this is why none of the other lords are interested in marriage?  We can't all marry Lady Hild, after all.
I think I'm convincing myself that this is more like a recommendation with conditions, instead?
Many of the changes appear to be made by people I have had discussions with in here before.  Those "my Nord Huskarls can beat your (insert alternate for bestest army ever here)" type of discussions.  The ones where after exchanging numerous flaming posts, they finally admit that "...IF there were no horses...and no bows...and everyone had to walk everywhere and hit things...THEN my Nords would win".  So they made a world just like that.  Everything that made life a living hell for the poor Nords in Mount & Blade has been removed from the game...or at least its simply much more difficult to have those things.  Viking Conquest is the poor Nords swan-song.  Even so, it's still pretty awesome and I do appreciate learning a different set of skills in order to enjoy this game.  I've been determined to develop my archery just to spite the developers though and by about level thirty, I'm only just becoming sufficiently deadly with it.  Of course, it's still the same Strong Long Bow I've had since about level four because there simply aren't any other options in loot, shops or for upgrades.
There is also some evidence of genuine historical love.  Place names are particularly interesting for example.  How much of it is true or accurate, I would never hazard a guess about but it is fun to try and decipher some of it.  Somebody clearly put some thought into it.  I'm also curious about this "Cantiga" song now too.
If you are new to the series and looking for a good, story-driven, RPG-type game then Viking Conquest most certainly is not for you!  Consider this more of a battle simulator that doesn't work all of the time.  Of the many reported hours put into this title, my guess is that almost all of it went into tweaking the online multiplayer aspects exclusively.  The single player parts were obviously left for last and abandoned just prior to release.  If your idea of a good story is "Ima gonna beat up everyone until there ain't no more people to beat up", then disregard everything I've written so far.
The BIG drawbacks include instability first and foremost.  Ignore anyone who tells you the game runs fine or that it "may have one or two bugs", etc.  So many people have already written about the exact same problems, the truth of the matter is plain enough for anyone to see for themselves.  My game crashing for various reasons has become totally commonplace such that I am in the habit of frequently saving my game because I know it will crash at any moment.  When you see code spliced into dialogue options, it's a rather clear indicator that the problems are not originating with the end-users.  PEBKAC certainly does not apply in all of these cases, sorry.
Another big one that cannot be overlooked is the rigidly confining mainquest storyline.  The player is hamfisted into ridiculous scenarios simply because the writers couldn't be bothered to do any play-testing whatsoever.  It can only make sense if you slavishly obey and follow it step by step without ever faltering.  Say for example, you think...geez, these guys seem tough, maybe I should go level up a bit before continuning?  DON'T do that.  I didn't find out that I would be given a free ship until AFTER I'd gone to England, kicked many arses and bought my own boat...and then went back to find out about the main quest...Arrrgh.  Later, it gets worse, a certain King expects you to swear an oath of fealty to him and unless you do so, the story simply stalls - I already had a King and I liked him, there is no way I was going to give up all of my towns and castles just to find out what the story says about my mom.
Besides, from what little I could gather about her fate, she seems to be doing rather well for herself.  Perhaps that is the biggest tragedy of all with this game?  The relationship between the player and their mother is central to the entire quest line and I actually couldn't care less about her.  That just sounds horrible, sorry mom.  It is true though.
Lastly, I have to bring up religion.  What a waste of everyone's time.  How wonderful it would be to have the option of playing as a blood-thirsty, Pagan warrior...perhaps one day we'll get that option?  This game seems to be about as open-minded about spiritual beliefs as a Baptist Minister might be.  The "Pagans" are murderous beasts spawned from Hell and are punished and hated for merely existing.  The Christians are all happy and loving and wonderful.  No priest or other Church funtionary is ever involved in anything untoward.  "The Church" is all squeaky-clean, just the way Grandma would want it to be.
I suppose I would recommend this, with reservations.

Recomendation: Yes, with reservations.
First, this is NOT anything like the gameplay of DX:HR.  DO NOT get this game thinking that it will be anything like DX:HR.  Most of the negative reviews I have read for this seem to not be able to understand that this is a direct port from tablet to PC.
Because this is a port, there are a few pieces that are missing that most PC gamers have gotten used to.  There is no manageable inventory.  Instead, you have a "Store" screen where you can purchase weapons, mods, ammo, and other items at any time.  Immersion breaking, yes, but it fits with the "merc style" storyline that the devs have gone with.  Having to find a "dropspot" for those items might have been more immersive, but would have upset some players who don't like "micromanagement"...
A few of the downfalls of The Fall:
This is easily described as a "Lite" version of DX:HR.
The controls are pre-determined and cannot be changed.
There are some audio and graphical bugs. (My crosshair disappeared in a New Game+)
The buttons are "touchy". (They work on the first click about 60% of the time)
Conversation choices are "double tap". (Select first, then confirm.  Suffers from above)
AI is predictable and almost oblivious.  (Some enemies seem to see you through cover, however.
"Heavy" NPCs don't drop heavy weapons (yet).
Hacking is decent, but there is no feedback on detection chances.
The Augmentations are much the same as HR, but the system is much less open.  It's mostly a simplified HR scheme, but there are some real differences, mostly in what augs you start out with.
The inventory is EXTREMELY simplified.  You buy individual weapons (or find them in the world).  You then "Equip" them into quickslots, and you can use them in the world.  From what I've seen, this means that you are carrying the entire arsenal in your pocket at all times, as long as you have the weapon available (bought or found).  Bundles are decent, but not really worthwhile once you actually get the weapon in the pack.  Everything you buy is immediately available in game, so there is no "shipping delay".  Buy ammo as you need it, rather than stocking up.
And now the highlights of The Fall:
A "Behind the Scenes" glimpse of the mercs you fought in DX:HR. (Barret Achievement ;D)
Nice foreshadowing of both DX:HR and DX from in game texts. (One Tyrant wants a Skul-gun)
The UI and controls make using health and energy boosts much easier than in DX:HR, especially while in the middle of the action. (Try doing multiple takedowns while cloaked.)
Enemies "evaporate", eliminating the need to hide evidence of your actions.
There is an interesting "Reset Story Progress" feature.  It resets you to the beginning of the game, except you keep anything unlocked in the store (supposedly).  Does delete the savegame, so turntable is reset, possibly achievements as well.  Use if you want to start from "Factory Zero".
There is a "New Game+" feature which unlocks at the end of the current content (Panama).  You keep all your Augs and Inventory, and the story starts over from the beginning.
This is a nice "easy access" DX title, especially if you are a DX lore lover.  The title boasts "The story will continue", so this could be a very interesting story if the devs keep on it.  It'd be really funny if this game is directly connected to DX:HR through Quinn. (Missing Link)
To summarize, buy this game if you are a DX fan and like the storylines.  The controls take a little getting used to, but overall it's a decent buy even at $10 USD.  A little polish by the dev team, as well as advancing the storyline, and this little gem will shine.

If there's one thing that both fans and critics of the sequel to 2012's violent and neon colored indie hit Hotline Miami can agree on, it's that Hotline Miami 2 is anything but more of the same. With tons more characters, stories, and world building, HM2 is definitely a much farther reaching and ambitious game. There's a non linear and cryptic story which jumps to the future, present, and past of the first games events in no set order. It goes on to show us such things as Jackets past and motivations. What other agents of 50 Blessings were doing at the time and why. How 50 Blessings functions and what it's real goals are. And how the world itself has reacted to one mans vigilante murder spree and how it now tries to understand and make sense of it. You'll most likely have no idea as to what the story means or how the events of each protagonists story relates to one another after your first playthrough. It might take multiple playthroughs, and it might even take looking up forums or other websites to finally get the full picture. Once you do however, you'll gain a whole new understanding of not only HM2, but it's predecessor as well.
Now that I've talked at length about the story, let's talk about the gameplay. Like the story, the gameplay of HM2 is also quite different. Levels are now large and sprawling labyrinths filled with enemies that are well out of your field of view. Patience, stretching out your view with shift as far as possible, and baiting enemies you can't safely reach or attack are now the name of the game. Each character you will play as has their own styles of play as well. Some have different weapons, some have masks, some have multiple people, and some simply start with nothing. Because you never know who you'll be playing as next, becoming competent with each character is also important. None of these elements are outright bad or broken. Again, it's subjective and whether or not you enjoy it will come down to your own preferences.
In conclusion, Hotline Miami 2 is a game that does almost everything differently then it's predecessor, and your enjoyment of it will come down to how much you either hate, love, or just accept these changes. But hey, at least the series went out with a bang, am I right?
