This is one of those times I wish I could give a NEUTRAL rating to a game. I DO recommend the game for families with children, and to anyone who loved the "Monster Loves You" game with its graphical and writing style. It's very cute and some would surely find it entertaining and worthwhile. However, it has a lot of issues, and after a handful of playthroughs, I don't feel like I can recommend it to the average player.
(See my video review and showcase of the game here:
)
PROS
+Cute graphical style
+Funny, family-friendly writing
+Create a cute story alone or with a friend/family member
+A decent amount of story-based content to explore
+Local multiplayer with a friend or against the computer
CONS
-LOTS of grammatical errors and typos. I mean... lots. For a game that is so heavily dependent on text, this is a real detriment.
-"Single-player" is just multiplayer with a computer opponent choosing options completely at random (so results are entirely based on RNG), and there is no online multiplayer.
-No randomization of event results. Each action gives the same event every time, which means that two players both familiar with the game will likely end up with a stalemate every time.
-Lack of transparency with some of the game info (reputation is displayed in percentage but awarded in points, no indication of how many turns you have left the first time you play, etc.)
My main problems are the predictability and the grammatical errors. The game might be fun for a handful of playthroughs, as you are still learning the results of each event, but there comes a point where you know the "correct" answer to every encounter and there's not much replayability left. And as I mentioned, the writing errors really break the immersion of the game, since it's almost entirely text-based. If no one on the team is a grammar expert, they really ought to have hired a proofreader for the text. I understand that it's a small team making this game, but if they can't produce accurate English text, they might be better off focusing on a different type of gameplay.
Overall, I do not hate the game, and it's not bad at all, just lacking. A bit of randomization for the event outcomes (a percent chance for a different outcome of each event would make a huge difference) and a professional proofreader would go a long way towards changing my review to a positive one. And as I said above, it is definitely fun as-is for kids and families.

The Last Federation is a 2D (4-1)X space strategy game that combines politics and battles. It is (4-1)X because exploration does not exist. Also, player does not control a race but manipulates other races by using politics and by helping battles.
In this game, player is the last survivor of a murdered race (Hydrals) that was the dictators of the solar system. But one of them betrayed the race. His (Its?) goal was to make the space technology available to other races and then creating a federation to unify the solar system. After Hydrals' homeworld got destroyed, the last hydral (i.e. the player) crashed into one of the rivals' planet. When that rival race built their first capital ship, he managed to steal it and escaped. That's all the story the game has. It is not deep but enough to make things clear, at least to a point.
The game does not have a separate tutorial. Instead, when player starts his/her first game, most of the game elements are locked and these elements are unlocked and explained as the game progress. Its execution is very good. Although there are lots of things to learn, player is never overwhelmed by them. Most of the information and choices have very informative tooltips. They are especially useful when some option is not eligible. This way, only thing the player needs to do is reading the tooltip which explains the reason. That said, some of the advanced information, such as which conditions are required to capture a planet, are never explained.
Every race has a different political structure and has a different opinion of life. Some values military strength and are more aggressive, another is all about peace and quiet. This makes the player approach them in different ways to gain influence and convince them to join the federation. It is also possible to agitate a race against another, resulting in starting a war. Of course, these actions do not happen directly. There are lots of friendly and hostile actions player can take. When player visits a planet, possible "missions" are listed under their own menu. These missions are the main tools to manipulate races. By using these "tools", player achieves his/her goal for a certain race. I won’t go into details because this is not a guide.
Combat is different than classic turn-based combat. Units don't move/attack like in a chess game. It is actually more like Dragon Age's pause-order-continue style but pausing happens in periodic intervals called "turns". In each turn player issues a move order, then an attack order, and fight continues until next turn. There are also abilities that consumes one full turn. Player can select 6 abilities to use in battle and if an ability's ammo is depleted it is replaced with another ability of the same type during battle (Abilities have three types, i.e. "offensive ability", "operations" and special ability”). Starting abilities are random, but how many abilities of a certain ability type a player can use, depends on which race's first ship was stolen by the player at the beginning of the game.
There are some points that make the game less “believable”. For example you can make a planet’s environment go bad, but race itself does not take any counter-actions to fix it. It will stay as it is, even if it cost billions of inhabitants.
The main soundtrack is similar to 90s arcade games’ low bitrate sounds. Other soundtracks are smoother and easy on the ears. Sound effects are decent. Also when a very important event occurs, a female –I am guessing AI- makes funny comments.
Every planet advances depending on the status of planet and race. Strategic elements and properties of the races affect outcome.
Game has some humor in comments, descriptions etc. It is always a good thing.
This is both good and bad. Bad side is below. Good side is that it makes battles more challenging.
Every time a new game starts, planets and their inhabitants change. Due to compatibility factor between a race and planet type, a different race becomes more effective. This effectively changes how that game progress.
Finding which information is important and which is just for "decoration", takes too much time.
This means, UI size is static and the higher the resolution is, the smaller the UI becomes. Therefore, when the resolution is set to full HD, UI elements become too small and very crammed.
Bad side of this is what the name suggests. When every small dot-sized ship fires another dot, screen gets covered with dots.
Game has a different approach to space strategy games and the formula worked well, enough to keep me in the game until I unified the solar system without taking a break. So I recommend it.

Vermintide is a fabulously fun and addictive four-player-co-op melee-oriented chop-'em-up. It's easily the the best coop game I've played in a long time. It's got the best melee combat system I've ever seen that is both vicious and visceral, and makes you feel like you're swinging an actual weapon instead of a piece of code. And with its strong sense of cooperative comraderie and gritty dread, this game is THE choice for gamers looking for something to play with their buddies over a weekend.
So basically, you start with five heroes with only white-level weapons. Every time you complete a mission, you'll get a new weapon. Playing on higher difficulties allows for the possibility of higher level weapons, but is obviously harder to finish. Still, this game has a satisfying progression system that makes for good replayability. All five heroes feel fairly distinct, with each having exclusive weapons.
Overall, this is one of those co-op game I've played that makes my top-games list, the others being Killing Floor 2, Far Cry 4, PAYDAY 2, and a few others.

Song of the Deep is a wimsical, gorgeous fairytale journey into the darkness under the sea. While the controls take some getting used to, they do a great job of bringing the alien feeling of being underwater home.
If you played Aquaria and loved it as much as I did, grab this. Aquaria's story is more mature and darker - which I liked -, but Song of the Deep is very clear in its inspiration. It is a light-hearted, modern-day Aquaria.

Song of the Deep is a beautiful game no doubt. The atmosphere is established so masterfully by the story, the soundtrack and the narrator. But I can't help but feel so frustrated by the combat that it completely breaks this atmosphere for me.
So what's wrong with the combat?
Well, it begins quite solid, you get some sea creatures to fight and its all fun and stuff. Until you realize that over the course of the game you will fight the same kind of enemies over and over again. There are some exceptions to this and the different enemy types will be stronger at the end of the game. However the problem is that the game just drowns you in waves of waves of enemies that never really challenge you enough that you would enjoy the combat, but are annoying enough that you have to deal with them (not to speak of the number of times where you have to defeat a set amount of enemies to open a door).
The puzzles and movement are the more fun part of the game and I really enjoy them, but I feel like every moment of "Hey that was a interesting puzzle" is followed by "Yeah, kill these 20 jellyfish that you fight since the first hour of the game for a minute or so until you can progress".
Also, the bosses are really lame, with the exception of
. They just serve as a glorified combat room where you fight waves of enemies until you pull a thing.
So you still might enjoy the game regardless, especially if you are into Metroidvanias, but this one just didn't click with me...

Its extremely beautiful art, atmospheric soundtrack, tight controls and sweet, interesting story make
a really great Metroidvania.
Its world is full of secrets to discover (conveniently displayed in your map, but some of them *really* hard to obtain), abilities to unlock and puzzles to solve (none of them too hard, if some can be slightly frustrating), and it's a real pleasure to explore all of the game areas, each with their own distinctive art style, enemies and soundtrack.
Pretty much its only drawback for me is that the boss fights are a little lackluster, but the rest of the game more than makes up for it.
All in all, a highly recommended game, not just for Metroidvania lovers, but for anyone who appreciates a beautiful, entertaining game.

I had no expectations of Song of the Deep, coming in to it from a bundle package and simply installing it and trying it out. My first impression was: oh, another 2d game about a kid's weird relationship with their parents. Yawn.

But I decided to give it a fair whirl to see what the gameplay was like, and wow, this game's initial package is GREAT. Hook style gameplay, using improvised weapons to combat sea creatures, light and dark effects that make sense, enemies that actually leave an impression, on top of solid level design and great voice acting.

Little things to watch for at the beginning: your life bar is the green bar, and it drains from the bottom to the mid left. That threw me at first, conditioned as I am on red bars that go from top to bottom.

Stationary enemies HURT A LOT. Think of Sea Pens as SPIKES in mario. It's not 1-hit die, but it will deal about 80% of your life bar with just a nudge so if you've taken any electrical hits earlier you will be RIP.
Lovely relaxing game, not too difficult, but I thought it was fun to explore the locations. Beautifully drawn. Controls were fine on a PC, I had no problems with them.
Solid Metroidvania with cool visuals and interesting mechanics. It's like Aquaria, but better :). All in all, if you find it discounted or if you have 10hours to spare - give it a try.

The most generic RPG-RTS you will ever play, also one of the best.
It's an RPG/RTS that lets you carry hero stats over from game-to-game, it also has an expansive open RPG style single player campaign that's a lot of fun, it also has a hardcore mode for heroes that includes perma-death.
Units also gain EXP and levels, and what's really cool is your heroes get to carry over some units at the end of each game if you'd like, so on top of game-to-game hero stats you also get to try and hold on to a group of elite units that you try to foster into high level killing machines, as long as they don't die.
I grew up playing this game, and graphically, mechanically, it's nothing special, but the sheer BULK of units, races, heroes, and fun is enough to make this game worth every penny you will spend on it.
I'm getting some thumbs down so maybe I'm not being clear enough. This is a very good RTS-RPG on all levels with a huge amount of content, but it is simply very generic in its theme, that's all.
It's not even generic in a bad way, it just has all the classic units and races you'd expect or want.
The weakest part of the game overall is probably the graphics which were not that great when it came out in the first place, some units also feel a bit out of place graphically when you take the art themes into account, sort of like when units are added with a mod and they don't look like the same person made them.
Oh, and it would be best if you didn't buy this for the MP, I'm not sure what sort of hoops you're going to need to jump through to get it working.

An absolutely incredible RTS with heavy RPG elements, Warlords Battlecry III is still one of my favorite games to this day.  With almost a dozen and a half well-balanced races to choose from, the replayability value is absolutely insane and every race has several viable strategies that will work to use their strengths against their opponents' weaknesses.  Creating your leader, a hero, is also extremely rewarding from the nearly infinite number of builds that you could create.
The gameplay and story are a worthy pairing for the mechanics even if it does sound somewhat familiar to that of a standard adventure RPG cliche.  A great evil is rising and threatens to overtake the world.  Your chosen faction is determined to defeat it and, through your choices, you will make many allies and enemies of the other factions as you travel throughout the world accomplishing what you must to do so.  The world map is interesting with lore behind every location and tons and tons of content to explore as the game is very non-linear.  Combat is also a fun experience where each faction's strengths and weaknesses can be used to your advantage.  Each faction has its own unique units and buildings as well as its own level of priority for the four resources of the game.  For example, the Dwarves faction uses a ton of metal, the Daemons are heavily based on stone and crystal, and the Empire prioritizes gold, though, each of these factions will find itself needed at least a little of these key resources to truly build a respectable army.
Your faction, whether you choose a fantasy classic like the Knights or Dark Elves, or a more unique one like the disease-carrying Plague Lords, or the lizardman-like Ssrathi, is an absolute blast to play.  Each has a list of armies and buildings that are almost entirely different from the other races as well as a separate tech tree.  Your hero, however, is the ultimate icing on the cake in my opinion.  With sixteen races and twenty-eight classes to choose from you could never tire of trying out different combinations to create vastly different heroes.  Each race provides six skills for you hero and each class does the same.  Each level that you achieve in the game provides you with a point to improve these skills and further improve and specialize your build.
I would recommend this game to all RTS fans as well as those who love fantasy RPGs.  This is a great game that to this day I don't tire of.  I purchased it instantly as soon as I saw it on Steam and wanted to get the word out that it is an absolute gem!

The game itself is fun to play, leveling is on the grindy side.
If you are playing this game to sit in the bushes and snipe hapless players as they run across open fields to capture points, you will be grinding a long time. I estimate I have about 300+ hours  into the game and still can't get recon(sniper class) hours played in steam is inaccurate due to the game idling in the background a lot.
This game needs a lot of work still, for most players using anything other than infantry will slowly kill your credit balance until you have to pay real money. Destoying tanks with anything other that another tank will lose you credits, long games lose credit, up agianst superior players losing credits. Mods on you gun = losing credits. You can counter this somewhat by buying a veteran membership, which costs about $10 monthly or $20 for 3 months, with this you get xp boost and a second badge slot (this is marginally pay to win). If F2P player can't enjoy the game you will be playing with a very small community.
Some of the higher tier weapons and tanks are over powered, and as an infantry you have very little you can do against tanks. Right now the cost of using a bazooka, anti tank greanades etc. is more than you get for actually destroying the armor. So the tanks sit on the hills shelling the infantry, The ariplane bomb and strafe the infantry, and the snipers snipe the infantry. If you manage to run that gauntlet you will likely die from the other sides infantry.
If the devs don't listen to the player this game will die, and anymoney you put into unlocking stuff early will die with it. They need to turn down the grind about 50% and up the amount you get for using weapons for thier intended purpose. Throw in some vanity items and reasonably priced unlocks and the game will make money.
I would encourage you to try the game still and go in with the mindset that it is still early developement and you are playing to have fun not grind. be careful with spending though this game may not make it.

Contrary to what certain reviewers say, the weapons don't feel real and heavy at all and because you mostly use melee weapons, the typical aiming component of FPS games only plays a minor role in this game. It feels like you're just clicking the enemies dead with your mouse without aiming while backing up a couple of times. It's terribly boring. (Platformer-adventure)
Options include Subtitles, Resolution, Brightness and Language, plus separate sliders for Music, Sound Effects and Speech.  You can play with Gamepad or Keyboard & Mouse, but they are NOT remappable. There are also three Difficulties to choose from: Beginner, Intermediate and Advanced.
Despite the fact that we are underwater, our sub (and later Merryn, herself) is highly maneuverable, though I might have felt differently if I had been playing with keyboard and mouse.  I
recommend a controller with this title, as I have a feeling that it would have become very frustrating for me if I hadn't been using one.
is a story-driven underwater "platformer" adventure, with heavy emphasis on puzzles.  There are enemies down there in the deep, but if you prefer exploration, you can usually avoid them.  There will be times when you can't advance unless you fight, and you're going to want to stop down and take out some of these enemies, if only for the coins that you'll gain from defeating them... but I'll come back to that later.
The story is what drives the game, and it's beautifully interwoven with the gameplay.  Pay attention to what it says the first time you die, as even that becomes part of the tale.  Between the narrator and the environment, I felt like I was immersed in a fable... and it's no wonder, as it turns out that the game is based on Irish/Celtic lore!
The puzzles are many, and were sometimes a source of frustration.  There were times when I simply could NOT figure out what to do and had to resort to Youtube.  Sometimes I had simply missed seeing something interactable on the scene, and sometimes it was more like, "OH! So that's how you get x-treasure from x-area/creature/whatever in the environment.
Be sure to visit the save spots (aka
) often, as you will lose all progress if you die.  That amazing treasure you just got will *poof* disappear if you die before you save.  The only exception is the item-upgrades that you find - the game will save as soon as you pick those up.  These items are things that increase your energy and health, so you'll definitely want to seek them out!
There are a lot of things you will not be able to get until you've progressed in the game and gotten some upgrades, meaning that you will have to revisit areas multiple times.  We do have fast-travel portals (aka
), but they are spaced out quite a bit.  Still, they do save quite a bit on travel time!
The
is our friendly traveling shopkeeper, and will give you items to help upgrade your sub... for a price, of course.  All of those coins and treasures you've been gathering can be spent here.
All treasures, save points, item-upgrades, shops and warp points are marked on your handy-dandy
... provided that you've discovered the area in which they reside.  Search carefully, as there are hidden passages scattered throughout The Deep.  There is an upgrade that will help you to find them, but you won't obtain it until late in the game.  It is possible to finish the game without fully-exploring, and even to miss some parts of the story (which I discovered after I actually finished the game.)
I had mentioned that our character, Merryn, will eventually be able to
, but in theory that could cause problems, right?  Some areas only Merryn can fit in, sometimes you'll need to separate for a puzzle, maybe you've just obtained something that you really don't want to lose if you die, or maybe she's trapped in the environment! :oh:  The good news is that the devs thought of all of those things, and you can therefore reunite with the sub by holding down a button for a few seconds.  Voilà~!  Issue no more!

After you finish the game, you can still "Continue" from the main menu if you would like to go back and finish up achievements and/or collect all of the treasures and items - it will take you back to the save point immediately before the final battle.
If you're hunting down 100% completion (NOT an achievement, but the way), I highly recommend checking out this
, which explains the puzzle mechanics involved for many of those seemingly-impossible-to-get treasures.  Keep an eye on the loading screens, as well, as they will give you some helpful tips.
The graphics are beautiful, the music and narration very fitting, and the gameplay is quite well done.  Some of the puzzles were, as mentioned, frustrating, but not so much that I would steer anyone away from the game.
Overall, I'd say that this is a solid adventure that deserves more attention.  Definitely recommended!

Think Civilization (or Master of Orion, if you're familiar with that) except instead of playing a civilization, you play an independent demi-god that gets to freely meddle in and shape everyone's affairs. And while the writing is very funny and the soundtrack is lovely, some design decisions turn the game part of this into a bit of a farce.
You have way too much power over the entire simulated world. Pretty much every variable is directly and easily changed by a metaphorical snap of your fingers and a selection on a menu. You can make anyone like or dislike anyone else. You can quickly ravage anyone's homeworld by messing with their 4 economic indicators and there's nothing they can do about that. Alternatively, you can quickly turn them into an obscene super power, and they cannot do that on their own. Owing to the fact you're completely and instantly healed at the end of every battle, which you can escape from anytime you like, you can destroy virtually infinite numbers of ships, if you but have the patience. You can be delayed, but never stopped. Nothing in the game will ever challenge you; nothing *can* challenge you when you are given this much control over everything. Higher difficulty settings only cause things to take longer; they don't make you any less likely to succeed. The irony here is that beneath the dozens of daunting menus and hardcore aesthetic, what you have is an ultra casual game. And that's what ultimately makes The Last Federation pointless to play.

Note that the early versions of the game had some balance issues and the turn-based combat wasn't as complicated and interesting as it has evolved into with v2, so the mixed reviews from early on are fair, but recent reviews are much more positive.
Anyway, absolutely get this together with the Betrayed Hope DLC, which complements the original version of the game perfectly by letting you switch from being nice (trying to persuade/coerce/threaten the races into a unified federation) to being pure evil (aka Dalek-style exterminate everyone left alive).
Betrayed Hope also seems to double the number of background songs playing for each of the planets, and the music is outstanding.  Beyond that, the gameplay and AI diplomacy on the system map is as finely crafted as anything else I can think of.
Turn-based combat is much more fluid in practice than it sounds like, and it can often be a spectacular visual riot of shots blasting in assorted patterns, and being able to wisely choose a path and speed of each segment of movement makes a big difference in how much damage you take.

About halfway through the game, you will most likely already know whether you've won or not.  This means that the late game can result in a lot of tedium where it feels as though you are simply mopping up.  However, getting to that point is one hell of a lot of fun, and there are enough surprises along the way to keep even the late game interesting.
Arcen do claim that you should use the fast forward often and as much as possible, but for me I've found that this is usually suicidal.  The problem with the interface is that it tends to be moderate-to-long periods of tedium interspersed with sudden and astounding events that suddenly change the game world to such an extent that it isn't possible to avoid; more work should have gone into a system that allows interruptions of "dispatches" when various events occur.  Pair that with the fact that some things you do will have absolutely no consequence (e.g., after I wiped out a five-armada Burlust invasion of the Evuck homeworld, somehow the Burlusts still instantly conquered the planet) and the game can be an exercise in frustration.
But what an exercise!  If you look past its small faults, you'll find a lot to love.

In one word: obsolete.
As you can tell from my hours played, I used to play this game. A lot. And this is only the hours logged on this character on steam, I had probably double this overall. However, I haven't touched this game in over a year. It runs on an obsolete version of java and the creators show no real intentions on updating it anytime soon. When I first started, it was a very vibrant game, full of excitement and fun. However, like so many others have commented, it's not what it used to be. The fighting system has been revamped over and over, so much so that it's just not fun to learn a new system every three months. It's not fun to deal with terrible support and a system that barely scrapes by.
It's a shame, because this game used to be amazing. The music for this game is incredible, to this day I still go back and look up my favorite songs and listen to them on youtube. Like everyone else has said, the creators have pushed themselves into a corner by alienating the fanbase by removing exciting features, putting crap into the game, and punishing players for the actions of the few.
I wish I could recommend this game, I really do. There was a time when I could; that time is gone. This game is on the downhill slope, which is sad considering where it has fallen from.
That being said, if you want to give it a try, go for it. It's free and you can always use this as a time sink. But this game had its glory days, and those days are passed.

text:
More like Deus Ex: The Fail!!! About the only thing forgivable about this game is that it is a port of a mobile game. So, its understandable that the quality is unlikely to match the heights that the game's big brother, Deus Ex: Human Revolution did.
The voice-acting was surprisingly horrendous, you'd think like DX:HR, they'd put some effort there but they didn't. The controls were alright but not exactly smooth. The audio cuts out during cutscenes and takedowns although it doesn't happen all the time. And certain aspects of gameplay like moving heavy boxes were simplified and there's no jumping even though I have to admit that was expected because again, this is a port from a mobile game.
The story wasn't bad but it still wasn't enough to salvage the game. There's plenty of potential but it falls flat in presentation, not helped by the surprisingly poor dialogue and bad VA. The characters weren't as interesting as Adam Jensen and company in the main Human Revolution game and despite some familliar characters appearing (the Tyrants), their appearance was quite lacking. About the only thing I liked about the game was hearing Bob Page's (main villain in the original Deus Ex) evil voice once again.
Overall, this game is to Human Revolution what Invisible War was to the original Deus Ex. A massive let-down. This isn't my worst purchase as I got a copy of the original Deus Ex GOTY version (the greatest game of all time) with my preorder. If you're in anyway interested to play this game, wait for a Steam sale. Its already cheap at $10, but it would probably feel more worth it if you get it for cheaper.

No customizable binds is an unholy sin right out of the gate. The voiceovers are lackluster and most of the accents are noticeably forced and fake. The writing is mediocre at best, the script is in dire need of an editor to add some narrative and not just exposition for its own sake.
The gameplay is par for par same mechanics as Human Revolution but the in-inventory purchasing reeks of laziness, not to mention it makes no practical sense. As usual the aesthetics are gorgeous if somewhat buggy here and there. Facial expressions are mostly emotionless and cutscenes models have that subtle sickening jerk to them like their limbs are taut rubberbands.
Despite all this, it wouldn't be half bad but for the non customizable keybinds. What in the hell was the rush? All this time was taken to introduce these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t unskippable tutorial popup menus in some vapid attempt to not lose someone who may not be familiar with the series' mechanics and then you don't give them free range of keybinds in an ostensible action RPG?
This game reeks of the typical Square Enix approach to every game it regurgitates. Gorgeous visuals that play like♥♥♥♥♥with writing that is reminiscient of tween anime crossover fanfiction. Which is a shame given the setting.

My only complaint about this, is that it's not yet finished.  And I don't mean that the game has bugs that cripple it, that's to be expected with Early Access.  It's why I generally avoid them like the plague.
But, with that said...  I watched some videos, read some reviews and figured I'd give it a shot.  It's only a fiver atm after all right?
But no, the game is literally, not finished.  I got a part way through the fourth part (don't want to say anymore as I don't want to spoil it) and it just stopped and said 'Thanks for playing, hope you enjoy more later'.  I at least come to expect the main part of the story to be in the game when you're paying money for it!  So, to me, this is a major point of concern.  If the dev's now decide to say sod it, I'm never going to know the ending.  That, my friends, would be unforgivable.
But, with that said, I am going to risk giving this a thumbs up.  Why?  Because it's cheap.  I played near 3.5 hours investigating things and at times, my heart was pounding and I 'wanted' to know where the story was going.  I have my suspicions, as we all probably do, but I want to see it there, done and dusted right in front of me.  So, for this reason I would say it's worth a £5 one off payment.  Besides, it's only 90 minutes off my normal £1/hour preferred rate, so can't really complain there either.
Just keep in mind, there are some bugs (had a draw in the bedroom move into the chest-of-drawers itself when I moved) and the game isn't yet complete.  But if you're a fan of psychological horror that's not just 'run and hide until it goes away', definitely take a look.

Full playthrough of game playing as the wolf in solo mode:
Really fun boardgame-esque game. Have only played in solo mode so far yet still entertaining. Sadly there isn't any online multiplayer, but it's a point-and-click kind of game so one player can just click the opponent's choices for them.

This is a cute game centered around the Big Bad Wolf who decided to give up demoltion work to run his own fancy restaurant, but he has only a week to get the place running smoothly, and that is more than enough time for the Three Pigs to put a big dent in his business plans.
That's pretty much the gist of this game. It's basically a Choose Your Own Adventure where up to two players (as the wolf and/or the pigs) take turns each week to either help your business (as the wolf) or to ruin it (as the pigs). Each area (lake, neighbourhood, etc) helps, or hinders, each side with various choices that you ultimately have to choose from. After seven days, the game ends in a form of a short story that shows the end results of your actions. Whether The Wolf's Bite succeeds or fails depends on you did (or not do).
The adorable artwork and story will make you want to choose every single choice when they come up, just to see what happens next. I will even pick what I know are bad choices, just to see the (often) hilarious result. According to the store blurb, there's over 350-ish choices/paths/whatever, so that's a lot of replayability right there. With that many results though, you will encounter the same ones quite often long before you exhaust them all. The outcomes of the choices (what you pick) never change though. There's also 'over 20' different endings too so it's fun to try to see them all.
I like how the game is obviously in favour of the wolf and he is seen in quite a heroic (most of the time anyway) light compared to the pigs, who vandalize, hangs out with tough gangs, and basically wreck havoc in the city just to frame, or sabotage the wolf from achieving his dream. The media often portrays wolves badly, so it's nice to see a good wolf for once because it's not very common.
I would recommend this game to anyone who likes fairy tales, animals, cute/funny stories, and 'quickie' games. Each round only lasts roughly 15 mins. The Wolf's Bite is a casual adventure game involving the old fable of the Big Bad Wolf and the Three Little Pigs. In this twist on the tale, the Wolf has left behind his bad-boy life and is looking to start a restaurant chain. The Three Little Pigs are naughty little tricksters and want to do everything in their power to sabotage his efforts and get revenge!
It can be played in local multiplayer (but not online unfortunately - possibly it's biggest downfall) and is turned based. If you don't have a friend to play with, you face the AI. You choose whether to play the Wolf or the Pigs and then have a game board which is a series of locations such as The Restaurant, The Grocery Store, The Neighbourhood or The Lake. At each location you have two options and picking an option will result in a static event happening and then a random event will occur. For example if I choose to work in the restaurant as the wolf, I will improve the quality of my food. Then, a fairy-tale character will visit and I'll have three options as to what to serve them. Wrong choice? Big mistake!
The AI (or player two) will then take their turn, which is fast and you can watch take place so both players get to experience all the dialogue / story. After 7 days (turns) the game ends and you'll get a result out of 20 endings based on your wealth, reputation and quality rating. There's no "winning" the game exactly, but the story results have some positive and some negative. At one point I thought I'd have a very positive rating because I had a lot of a certain stat but it turned out to be quite a bad ending for me! I won't go into any details because spoilers, but it's definitely hard to predict what's coming.
There are 375 "paths" to the game, but if you choose the same locations you will eventually see the same scenarios pop up. Once you know the choices, it's very easy to pick the "right" one but of course, that's a little boring. The fun is in doing new things and seeing where it leads - often with comical or disastrous results. Since the aim of the game isn't simply to get the highest stat possible but to experience the stories and have fun with the scenarios, this does have a lot of replayability and it's very hard to predict what ending you're going to get.
It's a cute game with lovely hand drawn illustrations and very family friendly. This is definitely playable by all age ranges - anyone who can read. This would be a great family game for parents to play with their kids, or for kids to play together but it is a very casual game and after 10 solo games (each solo game takes about 15 minutes for me with a fast reading speed) I would only return if I had someone else to play with.
My son is a ways off being able to read; but this is definitely a game I'm tagging as family suitable and I'll be returning to it once he can enjoy it too. Even a very young child could be engaged in this as an "interactive story book" if you read out the choices to them and in that regards, this could be a really fun and entertaining but also educational tool!

This game is really different from what I'm used to play and that is really refreshing. For me it is like an adventure game but with a much more dynamic format to it.
You can even say it is "simpler" than your common adventure game, but it has this kind of way where it makes you feel like you are playing a tabletop game which is really cool. It gets you to the story and action really fast with really a fun story and approach to the Three Little Pigs classic.
I would LOVE to see this translated to other languages as the english version uses unusual terms, probably recurrent in classical kids literature, but that can make it hard for a non-native speaker (and reader) to grasp it all. As I'm playing with my son, it can be hard to translate some of the phrases on the spot. I guess that is more a problem with me than with the game itself so no harm done to the experience overall.
In all, this is a really fun adventure game with a more dynamic feel to it, very good writing and is, for sure, a cool game to play with someone on the couch. Recommended!

Full play of the game:
Ideal audience: Parents with Kids or Casual players
The Wolf's Bite is a silly boardgame-like game where the Big Bad Wolf is trying to make a successful Restaurant over 7 days, while the Three Little Pigs try to sabotage him.
It can be played 1v1 or 1vAI.
Each player gets 7 turns, the Wolf player can go to a variety of locations to try to increase his reputation, wealth, and quality of restaurant; while the Pigs have to worry about their own Reputation and Wealth while trying to decrease the Wolf's stats. A special event happens for each player after they take a turn and they have to make a choice, these events can be very helpful or disasterous for the players. Every event can be quite humorous.
The game is very casual though; there is no tutorial so you'll suffer a lot of trial and error trying to figure out the best course of action. So I suggest this game is for people who want a fun little bit of casual fun or parents playing with their kids.

This game lacks online multiplayer. That's its biggest downfall to be honest. A Full run of the game and review here aswell.
Otherwise. It's funny, quirky and a nice spin to the Big Bad Wolf and Three little piggies. 1vs1. Over a 7day period, one action per day per player. It's a bit one sided though. The wolf player only does things to improve himself and the pigs both improve themself and discredit the wolf. Could have been nice with some things to reduce the pigs influence etc.
The AI isn't that good, since it seem to do everything randomly and not in response to your highest points. So it's easier to face the pigs since sometime they disregard everything and just go drunk.
The points are in either
Quality, Reputation or Wealth. The pigs does not have Quality since it's only grades the food level.
You win by having higher scores than you opponent, but it's a bit of a grey area about which matters most since I have had ties and still come up on top in my 5 games. There is said to be 20 different endings and I've only got the same ending twice.
Get it on a discount as of this release, or if this scratches your niche. I can see this get dull after a few hours for some, (since a game is around 20-30min) since the AI isn't that good. So it's all about local multiplayer. If it had online. I could probably play this ALOT more.
Still a good game all things considered.

I'm not going to give this game a score.
If your are expecting to be scared till you pee well unless you are a Baby this game will not scare you. Resident Evil Within, that should have been the title of this game, it is too much like Resident Evil. It has good ideas and the game tries not to be Resident Evil but it just can't help itself. For starters nothing makes sense and I'm sure that was the intention but it doesn't work. At the beginning the game was interesting, somewhat scary and tense but once you start getting weapons and upgrades it losses its horror factor. I just can't avoid the filling that this is mostly an action game.
Playing through so many Resident Evil style levels just boggled my mind and straight♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. Some bosses (some of them are too fast) and enemy heavy areas are just straight out frustrating due to lack of ammo. I enjoyed the game play because it is pretty solid but the game tries to be something that it isn't and that is a horror game. I suppose blood and bodies everywhere make it horrific and scary, "Woooooh scary...... -_-" Some enemies are creepy but enemies wielding firearms, "COME ONE SHINJI YOU PROMISED HORROR!"
There are game play mechanics introduced early in the game that are useless (hiding) or you just completely forget they existed (stealth kill which sometimes doesn't function.) The game is basically Zombies, Zombies with Guns, Zombie with Cross Bows, Zombies with Dynamite, Zombies setting traps, Zombies that Drive, Zombies that use Machine Guns, Zombie Giants, Traps and more Traps, Zombie wielding a Chainsaw, did I mention Zombies?
Does this remind you of something? Everything seems so familiar and out of place that it is hard to see the game as its own. The vague plot doesn't help it either and the design doesn't fit into the theme of the world.   **MINI SPOILER ALERT**  I mean come on we are inside this guys head and all he can think about is stupid Zombies and Booby Traps? Some levels are just ridiculous where you find yourself avoiding nothing but traps and Saw equipped Roomba Vacuums.
To me this is pretty much your typical RE 4 and later RE action oriented "horror" games. On that note if you are a RE fan then this games is great for you. I am an RE fan but Shinji promised the revival of "Survival Horror" not another Action Horror Game. For crying out loud you defeat the final boss with a FREAKING BAZOOKA!. This game offers nothing new to the Survival Horror Genre this would had made a better RE6 for sure but that is it. Shinji should have just reinvented Resident Evil the way Keiji is doing with Mighty No. 9. He could have even called it Biohazard in the US and Evil Resident in Japan.
Overall it is a good game but just don't go into to it with high hopes of playing a horror game.
I recommend this to Shinji fans who are not expecting anything new from his previous formula. Unless you find lighting enemies on fire with wooden matches something innovating. For those who aren't Shinji fans if you're looking for a solid action game with pretty good game mechanics you'll have some fun with this game.
Hopefully Kojima will do something fantastic with Silent Hills.

The combat is actually quite enjoyable if you liked games like Resident Evil 4 and Dead space, but it often seems to happen in all the wrong places.
The game starts itself as a horror game at the first few chapters, but it gradually turns itself into an action shooter with bad controls. Yeah it's a mess. The Evil Within is not a bad game by any means, but it isn't a good one either. If you are curious about the game, get it on sale.

An underwater Metroidvania.  Reminds me a little bit of Insanely Twisited Shadow Planet, due to the similar omnidirectional movement.  But I'd say it comes out on top because of its well told and acted story.  A little celtic girl build a submarine to find her father who was lost at sea.  There's some pretty good narration.  It's lacking in the core combat gameplay though, which is essential to this type of game.  What's the point of getting upgrades if all the fights are incredibly easy?

Few games on steam are made with the idea of "I want to make a game for my daughter."  And, while Sing of the Deep is not unique in its gameplay, it's heart is definitely in the right place.  Song of the deep is a unique spin on the action/adventure "Metroidvania" style of gameplay by Insomniac Games, that thrusts the player into the control of Merryn, a young and crafty girl who creates her own submarine to find her missing father.  Released on July 12, 2016, Song of the Deep does not utilize standard Metroidvania tropes such as platforming, in favor of swimming and underwater mechanics familiar to Ecco the Dolphin  or "That One Dammed NES Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles Level." Much like the former game, Ecco the Doplhin, the game's focus is more towards exploration and puzzles and less on combat.  While the combat is secondary, it is serviceable as a competent with clever weapons and "shield" techniques granted to a certain weapon type.  Individuals looking for a longer game experience will find this game lacking in length as it is roughly 5-7 hours in total to beat without hunting down collectibles.
The music in Song of the Deep ranges from oceanic ambiance to epic fantasy with uplifting orchestral flairs during strenuous combat encounters.  The score lends itself very well to the colorfully bright adventure through vivacious and colorful kelp forests, ruined ancient "water folk" cities old rickety boat graveyards and deep, dark chasms.  The animation quality is simple, but suits the pop-up book ascetic quite well.  Most npcs and monsters you will encounter resemble papercraft puppets in some regard, with sharp angular features.  The sound quality is good, but far too often are present audio glitches where the sound gets ridiculously loud after gathering loot or killing a mob.
Song of the Deep is geared towards a younger audience, or someone who is looking to introduce their child to gaming at around 6-8.  The puzzle-centric mechanics are easy, and won't keep an adult stumped for more than a few minutes while you try to circumnavigate through clever but simple puzzles.  In the later game, Song of the Deep has a strange pitch towards arena combat, where you are locked in a room and need to destroy "x" number of sea mobs before a door will open, which does not suit its puzzle and exploratory ideology.
Despite this, I recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a quick delve into action adventure games, a newcomer to the genre, or a parent who is looking to play a game with their children.

Although I'm sure whoever spearheaded the project had a heart in the right place, so much is stolen from Aquaria you almost feel like it's infringement, to the extent that some enemy designs and movements are directly from aquaria.
Unfortunately, unlike that game, Song of the Deep has no soul.
It cauterizes the player upon entry, telling them in a hamfisted heavily-cut opening that their dad is somewhere down in the water, and somehow this young girl can build a submarine, and we're expected to buy into it and go 'ooh, mysterious and aaaah, quaint', when the feel is anything but.
From word 'go' this feels like what a AAA company does when it tries to emulate indie titles. Nothing in the game makes sense, there are tons of random collectibles (apparently to help 'gamify' the experience), shops, upgrades that don't interact with or serve the story, and no explanation of how the girl's dad knew all this stuff when he was a sailor, not a submariner, and is presumably dead anyway.

For all the triple-A gloss, it is unfortunately a worse game. Somehow a team of two people, ten years ago, with no budget, managed to out-game a title made by a AAA company in 2016.

Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is the co-op game I've been looking for for a very long time.  Everything that makes L4D2 great is there, plus a whole lot of things I always wished L4D2 would have.  Imagine Chivalry: Medieval Warfare plus L4D2 plus a pretty robust, rarity-based loot system, plus a good range of five classes that have reasonably unique playstyles and roles.  The graphics and level design is also just fantastic.
I'm honestly baffled as to why the playerbase is shrinking -- L4D2 has much less replayability than Vermintide (no loot, no level-ups, no different playstyles and character builds, fewer difficulty tiers).  New maps are coming out very soon, and there's already 14 of them, which is plenty for a game like this.  Yeah, there are some bugs (occasionally an enemy will clip through a wall or get stuck on something), but nothing that utterly breaks or ruins the game, and the only serious frustration is if the game's host disconnects right before the end of a map.
Seriously, buy this game.  Help us rekindle the playerbase -- this game is really good!

This game was a toss up. I read some of the reviews and wishlisted it for a long time. It looked really different and exciting so went it on sale in the summer sale, I picked it up. I only played it for 10 hours or so, but I just don't see myself trying it anymore.
Pluses:
+1 star for gameplay. It runs stable. doesn't seem to have any bugs. Never crashed, or froze.
+1 star for graphics. I like 8-bit style graphics, the planetary icons are well developed and informative.
+1 star for combat. The combat runs like Star Control's melee mode, only a bit more strategic. This was really entertaining at first, but then became a serious bore later on.
+1 star for concept. It really is interesting idea and gameplay was random/fresh each play through. Different events occur that you have to respond and adapt to.
+1 star for the comedy. A lot of the dialogue and events really get a laugh. They did a good job there.
Minuses
-1 star for gameplay. It was interesting at first, but in the long run, I was bored. I think I spent an hour on maximum speed trying to get the last race to join the federation. Just got tedious trying to achieve the goals.
-1 star for balance. even with the entire galaxy blockading/bombarding the murderous bug people from basically day 1, they still didn't die and would continue to send out fleets to attack the others' home planets.
-1 star for size. The galaxy is really small. So small in fact that its really quite boring. it might have been more fun if the races could colonize other star systems and attempt to conquer the galaxy or something. But instead, you just have 7 planets to work with.
-1 star for notifications. There can be a ton of notifications but they don't really detail anything. Andor science station attacked. Ok which one? Where? Can I repair it? Steal it?....
-1 star for story. The story was interesting but not really developed. Apparently your entire race of powerful, nearly omnipotent beings is destroyed by 7 races that don't even have warp capability...

Pros:

Cons:

I've only clocked 131 hours on Steam, but I played for years on the normal client, and I've been on/off alpha/beta testing this game since 2006. I'll go into detail as to why I think this game is good and why I think the devs killed it years ago and are just milking what's left.
Pro:
The game is amazing. Period. If you like Fire Emblem or Tactics Ogre, this is the game for you. The characters are a bit cartoonish and anime-esque, but that just adds to the fun. The character designs are relatively unique and you feel a serious sense of accomplishment when you finally get the awesome-looking gear you want. You can choose out of 17 classes and, believe me, each one feels so dramatically different than the next that you'll be begging for the ability to just play them all at once.
When you level up, you notice it. You'll constantly debate leveling up one stat or another to benefit you more. What's more, you have 15 elemental spells to choose from. You can be a single element, duo element, or tri elemental as you pick and choose your favorite spell tree(s). The game is less about grinding out levels to finally unlock a spell and more about slowly learning how to play the game, then unlocking all of your spells and choosing from there.
The combat is spectacular. Unlike most turn-based strategy games, you have to constantly consider your position to the enemy's, even once you're engaged in melee. The myriad of movement and area damage can make your whole team wipe in two turns if you're not careful. Because it's a MMO, as well, you can simply out-level the enemies and go back to wreck their faces. The choice is yours. This isn't a "plan to whittle them down with ranged fire then melee them" like most other turn-based games, either. If you want to get into a boss' face, get into their face. They might have a wreck-all spell that turns you to mush, but most tank classes have something they can do to prevent it for a turn or two.
The lore is spectacular. It leaves a lot to find and compile, but it's there (or was when I was last active). Each bit and piece you may find tells a small bit about the history of events going on. From there, imagination takes hold and you can create your perspective of the world.
It's an anime-styled game. The women are busty and the hips are extremely wide. The graphics are a little cartoony, but the subtle vulgarity and brutality make up for it. It is really one of those games that you can let your kids play while still enjoying it yourself.
Cons:
The devs... Don't get me started on Ankama. They are, by far, the worst company I have ever dealt with. Their first priority is to appease the French playerbase, period. They do not care what the English-speaking players have to say. Your opinion will be moot if you do not speak French. I've played in several of the game's alphas/betas, and they ignored the English speakers like myself through and through. Things that were just added to the game last year I had been talking about since 2008, which is just sad and annoying to watch.
The game was running off of promise of content to the level cap. The ideal level cap being 200, just like in the previous game, Dofus. The problem? The level cap has been hit. The content now will satisfy people to that level cap, and nothing more. The game is slowly churning out meaningless updates that give little/no substantial changes that were promised years ago. It's more or less stagnant, even though they are still adding bits of content.
There were more systems in place when the game was released. There were even more before that. Things were added and removed because the developers didn't want to un-bug them. Governors, for instance, were elected and managed all things in the nation from the tax rates to the laws, given options in the dozens on what is legal/illegal, as well as challenges in each area, which were small tasks you could compete against other players to get unique gear. The government positions, now, however, are almost aesthetic. They can make some things illegal to do, but it's almost insulting and redundent on how they can manage it.
The player base is constantly dying then picking up again once something new comes out. Honestly, the game would be very nice if more people would play it. But, sadly, it goes through ups and downs, with the downs being extremely, extremely down. Finding someone to do something with that's not end-game or very early on is difficult and hording friends so you can play with them is common-place.
This goes back to the devs again. They locked the two French servers to anyone not in France. It didn't used to be, but there were a lot of issues with arabian players spamming the chat. It's understandable, but the population on either of those servers is almost always higher than every other server combined.
There are bugs in the game. Some of them are game-breaking. Most of them are annoying at best. If you run a decent system and don't try to push the limits on what you can do in the game, you will run this game almost entirely bug-free. These bugs, however, have been present for years and will likely continue forevermore.
All in all, I can't recommend this game to anyone. It might be worth a try if you like Fire Emblem or Tactics Ogre, but the developers killed it years ago. I want to like this game, I really do, but I can't. It's a grind fest once you hit level 100, for anything from gear to experience. The redundency is constant and unforgiving after a certain point. The most fun I've had is playing this game at the lower levels with people, but after a certain point it just becomes tedious and annoying. They will try to milk money from you. I will tell you now don't do it. It's not worth it.
If this still appeals to you, then go ahead. Don't say I didn't warn you though.

I've been a huge fan of the Deus Ex universe ever since I played the original when it first came out. Unfortunately, this game does not live up to the legacy of its forebears.
Deus Ex: The Fall retains the stylized golden appearance of Deus Ex: Human Revolution. I quite liked HR's art syle, which set it apart from the common browns and blacks of both the older Deus Ex games and so many others in the first person space. So, The Fall gets points for at least staying true to the style of HR. However, since this is a port to PC from an iOS/Android game, the graphics are severely lacking, even when compared with games several years old, such as HR.
The mechanics of The Fall are significantly different from HR. Egregiously, your character cannot jump. The game has only a single "save slot" which is overwritten by every quicksave or even when changing areas. Controls are awkward at best, given that they cannot be remapped and the "quickslot" system is anything but quick. These limitations make sense for a mobile game. However, it's quite jaring when compared to other PC games, or even ports to PC from console (such has HR).
Furthermore, aiming is simply awkward. For example, aiming a weapon with a scope without firing seems to be impossible. A single button controls both. Press and hold to aim, release to fire. The non-scoped weapons are only slightly easier to use. Gone are the "iron sights" aiming of HR.
Other than by-design limitations of the game, it is also unfortunate that The Fall also riddled with bugs. The most glaring is that any system with more than stereo speakers is completely broken. Music consistently plays, but all other sounds drop out at random, taking captions along for the ride! There is a work-around: in Window's Sound settings, change your speakers back to simple stereo (from 5.1, 7.1, etc).
More minor bugs abound, such as achievements that are listed as completed in-game but not in Steam. One must activate an ability, consume an item, or change areas in order to trigger the acheivement. While this is a minor annoyance, it illustrates the lack of effort put into the port. Since the game knows the achievement unlocked, it's inexcusable for the Steam unlock to be lagging.
Not all is bad. The "spirit" of Deus Ex is present in that most missions can be completed in multiple ways. I suspect that shooting enthusiasts will be disappointed, but non-lethal stealth is quite possible. Oddly enough, bodies auto-disapear instead of sticking around to alert your enemies. This makes "stealth" almost trivial.

1) There are only about 3 servers that have more than 5 people on them at any given time, which is a big problem in and of itself, but especially when you are bored of playing the Island map (there is a server that only uses Island), it can be frustrating.

I have dealt with racism while playing other multiplayer games, but it usually just amounts to some 12 year old calling you a dirty n-word before he impales you. However, because there are no other servers and the Admin was away, I couldn't really do a thing about it.
IN CLOSING, if you don't want to put up with  bad community, stale maps, a lack of servers, or just general boredom, don't bother putting too much time into it.

I am a fan of horror games, and indie games. So you would think that a horror indie game like Layers of fear would be right up my alley, but sadly this game misses the mark at least for now. The play style is reminiscent of "Going Home"; set points you have to walk through as a story line evolves. The game style is less a "game" than an interactive movie, you have few choices in how to proceed and the game pulls you forward along the plot with little more than a few mouse clicks required on your part. Now this would not necessarily be a bad thing, but the plot of Layers of Fear is simply not moving. I found myself looking more forward to the jump scares than the vague and somewhat dull plot you clue into on various pieces of paper found in the mansion that is the setting of the game. There are a few storytelling elements that I found to be interesting; Rooms change you look around, that is to say you enter a room with only one door but when you turn back to see the door you entered it has transformed into a hallway. Kinda fun...... At least the first dozen times. Soon you find yourself lackadaisicaly spinning around every new room looking for the next door to open. An interesting visual device that quickly loses its power to affect. Also the sound and music of the game are well used, and  really add to the ambiance of the setting, but again the repetition lessens the effect.
I do have a few questions about parts of the game. A few times you seem to be attacked/eaten by who I assume is your dead wife, after which you appear in another room on the floor. Is the relocation aa penalty for being eaten? Is Zombie wife a monster or a story point? Can she be avoided? Fought? Does it matter? I am unsure what is being communicated by this part in the game. And the confusion errodes my enjoyment.
I also experienced a number of graphic glitches and some loading problems but let me stress that this game is still early access so a few bugs  are to be expected. Overall the bugs are not a deal breaker, annoying but hey, early access. I should also throw in that because this game is early access it is VERY SHORT. Just as I was starting to get a handle on the story and the play style, BOOM! Game ends! A little irritating, and in the end makes me feel like I should have saved my $8 for a couple of coffees at starbux.
Overall, this game has potential. But much is yet to be done in both mechanics and story. I will be keeping an eye on this title but for now I would advise that unless you are really really into early access, you would be better off dropping your money in another location.

I love AE. I've played hundreds of hours in dragonfable and spent a bit over $200 on that game. I bought the founders thing in this game in hopes that the game would be fun and like all of their other games. However I can't say that this game is really too good at the moment. The biggest problem is the amount of grinding. Unlike other AE games where you can grind to do more interesting quests and get cool gear, the only reward for all the grinding in this game is the gratification of more quests to grind out. The second big issue with the game is also about the quests. There doesn't seem to be much story to them at all, I know the game is very early, but I still expect better from these guys. The last major problem I have with the game is the combat. While all of AE's games have varried types of combat ranging from AQ's simple combat using elements to deal more damage, to dragonfable's well thought out multiple skill based combat. However so far the combat in AQ3D has been press this button until they die. It's incredibly boring even compared to AQ, because at least AQ you have to consider elements in everything. However the reason this problem is mildly forgivable is because the reason for its boring simplicity is to make the UI better on the mobile version of the game.
Which brings me to the pros that I've felt. The greatest part of the game is being able to play it anywhere. Regardless of how well it responds at times, the ability to while bored waiting for something to pull out my phone and play the game makes me feel better about spending the money on the founders upgrade. The other big pro for the game is purely nostalgia and isn't a bonus to any players new to AE, but being able to see their world in 3d is quite fun to me.
And sadly that's all the good I have to say about this new expansion from my favorite company.

I played this game for a couple years before it ported to steam.  The entire time I played, all I ever noticed was players leaving.   Every guild I was in, went defunct.  People stopped playing.
If you had followed the conversations on ankama's own forum, you would have seen alot of unhappy players complaining about things that never got changed or fixed for the better over the years.
The games population bled out.  The it came to steam, and some new players showed up.  But not enough to replace the lost content.  The game was still empty.
Many people who wanted to buy the games currency were unable.  Many peoples credit cards were being rejected for no apparent reason.   Popular content was being changed or nerfed or removed, and new, unpopular content was being added or built upon depite many complaints.   No explanations, no understanding of the ankama logic was to be had.
Grouping for dungeons became obsolete with the return of the token system and people could just use their own store bought NPC groupies when they changed the loot requirments to allow NPC group members to count in the prospecting totals.  No longer needed a full group of actual players to get the best loot rolls.  They did that so everyone could compete with the multi boxers.
Some people think it was a good thing, but it was actually bad.  They wouldnt just ban multiboxing....they should have.  Instead they embraced it.  Real players didnt like it, and quit the game.
If you started playing the game now you would quickly discover how unpopulated the game is.   There once was a time when merhcant bags dotted the landscape and hordes of people hanging out at the temples.   The time has past and gone forever.
Servers have been combined several times because their populations were so low.  Its only a matter of time before the game is finally put in the grave.  Its a tragedy.   This once great game is a mere shadow of its past glory.   The game is free to play of course...   waste your time on it if you choose.
UPDATE:  I recently watched the wakfu cartoon series on netflix, not bad really.  It got me interested in playing wakfu again.  And I did.  For a few days.  More stuff had been changed.  The game is now even worse than before and less populated than ever.  There is only 1 server left with a decent population, but the gameplay is so bad now it doesnt matter.  They turned a fun relazing game into an absolute boring asf♥♥♥♥♥♥grind.   Somebody please buy out this company, fire everyone and do a 5 year rollback.

Hi there! I've been playing since closed beta and I promise that this game hasn't always been this terrible.
The game overall is so very unique, I loved it. The character classes, the environment, the stupid politic shenaniganry. The fun stuff back when this game was fun. I don't think there are or will be any games similar to it, unless someone actually wants to put forth the effort.
I have to say that steam release brought in droves of players, but the lack of Ankama caring enough was something that killed off the player base. They're so focused money, end game content, nerfing every class ten times over, and their other games,  that they don't really realize what's happening here (unless they just don't care?). I used to love this game, but now it's just super depressing. The once full streets and markets of the nations are now completely devoid of life. Nothing is geared towards new players or keeping them, everything is for high levels and end game content.
The creativity has seemingly vanished over the years and I have watched this game go from an amazingly unique and thriving game with a great community to... whatever it is now. I have noticed with my return that most of the players above a certain level tend to treat low level players as though they are the scum of the Earth instead of welcoming them or answering questions. I don't know if this is just on Nox or if other servers have the same issue.
The customer service from Ankama is absolutely terrible. It takes them ages to answer tickets, if they even get to them at all (they just recently closed a ticket that I've had open since 2013 that no longer even applies to the game or class I have, they didn't even answer the ticket to begin with). I do understand that they added heroes, but they also charge an arm and a leg for ogrines or any means necessary to actually buy booster packs. This is basically pay to win, the exp difference if pretty bad when playing with friends.
The community is... fairly toxic now. A lot of people will randomly gank you, so having the heroes system is almost a necessity.
I'm mostly upset because of how fast the game died and how little Ankama actually did to prevent that. No advertisements like Dofus had, nothing. I know some of you guys still love the game, but it's just... depressing.
I still play every once in a while to check up on old friends that refuse to abandon the game, but I really wouldn't recommend it unless you have the time and patience. I know this whole review has been all over the place, but I will always have mixed feelings about this game until Ankama starts caring again.

If you needed a bridge to cross the water, build it. If you wanted to created a sniper bunker to defend an area, build it. If you wanted to sneak across enemy territory, dig underneath the surface via a tunnel. Almost anything was possible with the tools at hand. The game's first and only weapon at the start of devlopment was the most balanced. You could get a one shot kill via headshot or 2-3 shot kill anywhere else. It made firefights intense and realistic to say the least. If I was able to go back and play the first version of Ace of Spades, I definitely would.
Unfortunately, towards to release of this game, classes with diffrent weapons were introduced. When I did play this updated version the weapon balance felt diluted and clunky. The submachine gun didn't deal as much damage as you would expect and the shotgun had too much range. Then Jagex releases this game with TF2 inspired class system and game modes that distanced itself from the original content. There were no 64+ servers with large maps and no Classic CTF mode. In fact the game modes were so poorly designed that none of them were fun to me. For example, one mode's objective is to destroy the other team's base while protecting yours. What is pretty sketchy about this is that you can rebuild your base just by randomly placing blocks in the area. Though the classes at the time had overpowered weapons, like the miner's drill gun. Imagine a gigantic drill breaking through an area and then exploding. The match was over in two minutes thanks to the entire team spawning as this class. It was a blatant example of imbalance and zero play testing.
This isn't Ace of Spades anymore.

I would like to say I'm a HUGE fan of Deus Ex: Human Revolution. I preordered this game knowing full well it was an iPad port. I didn't have super expectations giving the price of the game. I figured it would be ok for the story and expansion of the Deus Ex universe. Little did I know the full craptitude that would be unleashed onto my eyeballs and brain.
First of all, there absolutely NO JUMPING! What gives?! I was hoping for multiple paths to complete missions and find extra goodies. You also can't just pickup boxes to throw at people. I got the strength mod only to find out it's to slide stuff around and not be like "HULK SMASH!" vending machine throw. The controls are really awkward and seem broken at times. Like I'll be hugging the wall crouched backing up, then my character gets kinda stuck and will still be in cover mode when I'm clearly in the middle of a doorway or edge of a box. Also, in menus and various prompts where you have to choose stuff, I've had to click a bunch of times to get the option to register. In the main menu for inventory and stuff like that, sometimes clicking works, others you have to highlight what you want, then hit enter.
The environment graphics are ok, but the random npc models are awful. Alot of them look like mutated elf people. Also, the lighting doesn't look right on alot of things, like some polygons on a models face will be shadowed even when the light source is right infront of them. In the nightclub at Panama, there was this npc dancing like a derp, I actually thought it was a dude until she spoke because I thought I saw a 5 o'clock shadow. It's pretty bad when a player can't tell what they're looking at because of super low polys and the crappy lighting ingame. Facial movements are wonky as well. I've noticed that parts of the face don't move properly when the main characters are talking, like the upper lip doesn't move. Ben's and Anna's eyes are WAY too big, almost animeish. Barret's and Namir's models really look like they don't belong in this game. You can tell their models weren't made for the facial rigging in this game.
The voice acting, oh dear lord, the voice acting is TERRIBLE. If you wanna hear Skwisgaar Skwigelf pretend to be Russian, or other borderline stereotype/horrendous accents, then this shouldn't bother you. The main characters are meh at best. I don't really have a problem for the characters you see in Human Revolution though, they're ok. I've also noticed some glitching with voices in cutscenes.
The writing is lackluster. I found myself already clicking though emails not giving a flip what's going on in the world. There are plotholes as big as galaxies, and listening to the news reports and voice messages gave me a brain aneurysm. For example, in one message Anna says she would've cried if they didn't already take her eyes. That doesn't make any sense because tears don't come from your eyeballs. This is just one of many things that will make ocd people like me super mad.
The help system is absolutely annoying. It's not like H.R. where you can just ignore it like a boss. It FORCES you to look at crap and doesn't go away till you click the stuff it wants you to.
I feel Ben is just a bargain-bin version of Adam Jenson and this game is not worth the money. Overall I give the game a 2/10.

New Review: Are you ready for some hardcore Demon hunting badass cool paint warrior action!? Well this isn't that. Layers of Fear walks the same sort of line as Amnesia and P.T., and places you in the shoes of an insane painter wandering though his house, remembering the events that brought him to his current state, while attempting to complete his magnum opus, his greatest masterpiece. As his sanity slips further and further, experience twisting hallways, repeating rooms, and a dangerous new definition of 'art' that will produce fear and anxiety. Atmosphere fit for even the most hardcore horror fan is abounds. There are no Monsters, there are no Demons, there are no NPCs. Just you, a house, and a painting.
Pros:
EXCELLENT environment
Not reliant on jumpscares
Mostly unpredictable
Heart-stoppingly scary sometimes
Great Voice-Acting
Cons:
Graphically intensive
Short, somewhere bordering on 3 to 4 hours.
Early Access Review: Okay, I agree with most people: Layers of Fear is a LOT like P.T./Silent Hills in it's execution. There's no monsters, no villains, just you, an old house, and lots and lots of paintings. Put your fancy beret on, grab your brush, and delve into a dark and stormy night as you attempt to complete your greatest painting. Twisting hallways and changing rooms leave you wondering if you're crazy, painting watch you, the walls melt, and you keep pressing forward into madness. An EXCELLENT game, very well done, perfect for the artist and horror-lover in everyone.
