16bit Trader is a merchant simulation game where you play as a merchant and trying to collect money to be the richest merchant in the world. Although i said the richest, the game actually ends after you earn 1M gold. There is no time limit in collecting the money. However, an achievement will unlock if you collect it before the 1500th day.
If you are thinking that this game is 16bit because of the title, you are wrong. Although the graphics are just okay, it's not even close to 16bit.
The music is relaxing. It sounds like a market in the old games, with a soft tone on it. I like it very much.
You'll basically travel from and to places. There are a lot of cities and villages to move into, and sometimes, there will be an event which will rob your money or delay your trip (or both). However, these events can be "cheated" by saving and loading before moving to other places, making this game mostly becomes saving and loading. Luckily, you can do it fast.
You can hire mercenaries to reduce the random event chance. However, doing so will be costly because your traveling cost will be increased. Mercenaries can also be used to help farming diamonds, which is one of the money sources in this game. Note that hiring and firing tons of mercenaries can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because the game only offers you to buy a maximum of 5 mercenaries at once.
You can earn money by doing two things: trading and mining. However, these methods are unbalanced because mining will net you more money faster than trading. You just need to hire tons of mercenaries to mine diamonds and sell them back in the city to earn a lot of money. Note that diamonds are sold around 50-150 gold, while you can only get around 10 gold profit per item by trading (not to mention the carts and mercenaries which you have to hire in order to deliver more items, which will increase your traveling cost). With the same amount of money, i can get more profit from mining.
There are some side quests, each appears randomly in big cities or ports. Most of the time, the side quests will require you to travel back and forth, which can be costly. They will reward you from hundreds to thousands gold.
After you are having 1M gold, the game will end, and you can't continue after that. Some achievements won't unlock if you have 1M gold and there is still unlocked achievements needed to be unlocked.
There is an in-game achievement, although you can't see the list.
Pros:
- Random events
- Mining
Cons:
- Mining and trading are not balanced
- Too much relying on saving and loading
- No options to hire and fire merchants in bulk
Although this is a decent merchant simulation game, the saving and loading can make your brain explode. It also took a while to figure out on how to earn money efficiently (and when you already figure it out, you'll be bored doing it).

16bit Trader is very unique compared to other games I usually play. In 16bit Trader you are the heir to your family\'s throne and you must try and restore its former glory. Selling the only diamonds your family has left you must travel from city to city buying and selling goods and accepting quests from strangers. Although I highly recommend that you buy your own drinks, It seems the people in this game have no problem accepting drink after drink and spilling their secrets.
Although the game does not involve action or dedication to become succesful it does require a certain amount of skill combined with luck. You will need to know the knowledge of buying and selling products. It will take you a lot of tries in order to win but you quickly get the hang of it.
Quick Tips: Visit the mines frequently for easy diamonds right of the bat.
PROS: Cozy, Relaxing Feel. Easy on the eye graphics, interesting quest, and much much more.
CONS: Although I am sure there are flaws in the game as far as I can tell it is well put together.
RATING: 7/10

Where to Start....
Deus Ex: Human Revolution was one of my favorite games to play. I played it so much that I literally mastered the game, (Got every ending, got every achievement). So when I saw that Deus Ex: The Fall was on steam, of course I was excited about buying it...But given the couple hours I've sat and played it, my excitefulness has changed to a much more negative feeling..
Deus Ex: The Fall follows Ben Saxon, a Former British SAS Agent turned Aug, as well as Government Agent gone rogue Anna Kelso, as they hide from the Illuminati and their elite team of mercenaries known as the Tyrants. That's pretty much all I can really say in terms of a story, otherwise I'd be spoiling the game..
Many previous Human Revolution players will find the same gameplay elements in The Fall, however this time around, there's much more problems. Above all, I noticed constant glitches or stutters during gameplay, many bugs such as getting stuck on cover, being unable to click out of a menu, trying to grab an item with an NPC standing nearby and the game thinks you're trying to talk to the NPC, little to no ammo for non-lethal weaponry, and an in-game market you can use to buy new guns, ammo, or various items with the in-game "Credits", however everything is overpriced making the system completely pointless. One thing I was very annoyed about, was the inability to sell weapons picked up from enemies back to the market for credits...
Despite knowing it was previously a mobile game, Deus Ex: The Fall is just ugly, running the game on the highest settings, character models look dreadful, the world looks bland, and many graphical glitches occur at various times for no explained reason. Players who do not like the layout of the control system will find no way of reconfiguring the controls, which is problematic for some.
All in All, Deus Ex: The Fall is not worth the $10.00 asking price. The game is no longer than one and a half to two hours long (pending you do the sidequests), and doesn't offer much difficulty. Even on New Game Plus, where supposedly the difficulty is "increased", I never had a problem completing the game. If you really want to play it, at least wait for it to be on Sale for $3.00 or less...or if you want to experience the story without playing the game, then you should know that the game follows the exact same story as the book "Deus Ex: The Icarus Effect" by James Swallow. This is one time when the book is definitely better than the Game!
(Time Played: 7.6 Hours, Completed the game Three (3) Times, and earned all 28 Achievements)

I recommend this game only for people that really enjoyed Deus Ex: Human Revolution and want more of that type of gameplay.

The story is pretty compelling, and is at least as interesting as Human Revolution's. However, the game ends on a GIGANTIC cliffhanger, and there's no sequel currently planned.
All in all, a solid buy for $7.50 or less if you want more Human Revolution. I do not regret picking this up.

I can't stand the experience point system in this game. This unresolved problem seriously harms gameplay. It's not the grind that's the problem. The game is largely based on levels where you capture checkpoints.  Capturing the checkpoints are literally the only way you make any substantial experience. Killing someboy, you gain 7-8 exp. Wound somebody, one or two exp.  Capture a point by standing on it? 60-150 exp.  This makes the gameplay stupid.  I feel like killing somebody isn't really worth it. Just run to the next point and hope you don't die.  There's also vehicles with mounted guns that you can drive around and have another player killing people with the mounted gun. Cool right? Guess what? The driver couldn't care less about helping the other guys because there's no assist exp in this game.
What about killing the enemy when you're at their checkpoint? No extra exp for that. People just hide and hope someone else will kill the enemy because if you die you won't get as many point for capturing the point.
That said, this game isn't quite pay to win as you can theoretically grind your way to get all the better weapons. However, the experience point systems ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the gameplay as it motivates behavior. Yes, I think exp wise, they should take tips from Call of Duty.

16bit Trader is better than alleged paragon of the genre Tradewind series, as it does not make you fight pirates and bandits instead of trading...
Indeed, you can not do that at all. Instead highway thieves peacefully rob you of cash and wares, regardless of the size of your retinue, social standing and exploit foul play (reloading an autosave will only help you so far, as it does not work for long: first you loose the ability to save, then you find yourself no longer able to autosave).
To further boost robbers' moral your character is prohibited to store cash in banks (feature not implemented) or at least cars (500 gold pieces being the selling price and 1500 the acquisition price). Thus, these devils attack you once in every 3-4 land moves, while on sea mighty crackens stand guard. The most perilious place is not thieves guild base too, but rather royal army training grounds.
Porcelain makers village does not sell porcelain, hamlets will sell food for the same price as big cities.
The only way to recieve your margin is to buy at the lowest level of prices (yes, prices for food and jewels do only rise and fall simultaneously), wait for 100 days or so and sell at the highest possible price (amplitude does not change throughout the game, even if an undead army scourges the southern lands), after which there is more waiting, untill the prices fully recede.
So if you deal in jewelry, of which you can load 250 units on one car, you can expect roughly 30gold*250u=7500gold margin, which gives you 7500gold/200days=37g/d. With the base travelling cost ranging from 2 to 7 as well as bridge tolls, that leaves you (at the very best) 960 gold to give to the robbers, taken that they will usaully rob you once in 16 days.
Therefore, you must either take pleasure in a very slow growth rate(expect 10h of gameplay and remember YOU CAN'T SAVE) or loiter around looking for diamonds and doing quests, which will result in a slightly faster my farm-like experience.

I loved Hotline Miami. Sadly, I just cannot recommend this one. It just doesn't have what made Hotline Miami fun to me.
What I loved about Hotline Miami was that each level was a bit like a puzzle. You worked your way through it, with each death teaching you something new until you found the optimal route through the level. The levels were often small and claustrophobic, with narrow corridors and many rooms. Melee was a very viable strategy as you could lure enemies through chokepoints. Hotline Miami 2 throws this all out in favor of big open levels that rely more on guns and often render melee unfeasible. I find myself moving slowly through levels, hiding behind walls while waiting for enemies to come into range of my gun so I can safely dispatch them. I am often killed by off-screen enemies who I cannot even see when using Shift to extend my view range. Many deaths are a case of bad luck instead of a mistake on behalf of the player. Whereas my experience with Hotline Miami was fast and frantic, my experience with Hotline Miami 2 is slow and ponderous.
The final nail in the coffin for me is the technical issues. If I enable V-sync, I get mouse lag which often gets me killed as I cannot turn fast enough to kill enemies. If I disable V-sync, I get terrible screen tearing that makes the game unbearable to look at. If I try to play in Borderless Fullscreen mode, I have to put up with the mouse lag again.
Sad to say, as much as I loved the original Hotline Miami, I'm getting a refund on this one.

PT meets Silent Hill 4: The Room, minus enemies, minus combat.
So, walking simulator then? I guess it starts that way...
This game is an absolute masterpiece of atmospheric terror and a great example of how to take primal fears and play them against the player. You don't need to be stalked by an enemy (ie Demento/Haunting Ground) for a large house to be scary. In fact you don't need anything LIVING in it, at all... (emphasis...).
I have never been so afraid of an empty house, ever... Yet at the same time compelled to keep going to unveil the truth. As you keep going, the game begins to feel more like SH4 in that the 'sanctuary' (for lack of any term...) being the art studio itself becomes more and more corrupted by evil. Yet its not a 'fantasy' evil, which is why this game is so horrendously frightening...
The story is one of madness, and an 'evil' borne of madness. It is not fantasy, it is all reality, and a very deep, dark disturbing look at exactly how low the human psyche can fall. It is an 'evil' that exists in the hearts of many, and because its something we can associate with, it simply makes the entire premise all the more frightening.
If having no combat makes this a walking simulator, then 10/10 would walk and♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants all over again.

"Cujo, Cujo!"
Ever wanted to play a Mummy wolf out to hunt and kill all the bad humans who've stolen her wolf cub? Of course you have. We ALL have.
In Nocturnal Hunt you get to do just that, using stealth and heightened senses to attack or sneak past a pack of evil hunters who stand between you and your offspring. It's a short but compelling - and even surprisingly heart-tugging! - little game which positively drools quality, on every conceivable level.
Magnificent graphics, fantastic world and character design, brilliant mapping, highly intuitive gameplay...it's all here, suggesting that these devs may be ready to go toe-to-toe with the AAAs in no time. They might have to make a slightly LONGER game to do so, though, given that this one can apparently be beaten in under fifteen minutes...a fact which arguably makes its six dollar price tag a tad steep, though the sheer volume and variety of Achievements ensures considerable replayability for those to whom such things matter.
If, like me, you occasionally crave a brief bit of stealth-kill gameplay without the obligation of starting up a twenty-hour game in which your body count slowly, steadily (and ultimately quite tediously) soars into the hundreds, then this is the game for you. Your wolf can even SWIM, which is pretty impressive in a world chock-full of video game characters who perish the instant they come into contact with any sizeable body of water.
Devs of the world: more first-person games with animal protagonists, please. We've already done guns to death; time for more variety, methinks.
Verdict: 9/10.

So far, I've only played through the tutorial part of the story, and it is absolutely riddled with bugs.
-Spoken dialog being skipped altogether
-Spoken dialog being silent
-Constant bugged sounds (no gunshot sound, no walking sound, no explosion, no takedown noises, etc)
-Laggy video screen (my character kept jumping all around)
-The tutorial popups, although I'm sure is easy to turn off, were extremely annoying and prohibitive during the tutorial

-"Throw Grenade" isn't on its own hotkey; must be switched to as a separate weapon--(I hate this, but maybe that's just me)

Other than those few gripes I really get a kick out of playing this game with my friends, quite entertaining on its own though-- a great pick up and play game.

I don't even remember when I got this game, but I installed it on a whim and after a few hours of playing, I'm really quite pleased. Fair warning, it's really deep; that may be a good or bad thing, depending on what you're looking for. I personally love it. Getting into the nuts and bolts of the mechanics of the game can be a little overwhelming but they do at the least seem quite intuitive and natural.
This game is one part space civilization sim, and one part tatical turn-based combat, both of which often affect each other. The end result is an amazingly engrossing experience. I've found myself really mulling over decisions like which race to aid in building up thier forces (and currying thier favor in the process) and how to advance my own technology.
If you want a smart game to really sink your teeth into, I strongly reccomend this.
(Also, the music is pretty awesome)

Cons:
- dwindling player base

Theres seems to be a lot of negative seniment and reviews around this game and I think they are all overexxagerated. At least for me, it wasn't that bad of an experience.
First of all, I'm just going to say I beat the whole game. The game starts off rather annoyingly hard when you have no comparison for price. However, once you get the hang of the highs and lows for the prices, the game becomes rather easy actually. But the beginning part was fun to explore. (Also doing quests is not worth it.) The concept itself is simple and the interface is pretty user friendly.
The bad parts of this include the saving. The saving completely died on me after 1150 days and I couldn't autosave, save slot, or load saves. This was annoying at first since I was constantly reloading to try to avoid bandits. However, after it stoppped working, I traded like a real merchant and took losses from bandits. Nevertheless, the save function is bugged up after a while. My second concern is how easily exploitable this game is. I got to 1,000,000 frm just going back and forth between 3 cities. Sell to one, buy from another, sell to one, buy frm another. The game goes in cycles for the price increases and decreases, so once you figure out the cycle, it becomes really really easy to play.
Overall, I would not go nearly as far as some of the other reivews here and I'd say that this game is fun, for at least 1-2 hours before it becomes a grindfest and you lose your save option. If you have a bunch of hours to play a game in one sitting, this game may not be too bad for you.

Vermintide was the first game that i bought when it came out. I was on the hype train, and i made a huge mistake.
I got the game at the 2nd beta weekend, almost spent 50 hours in the beta, and i thought it's awsome. Unfortunately i didn't see the bigger picture.
First, the melee combat. It's not bad, it's just mediocore. Almost identical to Skyrim, but you can push. I was expecting something like Chivalry, but no drags, ripostes, nothing, just brainless lmbspam.
Enemies mostly coming from L4d, but it's not a problem, works very well in coop games. The Ai of these creatures, is just meh, cannot say a single positive aspect about it.
Graphics are extremly good in my opinion, but the optimization is beyond bad. it seems none of the options has impact on the fps. For me, the FPS drops are identical on the lowest to medium settings. FPS drops usually followed by a big game slowdown, causes a huge input lag, and driving me crazy.
Maps are well designed, and looking awsome, but there are only 12. (?)
The Networking. This is when the♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan. No hostmigration, No dedicated servers, why ?
Imo, the dedicated servers won't solve the problem. P2P is not as bad as most of the community thinks. I only played l4d in P2P, and it was awsome. My buddies are close to me, so everybody got like 10-30 ms delay, which is fantastic, and everything worked smoothly. However, in Vermintide, even with the same ppl, the delays are insane. The fact that a lot of different rules apply to the host and the guests is bad. When you are playing as a host, the game is great, everything smooth, everything works just as expected. When you are a guest (even with very low ping), first you will start to notice the delays, which is like increasing through the game, and then, the thing that are never happening as a host, like getting hit while pushing, dodge seems a 50 - 50 game as a guest, and a tons of hittrades, which again, doesn't happen when you are the host. Some guy on the forums actually mentioned, that even in lan, the host - guest difference is very noticable, because the game is not synchronizing properly.
There are a millions of bugs that influencing every map you play, just like cannot help your teamate up, because he sank into the textures, getting hit while using potion/nade, sometimes multiplies it, and there are a tons of other bugs that i could mention. That's why i gave a negative review, because they seem to not care about those problems and bugs that i mention above, but they are forcing the console version, and "so-called new", recycled content.
About the game's difficulty. I've seen that a lot of people complaining, because it's too hard, which the achievment charts kinda approves, but it's really not that hard. If you played l4d on expert realism, you know what can you expect on cataclysm. After 350 hours, I usually fight with the bugs and the netcode inconsistencies rather then the rats.
Again, the game has a great concept, characters, maps, lore everything is fine, except the optimalization and netcode, which is far below avarage.

Review Updated (3/1/2018)
Thankfully the polish company
eventually woke from their drunken taverns and fixed a long standing issue with regards to broken achievements since the games release. They also tinkered with a known save file issue which was causing them occasionally not to work. While their customer service was slower than a Monday at a pub, many our thankful that it at least eventually happened.
There are a LOT of negative reviews despite the fact that a lot of time and effort has already been put into this game by the designers to make the graphics eye pleasing and the delightful background sound that accompanies the adventure to be very fitting indeed. So why then all the negative reviews? It boils down to a number of things...
1) Gamers waited several years for them to fix five broken achievements and a corrupt save file issue.
2) Developers still never responded to the customers personally or in the forums. This means that you might as well pull out your favourite teddy bear in your room and go to town on him/her venting all your frustration as you will more likely get a listening ear from it than you will from the customer service of this company. I guess partly broken game and never responding developers is what they mean when they call their company 'FOREVER entertainment'...
3) The game itself was designed to be a 'trading game'. IT ISNT! It’s more a save your game every five seconds because the thieves are coming to take everything you own. In game it doesn't matter what you do, the thieves will steal everything you have built up in no time whatsoever. In fact it is so frustrating I'm not sure why they put them in at all. Take the thieves and kraken out of the game and the game has some merit to it, and it wouldn't matter at all the fact that the save files don't work for many people. As I said it doesn't matter what you do, you can have an army of 3,000 people and the 2 thieves will still take everything. For this reason there is no point at all to learn any trading strategies to play this game instead you will have to fleece the game in another way to win.
For those that have purchased this game, this is how to win.
As soon as you appear go to pub buy a 1 gold coin drink for all 3 customers until one offers you a treasure map. Go hire about 5 -7 people at the pub. Go sell the two diamonds you already have at the bank. Now travel to the closest mine. Search the mine and you should get a handful of diamonds. SAVE GAME. Travel back to the start. Fire the seven people at the pub. Sell the diamonds you have at the bank. IGNORE all markets. SAVE GAME. Slowly travel down to the bottom of the map to Lousifa or Zannadar IGNORING all the markets. You can buy drinks at pubs for the customers to get treasure maps or perform side quests. You can only do 3 side quests at any given time, you have to complete one to get another one. Once you’re at one of the two places mentioned above. Hire as many people as you can afford knowing there is going to be some travel expense. You should be able to still get quite a few maybe 50 people. Once you have them SAVE, travel to the closest mine, search the mine, go back to the town you have come from, fire all the people at the pub and then go to the bank and sell all the diamonds you have collected. SAVE GAME. Roam around for a handful of turns doing side quests and buying drinks and then repeat that process again at one of the two places mentioned. Congratulations that's it you have beaten the game.
It's just very tedious hiring and firing people, but using that above strategy you will get about 15,000 diamonds and win the game in about half an hour meaning you don't have to learn trading at all because it will never help you.
In a nutshell, a long time once broken game, non-existent customer service, rage quitting unfair events in the game that thwart every progress you have made and a game that complete misses the mark of being a trading game which it was originally intended to be and advertised as, makes this game a FOREVER THUMBS DOWN!

Ingredients
2 large eggs
Salt and pepper
2 to 3 tablespoons shredded cheese (optional)
1/4 to 1/2 cup filling, pre-cooked if necessary (optional)
2 teaspoons unsalted butter
Minced parsley, to garnish (optional)
Equipment
Mixing bowl
Whisk
8-inch nonstick skillet
Spatula
Dinner plate
Instructions
1. Whisk the eggs: Crack both eggs into a mixing bowl. Whisk the eggs until completely combined, and season with salt and pepper. If you\'re adding cheese or other fillings, make sure they are prepped and nearby.
2. Warm the skillet and melt the butter: Place an 8-inch skillet over medium-high heat and melt the butter. Tilt the skillet as the butter melts to evenly coat the bottom. When the butter stops sizzling, the pan is heated and ready.
3. Pour the eggs into the skillet: Pour the whisked eggs into the skillet. Immediately tilt the pan so the eggs coat the entire bottom. The eggs should sizzle on contact; if not, continue cooking, but remember to heat the pan a little longer next time.
4. Drag and push the eggs to form waves: Use a spatula to gently drag and push the cooked eggs from the edges toward the center of the pan, making space for the uncooked eggs and forming waves in the omelette. Tilt the skillet so that the uncooked eggs flow into the open spaces.
5. Cook the omelette for 1 to 2 minutes: The omelette will finish cooking in 1 to 2 minutes. When done, the bottom will be set and the edges will look crisp. The top of the omelette should still look fairly wet and uncooked, but there will no longer be any loose, easily flowing liquid egg — the omelette will continue cooking off the heat, so finish when you think the top still seems a bit underdone.
6. Top with cheese and fillings: If using, sprinkle the cheese and fillings down the center of the omelette.
7. Fold the omelette: Fold the bottom third of the omelette over the center, and then fold the top third down. Alternatively, fold the omelette in half.
8. Slide the omelette onto a plate: Gently slide the omelette onto a plate and garnish with parsley. Eat right away while still hot.

I loved Final Fantasy Tactics A2 and the Pokemon Mystery Dungeon series and always wished for a multiplayer version of those games. This game does a pretty good job of putting the combat experiences of those games in a multiplayer setting.
Besides the combat, I also enjoyed the game's environmental mechanics because it kind of gives me a Harvest Moon or Animal Crossing kind of vibe where the world gives you these resources to do things with, and the players are responsible for tending to them or making something out of them.
As for the grinding, I personally don't know if it is actually necessary or not, but in any case I managed to skip the first story quests altogether and head to my chosen nation (Bonta) and then proceeded to grind the highest level mobs and dungeons that I could manage, purely because I love overwhelming myself in these tactics games and barely pulling through.
It also helps that the only punishment for death is no exp gain for a lost battle, reduced stats for about 3 minutes and a respawn back to the previous checkpoint area of your choosing.
I've spent no money on the game so far, but I might in the future if I keep playing. Paying players get some nice bonuses, but I've been playing comfortably without them. There's also some nifty costumes and stuff too.
I recommend the game because it's free and I enjoy it.
If you get it, I'd definitely recommend doing the tutorial and trying out a few different classes. I went through a couple classes and then went with the Elitrope as my main because I personally loved the portal mechanic. My brother went with the archer because he loved the obscene range and then the huppermage because of the elemental/light attack dynamic. There's a lot of variety, so don't be afraid to try a few out. Also, your lower level alts will gain an experience multiplier to make grinding levels faster,

I expected a stealth based horror game, but The Evil Within is a below average, mission based action game. The comparisons to RE4 are somewhat understandable (Mikami, horror) but misguided. The core mechanics of RE4 are far more polished, the enemies are better designed and the encounters are infintely more engaging.
The game peaks early with the stealth and tactical based gameplay of the "RE4" village of chapter 3, and it's more or less downhill from there. Aiming with a controller is terrible, even with accuracy maxed out. Whenever you go into the aiming stance the camera zooms in an absurd amount -- it's basically a shoulder shifted FPS, and it's extreamly disorienting -- the controls reorientate costing you a precious second or two. What's reallly mindboggling, once the enemies cross a certain closeness threshold, say five or six feet, the closer they are the more difficult it is to land a shot. I suspect encounters were too easy with the over the shoulder camera shown in earlier builds and this was a lazy last minute fix. Haunted AI is pretty dumb (even when multiple bullets whiz by their head they don't know what's going on for a bit), and hit reactions and player feedback are incredibly basic, culminating in lackluster encouters. You can try to play tactically but in most cases it's better to brute force your way and shoot everything.

Lots of design issues; invisible walls, you can't pick up The Haunted's weapons (no reason is given why), some bottles you can pick up, the rest are props. Some ledges you can get up on, other similar ones, it's a no go. Stealth is very basic, you can't shoot or open a door from stealth, and Sebastian has hardly any transistion animations leading to many a moment where his actions don't match the tone and sequence on screen.
Enemy designs are generally uninspired and not creepy in any fashion. The majority of The Haunted look like Hellraiser III rejects, generic zombies or something ripped straight from 13 Ghosts. Low poly design and textures don't help either. Two boss characters fare better; The Keeper is imposing and Laura is a complete nightmare, even if they're more than just a little familiar.
The environments look decent but they're ultimately forgettable; they lack character and all feel similar. The nonsensical story takes place in the psyche, there's no sence of presence or progression and one place is the same as the next. Blood's smeared everywhere, I mean EVERYWHERE, and far from being disturbing, it has the complete opposite effect.
I did like the "Silent Hill" level.
Lots of trial and error gameplay, the puzzles are dead simple... and I hope you like turning gears, you'll be doing it lots with boring encounters telegraphed from a mile a way. FIVE out of TEN.

The Evil Within is one of the best horror games I've ever played, with a clear emphasis on the word 'games'.
No matter how much scarier you think other games might be, the fact remains that this one provides much more variety and depth in its gameplay. Also, it generally does a better job of tying in scares with level design and gameplay mechanics, not to mention that 'scares' alone are highly subjective and rarely a factor in replayability (i.e. you might as well just watch a movie if all you want is to see/hear really creepy stuff).
Speaking of subjective factors, I liked the story - even its main protagonist. Yes, there are cheesy moments here and there, but overall it does a good job of ♥♥♥♥ing with your mind and keeping you guessing. And perhaps more importantly, everything is presented in a very polished and atmospheric setting, with plenty of morbid details to keep you immersed and uneasy.
It is ultimately a linear experience, but exploration is rewarded with both items and story bits. And as I've already hinted at, this game offers multiple, organic approaches to solving each encounter and is therefore highly replayable, especially in new game+ mode. I rarely felt like there were a fixed number of  options, pre-determined  by the developers. It always felt more like a creative survival effort - tense and satisfying.
I don't remember the last time a horror game kept me hooked for more than 7 hours straight, and I have played quite a few of them: the amnesia games, among the sleep, silent hill, resident evil, etc.
Of course, there are some issues with the game:
-too expensive in my opinion
-poorly optimized (especially considering the price they are charging on PC - thankfully most of the issues can be fixed)
-low fov
-giant black bars
-'cinematic' camera angles can mess up your gameplay occasionally
-a few crappy encounters with gun-wielding zombies... seriously don't ever do that again

The first game is every zone leading up to Ashfall in which it is a drag where you spent far too long in too small of a map just grindng away with missions that seem only to exist for you to collect enough crafting materials so you can make all of the gear in the zone and move onto the next zone and repeat. This s because there are no gear shops everything you do before Ashfall is crafting based and there are no gear checks in the game so you don't even have to do any of them. I personally got to the Bone Cliffs, two maps prior to Ashfall or the map directly before if you skip the Bridge which is the best EXP grind in the game, with the Alpha Knight gear that is level 2. I have heard rumors they do plan on revamping the game to flow more like Ashfall so that is why this is currently forgivable.
The second game is Ashfall where shops have been added, hidden map objects exist for players to dig out, and most importantly you rarely stay in one instance for too long because every instance drops crafting materials for the Dragonslayer camp instead of having a different shop for each map. Dungeons have their own crafting shops but that is fine as Dungeons are currently the end game activities so they should provide different gear than just playing the store.
Dungeons are random encounters ending in a fixed boss fight. They currently have a problem where the number of rooms and activities you can be rolled are very limited but as time goes on I do expect this to be fixed. They are currently working on a 20 man dungeon they are calling a raid but we will have to wait until it is released to see if it is mechanically different enough from dungeons to be called a raid.
It wouldn't be an MMO without classes and AQ3D tried to do it a little different. Instead of you picking your class at the work go you can switch it up at any time while you are not in combat. At the time of writing Warrior and Rogue are your best free classes with Guardian being the only paid class. Guardian is unlocked when your lifetime purchases of in game currency, used to speed up crafting times similar to Warframe but not nearly as long, reaches a threshold which I believe is $20 US. Warrior is your crowd control class specializing in an AoE attack as well as an area buff, most people play as warrior even when the situation doesn't call for it. Rogue and Guardian are your DPS classes as both have skills that add marks to your targets allowing you to trigger and cause massive damage. Guardian can also trigger those marks for a heal and is the only character that can taunt at this time. Mage is also a class if you like getting kill credits for fights you didn't take a part in.

The Fall is a standalone spinoff game that uses a ton of the same stuff from human revolution but has a different story, characters, locations, etc. (Like Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon and Assassin's Creed: Freedom Cry)
The major problem with the game is that it's a port of a mobile game which explains a lot.
Gameplay is basically Human Revolution but with changes that were made to make the game easier because it was on iOS.
The game plays fine but there were some changes I was a bit mixed on.
The changes that stood out to me are
-Ben Saxon has augmented pockets (Infinite inventory space)
-A merchant follows you everywhere (You can buy things at anytime)
-Ben Saxon isn't very athletic (No sprinting or Jumping)
-It just feels like a mobile game despite being on PC
Also, bugs, nothing game breaking though. Some people have run into problems like no music and such, worst I had was the world disappearing during takedowns.
Overall, the game feels like it's on easy by default (there's no difficulty settings) and I felt limited due to no jumping and sprinting.
Despite all that, I've been having fun with it so far (after the annoying tutorial of course)
Would I recommend it? Right now? No
If you're a fan that wants more Deus Ex, just to be safe, wait until it (hopefully) gets patched or until it goes on sale.
If you're deciding which of the newer Deus Ex games to buy, just go with Human Revolution, it's pretty cheap when it's on sale and it's a bigger game (It usually gets a 75% discount which ends up being 5 dollars cheaper than The Fall at full price)

A falling blocks game like no other, Tricky Towers delivers a multi-player puzzler with endless local and online replayability.
The physics engine lofts this game into a class above others in the genre, forcing players to cope with the delicate balancing of blocks even in the presence of wind and rain. No two games are ever alike, while perfect strategy can be thwarted by a cunning opponent armed with an astute special ability.
The developer is also attentive to community feedback, providing support and new features in an impressively timely manner. The game is plenty fun in its current form, but I'm always happy when new blocks are added to the mix.
Tricky Towers ranks among my favorites as a delightful and inviting experience for just about everyone.

All in all, not a bad little game. It'll be interesting to see what additional gameplay elements come after this first chapter. There appears to be an rpg system (hit points, etc) so I expect to see some combat eventually.
Art direction note: I noticed that many of the characters share the same facial structures. In truth the only real difference between some of them was skin tone and hair style. This was probably just a cost/time saving measure which I can understand. But it's a little sloppy. Considering the first chapter of the game was free I won't complain. However, I would prefer to see some more individuality in the cast. Even if it's only minor characters who get that treatment, it's still distracting. It's a small town, so you probably won't need too many different sprites. (Or don't even worry about individual portraits for people like in Final Fantasy 6) But it would go a long way (at least for me) to see that tweak.
One minor note to the game makers (should they read this), at one point during the dialog Sara refers to the storage at the back of the car as a "boot". We call them "trunks" in the U.S. so you should either change it to "trunk" or have (I believe his name was Phil) say that line since he's from England.
All in all, it's a decent introduction to what seems like it might be the child of a JRPG and Silent Hill. I'm interested in seeing the next episode and curious as to how much it will cost to unlock the entire game.

I loved Final Fantasy Tactics A2 and the Pokemon Mystery Dungeon series and always wished for a multiplayer version of those games. This game does a pretty good job of putting the combat experiences of those games in a multiplayer setting.
Besides the combat, I also enjoyed the game's environmental mechanics because it kind of gives me a Harvest Moon or Animal Crossing kind of vibe where the world gives you these resources to do things with, and the players are responsible for tending to them or making something out of them.
As for the grinding, I personally don't know if it is actually necessary or not, but in any case I managed to skip the first story quests altogether and head to my chosen nation (Bonta) and then proceeded to grind the highest level mobs and dungeons that I could manage, purely because I love overwhelming myself in these tactics games and barely pulling through.
It also helps that the only punishment for death is no exp gain for a lost battle, reduced stats for about 3 minutes and a respawn back to the previous checkpoint area of your choosing.
I've spent no money on the game so far, but I might in the future if I keep playing. Paying players get some nice bonuses, but I've been playing comfortably without them. There's also some nifty costumes and stuff too.
I recommend the game because it's free and I enjoy it.

I know it doesn't look very pretty, but once you start playing, you'll appreciate the depth.
The game doesn't have any "modes" or "classes" or "locked abilities", instead it has an excellent "gameplay curve". What I mean by this is that it feels like multiple games layered on top of each other, and the longer you play, the more there is to appreciate. At first, you'll be a mercenary, with ragtag soldiers escorting caravans, raiding villages, doing trade routes, handling mini-quests for local guilds, or maybe acting as a proxy fighter for one of the many kingdoms. There's lots of variety, and it doesn't feel "old" for a long time. There's a lot of replay to be had on the actual battlefield - setting up skirmish lines and leading your calvalry to flanks against opponents.
But then you decide to pledge an oath to one specific king. Great! You're granted a village to manage, and now the whole court is open to you. You can now play politics with all the other lords in the court, increasing or decreasing relations with them, fighting alongside them in larger battles with high-tier units, or even just chilling at feasts with them - getting to know them and their families (which you can use to marry into property and status!).
As the game goes on and you gain more renown, you can start being more aggressive with requesting land, and back it up with your political alliances and forces. Now you feel like you could do a better job than the marshal, who never seems to attack the key enemy positions when on campaign. Or even the King, who never seems to go to war with the right people. And *you can do that*, you can start your own kingdom, recruit lords you've met, and be your own master - convincing lords to defect and join your cause. You can do just about anything that feels like you should be able to do it within the confines of the game.
It's not a game with an overwhelming set of dimensions, but it has a surprising depth. It wants you to keep playing, it wants you to discover all the ways to play it. It doesn't spoon-feed you anything, but your own curiosity will naturally figure all of this out once you start getting bored with your current lot. It's the best example of game depth that I can conjure to mind, and the game is crazy fun.

This game defies normal genres- To summarise, it is a combination of traditional 'Death by a Wall of Solid Text' 4X gameplay (with some unconventional and brilliant omnipresent politicking) and a top-down bullet-hell shooter. With turn based gameplay, no less!
To clarify, the ship to ship combat is turn-based, while the strategic map can pause to show the state of the entire galaxy in one fraction of a second, or can skip many months in a minute, dependant upon the players wishes.
The main basis of the gameplay is that you play an unaligned mercenary piloting a stolen ship, aiming to herd 8 warring intergalactic factions into a galactic Federation (one of whom is somewhat perturbed, as you nick your ship off them in the first place). The races seem perfectly content to squabble among themselves for all eternity, and take a very apparent glee in making your job all the more difficult.
In terms of accessibility to levels of player dedication (and patience), it is varied in difficulty. The easiest difficulty still provides just enough challenge that your tactics will adapt beyond your comfort zone, allowing new 4X empire builders a campaign-length sandbox to test their strategies in, whilst the toughest difficulty is, I would presume, challenging enough for even a master of turn-based space combat.
I would not be able to say too much more about Hardest difficulty, as I can barely get past the tutorial level on it.
In conclusion, if you like the idea of a text-heavy 4X political strategy game with a refreshing turn-based top-down spacecraft shooter with dakka levels set to optimum, then look no further than this game.
If, however, you are attached to your retinas, then better luck elsewhere (those myriad bullets, shells and lasers dotting the screen can give some wicked migraines if you look too closely to the screen).

When I first saw this game, I was unsure if I would enjoy it, as I'd played AI Wars before and had issues getting "into" an abstract game.  Since it was on sale though, I decided to give it a shot, and was immediately surprised by how inuitive a lot of the aspects of the game were, but also how impressive the tutorial was(Perhaps a little too hand holdy for my taste, but definitely did a good job of teaching what was going on).
For a strategy game, the difficulty was probably just about right for my tastes, with a learning curve that was not too punishing, but still required you to master most of the game to get a perfect win on normal.  What I was not expecting however was the storytelling that the game managed to do, and while much of the story is determined by your own actions(and very much read between the lines subtle in a few spots), the setup and the closure was extremely good.
Replay value is a /little/ questionable, but that is more of a personal taste thing.  I felt the only weak points were in that department, and largely a consequence of the player's effect on the game being pretty Illuminati-ish.  Instead of the player taking immediate actions that had dramatic immediate effects, the most effective impacts are from long drawn out planning that typically leads to the same roads (dealing with the warmongering races typically boils down to crippling them by destroying their world's ability to make effective war, or by setting them against each other, and tipping the scale occasionally to be sure neither side ever comes out on top for instance).
I'd still give the game an arbitary 9/10, especially if you can pick it up on a sale, and enjoy turn based(this is "real time" in a lot of ways, but very much meant to be played with a lot of pausing) strategy, sci fi, abstract gameplay, or a combination of all three.

The Evil Within is one of the best horror games I've ever played, with a clear emphasis on the word 'games'.
No matter how much scarier you think other games might be, the fact remains that this one provides much more variety and depth in its gameplay. Also, it generally does a better job of tying in scares with level design and gameplay mechanics, not to mention that 'scares' alone are highly subjective and rarely a factor in replayability (i.e. you might as well just watch a movie if all you want is to see/hear really creepy stuff).
Speaking of subjective factors, I liked the story - even its main protagonist. Yes, there are cheesy moments here and there, but overall it does a good job of ♥♥♥♥ing with your mind and keeping you guessing. And perhaps more importantly, everything is presented in a very polished and atmospheric setting, with plenty of morbid details to keep you immersed and uneasy.
It is ultimately a linear experience, but exploration is rewarded with both items and story bits. And as I've already hinted at, this game offers multiple, organic approaches to solving each encounter and is therefore highly replayable, especially in new game+ mode. I rarely felt like there were a fixed number of  options, pre-determined  by the developers. It always felt more like a creative survival effort - tense and satisfying.
I don't remember the last time a horror game kept me hooked for more than 7 hours straight, and I have played quite a few of them: the amnesia games, among the sleep, silent hill, resident evil, etc.
Of course, there are some issues with the game:
-too expensive in my opinion
-poorly optimized (especially considering the price they are charging on PC - thankfully most of the issues can be fixed)
-low fov
-giant black bars
-'cinematic' camera angles can mess up your gameplay occasionally
-a few crappy encounters with gun-wielding zombies... seriously don't ever do that again

As I am a big fan of Deus Ex, I purchased immediately when this game came out on Apple store.
And finished it three times.
I have to admit this game is not as satisfy as Human Revolution in game play, graphic and difficulty.
But this is still a decent game. As a fan of it, I am quite enjoying it.
I am very happy that this Steam/PC version they take out the in-game microtransactions.

First off: Yes, it's a port of a mobile game. Ideally they'd have remade/reworked the entire game system to that of Human Revolution, but they didn't. That's reality, and to be fair they've marketed it as nothing less. So yes, most of the game systems are heavily simplified, and the interactive depth fails to touch Human Revolution. This is very much a port based on the idea that maybe you didn't play the original release for whatever reason (disliking iOS controls, not owning a decent mobile, etc), and so here's your chance. "Did you play The Fall? No? Well, here's a PC verison". Nothing more, nothing less.
While actual design quality and expectation is subjective, what IS inexcusable is technical issues that are fundamentally game breaker. At time of writing, The Fall has issues where sound (music) overrides all other audio effects. This includes footsteps, dialogue, gunshots, and so on. When this issue occurs dialogue will bug out, conversations missing audio and ending in half a second, leading to lost chunks of story and inability to hear your surroundings (NPC chatter, enemy footsteps). Reducing music volume to zero is not a solution, you pretty much have to luck it out. Additionally, the game has weird lag-like stutter on aiming and movement with certain augs. It's seriously like playing a multiplayer game with high ping: jerky movement.
And so, as it stands, Deus Ex: The Fall is a broken port. Maybe it's a game you want to play even though it's a mobile port. Maybe you expected a total revision and won't touch it because it's not. But end of the day, if the game does not work, if it's fundamentally broken, that is the biggest problem. And so The Fall is not worth a cent from anybody regardless of standing until these issues are fixed.

TL;DR: The first chapter of an investigation and mystery game saga promises an intriguing story line but lacks in its potentially coolest features.
RPGMaker game that is not an RPG, Silver Creek Falls puts you in the shoes of two police detectives who are presented with a case of ominous disappearances at the small town of Silver Creek Falls. I will try to keep this spoiler-free for the important bits, because the story is so short for the time being.
The case presented is indeed ominous: large pools of blood are found at the scenes with no bodies to be found. What's going on? It's for your pair of investigators to find out. There are hints of occultism, secret societies and a shroud of mystery around the case. Gameplay consists of looking for evidence at the crime scenes and a couple of times you need to make minor deductions based on the evidence.
The deductions part could have been so much better executed. You are presented with a multiple-choice questions and got to choose the right answer based on the evidence. However, guessing wrong is not penalized, instead you get to try another answer right away. Being right straight on is not rewarded in any way either, rendering these deductions dull. It would have been cool if you were to chase the wrong lead for a few minutes: done right it could have sparked an additional story arc or at least a source of humour. Think about it: the investigators going to a café instead of the right scene, enjoying a coffee and finally realizing that "Nope, there's no clues here. Where to next?" and then resume the story.
Also, the beginning lets you think that you should keep a keen eye at crime scenes but there's no actual deduction similar to e.g.
or
required. That would have been cool. Now it plays more like an interactive novel: find all the evidence and see the next set of dialogue.
Dialogue between the investigators and the local deputy is perhaps the strongest part of the game in addition to the storyline. Of the investigators, headstrong and impatient Sara is a nice contrast to the calm and patient Philip. They will discuss the evidence when found and offer remarks as to its significance. This has been done very well, as is the soundtrack and graphics, which fit the theme splendidly. The soundtrack manages to capture the mystery theme excellently. There's also one cutscene with voice-over, which was really cool.
You also have a map of the town that you can look at any time but it's not really used for anything useful. The town is empty of any people or other activity whatsoever, like a proper ghost town. Perhaps it's because of it being a really small town but it frankly looks just unfinished in that respect.
You should note that others have experienced game-breaking bugs of various kinds: I was lucky enough to have a smooth playthrough. Just be sure to save every now and then to avoid them.
Story lasts a mere hour and closes in on a cliffhanger that leaves you wanting for more. It's a thrilling story and it's even free, so if at all you like mystery games do give it a try! Little Marryn is desperate, for her father is lost at sea. But the twelve-year-old does not give up, builds a submarine, takes all her courage and heads off into the ocean to find him. Soon she sinks into a huge labyrinth of ancient myths and dangerous monsters.
Sounds fabulous? It is. But don't be deceived by the start of the game, which, with its children's books sketches may seem like a simple game for kids. It's not. 'Song of the Deep' is a challenging adventure that takes many hours to complete and is epic in the best sense. This is not a snack for fast treasure hunters, but a pleasantly demanding journey with refreshing new ideas that feels very unique.
Pros:
- huge open world
- fantastic graphics
- very precise controls
- tons of secrets
- many challenging and satisfying puzzles
- diverse underwater world
- very clever game mechanics like freezing items to make them float or blinding jellyfish to makes them move away or using light to attract specific fish or using sonar to find hidden chambers, etc.
- heart-warming story
- feels like a AAA title
- charming narrator
- plenty of sub-marine upgrades
- good music
- very good sound effects
- satisfying fights, especially in the late phase of the game after you collected all the weapon upgrades
- warp points to ease travel over long distances
- made me want to immediately re-start the game after finishing it
Cons:
'Song of the Deep' intentionally gives you no guidance. This allows you to experiment intuitively and is great to reach many unexpected, satisfying moments of discovery in terms of 'Ah, this is how it works!'. But this can also be frustrating at times if you don't know how to continue, especially in the early hours of the game where you haven't collected a lot of the available upgrades. At one point I seemed trapped because I hadn't found the knife for Merryn yet. But I had no idea a knife existed and that I had to find it. So I had to turn to the internet to find out. As an achievement hunter I tend to collect every secret I find and 'Song of the Deep' is full of treasures. But many of them can only be collected after your sub-marine has been upgraded. So in order to fully enjoy this game and prevent frustration, simply carry on if a treasure seems unreachable. The game expects you to return later. As a matter of fact you return to areas many times.

Howabout a review that looks at the
itself? I've poured enough hours into Wakfu to make it feel worth my salt, so stay awhile and listen.
If you're not sold by that phrase, then this game probably isn't for you.
If you are sold, then prepare for a good co-op experience.
That being said, this game mostly shines with its' co-op play. Unfortunately, there seems to be a big void between starting players and end-game players.
I'll put a + next to pros and a - next to cons.
Albeit, some are a mixture of these.
Want to learn a class quickly so you can get to smashing things up, whilst being as powerful as any other damage class? Iop's for you. Want a class that's difficult to master and has tons of things to learn about and with synergies to discover? Xelor might be your pick. I had to cycle through nearly all of the classes and test them out before I decided to settle with Rogue.
At-least, I haven't seen too much of a meta other than higher level stuff = more money, and pets/costumes/emotes/all that = a high price.
There's lots of demand for people who are high-enough level in professions, and some people will pay kilograms(tonnes?) worth of cash to just acquire the stuff they can make. From the Baker, who bakes bread(duh) to heal health and give small maxhealth boosts, to the Handyman who can make dungeon keys, crafting workshops, and more. Speaking of...
Haven Bags are basically transportable 'homes'. You can decorate them, expand them out with Haven Gems(acquired through multiple means that don't cost realworld money), craft using purchasable workstations(at a hefty price, those things don't come cheap), and even
Yeah, that's right. You can carry a farm with you. Crazy stuff.
You can do everything a Haven Bag can do there, and even more. Set your spawn point there, spawn mobs(usually penned up to stop them rampaging everywhere and breeding wildly), and probably lots of other stuff that I don't know about because I haven't done haven worlds too much and I can't be bothered to look at a wiki.
Not exactly. More like "Pay to make everything grindy a little easier", or "Pay to look cool". From EXP bonuses to emotes/costumes to restat scrolls to class switches. (The last two have 30 day cooldowns, I believe. Don't worry, Ankama has standards.)
Plus, costumes/emotes from the store are
, which means people can sell them on the market. No need to fork out realworld cash when you can earn it with blood, sweat, tears, and mostly time. Definitely a lot of time.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Which brings me to my first con:
Literally just that. Both your level /and/ your professions are going to be a total grindfest.
It does, however, pay off. Perhaps you can even make some money from it.
Wakfu does try to ease combat grinding with 'Challenges', though. Things like 'Do not get hit from the back', or 'Kill two enemies in one turn', which awards a bonus EXP/Loot percentage/chance/whatever. Only slightly eases it, though. It'll feel like a chore to some.
I believe this puts a lot of people off from continuing to play the game, too. Especially if you're soloing.
Wakfu's a 2.5D turnbased strategy RPG. These kinds of games are usually pretty boring on their own, and more allies/characters/players makes the game more engaging and fun,
when there's diversity, which Wakfu shines at with its 15+ classes. It leads to another problem, though, which I discussed at the very beginning.
Naturally, joining a Guild fixes this, though. Lots of guilds like recruiting at Astrub, the starting hub of the game.(Past Incarnum. That's the tutorial level.) Don't be shy! Ask a guildie to invite you. It'll be worth your while. (Certainly was for me. Big shoutout to 'The Secret Society' people, especially if they're reading this 'u')
And one final thing.
If you want friends to tag along, do your best to be nice and slow about it. Let them grasp the game by themselves. I find Wakfu to be a very 'learn at your own pace' kinda game. You can not know the inner works of your class, but you can still play it and win battles.
Even with  its' flaws and its' grind and its' poorish solo play, I still enjoy Wakfu and rate it one of the best MMORPGs I've played. Compared to every other standing MMORPG on the market, I'd say this is an amazing little gem in the rough that

WHAT THIS GAME IS:
Left 4 Warhammer.
A hectic fast paced hack and slash action game intended to be played co-op with friends. You play one of five characters each with slightly different play styles and each with a variety of possible weapon choices unique to them. You play through missions with simple objectives and recurring crescendo events against a horde of rat men, finding supplies on the way. You get a random piece of loot after each mission. Weapons can be upgraded/broken down/crafted with the Shrine and Anvil in the inn lobby.
WHAT THIS GAME IS NOT:
A deep RPG with lots of choices and builds with narrative and story.
I highly recommend playing with friends and I recommend not playing on difficulties higher than your item level. The experience is severely diminished by the crap AI bots. However, if you do try to play solo, I've compiled some useful information that may help.
TIPS FOR PLAYING SOLO:
-AI partners are awful in many ways. (EDIT: The devs are aware though and the bots have steadily been getting better since launch) Be prepared for frustrating deaths for stupid reasons.
-Get good with Sienna, Victor, and Markus. If you play as Sienna or Victor, you will get Kerillian Bot, Bardin Bot, and Markus Bot. If you play as Markus, you'll get Kerillian Bot, Bardin Bot, and Sienna Bot. There is no Victor Bot unless someone playing as Victor leaves your game. Kerillian Bot is by far the best, Bardin Bot is decent, Markus Bot is mediocre, and Sienna is wholly terrible in all ways. (EDIT FROM THE FUTURE: At some point Kerillian Bot got terrible too and now Markus Bot is actually pretty good, so maybe they shuffle around sometimes. Sienna's still completely worthless though. EDIT FROM FURTHER IN THE FUTURE: Kerillian's pretty okay again, Sienna's still terrible.)
-AI Bots have whatever weapons and equipment the host player has them equipped with. Recommendations from my experience: Bardin, axe and shield plus handgun or crossbow. Kerillian, sword and dagger plus swift bow or hagbane bow (EDIT, lately my Kerillian bot has been doing well with dual swords with Endurance). Markus, sword and shield (or mace and shield) plus handgun. Sienna, bolt staff with longsword or flaming sword.
-Bots approach enemies and wait for them to attack first a lot, so you can't count on bots to shove enemies who are about to attack you. You'll end up doing the majority of the killing yourself, so bring a reliable high offense but not poor defense weapon. Recommendations: Two handed hammers (Markus and Bardin), two handed swords (Markus and Victor), Victor's Rapier, Sword and Dagger for Kerillian (Glaive is better, but only if it has the Endurance or Perfect Balance perk), and Beam/Mace or Fireball/Sword for Sienna.
-Bots get regularely trounced by big armored enemies. This can be helped significantly if their weapons have the Devastating Blow perk. EDIT: In fact, all your weapons should have Devastating Blow, as it allows you to interrupt Stormvermin attacks. Other recommended perks for bots include Second Wind and Killing Blow. Recommended perks for you include Improved Pommel or Endurance, and some form of healing (Bloodlust for slower high damage weapons, Regrowth for faster lower damage weapons). When rolling for new sets of perks at higher levels, some combinations can't happen (for example, generally only one defensive perk is allowed, you can't have both Endurance AND Improved Pommel). There are guides available online that list literally every possible combination, so check to see if the combination you want is possible before wasting upgrade tokens.
-The AI will religiously persue ratling gunners and ignore everything else, including you and the gutter running stabbing your face, and the rats who are attacking them while they take cover. I recommend a handgun, crossbow, bolt or beam staff, or other such high power long ranged weapon so you can quickly deal with gunners yourself.
-Rat ogres will probably kill you, as the AI is bad at dealing with them. Keep a strength potion and a black powder bomb on hand. Strength potions double damage of bombs as well as your weapons, so take the potion and then throw the bomb at the ogre if you want to stand a chance. All of Victor's ranged weapons (especially volley crossbow) except for the regular crossbow, Kerillian's Hagbane bow, and Sienna's beam staff are very good at killing rat ogres.
-AI will only pick up healing items if you already have one. They won't pick up bombs or potions ever (EDIT: Now they do, and they'll give them to you if you don't have one, hooray!). The AI will pick up tomes, but only if no healing items are available and if you are already carrying a tome or healing item.
-Friendly Fire is active on Nightmare and Cataclysm difficulty only, and only applies to ranged weapons and bombs. Don't worry about friendly fire from the AI; they barely ever use their ranged weapons, and when they do they can generally be trusted to be accurate. The AI however does not take into account when you are using your ranged weapon. If you play as Victor or Sienna, be prepared to shoot your AI partners fairly often as they like to stand behind you when idle and then run through you when an enemy approaches. Try to use slightly higher ground when available, like standing on boxes or stairs.
-The AI does gain benefits from trinkets they carry. Trinket recommendations: reduced damage from poison gas, faster revival, healing all allies when healing self, healing self when healing an ally, and the Rainbow Fish. Do not equip bots with the luckstone; this only affects you when you open a chest, and bots will never open chests. In fact, probably don't take luckstones ever.
-The starting trinkets that purportedly increase the chances of getting loot for a specific character - EDIT - actually do stuff now.
-The AI is extremely bad at avoiding Stormvermin Patrols. If you hear one, run very very far away and hide in a corner until they pass.
-Man the Ramparts has no Stormvermin Patrols, nor a rat ogre. Good map for grinding.
-The AI does not do a good job of keeping up with you if there are any rats about. Move slowly and methodically clear locations before proceeding so you don't accidentally leave their stupid asses behind.
-Ignore Sack Rats if they are already running away. Be an ambush predator if you want to kill them. If you can, snipe them in the head with a handgun, but if you miss, don't chase them; the AI won't be able to keep up with you.
-The Healing Charm is the second most important trinket in the game. The healing to allies it provides can get them out of About-To-Die Black-and-White status.
-The Rainbow Fish is the most important trinket in the game.

If you're those crazy types who rate a game on what it PLAYS like  - Think Resi 4 pretending it's Tenchu in Silent Hill :-)
This is one of those games that gets full marks for being warped and creative, but at the same time feels like something you've played before so don’t expect anything revolutionary.
Like your Silent Hill's and Resi's, it paints a great picture of a world but ultimately directs you down corridors, so the game is more focused on stealth than map exploration.  This is where Tenchu comes in - for you to survive you'll need to do loads of sneaking and stealth attacks (although note you can't jump or climb so it's just attacks from behind ).  Hand to Hand direct confrontation with even a single enemy leads swiftly to death, plus health and ammo are at even greater premium than normal for these type of games so firefights are an absolute last resort.
It's utterly gruesome so gorehounds will love it, but is it scary? -
**Opening Level Spoiler ********
The first level is a tense cat and mouse game with a chainsaw wielding butcher.  One wrong move sees you very painfully and gore-splatteringly killed.   Like Alien Isolation, there is a definite sense of a predator semi-intelligently stalking you.   After that you face a more traditional "get through trapped locations filled with sneak killable enemies that you may survive a shootout with but only at great expense" level.
*End of spoiler*********
While the game does try to mix up the gameplay style a bit, at the same time it’s constantly reminding you that the barb wire ripped undead/possessed/whatever enemies are definitely more badd♥♥♥♥♥then little ol' you.   Whether that's scary or not depends on you, but it's definitely tense.  There's no rocket launcher or semi-automatic shotgun to rip out if things are getting a bit out of hand
So I'm really enjoying it.   The story is decently warped and the enemies definitely are.   Gore levels are extremely high.   The reliance on stealth as opposed to the size of your munitions is a welcome departure from the norm.   While it's not exactly scary for me, I’m on edge constantly listening out for noises and other telltale signs that I’m about to die.
The frame rate issues are not game breakers for me  - I’ve been playing on 1080p with all settings on Max and while the drop in frame rate is noticeable, I've never had it become so bad it's even remotely unplayable. The latest patch allows you to remove the black lines and up the max frame rate if you want so that’s those complaints taken care of.    The patch also makes it run a bit better – whereas previously bonfires dropped my FPS to mid 20s, they now run in mid 30s.
Absolutely recommended for horror fans who’s lives don’t completely fall apart over frame rates and some jagged edges.

I'm a big fan of 4x games and strategy in general.  This game makes almost no sense to me.  Strategy seems a vague and ambitious term for this.  You do your own thing and influence other civilizations in the vaguest possible sense in order to accomplish the feat of you, the civilization that was destroyed, starting a federation of the remaining others to win the game.  You do this by being omniprescent through their development and literally nudging them in the direction you want.
The concept is interesting but the gameplay is slow and impotent in that decisions have very little impact on the civilization you are "manipulating" which gives very little differentiation in games.
Now, that out of the way.  The battle.  You spend 80% of your time manipulating and 20% enjoying the hell out of excellent turn based strategy.
The interface is surprisingly intuitive and the perks/abilities actually make a difference in combat.  The strategy component is great, and aside from some short periods where you feel like you are grinding it really feels like the piece of this game that works.
That's the problem.  You have here a 1/2 great game here.  Bipolar in the worst of ways for a 4x, the strategy seems useless and the battles are great.  This is like the exact opposite of Endless Space, and there is going to be some people who love it, and others who don't.
Bottom line: buy it on sale if you want a varient rogue type 4x.  Not for everyone, don't expect a normal 4x or strategy.

Let me first talk about the developers, the developers are some of the most open people ever, they are very open to adressing concerns and if you have a problem with one of their games, for example not being able to play, they will respond within a week most of the time {you should probably post your issue on the forums and not the steam discussion page}. Also for this game in particular they have already given out tons of free content when they released the first expansion, and are giving out more now that the second expansion is almost done. In fact, they are on version 8 or something for one of their previous games, AI war, and they are almost done version 3 for this game.
Now let's talk about the game, this is a hard game to decribe so give me a break if I fail at describing it, it is a simulation sand-box like game with turn-based schump like combat, sort of. Basically you play as a Hydral, the last of your race, your goal is to unite the galaxy, whether you are doing this by making everyone friends or exterminating all the races except for 1 is up to you.
The simulation aspect involves you flying around to different planets helping the very unique alien races or hindering them. You can also start wars or end them. The biggest negative aspect of this simulation mode include some of the options not being as usefull as others and their is quite a bit of grinding late game. The positives are that each of the races are very unique, there are some very good stories that come out of this simulation aspect, and there are some very interesting thematical events that happen. *SPOILER ALERT, DONT READ THIS NEXT PART IF YOU DONT LIKE SPOILERS* An example of a good story that came out of the simulation aspect was when I created an alliance out of the Boarines (isolasionist ice boars), the Burlusts (hyper aggresive chicken people) and the Acutians (Capitalist Cruel Robots), I then backstabbed the Boarines by convincing the Skylaxians (honour bound stereotypical grey aliens) to wage a war of extermination on them so that there were only 2 races left in my grand federation. Wanting to fill the gap I recruited the Thoraxians (bug-like hive killing machines) into my federation. After years of fighting (the grinding I was talking about) it came down to my federation (about 5 planets) and the Skylaxian Empire (about 3 planets), and after all these years of fighting, my federation then betrays me and became an axis of evil, causing me great troubles.
The combat aspect is very schump like and turnbased (more turnbased than schump like). The combat is very hard to explain so I wont really try, but all I can really say is that it starts becoming repetitive after about 50 hours to the average person but otherwise is quite enjoyable.
Finally, just want to mention some things I did not mention before, the music is really great and the expansions add SO much to the game but sometimes the game is really hard to lose so you will get into positions where it would take about 5 hours of grinding to win and 5 hours of waiting to lose. Also the learning curve is super steep.
TL:DR
+Developers are awesome
+Races are unique
+Great stories come out of this game
+Game is very open about ways to complete your objective
+Great Expansion (soon to be Expansions)
+/- Combat is great but can get repetitive
-The late game is grindy
-The simulation aspect could be balanced better
-The learning curve is pretty insane

I picked this up again...and then remembered why I put it down.
Pretty much the only complaint I have is the combat: the enemies are too damned tanky. It takes hours just to kill one guy. And god help you if you want to challenge the burlusts (a race in this game that is all about war). Your fingers will die before the god damned enemy does. You could decrease the difficulty, but even on normal, it takes so damned long, and nothing damages you. Why even have a combat sequence at that point?
Other than that, the simulation aspect is pretty in depth, though it definitely seems species other than the warlike ones need constant babysitting. if you have it accelerated to x2 fast forward, a race is going to get wiped out before you even see the ships.
The aspect of play, though, is unique. You play as something of an agent behind the scenes...except for whenever someone's getting attacked, because no one can defend themselves. You run around, and do diplomatic stuff. But, not too much, or else those you've united will form an alliance that's opposed to your federation...even though you were the one making them not kill eachother...yeah. I don't get it either.
Talking about diplomacy: Each race has a drastically different diplomacy screens. So different you'd think they were from different games. And this would be fine if some of them weren't really clunky as hell. As mentioned above, if you want to talk with the burlusts, you have to commit to a 9 hour duel (as such, I almost always get everyone to gang up on them. they are such  pain in the♥♥♥♥♥. And the Peltions and their damned vote system. So few things give votes, and that's the only thing that powers their diplomacy. You need 300 votes to get them into your federation....you get .5 after taking out an entire pirate camp. And as mentioned, combat is this game's weakpoint.
Sure it gives the races "flavor", or "personality" or whatever people call it now, but it sacrifices functionality.
